en: Then the twenty-seventh chapter:
The Blessed One said— "O Lotus-born one, having thus performed [the rite] according to the scriptures in ancient times, the divine [deity]..."
Thereafter, one should indeed perform the ancestral rite according to the procedure prescribed by the rules. (Pauṣa 27.1)
Pauṣkara said:
"O Blessed One, I wish to know how the śrāddha for the ancestors should be performed by those abiding by your teaching, beginning with the preceptor."
For whom and for whom is that work intended; for whom and of what kind does it perform its fivefold function?
And how indeed?
For that which has been correctly accomplished.

The Blessed One said: "O Lotus-born One, one should always perform [actions] as a duty for those who have renounced action, for those initiated into liberation, and likewise for my devotees. (Pauṣa 27.4)
And likewise for those in the fourth stage of life (caturthāśramin) whose sequence [of duties] is not specified,
as well as for the wise ones who desire to attain the state of the Blessed One.
O Pauṣkara, [this is] for the delight of those who have attained perfection through mantras, as well as for practitioners,
for the constant attainment of auspicious births, and for the supreme accomplishment of mantras.

Out of compassion for those sons, the teachers and others should indeed always perform the duties for those who know the commitments (samaya), for the sake of the increase of the true Dharma. (Pauṣa 27.7)
"Indeed, for the sake of further attaining a good birth and for the attainment of the true dharma, he is likewise a kinsman to his other devotees. (Pausa 27.8)
Out of compassion, one who has renounced actions and is mature, taking refuge in his vows, should always practice this for the sake of immediately pacifying misdeeds. (Pauṣa 27.9)
One who is greedy for enjoyments during initiation has not been led to the state of nirvāṇa;
for one who lacks intense devotion is not perfected through the practice [of mantra]. (Pauṣa 27.10)

"O best of the twice-born, even a practitioner who lacks a lineage does not enter the sphere of accomplishment; this is surely so for those devoted to the true path and dedicated to ritual action. (Pauṣa 27.11)
Indeed, they should always be favored by means of hospitable treatment, so that upon reaching this [state], one attains the supreme divine station. (Pauṣa 27.12)

Therefore, for all those who have been consecrated but have not yet performed the sacrifice, this must be spoken though it is not to be spoken; and it is for the sake of bringing the rite to completion. (Pauṣa 27.13)

O Lotus-born One, at the time of the *śrāddha*, even when one has partaken [of the offerings], one should not perform elsewhere the rites of mantra, mudrā, and ritual action, nor meditation and other such acts, except for those performed without ignorance. (Pauṣa 27.14)

O twice-born one, it should not be practiced nor should it be applied by devotees who are merely occasional practitioners and the like, even while relying on specific signs such as place, time, and so forth. (Pauṣa 27.15)
Whatever is performed for the ancestors, by that a man becomes free from his debt;
through the power of that action, he too attains incomparable satisfaction. (Pauṣa 27.16)
Upon its arrival, they attain from it a state endowed with joy, whether for a single moment or for many times, until the characteristic signs of death appear. (Pauṣa 27.17)
O Pauṣkara, it is joined with the lunar day-count, the annual cycle,
the food obtained from the field, and the collection of specific causes.
For the sake of pacifying the suffering of saṃsāra and for the exhaustion of evil deeds—
whatever evil deed born of suffering has been committed by the self (karmātmā) throughout infinite kalpas when the wheel of the senses was manifest.
From which [arose] the lotus-born Brahmā.
Therefore, O Lotus-born One, this body composed of the elements is indeed immediately followed by the perception of suffering, for such is its nature.
Just as suffering is pacified by suffering when it has entered into another aggregate of suffering,
so too is the burden of those men who commit evil deeds heavier than their own aggregates.

Just as one who has fallen asleep emerges from his own body while sleeping, O Pauṣkara, so too, having entered the body of latent impressions (vāsanādeha), he performs various activities. (Pauṣkara 27.23)
Without a body composed of the elements, they find no peace;
likewise, the vital breath, which previously gathered the senses, finds no support without food. (Pauṣa 27.24)
O Great-Minded One, as long as the self has not been manifested by the embodied beings through the state of a body, how can there be the exhaustion of their karma? (Pausa 27.25)

Internally, for the sake of that metaphorical designation, by means of action preceded by knowledge, one accomplishes that through the power of which infinite happiness quickly increases. (Pauṣkara 27.26)
This common rite for Vaiṣṇavas, and especially for the Guru and others, known as the "General" (sādhāra) or "Principal" (saṃpradhāna), is now being described.

Or one who has been invited, or arrived spontaneously, or is a constant guest; such a preeminent twice-born man who knows the five times [for ritual action] and is devoted to the six duties. || Paus 27.28 ||
Having first performed his ablutions and other rites,
O Brahmin, he should again lie down with self-restraint, having purified his hand with the water of the *arghya* offering.
Having pacified him with the flower-weapon empowered by mantra, and having extracted the eye-mantra empowered by the meaning of the mantra; (Pauṣa 27.30)
Having recited the eye-mantra and looked [around], and then having uttered "kā vāstu" (or "vāstviti"), he should seat himself before the Blessed One on a seat empowered by the syllable *praṇava*.
Having placed it upon a consecrated, spread-out, and pure surface—either facing him or facing north—and likewise directed toward the northern quarter; Paus. 27.32.

Just as it is pierced by the spreading rays from the directions of the Lord of Mantras, one should worship with the mantra, meditate upon him, and speak with restrained speech: "O you who have arisen from the Word. (Paus 27.33)
O Lotus-born One, having concentrated the Lord of the World like the sun in the sky of the heart-lotus, [offer] seven vessels or two vessels of food. (Pauṣa 27.34)
Having thus established the foundation with effort in this rite,
one should offer a gift within the inner altar, dedicated to the ancestors.
Since the king of mantras establishes the best of the twice-born even while he remains within his worldly conduct,
that should be known as the "inner altar" (antarvedī), for it is indeed internal to both of these.
Whatever offering of a piṇḍa to worthy recipients one may make for the ancestors, that becomes divine and stainless, because it rests upon consciousness. (Pauṣa 27.37)
O Lotus-born One, at that time they remain sharing [the merit],
O Puṣkarasambhava, by virtue of the donor’s intention. Pausa 27.38.
One should place [the offering] upon the seat for either one person or for many;
furthermore, the seat should be made of *dābha* grass tied with knots and consisting of many *kuśa* blades.
The hairs of the pervasive Lord, whose body is the limbs of the sacrifice, are known as the *kuśa* grass; all those very blades of grass are the veins residing within his elemental body.
The rays within the bodies of living beings are indeed all the powers of the embodiment of consciousness;
for this very reason, O best of Brahmins, there is the seat of kusha grass for the ancestors.
But whatever is given with devotion after that time, following what is prescribed for those invited at the time of the *śrāddha*, becomes indeed identical with Brahman. (Pauṣa 27.42)
"O Lotus-born One, it was indeed for this reason that in former times the snare of karma was ordained for those men who do not know the Self. (Pauṣa 27.43)
O Brahmin, for those for whom the Lord Acyuta exists everywhere in the form of mantra,
because they abide in the reality of true being, there is indeed no need for them [to perform rituals].
Then,
with a pestle consecrated by recitation, or with smooth powder of stone, he should strike at the crossbars as before.
Outside that, on the seat, one should fashion [the area] in front, exceeding one śama in length;
however, in width it should be one śama in measure, and as before, one should bring it to a state of purification.
O twice-born one, he should also place there blades of *kuśa* grass with unbroken tips and roots facing north;
for the northern quarter is divine, while the southern is designated as ancestral (*pitrya*).
O twice-born one, they constantly cause those immortals to flourish with their own nectar-like vigor, just as the ancestors [are nourished] by a hundred blades of darbha grass.
The host of ancestors dwells within, resorting to the southern portion;
for men, it exists thus in the north as the very nature of a fraction of the power of consciousness (cit-kalā).
O twice-born one, you are that stainless, eternal, and imperishable digit known as Immortality (Amṛta), which has taken its seat [within].
Therefore, whatever is known by those from Brahmā downwards, O twice-born one, is indeed thus. (Pauṣa 27.50)
And that which is given to the ancestors with a hand [joined] in truth, directed toward Hari—the unborn one who is the source of the world and whose nature is mantra—[is offered]. (Pauṣa 27.51)
And they offer libations of water to the ancestors;
because they are the refuge for those [ancestors], it is said that there is no other cause [for their satisfaction]. (Paus 27.52)
And for those, O Mahāmati, for whom the supremacy of the task at hand flashes forth internally preceded by the propitiation of the mantra, [that task is accomplished]. Paus_27.53.

That which is performed with a non-conceptual mind, according to the sequence of one's own [mantra] and others, and by virtue of the direction facing the presence of the mantra, becomes inexhaustible. (Pauṣkara 27.54)
But, O Puṣkarasambhūta, those who dwell having firmly resolved in their minds that "sentient beings are rare upon this earth," [are truly wise]. || 27.55 ||

Having brought it to the state of truth, one should place it upon another heap of kuśa grass; likewise, having recited the mantra over sesame seeds and water, one should scatter them again above that. (Pauṣa 27.56)
But because of the tips of the *darbha* grass, O twice-born one, this pair known as *kuruvinda* is the progenitor of the entire web of enjoyments in the three worlds. (Pauṣa 27.57)

Because of the excellence of the substance offered to the ancestors and the gods, purified by faith, the Blessed One himself, whose nature is peace, appeared in the form of Agni and Soma. (Pauṣa 27.58)
Manifested as the embodiment of those whose nature is action for the sake of self-realization, he exists for the purpose of furthering both ancestral and divine activities. (Pauṣa 27.59)
That radiance exists as the essence of sesame seeds, while delight exists as its own nature;
for this very reason, O twice-born one, it is present both for the unawakened and for the awakened.
Through water mixed with sesame seeds, one attains the state of being worthy for the ancestral rite (*śrāddha*);
and for the *śrāddha*, these two provide supreme protection—these two should always be used without fail. (Pauṣa 27.61)
And for those who know its true nature, there is a distinction for those who understand the mantras;
one should place the weapons, the consecrated missiles, and the vessels there.
In that regard, the first [type] consists of circular pavilions made of gold and other precious materials when available; otherwise,
they may be made of leaves from the *pālāśa*, *kadalī*, or *tamāla* trees.
First, one should pour water for the feet— pure, containing other waters, and consisting of auspicious leaves—
into a vessel, starting from the right, even for the purpose of washing the feet.

Thereafter, one should worship from head to foot with water for the guest-offering (arghya), flowers, and unguents, as well as with garments, garlands, incense, and lamps, and with curd-rice accompanied by fruit and recitation.
O Great-minded One, with wealth consisting of betel leaves, according to one's ability,
one should dedicate it to all the ancestors and kinsmen in their proper order.

But for Brahmins who are numerous, one should perform the rites for the ancestors in this manner, according to the nature of the sounds, the state of the knower, the location, and the physical form. (Pauṣa 27.67)
O Brahmin, where two twice-born men have been appointed for the sake of the ancestors, the presence of one’s own ancestors should then be brought about in that single [officiant]. (Pauṣa 27.68)
In the second [case], there is the establishment of the mothers and likewise of others;
however, if all of them are joined together in the third [case], they attain a single state.
One should first utter the word "Oṃ," followed by the word "asmat" (us), and immediately thereafter, "to the ancestors.
At the end of that, one should recollect "this is the arghya," "this is the pādya," and finally, "svadhā. (Pauṣa 27.70)
At the conclusion of all these ritual services, while recollecting the Mantra "Vaṃ" or "Saṃ," one should utter "Namaḥ" or "Svadhā," ending either with "namaḥ" or with "svadhā."
In this very way, O Pauṣkara, one who should perform [this] as a duty toward those of equal status within one's own kin, let there be salutation only to him. (Pauṣkara 27.72)
O twice-born one, when the ritual procedure is inverted, the *svadhā* offering is prescribed as mandatory;
indeed, the renunciant himself bestows it upon those who seek its fruit. (Pauṣa 27.73)
He should always perform a salutation at the end of the *svadhā* offering;
for he who desires fruit bestows the eternal fruit upon those who seek it. (Pauṣa 27.74)
At the conclusion of the utterance of *svadhā*, one should always offer salutation for his welfare;
thus, O twice-born, having distributed [the offerings] among the ancestors according to one's desire. (Pauṣa 27.75)
Having asked again and again through the opening of the bowl whether [the guest] was fully satisfied,
he then placed a handful of water, resembling nectar, into the hand with the *hran* mantra.
One should give that which is equal to the full moon; it is to be meditated upon as its sixteen digits, distinguished by the sixteen vowels beginning with 'a' along with the *anusvāra*. (Pauṣa 27.77)
"O Lotus-born One, the mantra ending with the sound 'tvaṅkāra' and preceded by the syllable 'sa' along with the star (the vowel *u*), is said to be the designator of the full moon. (Pauṣkara 27.78)
Before washing one's hands,
one should drink as before that which contains the imperishable vitality of food situated within the city of nectar.
O Brahmin, you too should perform the satiation of the hosts of ancestors and gods;
having washed your hands from the wrist downwards with black gram flour and other substances.
Having sipped water and properly withdrawn the remnants [of the offering], and having purified the ground, he should place water with sesame seeds in his hand. (Pauṣa 27.81)
Then, having risen, one should perform the act of gratification before the Blessed One, saying:
"O Blessed One, may the host of ancestors likewise be pleased first. (Pauṣa 27.82)
The array of deities within the body is established according to the divisions of the quarters.
In this manner, one should perform [the rite] in the temple for the propitiation of Karmatva when it is well-spread out.
Furthermore, in a time of distress, the king of mantras, having been worshipped, may go elsewhere;
one should purify the site through rituals such as sprinkling with water and so forth.
One should remember the deity established by the power of pervasion as residing within the reservoir of water;
having first performed the worship of Maṇḍala, one should perform everything else before it. (Pauṣa 27.85)
One who is intent on smelling the vessel should offer that which is contained within it—
sweet oblation together with blades of *darbha* grass and sesame seeds.
Having performed the purification with fire using the heart-mantra and the tip of a blade of darbha grass,
one should meditate upon the great abode, which has the form of a tree, whose nature is consciousness, and which possesses great radiance.
O high-minded one, that food which is intended for the satisfaction of the deities and the ancestors completely consumes, on all sides, the entire mass of material defects. (Pausa 27.88)
And that means of accomplishment was ordained by the Ancient One in Sanskrit;
O Lotus-born One, it pertains to those two, beginning with the Preceptor. (Pauṣa 27.89)
Therefore, at that time, it is indeed beneficial for him to offer [the oblation] to others as well;
always, by means of this very rite, for that purpose, for the sake of attaining auspicious success. (Pauṣa 27.90)
Indeed, through the power of various karmas, one should contemplate the diversity of that single seed of the substratum by means of the intellect, based on the ancestral rites performed in the past.
That [offering] should be satisfied by that very self-born [deity] through its own nature;
one should contemplate the food and the vessel as being situated within, like my own stream.

Having consecrated two *darbha* blades, each as long as a palm and containing within them the essence of the *arhaṇā* mantra, one should extract [the tooth] together with those two, while reciting the *hrīṃ* mantra.
Having the nature of the essence of taste, it has attained the state of food through its grossness;
O Mahāmati, one should consume it by taking morsels only the size of four finger-breadths.
[He is] the one who abides as the support for Agni and Soma, and for the host of ancestors (pitṛgaṇa) mentioned previously;
he is, in reality, the seed of the ancestors and possesses the nature of consciousness.
And one should offer two balls of food originating from Agni and Soma;
those two blades of darbha grass, which are the very form of the channels, are indeed there together with the ball of food.

Having brought about dissolution by means of the second [syllable], one should then offer funeral cakes (piṇḍas) for the ancestors through the intellect of worldly activity; by that [means], others [attain] the present state. (Paus 27.97)
Gradually, through the designation of names, those lakes previously unseen [become known];
thus, having understood their manifested nature and their throbbing state, one perceives them.
O Brahmin, as before, with mantras beginning with *oṃ* and ending with *svadhā*, adorned with the *hṛn*-mantra and accompanied by the words of address, [one should perform the rite]. (Pauṣa 27.99)
Thinking, "I shall fashion the *piṇḍa*," one should then perform the ritual as before;
indeed, the worship is carried out with services such as collyrium and ointment. (Pauṣa 27.100)
Then, one should perform the libation in due order with water mixed with sesame seeds;
having bowed with the head and having placed both knees upon the ground. (Pauṣa 27.101)
With both hands placed upon the mouth and with single-minded focus, one should recite this:
"Oṃ, homage to you, O Fathers; homage indeed to you, O Puruṣottama! (Pauṣa 27.102).
Homage to those who abide at the feet of Viṣṇu; svadhā to you, O ancestors, homage!
Homage indeed to Hari, the lord of the ancestors, whose nature is that of Agni and Soma. Pausa 27.103.

O Viṣṇu, obeisance to you whose self is the drinker of the true soma; obeisance to you whose self dwells upon the sacrificial grass (barhis); O Acyuta, the Agniṣvāttas are those who have been born throughout the entire cycle of saṃsāra.
You are the grandfathers who drink the Soma, and you are the other great-grandfathers;
homage to you, the Blessed One, the embodiment of the ancestors, and the Unborn.
O Blessed One, having abandoned You alone—the Nārāyaṇa, the Haṃsa, Viṣṇu, whose self is the three Puruṣas—I bow to no one else, nor do I worship anyone else. (Pauṣa 27.106)
"O Lord of All, I do not satisfy another; I invoke no other," having thus praised the assembly of ancestors with supreme devotion once again. (Pauṣa 27.107)
When possible, one should perform the joining of the mass-form [of the deity];
and then, for the host of ancestors seated in order before that [deity], one should likewise act.
O best of the twice-born, having investigated through both [the breaths] or in one,
and having meditated upon the ancestral host of Pitṛs situated at the tip of the sibilant (ūṣman) in due order, [one should perform the offering].
Then, having arisen by means of the *praṇava* into one's own true nature,
one should stand at a distance from those who are not looking on, positioned transversely in the middle.
O twice-born one, facing either north or south, one should then place the heart-mantra from the heart according to that northern orientation. (Pauṣkara 27.111)
Beginning with the *praṇava* and ending with *namaḥ*, [this mantra] has the form of wind and space;
it belongs to the twice-born who is seated before the *piṇḍa*, through the power of his vital breath (*prāṇaśakti*). Paus. 27.112.
Or, having emerged outside with effort through one's own independence, and having meditated upon her, one quickly attains a state of oneness with her. (Pauṣa 27.113)

Having dissolved [the breath] into the power of the self (ātma-śakti), if it indeed possesses the characteristic known as "heat" (ūṣmā), and having thus performed this for the assembly of vital breaths within the body of the Brahmin ancestors; Paus 27.114.
Then, as before, having restrained [the guests] on their seats, one should feed them as previously described: "Oṃ, salutation! This food is for you, O Immortal One, preceded by Viṣṇu. (Pauṣa 27.115)
The gods, the rivers, as well as the cows, the sun, the moon, and the lord of the forest;
Oṃ Mādhava, the Blessed One, the great one whose form is composed of mantra. (Pauṣa 27.116)
Remaining in another state as honey, let it indeed bring satisfaction to you;
and for the gratification of the ancestors, one should perform [the rite] without abandoning one's seat. (Pauṣa 27.117)
O Lotus-Seated One, having dwelt in that very region of the earth and beheld that mass of offerings, I now abide there for the sake of all the ancestors. (Pausa 27.118)
Until the collection of the morsels of food, which have been properly rendered free of remnants and released from life, they do not depart; at the conclusion of that, they go forth.

O twice-born one, having bestowed blessings upon those who are healthy, the performer of the *śrāddha*, with focused intent, should place [the offerings] in their proper places—accompanied by nectar, water, and sesame seeds—through the power of the mantra. (Pauṣa 27.120)
The secluded and revealed path for returning once more, and the ritual of the excellent mantra known as Nārāyaṇa, performed with the speed of Brahmā. (Pauṣa 27.121)
Having mounted their own senses as chariots, they have gone, satisfied, to the abode of the Imperishable.
This is declared to be the Prājāpatya [initiation], endowed with the traditional transmission. Pausha 27.122.
One should always perform the offering to the ancestors, which increases the previously mentioned fruits, by arranging the mantras through the ritual application of mantras. (Pauṣa 27.123)
O Lotus-born One, this [mantra] should always be employed in the plural or in the dual;
and if even this is bodiless, then indeed it applies to every ritual act. (Pauṣkara 27.124)
O Lotus-born One, the primary deity (aṅgin) should be joined with the lake and other limbs and sub-limbs as before;
likewise, the syllable *oṃ* is used at the end of the ritual for those deities, mantras, and eyes who are to be worshipped. (Pauṣa 27.125)
In this matter, however, the modification preceded by mantra that was mentioned constitutes the *samaya* for the spiritual sons (*putraka*) and others whose minds are purified. (Pauṣkara 27.126)
O high-minded one, my mantra is prohibited for bestowal upon the preceptor and the foremost of practitioners; any other [mantra] besides that, however, does not cause such opposition. (Pauṣa 27.127)

O twice-born one, [this applies] to the initiates (samayin), the spiritual sons (putraka) and others, even to the Vaiṣṇavas, to the four [classes] ending with the Maudgala, and likewise to those belonging to the various stages of life (āśramin). Pausa 27.128.
O great sage, for those who have been consecrated by initiation (*dīkṣā*) and are thus initiated,
this [mantra] is everywhere common, complete with its limbs, perfected, and well-honored.
Listen now to that arrangement of mantras which is to be taught to them: the twelve-syllable mantra is "Oṃ namo brahmaṇe kavacāya. (Pauṣa 27.130)
Thus, "netram" for the Viśvātman and "astram" for the Paramātman—
these, all accompanied by the Praṇava, are suitable for Śūdras according to their fitness.
And for those who have been duly initiated, [the rites] are indeed performed without the *praṇava*;
and they are likewise prescribed for women according to the requirements of proper conduct.
But for Śūdras who have practiced incorrectly, O Mahāmati, one should not break the mantras; rather, there should simply be an act of salutation. (Pausa 27.133)
For the twelve-syllable, the eight-syllable,
and likewise for the six-syllable [mantra] of the same class, the [preceding syllable] should first be employed for the purpose of completion.
But when, having been addressed with the eight-syllable mantra, he is brought down by means of the eight-syllable [mantra],
then the preeminence of the twelve-syllable mantra is ordained.
The six-syllable mantra attains primacy by virtue of both [the preceding and following mantras];
therefore, the eight-syllable mantra should always be joined at the conclusion of the crest-lock (śikhā).
The preeminence of the *praṇava* [is established], and then the mantras consisting of twelve, eight, and six syllables,
beginning with the *hṛdaya*, are to be understood in their proper sequence.

If it is postulated that the mantras preceded by the *varma* [syllable] are the objects of expression, then their identity is established, as is that of the *praṇava* in their place. (Pauṣkara 27.138)

The deity, having been brought into presence while residing in the mind by means of the *jitantām* mantra, should then be joined with the six mantras of the limbs (*aṅga*) as they are established. (Pauṣa 27.139)
That which was proclaimed as the third [syllable], preceded by the twelve syllables,
and preceded by Brahmā as the third, is indeed the designator of Dharma and the others.
The *praṇava* is [the seed] of all mantras, and it is also used in the rite of the seat for those mantras beginning with the twelve syllables and for the general rites of mantras.
Through the ritual offerings of substances such as darbha grass, sesame seeds, and water,
once they have been released, a fiery tranquility arises for each respective rite.
Therefore, O Lotus-born One, there is a further accumulation of the very enjoyments that have been used toward another ritual act which is contrary [to the original purpose]. (Pauṣkara 27.143)
The individual manifestation is secondary because it exists from its very root as presided over by consciousness;
it proceeds by depending upon that supreme [consciousness] for the sake of the agent's attainment of the fruit.
For those parts of the mantras that are devoid of the universal consciousness (citsāmānya) are unfit, like [inert] bodies;
however, the stable portions of the mantras once again attain fitness.
"Sometimes, O twice-born one, through the power of mantras or by the cultivation of knowledge" (thus concludes the procedure for the daily śrāddha).
Now follows the procedure for the occasional śrāddha:
Therefore, understand the rules for the occasional *śrāddha*, which bestows a favorable rebirth upon the ancestors and grants abundant success in one's actions. (Pauṣa 27.146)
One should never perform it without the immediate attainment of a worthy recipient;
O Lotus-born One, the *śrāddha* must be free from such [faults] as these. (Pauṣa 27.147)
And if he remains for the sake of bestowing grace upon that which has been earnestly requested,
then he should observe the discipline [of fire], beginning with the wood used for kindling.
All defects such as pride, envy, cowardice, anger, greed, and the like, must be abandoned from afar until the very day of completion. (Pauṣa 27.149)
When fruits, roots, and other offerings are presented with a mind of great effort according to the ritual preceded by purification, they become superior even to nectar.

O Lotus-born One, when success is achieved solely through the power of the place and the recipient, one should perform that with faith for seven nights, even if it took only a single day [to prepare]. (Pauṣa 27.151)
O Lotus-born One, having resorted to an auspicious time for a single day,
he passes that time with supreme joy, not otherwise.
Relying upon these three, you, with a compassionate mind, established in the state of goodness, have performed this ancestral rite according to your ability and with pure wealth. (Pauṣa 27.153)
It inevitably leads that which is sought after to Satyaloka before long;
however, depending on the place and time, it also bestows Tapoloka.
Faithful people who rely on the proper place and recipient bestow [merit],
and through the power of the time and the recipient, they achieve the fruit of rebirth in Mahāloka.
A gift given merely by reaching a sacred place bestows heaven;
whereas that which is performed by relying on the proper time causes one to go to the world of the twice-born (the earth).
A Śrāddha performed for one who has taken refuge in a gentle recipient bestows rebirth in the world of the living;
such is the fruit of these three factors: the ordinary [recipient], the place, and so forth. (Pauṣa 27.157)
In that regard, O Lotus-born One, the body is well known as *puṣkara* (the lotus) because it is nourished (*puṣṭi*);
time, consisting of eclipses and so forth, is the object to be grasped, and the recipient (*pātra*) is composed of that [time], O Lotus-born One. (Pauṣkara 27.158)
Likewise, one who possesses self-restraint acts correctly for the sake of the *śrāddha* and not otherwise;
for that triad which was mentioned regarding the *śrāddha* is indeed distinguished once more. (Pauṣa 27.159)
O Blessed One, he who is a worthy recipient and consists of the Lord [Viṣṇu] indeed becomes a savior for men through his birth endowed with consciousness, having reached the renowned region of Viṣṇu.

The period known as the twelfth day, the great time (bṛhatkāla), and that which is refined by the sun's passage into a new sign—O one of great intelligence, if these three are present with their specific characteristics, [they are most auspicious]. Pausa 27.161.
O Lotus-born One, the Lord himself, manifesting in a single form and other ways, will surely become the savior of those dwelling in other bodies. (Pauṣa 27.162)
For from the beginning of creation, that particular region, along with its waters, was presided over by Him;
it is a place that brings success to all undertakings.
If, at that time appropriate for the twice-born, there should be even a single muhūrta endowed with a lunar mansion on the day called the twelfth (dvādaśī), it would thereby become sacred to Viṣṇu.
It is the deliverer of the ancestors, accompanied by the left arm,
endowed with the three perfect accomplishments, and devoted to the five times.

O twice-born one, he who has attained the goal in the supreme reality is a vessel for the single path; and because he is endowed with self-restraint and other virtues, he is indeed a vehicle for the great purpose.
The ancestors indeed attain a favorable rebirth forever; and that [merit] arises with great velocity, for it is of equal speed [to the act itself]. // Paus 27.167 //
In an auspicious land, there is an auspicious birth accompanied by knowledge and virtuous deeds;
from the three types of ancestors, respectively, there arise fruits that are increasingly more auspicious.
Knowing this, the qualities such as place and time, when combined with purity of mind and approached with serenity, are indeed conducive to the giving of *śrāddha*.

Indeed, all this assistance regarding ritual actions is achieved through such weapons and means for those whose souls are purified by devotion alone, even though they delight in worldly dharmas. (Pauṣa 27.170)
O you who are born from the lotus of your own duty, [this is for] the twice-born who are entitled [to it], who delight in knowledge and action,
and who are devoted to the five times.
Then, by means of the *avyāghāra* mantra and by circumambulation,
the Blessed Lord Hari bestowed upon them the state of being the Brahman-syllable (*brahmavarṇatva*) within the continuous stream.
The Lord himself, who is the embodiment of the sixfold policy and the cause of both creation and dissolution,
is joined with a multitude of qualities that are free from attributes and never fallen from his own essential nature.
Indeed, because of these six qualities, Time and the others arise; for they do not perceive anything as being superior to Acyuta, except for one another. (Pauṣkara 27.174)
Therefore, those devoted to the Blessed One and intent upon the knowledge of his mantra lead [the soul] from this world to that subtle, stainless substratum consisting of time and the rest.
O Lotus-born One, for all that exists, beginning with Time, is entirely contained within them;
by the power of their majesty, everything shines forth clearly.
Furthermore, since this universe— both external and internal— is under the sovereignty of that Lord,
its nature as the body [of the deity] was previously revealed to you.

Indeed, by means of the instruction on the paths, that very same [teaching] describes in detail the steadfast Vaiṣṇava who possesses knowledge, is devoted to the true practice, and is a knower of the body.
The ancestors desire a pure male descendant who will deliver them from their own lineage;
thus, relying upon the proper place, time, and other such factors, one should personally perform the rite with self-restraint.
O Lotus-born One, having first prepared with faith food that is free from husks, radiant, pure, accompanied by milk, and provided with various condiments; Pausa 27.180.
Or indeed with the twelve-syllable heart-mantra,
[one should perform the rite] over new vessels that have either just emerged from cooking or have been further sprinkled with oil.
Or rather, O twice-born one, it should be accomplished in this way by means of a son, a disciple, or oneself, or by means of a sister, a female practitioner of dharma,
or a wife.
By way of the path of friendship and kinship.
Clad in white garments, skillful, with a pure self, free from bodily disease, and devoid of hunger and thirst. (Pauṣa 27.183)
[He was afflicted] with cough and asthma... by those who were naturally blind, deaf, or dwarfish;
yet, being thus freed from defects and devoted with heartfelt devotion, [he attained success]. (Pauṣkara 27.184)
The *caru* for the purpose of the ancestral rite (*śrāddha*) must indeed be prepared by one of the same caste;
the preparation of the *caru* for the social classes is ordained according to the natural order (*anuloma*).

O Lotus-born one, in the case of divine or ancestral [offerings], that which is obtained through improper means causes fault; however, in the absence of such [proper sources], what is purchased by trade is not defective, as is the work of a pure artisan.
O Lotus-born One, even by that [practice], one is freed from the aforementioned defects;
likewise for those whose souls are solely devoted to austerity, who have shaken off decay and various [impurities].
Likewise, [one should avoid the food] of women in their menses, of eunuchs, and especially of those who have recently given birth, as well as that of dogs, pigs, cats, and monkeys. (Pauṣa 27.188)

Therefore, with every effort, one should [place it] in a place sheltered from the wind and covered by cloth, away from those who roam about—such as village pigs, jackals, vultures, and the like. (Pauṣa 27.189)
In a place that is free from chaff, paved with mosaic, well-smeared, and whitewashed,
one should perform the mantra-worship and the practice for the deity who is the father of the gods.
And when it is possible, O twice-born one, it is ordained for all that food, condiments, and vessels be provided at all times in their proper order.

At the time of the internal commencement, however, sesame seeds along with kuśa grass, honey, and clarified butter should be cast [into the fire] using the twelve-syllable mantra; furthermore, this should be done repeatedly during the collection of the perfected [substances].
Then, O Lotus-born One, one should carefully cover them with a cloth of eight syllables, so that no vapor arising from anything else escapes to the outside.
When the *ūrdhvapuṇḍra* has been applied, smeared, and washed away;
when the collection of vessels has been covered with armor or cloth and placed within the boundary.
Having appointed a guardian among that row [of attendants], one should perform the bathing and other rites;
O Pauṣkara, [this applies] to the fire, the Brahmins, the dwellings, and the place of worship. (Pauṣkara 27.195)
Having first made an allocation of the vessels, the portions [of food], and the assembly of good companions,
one should always perform the rite until its completion.
Having removed the outer garment, he should shake out the undergarment beneath it and discard that body-wrap. (Pauṣa 27.197)
Unshaken, stainless, and clear— whether it be without a thread, consisting of bark garments and the like,
or dyed blue, whatever clothing or such may exist.
Having cast away all objects of sense from the world outside,
one should then, through the intellect, focus upon the Supreme who has entered the form of the mantra.
And indeed, for the sake of showing favor to the ancestors, I shall perform the sacrifice once again;
having seated the twice-born ones on their seats in order, as before, I shall call them forth.
Before them, two of the best of the twice-born should first be seated facing east;
they occupy seats presided over by the triad [of deities] upon the twelve-spoked wheel, the support, and the abode.
Now, what are the six limbs common to all, which consist of the six vowels of the twice-born?
[They are] joined with the weapon-mantra and the crest-mantra, endowed with the six [limbs] in their proper order.

Having directed [the disciple], for the sake of attaining identity with the body, [the teacher] should [unite him] with his own designator—the true abode which consists of a single form and so forth—while standing facing the east. (Pauṣkara 27.203)
One should arrange the array of deities accompanied by the utterances *phaṭ* and *vauṣaṭ*, namely the two mantra-forms known as Nṛsiṃha and Varāha. (Pauṣa 27.204)
Indeed, for the sake of protection, one should always place those deities known as Agni and Soma on the northern side,
without looking at them, and install others beyond that.
There, first having placed the heart-mantra and the others in the bottom row,
one should likewise place the assemblies of those born from the excellent syllables with the [divine] gaze.
To its right and above, and likewise for the lineage of the Mother,
another [mantra] should be joined with the armor-mantra (kavaca), which is entirely composed of the Blessed One.
The second [is performed] in the name of the father; then, to the south of that,
the third is for the sake of attainment, and the fourth is indeed with the heart.
O twice-born one, the fifth [offering] should be joined with the mantra of the form named after the grandfather, and the Ekāyana [mantra] indeed with the name of the great-grandfather. (Pauṣa 27.209)

In the Father (Janaka), those three [syllables] that have passed beyond should be placed in sequence as the state of living beings by means of those mantras; and the pair likewise proceeds in sequence.
One should then place the three preceding ancestors, beginning with the great-grandfather, either by means of the general six-limbed [mantra] or by one's own [specific mantra]. (Pauṣkara 27.211)
The application of the mantra in the giving of *śrāddha* offerings and in the worship of the twice-born is now described as being in two states, according to the authority of the four forms.
O one of stainless vision, both worldly enjoyment and liberation are obtained from the first mantra; and absolute isolation alone is obtained from the second.
The King of Mantras, unmanifested, should perform the placement (nyāsa) for the group of mantras together with his friends;
then, in sequence, he should place those beginning with Pradyumna and ending with Vāsudeva for the three [deities].
That indeed is not with distinction; listen again to this:
for that which expresses [the state] of those previously mingled with friends is "Aniruddha. (Pauṣa 27.215)
From the group of mantras of Pradyumna, two [mantras] arise from desire;
then, by means of the *praṇava*, one attains the Great-Grandfather, whose nature is the Supreme Brahman.
O Mahāmati, that which is the satiation performed with a face radiant with great joy is now described as being of three types, according to the section on the nine forms.
O Pauṣkara, out of affection for his friends and the twice-born, Viṣṇu should then place [the seed-syllables] of the group of Mothers with the Vairāja mantra.

Know that by means of three Nārāyaṇa days, one should perform the triad for the ancestors and others in sequence; this is indeed called the "piercing" (viddha), and it is the knowledge of Śrāddha that bestows its fruit. (Pauṣa 27.219)
O Lotus-born One, even without the attainment of a physical body for the ancestors of the sacrificer,
[the rite] proceeds from the Vairāja-mantra up to the end of the Sāṅkarṣaṇa-mantra.
Know, O Pauṣkara, that the five mantras are for those whose ancestors have reached their ultimate goal, for they possess true faith. (Pauṣkara 27.221)
Indeed, through the mantra of the support—[the *vai* mantra]—it bestows the attainment of self even upon the ancestors of the performer of the *śrāddha*. (Pauṣa 27.222)
The enjoining of the five foremost of the twice-born in the rite of *śrāddha*, beginning with the circle of friends—this indeed is the supreme and ultimate [duty]. (Pauṣa 27.223)
When endowed with all the necessary conditions, it bestows supreme and complete nirvāṇa upon both the performer and the host of ancestors; how much more so, then, when performed repeatedly?
O Brahmin Pauṣkara, when the opportunity arises, one should offer food at the proper time with a mind purified by faith and out of compassion for one's equals.
In this optional performance of the śrāddha offering, however, one should not employ [the guests] in any other row;
rather, one should first arrange a single group of Brahmins facing north.
Then, with the heart-mantra, one should perform the placement (*nyāsa*) for all [the deities] born from the lotus;
likewise, with the *praṇava* and their own names, [one should place them] in the heart and other [limbs], as is known. (Pauṣkara 27.227)
O Lord of weapons, ornaments, and missiles, one should first employ the mantras within their proper range; or likewise, facing east, one should apply them with power by means of the *cakra* mantra.
One should join one *vipra* facing north with the *mukhyamantra*,
and there, having joined two [others] facing north, he should connect them with the *hrīṃ-mantra*. (Pauṣa 27.229)
O Lotus-born One, one should then remember one's friends, kinsmen, maternal lineage, and paternal lineage— entirely as they exist in another body. (Pauṣa 27.230)
In the mandala, one should worship either the wheel situated in a water-vessel or Nṛhari;
one should install a single Brahmin facing north as the primary figure with the principal mantra.
Just as for the satisfaction of the group of ancestors and the maternal family, he should satisfy all other people according to his ability for their pleasure. (Pauṣa 27.232)

Having picked up a morsel of grass, one should offer it soaked in ghee and honey, mixed with *darbha* grass and water containing sesame seeds; it should not be alkaline nor excessively salty. (Pauṣa 27.233)
One should perform [the rite] in this manner on account of one's own lineage; otherwise, it may be done for another out of priestly duty, compassion, or affection.
For in its production, his lineage is established as prior to that;
[the body] extends from the feet to the knees, from the knees to the navel, and from the navel to the middle of the chest.
Having established the four mantras beginning with Aniruddha, starting from the crown of the head down to the heart, from the heart down to the navel, and from the navel down to the feet.
O Brahmin, for the attainment of a happy rebirth and for the constant satisfaction of the ancestors,
one should indeed offer [the remnants] starting from Vāsudeva and others, down from the top of the head to the tips of the toes.

Furthermore, O Mahāmati, one should join the four [syllables] ending with *aniruddha* at the heart with the syllable *praṇava*, or else [meditate on] that which is peaceful and composed of pure consciousness, O Brahmin. (Paus 27.238)
The four [deities] beginning with Vāsudeva and ending with Adhyakṣa should be installed in sequence as the pervasive lords of the fire, water, disease, and spirits. Paus 27.239.

O twice-born one, having first placed Aniruddha according to the sequence of dependence within the four elements beginning with earth, and then having installed Nṛhari for the sake of protection, [one should place] the supreme [form] of the ninefold manifestation.

Then, one should sequentially place the eight [syllables] starting from the head, the face, the throat, the heart, the navel, the secret place, the two knees, and ending with the feet, down to the earth. Paus. 27.241.
But within the expanse of the heart, the Lord Vāsudeva, who is beyond the senses (Adhokṣaja),
[presides over] Saṅkarṣaṇa and the others, corresponding respectively to the elements ending with earth, preceded by the intellect.
Or rather, O Brahmin, it should be stated that the group of seven known as the "supporters of the earth" follows the sequence beginning with the earth and ending indeed with Saṅkarṣaṇa.
Then, O twice-born one, one should meditate upon Vāsudeva within the substratum of consciousness, [and likewise] within the fluids, blood, flesh, fat, marrow, and bones. (Pauṣkara 27.244)

One should gradually install the seven [deities] beginning with Saṅkarṣaṇa and ending with Varāha within the white element (śukladhātu) for the sake of accomplishing the gateway, starting from the very white [element]. (Pauṣkara 27.245)
O Lotus-born One, beginning with the mantra of Varāha and ending with Saṅkarṣaṇa, one should place the vessel as before for the purpose of expelling the wicked. (Pauṣkara 27.246)
By virtue of its pervasiveness, the Blessed One is both outside and within, like himself;
and Sāṅkarṣaṇa, like the individual soul (jīva), is the seed within the hollow of the heart-lotus.
"By means of the yoga of emanation and withdrawal, [one performs] the sevenfold [rite] upon the seven elements.
Pauṣkara said:
"When one's own mantra is present in its general form, indeed being in close proximity..."
In the application of the two *kāraya* [stomas], when they occur in the *vigraha*, they are flaming within; or as it is said: // Paus 27.248 //
How is the application of mantras—whether four or nine—to ritual acts appropriate for those who have been liberated through the rites of nyāsa, arcana, and so forth? (Pauṣa 27.249)

The Blessed One said: Indeed, the common mantra accompanied by its six limbs is always prescribed for all; however, for the practitioner, a mantra that is discordant would cause obstruction. (Pauṣkara 27.250)

O Great-minded One, having been authorized for everything, whatever belongs to the fourfold self and so forth, as well as one's own mantra and the like, depends here upon the will of the Guru. (Pausa 27.251)
For even there, for the sake of distinction, he is described by means of two [methods] for the faithful;
however, when the collection of mantras has been previously arranged according to the desire of the Brahmins.

Having withdrawn one’s own mantra and with a mind established in its own abode through the contemplation of Brahman, one should thus perform the visualization of the locus and so forth. (Pauṣkara 27.253)
That array of mantras which was distributed among the bodies of the Brahmins,
and that which was not to be employed,
he then caused to be placed within himself by means of his hands.
In this regard, O Brahmin, listen to this specific rule prescribed therein:
first, the Blessed One [should be worshipped] by pervading both the left and the right.
One should place the second [syllable] on the five fingers of the right hand;
indeed, the third is on the two sides, following the sequence beginning with the thumb.
One should then place Aniruddha on the two palms, beginning with the right;
or else, according to one's own will, one may place only one [deity] ending with Vāsudeva.
When the ninefold self is in the two thumbs of the hands, Acyuta is in the [remaining] eight, ending with the Varāha, in sequence from the forefingers as before.
Having placed the left-hand threatening gesture (*vāmatarjanī*) at the end, or indeed ending with Vāsudeva, and having positioned *svāhā* in the middle, this is the essence of worship.
Likewise, [it is] in the *cena* and *nala* [meters]. (Paus. 27.259)
Even that which has become fire through oblation would lead to purification as before;
thus, by the power of one's desire alone, there is a transformation of mantras.
Easy to propitiate for those who have reached the new state of steadiness, she causes no obstruction at the time of the ancestral rite (śrāddha).
Having thus performed the assignment and now honored her with his head bowed, [he should proceed]. (Pauṣa 27.261)
The teaching is a cluster within a flower-vessel consisting of the Blessed One;
in its center is the moving water, which is the mind endowed with the five sense-faculties.
One should place that [mantra] situated on the seat of the mantra in the center, at the edge, or in the heart; this is the time for the ritual sipping of water (*ācamana*).
But [I have done so] out of a desire to show favor to me.
In the presence of the twice-born, of the Lord, and of the blazing fire,
even a person who is all-knowing must remain strictly self-controlled.
Thus, by those lords of the twice-born,
with minds that were perfectly pure through wisdom and with hearts full of compassion, everything he said was accepted with faith.
Since the measure arising from the lotus is twofold in nature,
it has been repeatedly applied to all entities, especially in the rite of faith.
That [offering] should be applied at the proper time as the fulfillment of all rites;
it is purifying and generates satisfaction—how much more so, then, in the rite for the ancestors! Paus 27.267.

O twice-born one, having mentally received the mantra-empowered command along with [the gesture of] the head, and having internalized the śrāddha consisting of material substances by means of which it arises; Paus 27.268.
Indeed, it would be fruitful for the ancestors, for that is rooted in knowledge according to reality;
otherwise, by what cause could there be such a state of attainment for the ancestors? (Pauṣa 27.269)
Just as trees do not reach the earth without a root,
so too does knowledge bear fruit quickly through the path preceded by joy.
Having caused the entire collection of sense-faculties, which had indeed been engaged in external activity, to dissolve by itself within the self in the space of the heart-lotus— Pausa 27.271.
Having fully realized it through the power of its own nature,
one should now perform salutation to the All-pervading Lord, the Sovereign of all, from his true essential form.

One should contemplate the consciousness that has itself transformed as the unswerving vibration of the Self, whose nature is peaceful awareness and which consists of the bliss of pulsation. (Pauṣkara 27.273)
Blazing with the radiance of a thousand moons, suns, and fires, it is steadfast,
its conscious core filled with a wheel of rays, and facing in all directions.
The state of the Blessed One, which abides within the expanse of consciousness, is perfectly tranquil;
for it is indeed far more distinct from the channel of knowledge that constitutes its power (or its manifoldness).
One should visualize one's own assembly of ancestors, shimmering for the sake of pacifying karma, as a mass of innate bliss situated within the corner of a mirage.
Just as the power of a great fire, characterized by burning, O Pauṣkara, emerges externally by relying upon a spark of charcoal; (27.277)
For he departed in that very manner, yet by virtue of his concise resolve;
having taken refuge in Agni and Soma, the ancestors [followed] by the will of the Lord.

O twice-born one, by the power of the space of illusion (māyākāśa), that which is external to the king of mantras, Prakāśa, gradually results in either happiness or greater suffering for those very beings. (Pauṣkarasaṃhitā 27.279)
O Lotus-born one, with the very internal organ (antaḥkaraṇa) together with the senses,
enveloped by the space of Māyā, one should then cause the heart-mantra to revolve.
O Lotus-eyed One, for the sake of pacifying that suffering, [the light] enters through some aperture of the rays;
and by means of knowledge, it extends again as far as the limit of space.
At that time, O twice-born one, by the power of its influence, that very mass of consciousness (citpiṇḍa), residing within the locus of Agni and Soma, arises from that family in due course.
The seed of the internal organ, however, is freed from the power of great delusion;
it resides within the limit of knowledge and the limit of space, being extremely subtle and eternally manifest.
It is presided over by those beginning with Nārāyaṇa ending with Kṣmānta,
or alternatively, by those beginning with Vāsudeva ending with Prāṇabrahman, in due order.

By means of the five limbs of mantra—which are pervaded by the intellect, which exist according to their actual state, which are characterized by origination and stability, which are of the nature of the Knower, and which are devoid of the eyes (the sixth sense)—[one attains the goal]. // Pauṣa 27.285 //
Because of which the practitioner’s performance indeed becomes perfectly clear;
therefore, by virtue of this arrangement, [the rite] takes place within this heart during the libation to the ancestors.
Remembering the arising of the mantras by virtue of his own practice,
he should contemplate them either as formless or as embodied, according to the arrangement of the presiding deities.
That which was previously described as consisting of the two [elements], the support for the accumulation of the seeds of consciousness,
is filled within by those powers of the internal organ.

O Mahāmati, one should meditate with the *praṇava*, which possesses an indivisible characteristic, upon the earth that has attained the state of a seed within the center of the chosen pericarp. (Paus 27.289)
One should meditate upon that which has emerged from it— unpolluted by the qualities such as sattva and the rest, which are inseparable from it— and colored by the triad.
O Pauṣkara, that which is known as the Great-Grandfather (Pratitāmaha), by virtue of its consciousness,
has attained the state of deep sleep (suṣupti) and has become slightly turbid. (Pauṣkara 27.291)
One should contemplate that [consciousness] resting in the space of the pericarp within the belly of the sun of consciousness, and then as having emerged from that very region of pure awareness.
He colored his own grandfather with his very own inner organ, by means of the letter *e* and his own name, and through a dream that was not made manifest externally. (Pauṣa 27.293)

One should recollect the abiding of that [consciousness] which has resorted to a dual nature, as well as the aspect of consciousness itself, in the region of the throat and in the space within the navel. (Pauṣkara 27.294)
Then, O Lotus-born One, one should recollect the consciousness colored by the mind, the intellect, and the ego, which is undisturbed even while awake. Pausa 27.295.
In the inner space of Brahman, upon the ground of the path of the *brahmarandhra*,
within the sheath of the individual soul (*jīva*) consisting of the two [subtle] bodies, which is the causal state characterized by the fourth (*turya*).
One should understand that the two deities known as Viśva are Vāsudeva and Daivatyā, who possess forms like the orb of the sun and are identical with that [divine] self. (Pauṣa 27.297)
For that is the root from which all the gathering of ancestors for those who perform rites arises;
it exists either by presiding over the one known as the great-grandfather.
O Lotus-born One, this consciousness of Brahmā is indeed like the midday sun, either embodied or bearing the form of pure knowledge. (Pauṣa 27.299)
One should meditate upon [the deity] presided over by Pradyumna according to its previously described own-place;
thereafter, one should contemplate Aniruddha, who is the form of the tutelary deity here.
When entering through the aperture at the crown of the head, one should— whether formless or indeed embodied—
worship with the mantra and make the place richly empowered and presided over.

O Brahmin, one should meditate upon the other [mantra] with the heart-mantra, that supreme one with the head-mantra, and indeed always the fourth as the presiding deity of the crest-lock (śikhā). (Pauṣkara 27.302)
One should meditate upon the body [of the deity] accompanied by the Śakti-mantra, followed by the heart-mantra;
likewise, the one called Astra with the head-mantra, and the eye with the Śikhā-mantra. (Pauṣkara 27.303)
The tetrad of the ninefold form, which is purely of the nature of consciousness within the heart,
is differentiated by the powers of the qualities whose essential nature is pure existence alone.
Saying "Oṃ tat sat," one should clearly perform [the rite] within the interior of the dense pericarp, extending down as far as the throat, by means of the Garuḍagādi mantra.
One should meditate upon the one who is both the sky and the boar and the man-lion at the tip of the aperture of Brahmā;
for when there is a state of division, it arises as if within a single reality through the intellect of differentiation.
One water is naturally cool and the other is warm and sweet;
thus, one should act for the sake of attaining enjoyments, for from this [duality] comes the transgression of those who [act otherwise].
O Brahmin, that which bestows liberation should always be known by those who do not seek fruits;
these mantras, from the heart-mantra up to the *masataka*, are like armor and weapons for the vision.
The heart and the other centers are to be deposited as presiding deities and as powers (śaktis),
because the three— namely strength and the rest— are indeed the objects of enjoyment for knowledge and the other faculties. (Pauṣkara 27.309)
And those six, beginning with the heart, have indeed been determined previously;
thus, one should [visualize] the host of ancestors in sequence as the causal root within the body.
Having placed [the offerings] together with other desired ancestors who are of the nature of consciousness,
he should then perform the satiation ceremony at his side, preceded by the Viśvedevas.
First, those two should be satiated with the characteristic of water by means of the *praṇava*, which contains supreme bliss and possesses a thousand rays. (Pauṣa 27.312)
One should meditate on the Praṇava rising from the root of the vital energy (prāṇakalā) at the heart—[the Praṇava] resembling a bubble of milk, nectar-like, and cool as ice. (Pauṣa 27.313)
And that great sequence of the channel of knowledge, which is the essence of the stars (or the essence of the savior).
And depending upon it, the Viśvedevas and others remain stationed.

One should meditate upon the ancestors as having the form of the Blessed One, possessing a physical form with the appearance of fire, spreading upward as far as the aperture of Brahmā (brahmarandhra). And one should [meditate] upon that. (Pauṣa 27.315)

O twice-born one, one should meditate there upon that mantra dedicated to the ancestors and the deities, which has attained the state of the full moon and is situated above the aperture of Brahmā (brahmarandhra).
One should meditate upon his vital power (*prāṇaśakti*), blazing in form,
situated above his head in the center of the solar disc, like the fire at the end of an eon.
That nectar-mandala, absorbed by his splendor, was meditated upon;
it was then made to flow back again through the cranial aperture of Janaka.
(Here, there appears to be a gap in the text) One should meditate with a pure mind upon that which is rooted in the source (*mūla*) in due order;
thus, having attained the state where thirst for objects has ceased, one should utter the syllable *oṃ* as before. (Pauṣkara-saṃhitā 27.319)

O best of the twice-born, one should lead [the soul] to the fourth stage by means of the meditative intellect that effects the dissolution of the father and other [ancestors]; thus should one act repeatedly for the attainment of enjoyment. (Pauṣa 27.320)
The Śrāddha rite is the nectar for the ancestors, bestowing the destruction of all suffering;
indeed, having placed the host of ancestors within the offering-cake (piṇḍa) which consists of light and bliss. (Pauṣa 27.321)
From the interior of the illusory ether (māyāmbara) to its very end, characterized by the cessation of all latent impressions (saṃskāra),
it surges forth from the root upward, with reference to the upper body.
Just as the solar disc in the sky [appears] through the sequence of its rising, one should again dissolve that very thing by means of the meditation on the moon. (Pauṣa 27.323)
One does not fall ill again when the fruit of one's karma ripens;
likewise, if one should cast a morsel of food upon ground consecrated as a field of Brahmā, [the same result follows].

O twice-born one, know that within the infinite, vast, and full nature of consciousness, there exists that which is unmanifest—the deliverer of one's own lineage, who is devoted solely to knowledge and action. (Pauṣkara 27.325)
However, rare indeed is that person for whom this [practice] is truly a matter of realization,
whose self is purified by devotion to the Blessed One, and who is devoted solely to His mantra.
The ultimate refuge.
Then, for the sake of accomplishment, one should proceed with the external śrāddha rite in the presence of the Lord of Mantras, the Fire, and the Brahmins, in their proper order.
O Blessed One, O Lotus-eyed One, the mantra known as Abhyarthāsanakarma, which has been brought down, indeed belongs to my ancestral lineage. (Pausa 27.328)
Becoming yourself one whose soul is devoted to the ancestral rites (*śrāddha*), lift yourself up from the ocean of existence;
enjoy [the fruits] yourself through [the practice of] knowledge and so forth, which is grounded in power (*śakti*).
For by means of the instrument, the web of enjoyments characterized by the three qualities arises through power;
having thus petitioned and intended this with the mind, [one should proceed].
Then, having recited this entire list of the ancestral groups in sequence, [one should say]:
"Oṃ Oṃ Oṃ Oṃ, O Supreme Lord, for the satisfaction of the ancestors."
Indeed, for the sake of deliverance, I offer this sacrifice—*Oṃ*, *Oṃ*, *Namaḥ*, *Namaḥ*—having mentally uttered it once, fourfold, and ninefold. (Pauṣa 27.332)
Recalling that which was placed within the Supreme Self while residing in the outer garment,
he should then, according to his means, honor it with all offerings, beginning with the arghya and pādya.
O twice-born one, one should worship the Lord of Mantras with enjoyments ending with betel;
in this regard, the following is the general procedure for the act of procuring those enjoyments.
And the mantra to be recited at all times during offerings made with faith is:
"Oṃ vauṣaṭ! This [offering] has the luster of nectar and consists of strength and vigor. (Paus 27.335)
"Oṃ, homage, homage! Enjoy this stainless enjoyment whose nature is splendor.
Then, having sprinkled the available food offering with the gaze of the Great One— Pausa 27.336.
In this way, that which was not large in form, having been placed in the hand, likewise entered the bowl;
and thus, that which was non-existent was held by means of the mind through meditative concentration.
Having thus worshipped Mantreśvara for the satisfaction of the ancestors,
one should then offer that "body-modaka" upon the removal of the darbha grass.
Oṃ, salutations! O you who pervade the world, be pleased with our assembly of ancestors;
may this [offering] be inexhaustible for them, as well as whatever has been performed by you and made your own.
That very procedure indeed leads one from the state of the ancestors to one's own self;
it impels the inner disposition of the hair-pores of the Lord of Mantras like the rising sun.
One should sequentially visualize the host of ancestors in the region outside the heart-lotus;
then, one should indeed worship those established within the internal measure with offerings such as *arghya* and collections of enjoyments.
One should meditate on [the deity] as white as the full moon, filled with a mass of rays,
entering by means of its own power into that which abides in the nature of the mantra.
Within that host of ancestors consisting of radiant energy, one should again meditate upon that assembly of manes,
possessing the luster of ten thousand midday suns and flashing with brilliant light.
Then, once that activity has ceased, one should meditate on how they gradually enter the space of the heart-lotus through the pores of the skin.
Then, taking the mantra situated upon the seat with the thought that it is the moon,
one should go near the fire and meditate there upon the Lord who has arisen therein.
Then, having gratified [the deities] with devotion according to the rite until completion, the king of mantras is invoked there;
likewise, the sacrificial porridge (caru) and the rice for the *piṇḍas* are prepared as before.

Having worshipped [the deity] within a vessel containing honey, clarified butter, sesame seeds, and *darbha* grass, joined with silver, one should perform the rites of striking and so forth, empowered by those mantras.
Having led it to faultlessness, one should subsequently cover it with a cloth or similar material;
then, preceded by a mental connection, one should worship the common seat.
Then, having sprinkled water mixed with sesame seeds over the kuśa grasses in sequence, according to their respective positions, while reciting the *praṇava* (OM).
There, one should first place the vessels made of gold in due order,
following the sequence beginning with the ancestors; at the very beginning and at the end, they should be placed in front of those.
One should offer that [water] with the name preceded by the mantra and followed by "namaḥ," while reciting in sequence:
"The sesame seeds, the water, and the tips of kuśa grass—this is the arghya for you. (Pauṣa 27.351)

O twice-born one, having thus prepared the arghya offerings up to the great-grandfather, one may offer according to one's desire in another śrāddha gift; for it is the same with other [offerings] as well. (Pauṣa 27.352)

As before, having offered the arghya water into the vessels according to their names and lineages—either separately for each vessel or according to the number of seated twice-born—the [offering] should be presented. (Pauṣa 27.353)
Then, having brought the food prepared for each individual along with the sacrificial fee (sādhya),
one should place it, together with *kuśa* grass, into the hands of those who have reached the end of their great-grandfathers' lineages.
Having likewise presented the water-offering with the remainder in the hands of others,
he should perform it within well-defined boundaries for those who possess both the arghya-water and the ritual water.
When the water for the *arghya* offering has been given, he should offer the shape of the entire vessel;
then, with the clarified butter held in the hand of the Brahmin and with that *arghya* water, [he should perform the rite].
O twice-born one, having indeed cast his own eyes upon another vessel,
he should then draw up that water in due order and proceed to the vicinity of the fire.
Then, having placed that vessel filled with sesame seeds and water before him,
he should mentally meditate upon the Supreme Lord as a seat within it.
Having divided the array of the ancestors there, one should meditate upon it with the syllable Oṃ,
situated in the stainless sky like a multitude of stars.
Likewise, O Kamalasambhava, when that [nectar] has been placed in another vessel,
one should contemplate it as being in the space above the palate, within the state of blissful activity.
Having first performed worship of those [deities] with excellent flowers and perfumes, one should [worship] the Lord of All, the God who vibrates within by His own splendor. (Pauṣa 27.361)
There, one should place two blades of *kuśa* grass smeared with honey into the water,
having covered them with another vessel made of *kaja*.
O twice-born one, you should understand that the two vessels, Heaven and Earth, are filled;
having placed them and caused them to be honored, [one should proceed] from the root upwards, each higher than the last.
Within those [energies], the subtle manifestation of the Father (pitṛ),
whose nature is the universal consciousness, has attained oneness with the sound *tāra*.
One should block [the breath] that has arrived via its own functional path while seated on kusha grass;
one should contemplate it through its power according to the sequence previously taught. (Pauṣkara 27.365)
In some places, however, there was the ancestral form manifested as a single manifestation of sound, appearing as a row of beings characterized by the previously described marks.

O twice-born one, having filled the hollow of your cupped hands from the arghya vessel with sesame-water, you should offer a continuous stream of it while reciting that [mantra] in sequence. (Pausa 27.367)
"O [Name], this water for the feet, which culminates in the *praṇava*, be yours.
Then, having taken another vessel, he should offer it into the fire as before.
With his hand adorned with a ring and rendered pure by a sacred thread,
he— whose nature is all-pervasive consciousness— bore the form of the primordial element.
Having resolved with the mind upon the ultimate through the contemplation of Brahman,
this is the supreme support for those of intense [aspiration] and the highest means of nourishment.
It is the source of manifestation, the locus of dissolution, and characterized by supreme bliss;
therefore, one should first worship it while situated in the vessel with water for honor (*arghya*), flowers, and unguents.
It is to be worshipped with the *praṇava*, and by means of that very [syllable], one should then indeed remove all evil;
reciting it mentally, one should contemplate it in the form of a sphere (*golaka*).
Since it consists of the power of all [deities], they assume that specific form through their actions in order to accomplish their respective functions.

Having honored all the ancestors, including those who share the same lineage and those who are not to be favored, with abundant enjoyments and according to the rites of the previous [ancestors] through the Lord of Mantras, as is desired. (Pauṣa 27.374)
Likewise, one should worship those [deities] who have assumed the form of food in their proper sequence;
for the vessel, beginning with Alaka, should indeed be filled with strained water.
Having prepared food there accompanied by honey, *darbha* grass, and sesame seeds,
one should indeed meditate upon the Lord of Mantras, formless and of immeasurable splendor, seated within the orb of the moon.
One should meditate on the pure, cool spray as it wells up from within oneself and is poured out from the pitcher along with that water. (Pauṣa 27.377)
Then, O twice-born one, taking a sesame seed soaked in honey with both hands, and filling [the vessel] again and again with supreme faith for each one, Paus_27.378.
With that [handful], together with sesame seeds and the sacred syllable *bhagavān*,
one should offer [an *añjali*] to the ancestors in succession for their satisfaction.
...the mantras were recited over them. // Paus 27.379 //
Then, one should perform the rite for the foremost of the twice-born facing east, as before, but with particular care and endowed with faith during one's own śrāddha. (Pauṣa 27.380)
O Brahmin, [he should worship] the entire body, gradually from the feet up to the head,
with flowers mixed with water for the *arghya* offering and with unguents such as sandalwood paste.
Then,
having fanned them with the fans of his wings to stir up the wind,
he subsequently offered various garments perfumed with incense.
Then, having adorned them according to one's ability with bracelets and other ornaments,
one should immediately give them sacred threads along with upper garments.
Then white garlands for the head and neck-strings, and then divine-smelling powdered incense mixed with camphor [should be placed] upon the head. (Pauṣa 27.384)
Then, having offered them that supreme collyrium for the eyes,
he should afterwards show them a mirror and scatter flowers before them.
Then, O Mahāmati, one should fumigate them in due order with incense purified by fragrant smoke, and they should be worshipped with a brightly shining lamp. Pausa 27.386.
Their sandals, various umbrellas, wooden shoes, footstools, and those very seats. (Pausa 27.387)
Indeed, having fashioned various beds, palanquins, horses, and so forth, as well as all the necessary articles made of silver and other materials, for everyone.
Or else, having offered that root [offering] to all according to one's ability,
he should perform a communal assembly and a shared distribution for the complete satisfaction of their minds.
Again, having placed water for the respectful offering (arghya) in their hands while reciting the mantra,
he should perform their worship in sequence, just like the sacrifice to the Blessed One.
Then, with the honey-mixture (madhuparka), with various kinds of food offered with faith, with edible fruits and roots, and with purifying drinks; Paus_27.391.
It should be eaten first with fragrant *rasālā* and boiled milk, either in small quantities or in leaf-cups.
For the pleasure of all the Brahmins, having offered [the food] equally and presented it,
he should give water for the *arghya* into their hands as before, and also for them to sip.
Recalling the mantra mentally and receiving it from the twice-born with water, he remains before him with one-pointed mind, muttering and meditating upon the weapon-mantra.
Indeed, for their satisfaction, this Dharma-śāstra— which yields the great fruit of easy awakening— is superior to mere ritual arts; it is the supreme Śāstra of Liberation.
Proclaiming his virtues,
whatever is useful to him should be offered to him; then, when the twice-born is satisfied— [Pausa 27.396]

And when the connection has been established as before, at all times one should perform the offering of water; furthermore, O twice-born, one should satisfy [the ancestors] with libations. (Pauṣa 27.397)
With the water remaining from the offering of the funeral cake (piṇḍa),
together with honey-mixture (madhuparka), sesame, milk, clarified butter, and various side dishes.
Having filled his hollowed palms with water, he should then cast the rice-ball (piṇḍa) outside,
in front of the twice-born, along with a stream of water.
One should cast [the remains] toward the northern direction and lead them to the abode of Antaka;
then, having discarded the *pavitraka* and the *pratiśāṭaka*, [one should proceed].
Then, having changed his garment, or else while recollecting [the deity] above in his heart,
he should afterwards perform the ritual sipping of water (ācamana) with his own mantra, using the *hṛdaya-mantra* of the stainless self.

"O sir, may everything be complete!"—thus he should urge those twice-born who are seated on their mats; then, once they have expressed their satisfaction, he should offer the final oblation (pūrṇāhuti).
Then, as before, the annual rites should be performed in their proper sequence;
from this point on, they should be performed by all standing, except for the two who face eastward.

Then, at the conclusion of those two, having extracted everything from the vessel—including the fruit and roots—and having infused it with honey, clarified butter, and sesame seeds, one should offer the *codana* [oblation] to them. (Pauṣa 27.404)
"Now, let him make an offering of the remains of the meal to the twice-born;
O sir, let them speak without agitation and declare how it should be employed. (Paus 27.405)
Indeed, our own vessel was taken out according to one's desire for wealth;
then there was the ancestral food-ball (annagolaka) which had been honored. Paus 27.406.
Having extracted that which was brought into the body as if it were a separate spark,
one should then indeed contemplate it from one's own body by means of the *recaka* breath.

Having meditated upon [the deity] situated within the vessel of nectar, equal to the moon, with the heart-mantra, and having performed twelve recitations for the sake of the twice-born who has bowed down according to his desire; Pausa 27.408.
Having presented the remainder to his own wife out of consideration for the brahmin,
and having applied it and withdrawn it from the cows, he offered water into the fire of the twice-born.
Having first performed the fire-ritual for the eating-vessels [of those who have] remnants, one should then offer there, in the presence of the Blessed Lady, water mixed with sesame seeds.
O Lotus-born One, one should gradually give gifts accompanied by gold to the ancestors for their gratification, and one must protect [the offerings] from jackals at present. (Pauṣa 27.411)
In the rite for the ancestors,
within this vessel consisting of the proper placement and ritual action,
the *piṇḍa* offering— accomplished by means of the ritual foods and to be conveyed [to the ancestors]— is to be completed following the meal. (Pauṣa 27.412)
One should not recite the *akṣayyā* formula, nor perform the water-libation intended for [the deceased], nor offer the *pūrṇāhuti*, nor perform the ritual turning back of the water. (Pauṣa 27.413)
Then, having opened the vessel for the ancestors, he should pour forth from the lotus of his heart his own mantra—
blazing with the brilliance of the fire at the end of an aeon— to the deity with food.
That vessel is in the expanse of the sky, and that [point] is far from the twelve fingers;
for that is the Pitṛya-dvādaśānta, which attains unity with the vessel in due order.
One should behold these lords of mantras and meditate upon the ancestors with a contemplative mind; likewise, one should visualize a mountain of blazing fire at night as a protective shield.
Thus having attained oneness with that mantra,
they [the goddesses] then beheld Hari, the Lord of Mantras, who resembled a hundred moons.
