Having meditated upon [the deity] as devoid of parts, one should then cause the sovereign powers (śaktis) to dissolve there, like the assembly of ancestors (pitṛvyūha), following which the king of mantras [should be dissolved]. Paus 27.418.
Having made that water his own through the ancestral path, the Lotus-born One wiped his eyes once more with it and, together with his wife, gazed [upon him].
Having cast into the water that which was previously offered along with the liquid,
and having approached the abode of worship where the deity has entered the extinguished fire, [one should proceed].
O twice-born one, having worshipped the Lord of Mantras as before, one should gratify him;
then, having offered that oblation, one should partake of a meal.

Then, O Pauṣkara, meditating upon the Lord of Mantras within the interior of the lotus of the heart together with his kinsmen, one should remain restrained in speech and consume morsels of food resembling nectar.
Then, when the ground has been cleared of remnants and thoroughly washed,
he [should offer] the rice with its condiments—
which is purified by darbha grass— with his hand.
Having brought that [food] and placed it in another vessel provided with *darbha* grass and sesame seeds,
one should set it down outside to the south, accompanied by a lamp.
Having recited the mantra in a pure place and spread a layer of *darbha* grass, he should then pass the night with discourses on Dharma or through the practice of yoga.
O twice-born one, the śrāddha for the ancestors has been ordained by this rule;
it pacifies the suffering of saṃsāra and bestows liberation before long. (Pausa 27.426)
Having performed that which is of a single type and that which consists of both through faith,
it is employed in the application of knowledge and action.
Abiding in the worldly dharmas, she undergoes the impression (*vāsanā*) of fulfillment;
therefore, indeed, by that karma, a manifold state of grace arises.
Those born of mantra should practice with effort for the sake of attaining expansion;
then, one should perform the mental refinement for those who have attained perfection. (Paus 27.429)

Now listen as I describe the ritual procedure known as the *aurdhvadehika*, which must be performed immediately thereafter for the sake of accomplishing the previously mentioned results. (Pauṣa 27.430)
And know that this too is twofold and doubled, O Lotus-born one;
it belongs to all those who have been well-initiated and are liberated by means of the nectar and other [substances]. (Pauṣkara 27.431)

Indeed, when the mantra has been propitiated as before with faith, it bestows that very [attainment] which is beneficial at all times in the states of manifestation and so forth, as if it were being granted. Paus. 27.432.
O Amalekṣaṇa, until one is satisfied, up to the limit of the Lord’s pleasure; when the Lord of Mantras has been made present upon the second Amalāgra— Pausa 27.433.
A meal consisting solely of boiled rice, free from elaborate preparation, is always beneficial for all beings of little strength until they are fully satiated. (Pauṣa 27.434)
Then it exists, established within the blazing, unmanifest seed;
it is of gentle activity, subtle, and characterized by the supreme power of the vital breath (prāṇa).
Having relied upon that external time characterized by days, which is indeed a tenth part of that [internal duration],
the agent, possessing the corresponding ritual procedure, should perform it in due order.
And that which is permeated by the portions of the vital breaths—
the manifest characterized by the senses—
is brought forth from the unmanifest under the guise of the form of food. (Pauṣkara 27.437)
The sense organs beginning with the ear and ending with the organ of generation— by relying upon these, one may quickly attain [the goal] once ten days have passed.
On the eleventh day, O best of Brahmins, there is indeed the state of Śakti;
O Brahmin, this occurs through the thirty-third-day rite in its manifest form.
O twice-born one, by means of the *vināḍī* preceded by truth, and again by its portion of breath characterized by twelve *kalās*, the remaining multitude of principles [is established]. Pausa 27.440.
O twice-born one, the darkness of the principle of intellect (buddhitattva) must be dispelled in due order: first in the year, and then by the second [year]. Pausa 27.441.
Then, from the subtle element of sound (śabda-tanmātra), the pentad [of gross elements] indeed arises through the five [subtle elements];
thereafter, the group beginning with space (ākāśa) is manifested from the subtle elements.
By a group of five months, the five elements indeed reach their end;
then, when one is fully clothed, [the state of] bathing and the discarding of what has been eaten likewise occur.
When the tooth-stick has been sipped with the *hṛdaya-mantra* and [the mouth] rinsed again with the five products of the cow (*pañcagavya*),
one should likewise properly place the mantra in its location and put on the garment.
Having sipped water with the *hṛdaya* mantra and then having performed the ritual placement (*nyāsa*) of the root mantra upon the palms of the hands, one should [then] from the head...
Having performed the ritual union with that very [deity], one should effect the identification of the body.

Then, O Brahmin, for the sake of showing favor to the deceased, one should briefly offer [the oblation] with the heart-mantra consecrated [with it], according to the rules of one's own lineage, while remaining free from worldly attachments.
O twice-born one, he should then offer three handfuls of water mixed with sesame seeds under that person's name, along with *darbha* grass and silver. Paus 27.447.

For the sake of purification, for the purpose of auspicious peace, one should recite one hundred and eight times either one's own mantra, the *astra* mantra, or the common twelve-syllable mantra. (Pauṣkara 27.448)
By the power of meditation, one may proceed according to the rules in the previously prescribed rite, either with the entire collection of the nine-syllable seed-mantras or with just one.
O twice-born one, a Śrāddha for the deceased performed by two [persons] at a sacred ford, on a riverbank, in a house, or in an auspicious sanctuary, brings exceedingly great merit. Paus 27.450.
Having encountered the darkness of the array of obstacles,
such as trembling and the like, it causes the destruction of resolve and renders one's actions deficient. (Pauṣa 27.451)
Therefore, by means of the power of the Brahma-mantra,
one must indeed protect one's own power from its very root, dispelling the form of darkness with radiant light.
Having first propitiated all [the materials], such as sesame and *darbha* grass, with the mantra,
one should indeed cast these aside and [employ] another? What [is it]?
Having performed other rites, he should then stand up facing the east.
Now one should perform the appropriation of the site as common to all;
through the meditation on Brahman, one should contemplate the root mantra as omnipresent. (Pauṣa 27.454)
O Lotus-born One, one should visualize the form of the mantra as radiant as the sun, situated within the eight directions between the earth and the sky.
Then, one should meditate upon the entire expanse of space as being contained within the mantra;
in the midst of it, one should contemplate Śiva as the pillar that supports the path of saṃsāra. (Pauṣa 27.456)
The pure and great nature of the Brahma-nāḍī should be meditated upon;
one should place the true reality within the external path characterized by conceptual construction. (Pauṣkara 27.457)
When there is mutual perception between the thoroughly pacified karma and Brahman,
one should remember that the eye therein acts as a gateway, like a window.
Then one should meditate upon that which is adorned by thousands of whirling sparks of fire,
ending with the feet of a royal swan, which removes all obstacles.
Thus have I declared the *āyatana*, the mantra-form, and the mantra for all rites and for the mantras beginning with the *ādhāra* and *āsana*. (Pauṣkara 27.460)
For those of purified self who have attained the ultimate goal of the swan-like [yogis],
there is no end or fixed abiding therein.
One should perform the ritual placement of mantras according to the prescribed rule.
Having sat upon a seat made of darbha grass, which has been permeated by the pervasiveness of the *praṇava*,
one should perform the three-fold breath control (*prāṇāyāma*) using the root mantra.
Then, by means of the two types of concentration (dhāraṇā), one should perform the purification of the body;
thereafter, one should perform the ritual placement of mantras (mantranyāsa) as before upon the hands and the body.
Having obtained the *arghya* and *pādya*, one should sprinkle [the offerings] with that water, having purified them with the *sarvamantra* while using a blade of *darbha* grass. (Pauṣa 27.464)
Having observed that [the object] there has been burnt by its intense radiance, one should remember it;
then, one should contemplate it as having attained the splendor of the sun through the root mantra. (Pauṣa 27.465)
One should sprinkle the hearth, together with its fire and fuel, with water consecrated by the *astra* mantra;
then one should kindle it with the *netra* mantra and awaken it with the *varma* mantra.
Having washed the vessel with water from the weapon-mantra, one should strike it immediately thereafter;
then, having covered it with the root of an *ambu-darbha* blade, one should seal it with the armor-mantra (*varman*).
Having washed the rice grains repeatedly with the weapon-mantra (*astramantra*),
one should place them together with honey, clarified butter, sesame seeds, and cow’s milk while reciting the root-mantra (*mūla*).
The knower of mantras should cook [the offering] on a ladle consecrated with the Astra mantra, using the Hṛdaya mantra;
once it is cooked, he should then take it out with the Mūla mantra.
Then, having washed and anointed the eyes with the *śikhā-mantra*,
one should apply the vertical sectarian mark (*ūrdhvapuṇḍra*) on the cardinal directions and protect oneself from the front with the *kavaca-mantra*.
One should perform [the rite] established upon a well-smeared portion of ground provided with sesame seeds and unbroken rice grains, situated on a bed of kuśa grass presided over by the Praṇava.

And having thus prepared the *caru* by covering it with the weapon-mantra (*astramantra*), at the time of the excellent performance of the rites for the spreading of the *brahmāstaraṇa*, [one should proceed]. (Pauṣa 27.472)
One should employ the heart-mantra, reciting it with the mind according to the path of mantra; thereafter,
one should perform the rites for the deceased by means of that [mantra].
The worldly [attainment] is through the threefold pervasion. (Paus 27.473)
There, in that divine place, having first performed the ritual worship according to the previous procedure,
one should duly dedicate offerings characterized as previously described for the sake of the deceased.
Indeed, that which arises from the wheel of the vessel by the mere act of eating [the] person,
having been filled with all kinds of food and anointed with [oil] and so forth, [is offered] with the heart-mantra. // Pauṣkara 27.475 //
Having touched it with the fire of his gaze and having prepared it with its various condiments, he offered it to the Lord, speaking thus out of a desire for His grace. (Pauṣa 27.476)

Having summoned the deceased by his own name from the sky— either as a clearly manifest form consisting of his own words or as the syllable *oṃ*— one should place him within the space of one's own heart.
And having contemplated it as being like a tiny spark of fire remaining from an extinguished flame,
joined with a slight portion of vital breath and brought under control by the power of karma; // Paus_27.478 //

And having gradually led forth the mere existence of the specific [deity] through the path of fire and established it in its own place within the object perceived by the mantra-visionary; Pausa 27.479.

Then, O Brahmin, one should meditate with the *praṇava* upon that which is imperishable, known as *prāṇa*, which is supported by the vigor of food and endowed with the multitude of the powers of the principles (*tattva*).
Then, by means of the path of that heat, while recollecting with the heart-mantra (hṛnmantra),
one should visualize the deceased as having emerged [from the body] because his vital breath has departed, enveloped by the faculty of hearing.
Know that its essential nature is a subtle state colored by knowledge,
and that it has, in reality, attained oneness with the departed spirit.
O Brahmin, by means of that [concentration], one should gradually contemplate whatever has entered the heart;
thus, through the sense organs of hearing and so forth, having attained unity with the single, manifest prāṇa.
O Lotus-born One, now that the vital breath has arisen from its food and is withdrawn, one should remember everything beneficial along with its root, just as one remembers the wind. (Pauṣa 27.484)

But that formless [element], impelled by the power of the vital breath (*prāṇa*) like a blow, one should meditate upon as the sense organ, having reached the state of the heart-mantra (*hṛnmantra*) within the heart. (Pauṣkara 27.485)

Having seated you upon a peaceful throne, previously purified through pervasive meditation, one should thereafter worship you as the Lord of Mantras with constant, auspicious offerings such as arghya and the rest.

O Lotus-born One, one should offer flowers, unguents, and incense up to the mother [of the deceased], and afterwards give water with sesame seeds by name and lineage, using the *hṛdaya* mantra. (Pauṣa 27.487)
Then, having gratified that sense-organ, which resides within the locus of fire and has the heart as its form, according to the rule and by the previously stated sequence; Paus_27.488.
Then, having summoned the previously mentioned vessel which consists of the Blessed One,
one should place it on the seat previously remembered, in front of the Blessed One.
Having placed the mantra upon the heart with the *hṛdaya-mantra*, one should then worship it with water for the guest-offering (*arghya*) and other offerings;
then, having sat down at ease, one should proceed to the place of propitiation.

One should meditate upon Him with the heart through the senses according to one's own capacity, as He has attained a formal manifestation; yet He remains established through His essence as the nature of taste within the power of food, and by means of differentiation.
One should meditate as before on the preta, and remember him with the *praṇava*, having brought him forth and established him in the state of presiding over the food. (Pauṣa 27.492)
And [he should perform] the end of the mantra of the lord of the twice-born together with the arghya water;
then, within the power of that [deity's] vital breath, it has attained oneness through the heart-mantra.
The food offering [extends] to the end of the sky.
O Kamalasambhava,
that [wind] then gradually enters the space of the heart along with the vital breath (prāṇa).
One should cause [the deity] to experience [the offering] as it proceeds into the auditory function for the sake of manifestation;
having thus established the deceased's self within the previously mentioned form of the Brahmin, one should proceed. (Pauṣkara 27.495)
Then he should place water in the hand as before for the purpose of sipping, provided that there is no doubt regarding the commencement of his meal. (Pauṣa 27.496)

Meditating with his intellect, he should stand at the forefront; by the power of the vitality of food, that [object] attained its true state through the heart and the sense of hearing. (Pauṣkara 27.497)
O best of the twice-born, once the meal was finished, that lord of the twice-born emitted the sound of the *praṇava* from his own body through the right channel. (Pauṣa 27.498)

O Brahmin, having drawn the deceased into the space of the lotus-heart by means of that [nectar], one should indeed endow the ear with existence through one's own heart as if with nectar. (Pauṣkara 27.499)
O tiger among brahmins, when the leftovers have been removed, the propitiation of the Lord is ordained as before; then the performer, having finished his meal, [should proceed]. (Pauṣa 27.500)

One who possesses the mantra as their very self should recite the Astra-mantra one hundred and eight times for the sake of pacifying obstacles and other hindrances; he should then perform the worship at the site according to its constituent parts.
Having withdrawn all that consists of the final vowels along with the *arghya*, flowers, and so forth,
and having cast it into a body of water, one should perform the *svāhā* [offering].
Then, at the arrival of night, he should perform the concentration on the mantra and its recitation;
likewise [he should guard] the ears,
the eyes, and the sense of taste.
And the fourfold [set] including the notion of the nose.
O Mahāmati, the four [vowels] are to be manifested over four days;
then the five [consonants], beginning with *va*, are to be placed upon the head in sequence.
O best of the twice-born, for the sake of attaining welfare for the deceased, one who has attained the state of existence should prepare the *yaru* when the eleventh day has arrived. (Pauṣa 27.505)
It should be provided with various side dishes and accompaniments, and be well-prepared with faith;
[the recipient] should have his feet washed, perform the ritual sipping of water (ācamana), and be struck and gazed upon.

Having placed [the disciple], who is purified by clear water, bowed down, and meditated upon the reality of the Blessed One, upon the seat that has been worshipped and permeated with the sense of pervasion; Pausa 27.507.
Then, having anointed him with devotion using ointments such as sandalwood and the like, and having wrapped him in fine garments, one should adorn him according to one's ability. (Pauṣa 27.508)
With excellent ornaments such as golden bracelets set with gems, with garlands, sacred threads and the like, and with purifying head-cloths; Paus_27.509.
Having placed that food and condiments in his hand, one should honor the Lord of Mantras with supreme faith, desiring to show favor to the deceased brahmin.
Having first performed the propitiation of the Lord as far as the celestial abodes,
one should then perform the ritual placement of mantras (*mantranyāsa*) for the most excellent Brahmin.
Then, [place] the root-mantra on both hands; on the fingers, the heart and the other [limbs];
on all the tips of the nails, the eyes; and then upon the body from the feet up to the head.

Having placed the feet at the conclusion [of the body], and having meditated upon the heart and the other [limbs] in their respective places, one should then contemplate the nature of the mantra, endowed with the sense of identity with it.
Having worshipped with the *praṇava* accompanied by the designation "Father," and with offerings such as *arghya* and flowers, but with special items as before.
Having bestowed upon him everything that serves as an instrument for the deceased, including cattle, land, and gold, he should provide whatever brings him satisfaction.
The deceased becomes free from debt and attains the supreme state;
then, as before, he should be satisfied with food provided in the proper manner. Pausa 27.516.
One should meditate upon the heart as being active, as before, by means of the root mantra;
however, it is indeed characterized by the arrival [of the deity] residing within the collection of the senses. (Pauṣkara 27.517)

One should always contemplate the *praṇava* together with the root mantra as the deceased; thus, having attained the state of "I-am-ness" (*asmitā*), it becomes properly joined with the powers of the senses. (Pauṣkara 27.518)
Having performed this with the mantras ending in *dhara* preceded by *buddhi*, one should please him;
one should act there for the sake of awakening and should draw [the diagram] with the *śikhā-mantra*.
O twice-born one, armor was ordained for the manifestation of the mind itself, and then, in due order, for the manifestation of the five subtle elements (tanmātras). Paus 27.520.
The weapon-mantra of the elements, indeed, is constantly sounded; for by twelve months, or by ten and eleven [months], it is truly attained. (Pauṣa 27.521)
O Blessed One, when the thirteenth month has arrived, one should indeed offer a funeral ball (piṇḍa) for the deceased;
this should be performed on the path of the ancestors, which consists of the Lord.
O Lotus-born One, listen clearly as I speak:
first, the ritual bath has been fully described; thereafter, one should perform that [rite]. Pausa 27.523.

For the sake of the śrāddha, one should seat the best of the twice-born—who have sipped water for purification (ācānta) and whose feet have been washed—upon abundant and well-prepared food with faith. Paus 27.524.
Whether they be sons, those who know the samaya, practitioners, or teachers;
whether householders, celibate students, forest-dwellers, or ascetics—Pausa 27.525.
O best of the twice-born, having placed four facing northward directly before the Lord of Mantras, one should likewise place two facing eastward.

Of those two, the rite of sakalīkaraṇa is indeed prescribed for one by means of the weapon-mantra (astra), and then for the second by means of the armor-mantra (varman); thus the ritual of placement (nyāsakarma) is ordained.
O twice-born one, during the rite of placement (*nyāsa*), the eye was first assigned to those facing north; thereafter, it was ordained that his head should be situated above that.
Then, the heart-mantra should be used for the second [placement], and the root-mantra for the fourth; indeed, the hand-placement (hastanyāsa) and other rites should be performed accordingly.
Then, one should assign the six crest-mantras (śikhā-mantra) beginning with *svā* and ending with *khāda* (*khādyasvānta*) into the [six limbs].
Then, having performed the worship of the Blessed One as far as the abode of Agni, [he should proceed].
Having performed [the ritual] exactly as described, one should worship with special care;
then, O best of the twice-born, that which has been assigned to the weapon (astra) should be worshipped with the weapon-mantra.
One should perform the worship of the armor and the form of the armor, excluding the two— the name and the lineage—
and thereafter perform the worship of others by means of their own names and lineages.
There, one should worship that deceased twice-born person with his own respective mantra, having performed the ritual placement (nyāsa) of the eye-mantra upon him. (Pauṣa 27.533)
O twice-born one, seated upon that and established there is the form characterized by the ancestors; for its worship, one's own head-mantra is prescribed.
O Brahmin, know that the heart-mantra which one worships is the Grandfather (Pitāmaha) himself;
one should perform the worship of the deceased by means of his name and lineage, indeed with the heart-mantra. (Pauṣkara 27.535)
Know that he who has performed the ritual placement (*nyāsa*) with the root mantra is your great-grandfather;
indeed, he is to be honored by that very name along with his lineage (*gotra*). (Pauṣa 27.536)
O Brahmin, for those who have now been honored, one should perform the internal unification of the rite intended for the ancestors, beginning with the *preta* stage, within their hearts.
O you who have arisen from that lotus, understand from me how the destruction of the food offering occurs gradually for those whose nature is the essence of food, as previously described.
Then, having mentally envisioned the host of deities, he should meditate upon them with his intellect as equal [to himself],
not abandoning his own abode, through devotion, [attaining] likeness to the full moon.
Having contemplated the *sāmā* mantra as mere food for the ancestors and the *netra* mantra [as the eye], one should likewise mentally recollect the *śiras* mantra as it has arrived. (Pauṣa 27.540)

Together with the power of the eye, having taken up the two powers called "the Eye" and "the Upper" from the vessel consecrated by the heart-mantra, he should then take up that which consists of the heart.
One should indeed contemplate the Śakti, who is contained within the food offering (naivedya), by means of the root mantras;
through the very guise of the power of the mantra, she is present in the form of the *praṇava* (Oṃ) along with the sacrificial food.
O Pauṣkara, one should then unify the mantra and the Brahman; having thus established it within oneself, one should take the vessel of the food offering (naivedya). Paus_27.543.
To the twice-born who are seated, along with the various kinds of food and edibles,
he should give water into their hands at the very end, when only cow’s milk remains. (Pauṣa 27.544)
O twice-born one, for the sake of the satisfaction of the ancestors, one should repeatedly ask what is required by each of those engaged in the meal and give it accordingly.
Then, O Pauṣkara, one should perform their placement there with those [mantras] ending in *svāhā*, according to this rule for the unification of the Śaktis. (Pauṣkara 27.546)
Having now extracted the deceased from his two-fold body, he is endowed with the qualities of reality and power, blazing like the sun as before.

Having recited [the mantra] within the heart-lotus by means of that splendor of the mantra, one should once again make it even more refined; then, indeed, having drawn it from there into the heart— // Pauṣa 27.548 //

Then, having purified [the element] in the paternal [lotus], for the sake of its increase, one should extract it from there and, being fully satisfied, place it within the heart by means of the heart-mantra. (Pausa 27.549)
Having placed [the two] within the range of the heart-lotus of one's great-grandfather,
and having made them radiant with the digits of the Mantra-Brahman, one should bring them there into the heart.
Then, having dissolved [the self] within one's own nature through the contemplation of peace by means of the syllable *praṇava*,
and having performed such a meditative synthesis (*anusandhāna*), from that time forth for him indeed—

The status of being a father [is attained] at the annual śrāddha, especially when the time has arrived; for those who have died other than by [natural] causes, it is ordained that this occurs once the year has passed. Paus 27.552.
O tiger among the twice-born, for other ancestors who long for the śrāddha,
as well as for a living being whose speech remains suspended, the state of being a preta has not yet been pacified.

"O Lotus-born One, it has been thus explained with its constituent parts by means of the mantra: that the state of being a father, having received the consecration, remains established in each successive stage."

Now, learn from me that ritual procedure known as the *aurdhvadaihika* (rites for the deceased) intended for those who are to come, performed with four mantras belonging to the fourfold self. Paus. 27.555.
Having established the ten sense organs, beginning with the ear and ending with the organ of generation,
he should perform the rite known as Vāsudeva by means of the mantra over ten days.
In this [rite], O Pauṣkara, one should perform the manifestation by means of Sāṅkarṣaṇa;
or, in the principle of intellect (buddhitattva), one should manifest it by means of the third [mantra] together with the mind (manas).
O Pauṣkara, when a year has passed in this manner, the earth element is to be manifested from the subtle element of space by Aniruddha, just as before.
O best among those who know mantras, one should perform the *sapiṇḍīkaraṇa* rite in sequence, beginning with Aniruddha and ending with Vāsudeva, using the four mantras. (Pauṣa 27.559)
O best of the twice-born, one who knows the Self should thus desire that arrangement of kinsmen by means of the nine-formed [rite], for the attainment of auspiciousness. (Pauṣa 27.560)
Therefore, now listen with one-pointed attention to this summary:
it is taught that a mountain serves for the gratification of the senses, such as hearing and the rest.

Nṛsiṃha is indeed for Bhūgā and others; in this [state], when the power resides on the seat of the bird, the reality of Brahman becomes manifest for the sake of the welfare of those whose intellects are accompanied by the mind. (Pauṣa 27.562)

O Mahāmati, having thus performed the recitation (japa) consisting of the retention of the mantras together with the subtle elements (tanmātra) and the gross elements (bhūta), and joined with the principles (tattva) and the digits (kalā); Paus_27.563.
Then, when a year has passed, one should bring about the contemplation of the Pitṛs with five [deities] beginning with Varāha, and subsequently with four beginning with Aniruddha.
By means of the previously described procedure, endowed with knowledge and meditation, and through divine and immutable action, one accomplishes manifold goals. (Pauṣkara 27.565)
That second arrangement has been indicated by me; having made it clearer for me as I speak, listen attentively. (Pauṣa 27.566)
Having performed all the previously mentioned procedures for the preparation of the sacrificial oblation (caru),
one should kindle the fire, consecrated by the purificatory rites as before.
Having meditated upon the Lord of Mantras within that [fire], one should offer sacrificial fuel sticks and oblations in sequence;
then, having spread *kuśa* grass with its tips pointing south in front of it, as before.
Having meditated on the seat of one's own residence, one should place above that the lotus-seat, and upon it,
as before, the ball of food (annagolaka) joined with the primordial [deities] and the others.
Having performed everything previously mentioned in that regard, immediately thereafter,
he should offer handfuls of water mixed with sesame seeds before it, under the name of the deceased.
Having given [the gift], then having withdrawn it, and having cast it into the midst of the water,
O twice-born one, he then makes it his own through the mantra. (Pausa 27.571)
Having collected everything in water and cast it away without fire, one should perform the rites in this manner for ten days; then, as before, on the eleventh day, [one should proceed].
One who knows the ritual procedure should perform the *śrāddha*, preceded by the offering of the rice-balls (*piṇḍa*),
once the year has been completed, in order to effect the attainment of the status of a *pitṛ*.
The previously mentioned meditation, together with the mantra, becomes superior to that [meditation on the father];
it resembles a blazing sun and has attained a state of singular capability. (Pausa 27.574)

One should meditate upon that mantra which constitutes the presiding principle (*adhyakṣatva*), characterized by the internal self (*adhyātma*), and having emerged from the physical body (*piṇḍa*) once it has entered the objective sphere (*adhibhūta*). (Pauṣkara 27.575)
One should closely observe its activity in the sky above that place;
thus, O Lotus-born One, when it is led away from the food and has departed, [the result follows]. (Pauṣa 27.576)
Then, with that mantra, taking from that mass consisting of the elements,
he took a handful of it and whatever fragments were there.
One should now properly remember the transformed [state] as all-pervasive;
then the primordial state, both with respect to the internal self (adhyātma) and the divine principle (adhidaiva), O Lotus-born One.
One should then lead that food, which was intended for the ancestral *piṇḍa*, upward and place it [there].
In this way, the deceased attains oneness with the individual consciousness (*cit*). (Pauṣkara 27.579)
Indeed, everything arising from the lotus should be performed like the *piṇḍa* offering for the *preta*s;
thereafter, one should perform his activity according to the ancestral tradition.
Therefore, that too— just as before— one should bring to a state of transcendence,
O best of the twice-born, in this aforementioned rite dedicated to Prajāpati.
From the eleventh day until the day on which the status of being a father is attained, one should perform the remaining rites previously mentioned;
that which remains [after the eleventh day] should be performed first.

However, at the place of the meal, while the twice-born are seated upon their seats, one should indeed offer the inexhaustible water mixed with sesame seeds while they are reciting prayers. (Pauṣa 27.583)
To this extent, the purport of this [treatise] known as the *Aurdhvadaihika* has been correctly elucidated; it is characterized by the quality of goodness (*sāttvika*).
When passion has arisen during creation,
it indeed vibrates within the heart; likewise, the two components of cognition— [the object and the subject]— are likewise [manifested], O Pauṣkara.
For their benefit, food along with water and rice-balls (piṇḍas) are prescribed for the rite of the deceased, each according to its own proper time and as is customary for the family. (Paus 27.586)

O Lotus-born One, the prohibition of the four types of pride has been prescribed during periods such as birth-impurity; indeed, O Source of the Waters, there is a prohibition for the householder until the end of his life.

O best of the twice-born, because of the power of those foremost among the twice-born who sacrifice with the single principle of the fourfold self, and because they are worthy of worship, there is no [such thing as death]— so it is said. (Pauṣa 27.588)
Therefore, one may indeed undertake the entitlement [to perform rites] during a period of impurity caused by death or birth,
whether in receiving gifts or in giving them, for that duration, provided there is no mixture of castes.
Indeed, this innate practice of those who do not sacrifice to the gods and of those who sacrifice to the Blessed One is mutually beyond doubt. (Pauṣa 27.590)
However, for one who desires the path and follows this [teaching] which is indeed infallible,
if the period of impurity has already passed, he should then observe the ten-day rite.
Thus it was spoken by the Lotus-born One, O Sarasvatī, concerning the eternal and supreme preliminary rite for the śrāddha, beginning with the formal transmission of the gift. Pausa 27.592.

Now follows the procedure for the optional *śrāddha*—another ritual injunction; listen further to it in this context, which bestows the fruits of heaven and liberation upon those devotees of purified souls. (Pauṣa 27.593)
That which pertains to a matter of legal procedure, when it has been interrupted by those whose intellects are [guided] by the treatises (or by their kinsmen).
But one who desires it himself may complete the entire [study] of the twice-born in twelve days.
I shall now relate that matter briefly and exactly as it happened:
in former times, having accumulated the necessary provisions and surrounded by excellent companions, [he set out].
Thus, many twice-born ones, who generate serenity of mind, having placed [the ancestors] at their head on a bright day prior to the fortnight of the ancestors (pitṛpakṣa). Paus 27.596.
This should be recited during the rainy season, but in the month of Mādhava, during the autumn,
one should go to the abode of Viṣṇu, which is crowded with people offering flowers and incense.
Or the bank of a great river, or a mountain slope with its peaks and water, free from danger and unoccupied by outcasts, Śabaras, and the like. (Pauṣa 27.598)
Having approached that [place], one should perform austerity and sacrifice according to the prescribed rules,
for the Gaṇas, for the Nāgas, for the Bhūtas, and for the Lord of the Forest.

On the following day, one should indeed perform the propitiation of one's own mantra with a sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) according to one's ability, through the very mouth of the resident of the sacred field (kṣetravāsin). Paus 27.600.
Immediately after that, one should pray to the mantra residing in the abode of Viṣṇu— whether its characteristics are unknown or clearly manifest— and which is worthy of worship.
One bows to the Lord, the Supreme Overseer, who is endowed with the seed of his own consciousness,
whose designations include the manifest and the unmanifest, and whose aggregate is known as the senses. (Pauṣkara 27.602)
I establish it by joining it with its constituent parts according to the ritual rule,
[unifying] the form of differentiation and the non-differentiated self of the accumulation of the impure body.

And for the sake of experiencing the fruits of my good deeds, O Supreme Lord, otherwise than this, the characteristic of the vital wind remains within me after I have departed from the body. (Pauṣa 27.604)
And she, possessed of both pleasure and pain, was completely enveloped by the desire for wealth.
It arises filled with agitation, appearing as if it were for a long time and inexhaustible.
And likewise, the activity of a living being— whether voluntary or involuntary—
is performed through the acquisition of another body, either perpetually or after a lapse of time.
That terrible and unbearable state, which in reality persists, goes to its destruction through your grace, O Lord; therefore, may food quickly be provided with water. (Pauṣya 27.607)
The aggregate known as the sense-faculties, once it has been brought to completion, is free from affliction;
it is without continuity, beyond doubt, devoid of hope, and yet it enters the net of karma.
Having taken us as your concern, you alone today provide protection for yourself;
you are the supreme refuge for those who have fallen into hell and are devoid of hope.
You alone are eternally capable of delivering those for whom the funeral cakes have been omitted; therefore,
you alone have eternally commenced that [work].
Sanātana. Pausa 27.610.
O Blessed One, until the day of completion, may the entire web of obstacles along with their latent tendencies depart from me; may there indeed be the accomplishment of my karma.
Having thus petitioned the Unborn One and filled the vessel with water,
he should perform the remaining full oblation and maintain self-restraint until its completion.
Having set aside all worldly conventions characterized by dharma, pleasure, and wealth, as previously described, one should thereafter become fully attentive.
Then, having performed the worship of the deity according to one's preference,
I shall indeed offer the libation (tarpaṇa) either in front of it or to its right.
Then, having seated the lord of the twice-born and having performed everything according to the prescribed rites,
he did so with a mind free from doubt and with an intellect directed in that very same way.

One should meditate upon one's own home as one's own consciousness, arrived in its presence; and one should remember that single, sinless state with the *praṇava* at the appropriate time. (Pauṣa 27.616)

Having gone to a dwelling, one should perform the great preparatory rite as prescribed in the scriptures; having become a mendicant, one should practice that which is ordained and for which initiation has been declared.
Having thus performed the collection of the bones according to the prescribed rule,
O Lotus-born One, one should then indeed perform the ritual bath accompanied by mantras there.

Then, he should perform the ritual bathing with the chief mantras associated with the Ṛg, Yajur, and Sāma Vedas, which contain references to water, by the best of the twice-born who have been initiated.
From among the twelve-syllable mantras previously mentioned,
one who has been initiated should indeed recite only a single mantra that possesses the characteristics described above.
Having thus performed the bath with either one's own mantra or the weapon-mantras (*astramantra*),
one should again meditate upon one's own twelve-syllable mantra within the lotus of the heart.
With single-minded focus, he remains reciting [the mantra] for half a muhūrta or a full muhūrta, [visualizing him] as having the color of molten gold or in that very same unmanifest form.

O Brahmin, by that [practice], the impurity arising from his own lineage is brought to an end like the fire at the end of an aeon, due to the intention of those men who possess the requisite qualification.
The mind is the reality for those born from others in their respective order;
however, it is not so for those born from the fire of bliss, who possess all-pervading power.
And for those twice-born who are practitioners of that [path], knowers of it, and authorized— having thus purified his body and prepared the food as before— Pauṣ 27.625.

Food fit for consumption, accompanied by condiments, was intended solely for the sacrifice to the Lord, as well as for the libation to the Fire and for the offering of funeral cakes (piṇḍa). Paus. 27.626.
Just as the body, which is like a vehicle and a second form of the elements,
meets its destruction through karma, so too does it for those seeking liberation through initiation and other such means.
Having thus given [the gift] himself at this time, that body which he previously attained for the sake of assisting through his actions returns within ten days or so. || 27.628 ||
O Lotus-born One, by means of that very Dharma which will arise after a long time,
through long practice over a vast duration, there occurs a great accumulation of karma.
Indeed, through the grace of the Lords of Mantras and by that pure deed, he surely attains peace and the state of being a father. (Pauṣa 27.630)
Furthermore, even that which is more weighty than this, or indeed that which is personally prepared, shall serve for the benefit of men for ten days and so forth. (Pauṣa 27.631)

When the daily [rite] has concluded, one should then perform the ritual dismissal (*saṃyaja*) of the deity who is to be worshipped for one's own sake, having mentally resolved upon it either by oneself or through the mouth of the Guru. (Pauṣa 27.632)

For indeed, by means of the *śrāddha* under the guise of a rite, one establishes a connection with the future body—the substratum of karma—through the limbs of the *Īśvara-tattva*, which exist separately from the state of the [current] body. (Pauṣkara 27.633)

Then, O Lotus-born One, having worshipped the Lord of Mantras as before with offerings possessing all complete characteristics, ending with the ritual gift of handfuls of sesame seeds according to the rule.
Then, according to the previously mentioned procedure, with devotion and faith, many Brahmins devoted to the five daily rites should [perform the rite] for one day. (Pauṣa 27.635)

For he who, having satisfied [the ancestors], desires prosperity through the sacrifice to the Blessed One and other rites, for him there is the cause of crossing over, whether while living or after death. (Pauṣa 27.636)
I do not see anyone who knows the truth of the origin and dissolution [of beings]— and who is free from the practice of mixed worship— except through this sacrifice preceded by mantras.
In this regard, those three vessels are eternally devoted to knowledge and ritual action;
they are intent upon the application of mantras, for there is no deviation from what ought to be done.
Endowed with devotion and faith, it is the supreme raft for crossing over; let it remain, O Pauṣkara, as the means for those who are free from sin. (Pauṣkara 27.639)
The sacrifice consisting of Brahman, which is pure and even prohibited by others, [is performed];
yet, because they have fallen, the offering of funeral cakes and water with sesame seeds must be made for them.
And by chanting their names, these beings attain the supreme goal;
this single utterance is most excellent—an effortless valor.
Or, preceded by the performance of the *ādhāra* and *ādhāna* rites, he should perform the *prājāpatya* penance;
however, O best of the twice-born, this should be done until the end of the *sapiṇḍīkaraṇa*, up to the tenth day.
When the fire has been first gratified and the Lord of Mantras residing within it has been satisfied,
one should then perform the offering of the funeral cakes (piṇḍa) according to the previously described procedure.

Having seated one Brahmin on a seat, or even many according to one's ability, they should be offered libations according to the rule for the sake of attaining the realization of the ultimate reality. (Pauṣa 27.644)
With fruits and roots as food, with various kinds of delicacies, and with diverse purifying drinks—whether to be licked, drunk, or sucked. (Pauṣa 27.645)
With sacrificial fees (*dakṣiṇā*), betel leaves accompanied by water-pots,
and with gifts such as umbrellas, sandals, and vehicles, according to one's desire and as is appropriate.

O Blessed One, one indeed attains devotion by means of that which is the assembly consisting of the Blessed One, or by knowing the resolve, as well as the strength and weakness of place and time. (Pauṣa 27.647)

Driven by greed for a worthy recipient, he quickly desires to perform a funeral rite (*śrāddha*) either ten days prior or at the conclusion of the transformation into the state of a *pitṛ*. (Pausa 27.648)
O twice-born one, even if it has been many days since the last meal of prepared food,
one should perform the worship of the Lord duly with leaves, flowers, and other offerings.
Intent on the propitiation of the fire, he should indeed offer to the ancestors for his own sake a vessel completely filled with rice grains sprinkled with honey and clarified butter. (Pauṣa 27.650)
Above the form, it is adorned with juices, fruits, and roots;
it is enriched with an upper garment and a sacred thread, and joined with a garland.
Having worshipped and offered [the gift] consisting of grain, accompanied by a single [piece of] cloth, provided with a water-pot, and endowed with incense, lamps, and so forth; Pausa 27.652.
Then, for the sake of the ancestors and for the sake of the twice-born (the living), one should offer water with sesame seeds;
this may be done by a single person, or indeed by many acting together for the same purpose.
The prepared food of the best of the twice-born,
having been honored and offered in due order, must indeed be presented to the Lord.

Or, having prepared a *piṇḍa* with rice grains sprinkled with honey and clarified butter as before, [he should offer it] in front of the Lord who has entered the womb of the fire, upon the darbha grass... [Pausa 27.655]
But as for that which was stated, he [attains it];
and here, as the occasion arises, [he attains] the vital breaths and the sense faculties.
One should perform the offering of scents as before, with a perfectly pure intellect,
according to the rite prescribed for the departed spirits, by oneself and for oneself.
Having completed the year according to the prescribed rite preceded by mantras,
one should perform the annual śrāddha ceremony every year for as long as one lives.
Endowed with various gifts and adorned with the essence of devotion, they follow the path as it has been prescribed; however, they are possessed of the [right] spiritual lineage (gotra).
At the end of the mantra, O twice-born one, they should be employed preceded by the word "sama";
one should meditate upon one's own form, known as the pride of knowledge.
Therefore, [one should meditate on the goddess] as pure and blazing in form, sometimes characterized by a specific shape,
and sometimes in the form of a sphere, resembling the midday sun.
And in some places it appears even more dull due to the influence of its activity;
having thus completed [the rite] according to the rule, preceded by the sacrifice to the Blessed One.
Everything previously enjoined, up to the satiation of the Brahmins,
is performed with the rice-balls and other offerings for the ancestors, which are concluded at the end of the fire-ritual.
O best of the twice-born, one should eat together with one's kinsmen what remains after [the guests] have been served;
this is the Prājāpatya rite for the divine rites pertaining to the ancestors.
In this ritual accompanied by mantras, is there success for those whose nature is knowledge, who are themselves the agents within their own selves, and who have mastered the mantras? (Pausa 27.665)
And by means of that [rite], the deceased quickly attains the state of reality;
therefore, one should perform the entire *śrāddha* ritual there with [the offerings] consecrated by mantras. (Paus 27.666)
O one of stainless eyes, until the completion of the satisfaction [of the ancestors],
one should perform everything with speech, preceded by the utterance of mantras, even if it does not constitute a formal rite for the assembly. (Pauṣa 27.667)
"Take it, bring it, restrain it"—O twice-born one, one should indeed mentally recollect every such activity from beginning to the end of the meal. (Pauṣa 27.668)
With the *praṇava*, one should enter oneself into the mantra, which resembles the combined radiance of the sun, moon, and fire, within the fire characterized by that very form. (Pauskara 27.669)
Or, know that within the Supreme Self, though it is undivided, there exists a fourfold nature;
it has the form of a Kadamba flower, possesses all powers, and is untainted.
Thus has been declared, O lotus-eyed one, the great procedure for the next world concerning one who remains in the state of a living being,
which is equal to the Mukha-kalpa.

In this regard, O Brahmin, one should remain composed and understand everything previously mentioned— both that which has been stated and that which has not— as culminating in the propitiation of the Blessed One.

Whatever great rite consisting of offerings for the ancestors and the deceased one performs according to this rule, for the sake of his satisfaction in the hereafter, they bestow upon him an auspicious progeny. (Pauṣa 27.673)

O twice-born one, even if incomplete in terms of ritual disposition, mantra, action, and material offerings, he who recites this chapter on the *śrāddha* for those partaking in the *śrāddha* is indeed possessed of yoga. (Pausa 27.674)
Indeed, by offering everything before the ancestors with devotion, one becomes free from debt;
how much more so, O high-minded one, when the mantra is the sacred Veda and the ritual action is that of the mantras? (Pauṣa 27.675)
Pauṣkara said:
"O Blessed One, by means of what merit does one [attain] Brahman..."
I have a doubt here as to whether [the Lord] exists in a manifest form.
The Blessed One said:
Just as for them the orb of the sun cannot exist outside of its rays,
so it is with the embodied form of the sixfold attributes of Lord Viṣṇu.
The light... [was] previously... the tip of the finger...
O Lotus-born one, these qualities are always manifested by none other than you;
for such is the distinction between the fourfold embodied Lord and the Supreme.
O twice-born one, that which exists as the mutual pervader of various juices— prepared for the sake of a single mass— that possess distinct forms, is established in the state of encompassing both.
Of the All-pervading Lord, the Sovereign of all, everything exists within all his powers, and they function just as... // Paus 27.681 //
(There is a gap in the text here) — ...is addressed with harsh words.
O Brahmin, the Lord Vāsudeva is the soul of the universe, the eternal one. (Pausa 27.682)
Furthermore, those whose speech consists of the density of consciousness manifest the form of the [Supreme] for the sake of correctly assisting in ritual action.
The complete characteristic of all phenomena shines forth;
moreover, within the Full Self,
all things abide as that very reality.
But those *kṛtyā*s perform their deeds through the agent, [who is] the Supreme Lord;
by means of the power of manifestation, they belong to the power of that which is... // Paus 27.685 //
O Lotus-born One, from the center of that which is covered by a web of rays,
he manifested himself together with the primordial principle (Ādi-tattva).
And regarding the preparation for meditative concentration, whether in its attainment or in the practice of dhyāna,
the Supreme Self has arisen as the all-pervading Lord.
For this very reason, it is inferred merely by its self-luminous aspect;
thus, the moon is indeed nothing more than a mere fraction of the power of bliss.
O lotus-eyed one, it should be known that for one who is pleased, there is no treasure higher than this.
In that very same way, the power of consciousness (*cit-śakti*) is to be fully understood as being like fire.
For whatever other entities exist in this world that imitate it,
even qualities such as knowledge and the like are obtained; therefore, they are born from power (*śaktija*) and born from the constituent parts (*yāṃśaja*).
In every respect, the Blessed One exists thus as the universal essence;
this form is not composed of illusion, nor is it joined with the qualities of inert power.
O Blessed One, O Lotus-born, for that which is dissolved within you truly exists;
for when examined by those who perceive the imperishable, it is indeed eternal.
One reaches the stage of non-existence, like a lord seen in a dream;
so too do the mantras that are equal in power when recited at a funeral rite (*śrāddha*), as well as those proclaimed for initiations (*dīkṣā*) and other such rites. (Pauṣa 27.693)
And in other activities as well, they likewise perceive that [object] as endowed with such majesty;
thus, preceded by mantra, they perform the activity enjoined by the scriptures through the intellect alone.
Indeed, through the nature of knowledge, he quickly attains mastery over the actions of those foremost of the twice-born, learned in the Vedas, who abide in the stages of life for your sake.
Just as there is no fault in accepting food from a Śūdra who has already eaten, because of the weight of his knowledge,
so it is indeed always for those who are pure and naturally radiant. (Pauṣkara 27.696)
A garland produced from fresh [flowers] would become impure through the acceptance of a Śūdra; yet,
for Śūdras themselves, there is no fault in this very matter, due to the weight of their ignorance.
There is no contradiction anywhere between the mantras and the commitments (samayas) of all [practitioners]; for this very reason, it is so. (Paus 27.698)
There exists for the twice-born a [place] that is the limit of the mantras consisting of the three Vedas, which bestow the fruit of active engagement.
O best of the twice-born, it was not by nature [so], but was illuminated by Brahmanic splendor and remained established under that name.
And for those [beings], that which exists is the unanointed, perfectly awakened state of enlightenment;
yet there is only mutual hostility toward one another.
O Lotus-born One, for the lords of the twice-born, the deer, and the mantras,
there is a single point of rest that is reached gradually, step by step.
And it is established, O Pauṣkara, for the fourth, known as the Śūdra,
[the lineages] Prabhākara and Vāha,
and Taikṣvya.
But indeed, it is due to the power of honey.
In that same way, O Brahmin, the three classes of fiery color likewise turn back;
for which purpose indeed has this been prohibited—[fill in the blank].
The mind alone is indeed the support for those mantras beginning with *tad-rig*;
and know that their purity is she who is the sovereign of all. (Paus 27.705)
Furthermore, the mantras of the Nivṛtticakra indeed bestow that fruit of cessation; likewise,
for those [mantras] in which doubts have been manifested, there are *svāhā*, *vauṣaṭ*, and *vaṣaṭ*.
O Blessed One, those mantras which were previously declared by me to you as prohibited for the sake of [attaining] completion are [rendered so] by the *praṇava*... // Paus_27.707 //
O twice-born one, although they are all equally cooks for the Omniscient One, even among them, some are engaged in their own specific duties by virtue of their particular role.
By which, O Mahāmati, they do not possess the quality of luminosity,
[as established] by the primordial Lord, the All-pervading One.
Within the threefold collection of sounds, people are of three kinds;
the Brahmins who do not worship other [deities] are devoted to the assembly of mantras, such as the *añcala* and others.
The four officiating priests— those who recite the Ṛg, Yajur, Sāman, and Atharva Vedas— are engaged in the ritual mixing [of the offerings] regarding the seed, the lump, the word, and so forth.
When the array of mantras is perfectly pure and free from the traces of passion and delusion,
[it is suitable for] the mantras of the passionate (rājasa) and the ignorant (tāmasa) classes.

For all those authorized by the ritual rule are indeed intended solely for the sake of attaining the Self; this must be done constantly with great self-restraint and especially with devotion. (Pauṣa 27.713)
A Śūdra who knows the mantras must always maintain the three states regarding the mantras of the Supreme Self, such as *bala* and the rest.
O Lotus-born One, for those who perform actions with the Rig, Yajur, and Sāma Vedas as their guides, there is the attainment of the fruit of absolute liberation. Paus. 27.715.
For that which culminates in heaven is indeed superior, fruitful, and complete with its limbs and [auxiliaries];
likewise, for those who have mastered all-knowing mantras, there is the power of atomization (aṇimā).
For it is indeed always unasked for and conjoined with liberation;
for this very reason, it belongs to one who has propitiated [the deity] entirely.

O Pauṣkara, that fruit for the attainment of which [the yogi] exerts himself— consisting of the powers such as *aṇimā* and so forth— is achieved through a portion, through greatness, and through the totality of conditions.
For the direct realization of that [mantra] yields the eternal fruit of absolute liberation, O Great-minded One, even from mantras that are rajasic or tamasic. (Pausa 27.719)
For it indeed bestows the fruit of mental excellence, consisting of self-refinement accompanied by a slight visible result and joined with excellence in one's birth.
Among these, that which is the primary fruit— considered in relation to what has been previously stated—
is that which pertains to the Sāttvika mantras and is based on a single portion.
For the sake of the conditions of liberation, it has been proclaimed for the sake of its accomplishment:
"The mantras are the makers of names; their success comes through the power of those rites. (Pauṣkara 27.722)
Action is understood from the scripture;
however, it is [perfected] through self-restraint preceded by complete purification, contentment, and devotion. (Pauṣkara 27.723)
That would come about through association with the virtuous—[is it not so?]—through the auspicious mantras of the best of the twice-born and through eternal ritual action. (Pauṣkara 27.724)
O twice-born one, in some cases the fruit arises from the conjunction of the triad; in other cases, the culmination of the rite is the great power of the mantras.
O twice-born one, [he saw] those who were present in their true forms, stationed there by the power of mantra to perform their respective offices in various places. (Pauṣkara 27.726)
The acts that enhance one's birth arise together with the causal conditions; indeed, for the sake of devotees, this application should always be performed in this manner. (Pauṣkara 27.727)
"O Brahmin, in this manifold array of mantras which bestows both worldly enjoyment and liberation.
Thus ends the twenty-seventh chapter, titled "The Exposition of Śrāddha," in the venerable Pauṣkara-saṃhitā of the venerable Pāñcarātra.
Now begins the twenty-eighth chapter— (here there is a break in the manuscript)—
The Blessed One said:

It is not for those intent on the recitation of the Vedas, nor for those who perform sacrifices for the sake of liberation, nor for those devoted to asceticism, nor for those who practice the duty of giving alone. (Pauṣa 28.1)
And for all those devoted to the *agnihotra*, O Pauṣkara, this [practice] has been declared by the Great One to be even more weighty than the *agnihotra* itself;
thus, how might there not be a pacification of the suffering of *saṃsāra* for human beings? (Pauṣkara 28.3)
— (here there is a significant omission of text)—
The Blessed Lord said: "It bestows the path to heaven and likewise grants the most excellent fruit."
And the Agnihotra alone belongs to the Brahmins who are exponents of the Vedas.

Furthermore, O Brahmin, those who remain therein, abiding in that which possesses the nature of that Dharma, [should be engaged] in the worship of that [deity], in meditative concentration, and indeed in the practice of recitation. // Pausa 28.5 //
Of those whose minds were uplifted, who understood the deeds of the Blessed One,
who were destined for existence, and who purified themselves through the true scriptures.
When performed with secret mantras along with complete oblations of substances such as guggulu and others, it shall become a deliverer from worldly existence.
With sacrificial implements made of *vaikaṅkata* wood, with wealth acquired through righteous means, and with both devotion and faith— Pausa 28.8.
Just as previously instructed, having properly established the sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa) according to the ritual rules, [one should act] when the fire produced from various wombs has been duly invoked.
And having brought it down into the midst of that [ocean], which had arisen from various wombs—
[here there is a break in the manuscript]— Pauṣkara said:
O Blessed One, I now wish to know the origins of fire,
exactly as they are, through your grace and with the desire for spiritual attainment. (Pausa 28.10)
The Blessed One said:
"O Lotus-born one, the source of fire is twofold: that which originates from the sun and is characterized by jewels, and the second, which arises from the contact of its rays with a mirror."
Arising from various wombs, it possesses manifold characteristics. (Paus 28.12)
That which is established in this world through the very process of churning,
indeed by means of various methods of friction and mutual rubbing.
Sometimes there may be the manifestation of that [state], which is devoid of any movement whatsoever.
O Lotus-born One, there are three kinds of stone; among them, this one alone is [auspicious] when, upon being rubbed against another on a completely auspicious rock, [it produces a sound].
It sets ablaze mountains with blazing fires; and with the iron-striking *lohaghātakī* [mudrā], characterized by the threatening forefinger, it causes them to fall. (Paus 28.16)
In the case of the third pair of folds,
there should likewise be a perfect joining of the edges with one another for those [vessels] originating from iron and stone.
Even in the eighth [chapter], the single characteristic of the churning-stick is described in brief.
And even a severe beating is not truly [greater] than that,
O Lotus-born One, for there is no [suffering] greater than that which arises from the loss of jewels;
this should be understood as the most excellent [consequence], occurring at the [proper] time.
From the tip of the flame and from the flickering hair, that manifestation [arose] at the summit...
/ O Great-Minded One, the fivefold station of these [goddesses], which ends with the Brāhmaṇī, exists together with various deities and is endowed with individual manifestations.
May Śakti, filled with hosts of attendants, become the pervader of the universal.
Therefore, fire should indeed be taken up in the form of its latent power (*śakti*);
for it is not possible for it to exist in contradiction with both [the householder and the ascetic], just as it is for a householder.
Therefore, O Lotus-born One, the power of all things arises from their essential nature;
however, fire indeed serves as the specific determinant when its own effect is present.
O Lotus-born One, this very narrative, which is proclaimed as being of four kinds, is now further described by you as being of seven types. (Pausa 28.27)
O Lotus-born One, there are the yakṣī, the pārthivī, the saurī, the śaikhī, and likewise the bhrāṣṭrī; there is the kāpālī, and the independent fire (agni) without that [other]. Paus 28.28.

O Brahmin, their stability is further said to be of two kinds: that called seedless and that with seed. First, the seedless is described: Pauṣkara 28.29: "O Brahmin, their stability is further said to be of two kinds: that called seedless and that with seed. First, the seedless is described:"
The vessel is of two kinds: that which is called "located therein" (*tatsthāna*) and the *kaicakī*; likewise, there is the *saloha* and the one made entirely of stone. Pausha 28.30.
This is declared to be seedless (*nirbījā*), and it is also described as having seeds (*sabījā*);
it is characterized by the fire of independence, [appearing] as a conch-shell, a frying pan, and a skull. (Pauṣkara 28.31)
O Lotus-born One, as for what was said by me to you—that the *hotrā* is indeed a bond—it is always without distinction and common to all alike. (Pausa 28.32)
Even though it has been understood that he was born from a lotus, listen nonetheless to the established order of the stages of life (*āśrama*) according to their specific origins. *Pauṣkara* 28.33.
For those practicing celibacy, the fire is prescribed as being characterized by iron and stone;
for householders, it is called *ādhāna*; and for forest-dwellers, it is made of wood.

And for the ascetics who are devoted to her worship, whose souls are intent on it, and who are engaged in the six duties, Sāvitrī indeed possesses the characteristic of a fire that consumes all other speech. (Pausa 28.35)
The two eyes of the supreme Fire were ordained as the two fire-drills (araṇīs);
by his permission, the celestial eye was likewise divided into two, becoming common to both.
These two, along with that authorization—this triad [constitutes] the boundary for the Vaiśya caste; and this triad is likewise for the Kṣatriya. (Pauṣa 28.37)
For the sake of accomplishing the sequence for a Śūdra, specifically with his permission,
[the rite] of the best of the twice-born among the twice-born [is performed].
O Pauṣkara, the first [daśā] belongs to the Brāhmaṇa, the second indeed to the Śūdra, and the others belong to the other [castes]. Paus_28.39.
In times of distress, however, one should not give [the sacred thread] to anyone else, nor to a Śūdra, nor to any other...
(in all four manuscripts, there is a gap in the text)... ...which causes contradiction.
Thus, this is the primary [teaching]; beyond this there is nothing further.
A transposition of the primary [deities] grants only minor success; all the various origins (yoni) have been prescribed according to the distinction of their respective fruits. (Pauṣa 28.42)
O you who arose from the eleven lotuses, listen to how it was:
for those desiring the earth, [the vessel] is made of jewels; for those seeking radiance, it is indeed made of bronze. (Pauṣa 28.43)
The *gopā* [lineage], characterized by the absence of passion (*araṇi*), is to be known as the *kaicakī* womb;
it bestows happiness, good fortune, and nourishment. (Paus 28.44)
O Lotus-born One, this ground bestows intelligence and vigor; it is renowned as the destroyer of enemies, adorned with iron and stones, and is celebrated as the source of all.
Dharma is the female disciple (śaikhī), while Bhrāṣṭrī is indeed the giver of land;
Saṃvedayoni is Kāpālī, and O Lotus-born One, she increases one's station.
In the codes of Manu, she is proclaimed as the auspicious source that brings about the pacification of diseases for those in all four stages of life.
There is no contradiction regarding the state of being an egg-born for all [beings] when there is mutual taking [of one another]; for at the time of their desire, all wombs indeed present themselves.
"For those devoted to the propitiation of mantras, these are indeed always non-contradictory;
as long as [the time] is not excessive, O twice-born one, let that which occurred previously not come to pass. (Pausa 28.49)
If, due to negligence, he is not pacified, another womb may take him away again;
this does not happen through force or confinement, nor by the mere honoring of one who remains in the state of worldly attachment.
One who has been formally accepted [as a disciple] should perform an expiation even more extensively;
indeed, it must be especially distinguished when done publicly, whereas it is otherwise when done privately.
Thus ends the twenty-eighth chapter, titled "The Classification of the Fire-Source," in the *Pauṣkarasaṃhitā* of the *Śrīpañcarātra*.
Then the twenty-ninth chapter.
The Blessed One said:
"In the *prājāpatya* [posture], in the *daiśikīya* [posture], and in that which is measured by the hands raised from the *śaiṣa* [posture]..."
One should gradually increase the field by one finger-breadth at a time until it reaches its full extent.

As far as a field measuring eight *karas* arises for the purpose of a sacrificial altar (*dhiṣṇya*), so too, by way of measurement, would there be one hundred and eighty-one [such fields]. (Pausa 29.2)
For all the sacrificial pits (kuṇḍas), the auspicious number located in the eight directions arises as eightfold. 29.3.
O twice-born one, the various types of rites for the fulfillment of desires arise from distinctions such as the square shape,
provided that there is equality of the sacred field according to this method.
They possess the characteristics of a garland of the seven precious gems, the Śrīvatsa mark, and a crown;
they resemble a conch, a discus, a mace, a lotus, a bow, and various arrows.
All [the seats] together with their pedestals are prescribed with four, three, two, or one rim;
they are marked with the discus, lotus, mace, and conch, either individually or collectively.
Likewise, they arise beautifully from their own limbs, which flow forth from the eight sources,
each according to its own specific extent, numbering two, two, and twelve respectively.
Know that one part to be a finger-breadth for the sake of establishing all the limbs; indeed, this is again for all [limbs] according to their various inherent proportions.
The division known as the "non-illumination of illumination" is remembered as being manifold;
it is the bondage characterized by worldly enjoyment, which yields infinite fruit for those who seek it. (Pauṣkara 29.9)
O Supreme Lord, she who is equal to Vyāsa and Svāhā bestows the perfection of all desires. (Pausa 29.10)
O Mahāmati, according to the principle of the characteristic of illumination, their [own] destruction occurs by itself.
The twelve sacrificial pits (kuṇḍas) up to the end of the hand are thirteen finger-breadths in height;
they possess all possible shapes, are mobile, and are devoid of girdles.
In the case of a substitute, however, mobile [images] are prescribed for the satiation with mantras;
likewise, those up to two cubits in length should be characterized by the great marks.
Having drawn lines upon the ground and filled them with grains, seeds, or even soil,
one should do so for the perpetual completion of the ritual, even in the absence of all other materials.
But in the case of a secondary or tertiary substitute, one should always act without contradiction,
using [wood] that is endowed with bark, symmetrical, full, succulent, straight, and firm.
But with wood split by fire, this city indeed should be constructed here. (Pauṣa 29.16)
O twice-born one, even for those made of metal that are twelve finger-breadths long and are mobile,
the same rule applies when they are to be filled with oblations.
Since there is no sacrificial oblation without a fire-pit that brings success to practitioners of mantra,
therefore a fire-pit must always be prepared— whether according to the sūtras, mobile, or fixed.
And specifically for the sacrificial ground (havyabhūmi), when it is yellow and twice as high [as the standard], it may be two-sided, four-sided, eight-sided, or circular. (Pauṣkara 29.19)
Having made it elevated by one-sixth or one-twelfth [of its height],
and having attained its own proper measure, it should be raised to the desired height as previously intended.
With bricks, either unburnt or burnt, according to one's preference;
otherwise, it is beneficial at another time.

Or one may make them equal, so that their share is the same; otherwise, from the ground being excavated, it should be made two finger-breadths larger than the previous dwelling, so that there may be a separate residence for each. (Pauṣa 29.22)
From the region as far as the Mekhalā mountain range, each respective [king] fell into a state of terror before the forest-fire of his own affection for the Lord.

O Mahāmati, the positioning of the twelve sacrificial pits (kuṇḍas) according to their actual measurements is as follows: one part is reduced by three-eighths, and another half is reduced by one-sixteenth, which constitutes the measurement of the rim (nemi).
O one with beautiful eyes, at some point, having divided those twelve [fingers]—each measuring twelve *aṅgulas*—into four parts or three here, [one should proceed]. (Pauṣa 29.25)
The measurement of the rims is equal to their height and breadth; they are always equal to the womb because they are fashioned from behind by its function.
But it should be raised by a measure of four finger-breadths from the rear boundary;
you, however, should increase it gradually according to the proportion up to the rim.
O Lotus-born One, the girdle should always be wider than its measurement by one-third of one's own finger-breadths, less by a quarter.
Then, having extended its tip by one-third of that [measurement],
the first girdle (mekhalā) should be made.
Like the reflection and the channel for the vital breath, that womb is the source of growth and sustenance; it is the method for the finality within the internal cavities, proceeding in due order.
Having attained a state that is even and smooth like the trunk of an elephant,
he rests upon his own manifold form, which is characterized by the qualities (guṇas).
They flow through the night by means of a stream of awakening that resounds without end,
into the fathomless ocean of the Self, which is the locus for the washing away of all impurities.
Having perceived the source [of the world] in the sky, with passion [prevailing], he was freed from the two wheels of rebirth by means of the two qualities of darkness. (Pauṣa 29.33)
"Know that which is formless, the Supreme Brahman, which, due to the very suppression of its qualities, possesses a waistband of calf-hair; it has entered into the sky. (Pauṣa 29.34)
In the sacrificial fire-pan (dhiṣṇya) which has four girdles,
he himself first placed the unmanifest fourfold Self there, within the four girdles, before the enclosing sticks (paridhi).
Equal to those of perfectly complete form, [I offer] to me— [the one born of liberation]—
that which consists of pairs of qualities, beginning with Acyuta, as the triad in sequence.
That is the source of all actions:
that action which, depending upon its continuous flow, attains identity with Brahman. (Pauṣa 29.37)
Of those whose origins are vast and infinite, who have long since assumed the form of forests, [the purification] of the sacrificial pits is as before— [free from the Māris]. Pausa 29.38.
With her limbs extended and made compliant, and with a steady wick [of breath], might she cause him to fall for a moment by means of the interior of her swelling breasts? // Paus 29.39 //
Moving steadily from its base, it should be raised for others;
it must be extended, well-positioned, and as smooth as the surface of a mirror. (Pauṣa 29.40)
Manuscript *ka* reads after 38ab: — *kuṇḍalānām ami* — — — — — — — *pūrvavat* / *vidheyā vitatāṅgī susthiravarti* — — — — — /
With darbha grass—
[the practitioner] should fashion [it] with a steady mind, intent upon the womb (yoni) for others who are striving;
it should be spread out, well-established, and like the surface of a mirror.
Now hear from me regarding the contraction of the *kuṇḍanemīs* at the appropriate time:
O Brahmin, the husks (*tuṣa*) consist of four parts, depending on whether they are classified as superior (*uttama*) or otherwise.
[The measurement] of the hands is [calculated] by five fingers less [the previous amount];
for those who are constantly heated and equal in measure, possessing various forms as their own nature,
and equal in width and length...
One should bind each finger-face individually; thus, the witnesses [should be] deficient...
but the two heights...
For others, it should be two cubits from the top, and likewise one hundred [of such units] should be equal to that.
Having first considered the place, time, and other factors,
as well as his own capability, he then performs the layout of the maṇḍala lines.
And in the presence [of the deity], with bricks and so forth,
O Lotus-born One, one should fashion the pits for the pedestals;
and above the pedestals, O Pauṣkara, there should be a pit for the eight-edged pedestal.
Now hear from me regarding the contraction of the *kuṇḍalas* at the improper time;
for that [contraction], O Brahmin, consists of four parts, depending on whether it is the best or other types. (Pauṣa 29.41)
One should increase the measurement of two cubits by one finger-breadth at a time for each [additional] cubit, until it reaches the witness-mark. Paus 29.42.
Even for those whose constant extent measures five finger-breadths, and who possess various forms throughout all directions, [the same applies]. (Pausa 29.43)
In the girdles of the celestial abodes of incomparable breadth and length,
[there is] a height of nine units above the entire summit, rising two units higher.
For others, it should be two cubits from the top of the head, and there should be a hundred [such measures] equal to that;
having thus previously considered the influence of place, time, and so forth.
Then, according to his own capacity, he should construct the arrangement there, including the fall [of the structure],
and have it built with bricks and other materials in the presence of artisans. (Pauṣa 29.46)
O Lotus-born One, above the pedestals— which are well-proportioned, octagonal, and possess four corners—
there is a cavity for the eight girdles; such is the emergence of the pedestal, O Pauṣkara.
Having realized through his own mind that [the world] is subject to decay and growth, he dissolved it with an intellect purified by wisdom. (Pauṣa 29.48)
For the sake of his own satisfaction, he should now lead [the offering] with a nature of twofold splendor;
for the power of the Lord’s fire, the supreme primordial nature consists of the flames and so forth. (Pauṣkara-saṃhitā 29.49)
Another [aspect] is that the various forms of the natural hearths arise from fire;
indeed, this very form of fire exists because of its presence within the sacrificial pit.
In the object of action. // Paus 29.50 //
What was ordained for the mouth of the Lord and for the Brahmins—that oblation which is indeed offered by the preceptor when the sacrificial vessel has fallen—[is here described]. Pausa 29.51.
Everything offered into the fire indeed bestows success, for it consumes everything;
previously, [the practitioner] himself duly obtained power through the sequence. (Pauṣa 29.52)
Whatever substance is prescribed as an oblation, when offered into a smokeless, leaping fire that rests upon its own bed, it yields a merit of ten million times ten thousand crores.
One should perform oblations numbering one hundred thousand, gathering the necessary materials;
this provides a staff for two fortnights and ensures inexhaustible sustenance.
Then, for others, it flows in a continuous stream...
O son, [place him] situated in the sky of logic upon the lotus of the Brahman-mantra. (Pausa 29.55)
