"But when the primary rite is lost, O Lotus-born One, what is appropriate? [Tell me] regarding the sacrificial pits, their dimensions, and the lineage, potency, and so forth. (Pauṣa 29.56)
Then follows the raising [of the vessel]: it should be made of copper or even of iron, with its interior like the womb of the abode of Kamalā. (Pauṣa 29.57)
By means of which the carriage of phenomena does not go to its own ground of being.
One should perform the consecration of the ritual preparations and subsequently install the sacrificial pit.
There, having generated the fire and brought it down, he should satisfy it with many *ājyadoha* mantras for the purpose of satiation. (Pauṣa 29.59)

O twice-born one, by the force of the syllable *oṃ* within the fire, one should quickly cause the essence of the *ājyadoha* to fall above, in the center of the pervasive Lord who is the self of the mantra. (Pauṣkara 29.60)
And likewise, for the attainment of liberation and enjoyment, [the breath] proceeds in sequence through the opening of the *brahmarandhra*,
becoming endowed with fragrance like a forest grove, completely full, and of equal radiance.
O Brahmin, having performed the worship of the Lord of Mantras together with the retinue, the limbs, and the secondary limbs, as well as the insignia and the enclosure; Pausa 29.62.

Then, having obtained the authorization, one who is free from sloth should perform ten thousand recitations or more of the mantra that has been commenced, preceded by the *brahmā-mantra*, for the sake of service.
For it is certain that, according to their capacity, [this occurs] at dawn when the sun has set,
or during the night.
But in the middle portion, it should be according to the injunctions of the scriptures.
After the rite of preliminary service (*pūrvasevā*) and for the sake of generating devotion toward the one who has been worshipped,
once the recitation of a hundred thousand (*lakṣajāpa*) and so forth has been accomplished on a day of Brahmā (*brahmadina*), [one should proceed].

When that equal oblation is completed—or, O Lotus-born One, when it is prescribed otherwise—with grains, seeds, sesame, or fruits, equal in measure to the [principal] limb or even equal to a fraction of a limb; Pauṣa 29.66.
Immediately after that, one should perform the oblation with the arrow-seal of the lion-faced [deity] known as the "lotus-born," due to its equality [with the previous]. Pausa 29.67.
O Pauṣkara, for a period equal to six months, or double that,
or even fourfold according to one's capacity, through the practice of yoga at intervals.
When [the time] is capable— [and] at the end of a hundred [years], when two and four are completed,
[it occurs] for those who have one, three, or four nights, with clarified butter in the vessel.
One should bring the abundant self into harmony; [one should bring it] into harmony... // Paus_29.70 //

In all the mantras, the practitioner of mantra (mantrī), reciting the Saṃhitā together with them, should do so correctly with his intellect, either collectively or individually according to his own capacity. (Pauṣa 29.71)

One should bring joy to the entire assembly of those whose mantras have been broken by means of oblations of clarified butter; and indeed, from the *dhruva* vessel, one should offer with the consecrated [oblation].
Now I shall describe the characteristics of the *tāla* tree, together with its measurements,
which originates from a well-known sacrificial tree, is firm, free from blemishes, and without wounds.
Having taken a very well-prepared piece of wood that is free from the fear of forest fires,
devoid of sap, and auspicious, [one should use it] which has not been kept overnight. (Pauṣa 29.74)
From the wrist to the middle finger of the arms, one should again multiply that [measurement] by the breadth of the thumbs. // Pausa 29.75 //
One should proceed by discarding eight [units] at each [stage], while the remaining [units] increase by one; indeed,
those eight [types of] conduct beginning with the Banner (dhvaja) are to be thoroughly understood in their proper order.
In that regard, whatever remains is considered auspicious from the auspicious;
and from the pair of you two, and from the third, the Lord of Beasts (the Moon) is the remainder.
The fourfold is the increase of the dog; the fivefold is known as the bull; [the sixfold is] the female elephant.
And indeed, from the remainder of the seven elephants. (Pauṣa 29.78)
In that regard, those known as the "single" and the "groups of seven" are considered pure and bestowers of auspiciousness;
likewise, those whose banners bear the elephant, the lord of elephants, the lion, the bull, and so forth, are granters of prosperity.
For the sake of destroying the unwholesome, and for the sake of increasing one's own wholesome [qualities].
One should insert a length of one finger-breadth or joined with two finger-breadths according to the proper method.

One should divide that length into five parts; for the sake of accomplishment, one should place the lotus (pauṣkara) there, where the center of the region is located, with its petals extending to the edge.
The first *kauśa* and the others, excluding the *ago*, should be applied in sequence according to their designation;
one should effect the reduction of the petals, filaments, wheels, and limbs of the grounds.
One should again project the elevated points up to the limit of the vani;
the ear-marks are to be turned out with a space between them from the two wheels and lotuses.
The length should be one-fifth [of the total], equal to its width;
and it should be joined at two parts, extending from the region of the branches to the tip.
The earth should be fashioned as one that perceives other forms,
situated between the tip of the plow and the irrigation channel, and adorned with various activities.
One should perform one's own respective perception, and by that, the auspicious non-perception;
then, indeed, by means of the first portion situated in the center of the circle of the earth.
Having fashioned a lotus endowed with its characteristic marks— consisting solely of sixteen petals, together with its stalk, filaments, and pericarp— Paus_29.87.
The seedless [mandala] consists of the pericarp and the calyx, slightly adorned,
and surrounded by Hetīśa, who is endowed with the characteristics as previously described.
One should fashion the ground as the rim of a wheel, marked on both sides at the corners;
the mandala should be adorned with *kaustubha* gems, swastikas, or conch shells and other such symbols. (Pauṣa 29.89)
Or [one should recite] "tārāttā egaṇāḍhyaṃ vā" and so forth; one should perform the rite with the weapon-mantra until the fierce goddess has appeared.

Therefore, for the purpose of reaching the end, one should again discard an eighth part belonging to the fortnight and perform a reduction so that it becomes like the trunk of an elephant. (Pauṣa 29.91)
The space between the two [outer] walls should be measured at one-eighth [of the total width], or it may be made equal to one-sixth; it should be auspiciously characterized by its breadth.
Having divided that width into two or five equal parts, [one should mark] the middle section... // Paus 29.93 //
One should divide [the remainder] into two parts for each of the two sides— one part and one non-part—
or according to one's desire, dividing them in front for the purpose of proportional distribution.
And another set of aggregates—like a fish, a mark, and so forth—in due order. // Pausa 29.95 //
From the sides, one should lead the space from the exterior toward the interior by means of the throat;
so that there may be the radiance in the cow’s-mouth [mudrā], the throat bestows great supernatural power.
But for conch shells and the like that are devoid of a pedestal,
[the measurement] from the end of one to the other should be joined with a cloth-band or by means of two lotuses.
One should remove [the measurement] from the two parts of the ground of the pedestal by proportional reduction;
starting from the shoulder and the neck, there are three [parts for] the neck as desired. (Pauṣkara 29.98)
Having first assigned the portion as previously described—indeed, there is the statement of Śaṅkha regarding one who has omitted the ritual procedure for the altar (vedikā). // Pauṣa 29.99 //
One should construct it measuring five parts along with an additional quarter-part;
or it may shine even if it is slightly greater or slightly less than its width.
One should gradually reduce three parts of the pitcher and two parts of the dwelling;
for the conch with a broad belly, one should reduce it by a fifth part.
Then one should worship the region of the belly in two parts with garlands and other offerings;
for that which extends from the base, occupying three portions in length, indeed proceeds [therefrom].
From among those, having first drawn the limb toward the region of the throat as previously described,
one should then divide the remainder into ten parts and measure it by seven limbs.
One should fashion a staff in the shape of a mace, its width at the neck being as specified;
it may be of two types, according to the prescribed method, and should be infused with salt.
In that case, the construction is said to be by means of exactly three parts;
one should make it approach the altar, resting upon a single part.

One should then fashion a svastika endowed with the proper characteristics, marked by a lotus in the center, and a collection of pericarp petals at the end, with each part being one-sixteenth [of the whole].
In the courtyard, with well-proportioned and well-placed *peta* [architectural elements] forming the interior,
and thus established by the arrangement of the *dhārācana* [flowing ornament], perfected by the twelvefold [set].
Circular or square, situated in the middle of the heap of [materials].

One should likewise fill the outer portion with a fist that holds the hand (karagrahavatī) and is characterized by the upward movement of the fingers, while the staff (daṇḍa) is slightly more than the measure. Paus 29.109.
One should fashion a hundred-petaled lotus with its face turned downward, broad, with an upward-pointing pericarp,
many leaves, and filaments, using the fists as the weapons for striking. (Pauṣa 29.110)
Or should one cast it upon the altar? Listen now to another characteristic of the pedestal (pīṭha), which has been prescribed in the Ardhakalpa.
Auspicious, like the throne of a god.
Having divided [the area] up to the edge of the *uṣṇīṣa* into nine parts by the preceptor,
twelve [parts] are said to be prescribed here as previously [stated]. // PauṣS 29.112 //
The lotus, the wheel, or the aravinda is marked with the [proper] characteristics; however, listen further to the measurement and the divisions according to the specific site. Pausa 29.113.
Having established the field with Brahmasthāna as its limit and divided it into six parts,
one should adorn two parts in the center for the purpose of establishing the position of the pericarp (karṇikā).
The perimeter should be made with one-eighth part, the row of filaments with half of that,
the mass of petals with one and a half parts, and the space outside that with half a part.
O Pauṣkara, having reached these inner fields, one attains a terrestrial city endowed with various wonderful arrangements. Paus_29.116.

O Brahmin, having taken up small portions from each of the elevated parts, and having surrounded the [central] syllable with the verbal suffixes, one should arrange the petals and the base in due order.
And one should slightly lower the ground from one field to another as prescribed;
otherwise, having traversed and leveled the remainder, one should proceed differently.
The measurement of the field for the filaments within the pit is as previously stated;
having fashioned the network of petals together with the sky [the central circle], it is done by means of a fractional part.
Outside of that, one should construct a field with a circumference equal to the wheel and its rim plus half a part,
according to the characteristics previously described.
Behind [the deity], one should fashion either a lotus with its stalk or a solitary lotus;
and at the mouth, a cluster of lotus petals.

This is the [section on] the construction of the measures; at that time, the object of knowledge (prameya) within this [system] must indeed be understood for the sake of accomplishing the ritual action. Pauṣkarasaṃhitā 29.122.
Ananta, having become the nature of the hundred-petaled lotus, holds the fist here;
remaining within as the nature of the seed-syllable, he then rises with his face upward.

That great vital wind, which has the noble self as its essence and moves within the body, being impelled through the aperture of Brahmā (brahmarandhra), returns again by the power of one's will. (Pauṣkara 29.124)
The seven netherworlds are its stalk, and the skin is its lotus-petal;
resting upon which, the nectar remains like water within its own flow.
Abiding within the lattice of the arrangement of the wheel, you assume the form of a sacrificial session;
then you take on the body of a conch, and from that, the wind, the royal treasury, and space.
Seedless, unborn, unshakeable, and primordial, it is the supreme deity of the garland-deity;
it is the true reality, immeasurable, the object of knowledge, and this infallible one. (Pauṣa 29.127)
However, at the time of consecration, having placed [the image] there and constantly recited the mantra during the libation,
one should discard its height as well as the width of the altar.
Having fashioned the mace-staff according to the specified proportions, it should be well-knit, very firm, and indeed very solid.
Neither too thick nor too thin, it should be joined with a straight line;
thus one should fashion it out of material substances or else from auspicious wood.
Now, the characteristics of the sacrificial ladles (sruva) and the large offering-spoons (sruc) for the purpose of oblation are described.
Having taken pure iron that possesses the previously mentioned numerical characteristics, [one should fashion them]. Paus 29.131.
One should divide the length of the *sruc* into eight parts, excluding three;
by that measure of a part, its width is prescribed.
Having divided that [area] into equal parts with clear lines in due order,
one should fashion the pitcher (kalaśa) from the base as an eight-part square.
Then, having avoided excessive bulk, one should indeed fashion it with half the width;
one should create a lotus resting upon its base, complete with its stalk.

That conch, with its mouth expanded, possessing the *nandyāvarta* mark and auspicious characteristics, is known as the "Four-Part" (*caturaṃśa*) when both side portions have been omitted. (Pauṣa 29.135)
Bound in the middle like a noose, well-proportioned and circular,
the staff has four parts and extends from the mouth of the pitcher.
From the conch-mouth, one should fashion the canopy joined with the three [elements],
and create two stalks for the stream, measuring eight parts.
Having completed the square neck-base like the pedestal,
one should carve a lotus upon it, enclosed within a circular rim.
The thread [of the neck] is like a net of pearls at the four corners of the conch-shell [shape];
the neck is elevated by one part and its width is measured by two parts.
The face should be slightly turned; it should not be raised more than one-eighth part [of its height], leaving a space of one part [between the chin and the neck].
The head should be like a lotus, with the neck as its stalk and the ears as its pericarp.
The circle of the pericarp is surrounded by the edges of infinite filaments;
outside of that is the network of petals, which is equal in height to the protrusion of the filaments.
Without division—behind, across, and facing forward—one should form [the seal] in the center of the pericarp, sealed by means of a sphere alone. (Pauṣkara 29.142)

It should be marked with the Kaustubha gem or with the mark of Saurabheyī, and it must be capable of holding an oblation of clarified butter and other substances equal to one and a half *homapramāṇas*. (Pauṣa 29.143)

The definition of the characteristics of the valid means of knowledge has been fully proclaimed; it is remembered as being for the purpose of the oblation of clarified butter. Now, understand the remainder concerning the carrying away [of the remnants]. Paus 29.144.
Varuṇa himself, indeed the very embodiment of nectar, exists in the form of the lotus;
and that weapon, existing in the form of its stalk, creates fear for the obstructors.
The moon, which causes the nourishment of the world, is at the tip of the lotus;
for that capacity known as bliss should be understood as the Supreme Lord. (Pauṣkara 29.146)
But the preceptor, being self-restrained and seeking to accomplish that installation,
should proceed by relying upon this divine conceit.
In the arcane fire-ritual, however, all the implements and the noble ones remain together within a single locus of their own respective instruments.
With this entire body as the vessel for the offering, they are endowed with the conch, the discus, and other [emblems]. (Pauṣkara-saṃhitā 29.149)
[This] must be performed for the sake of attaining one's desired goal;
therefore, one who is not qualified [for other rites], as well as one devoted to the deities of food, [should perform it]. Pausa 29.150.
One should resort to the Damaha [practice];
the removal of the body, though forbidden, is auspicious. (Paus 29.151)
Having attained that state, he who stands in a position of authority bestows, in return, the permissions favored by you upon those devoted to you. (Pauṣa 29.152)
In the description of the great Brahman [altar], one should fashion the *ājyasthālī* (ghee-pot) with the interior of a lotus; these are auspicious for the southern journey from the self. Paus 29.153.
Having properly grasped the self as immortal and having offered praise, one obtains [the fruit] through the fire.
It is certainly the stalk of the means of valid cognition (pramāṇa), possessing auspicious characteristics at its base.
One should fashion [the image] from pure essence, born from the seed-syllable;
it should be capable of that [function], designated as its stalk, and attended by Śrī. Paus 29.155.
Having prepared a divine lotus pond filled with fully blossomed, half-blossomed, and budding lotuses,
as well as with lotus plants interspersed among them.
And likewise, the guardians of the directions [should be placed] in the south and north;
[the ground] should have four faces of equal extent and be made to contain blossoming lotuses in its interior.
By means of a third part of the wheel-space, [the tongue] is depressed by the wind-leaf; it should root itself in the region of the throat, having indeed reached one after another. (Pauṣa 29.158)
The crown, adorned with a blue lotus, is perfected by fragrant sounds;
the lotus with its stalk belongs to them—that is the supreme vessel of the Lord.
And it is always known as the bed and seat, and the ocean of immortality;
[it is] the support of heaven and earth... // Paus 29.160 //
A fragrant garland, three [offerings], and two stones with flowers; also whatever vessels are suitable, such as the *praṇītā* and others. (Pausa 29.161)
All those [images], joined with the conch, lotus, trident, and lord [Śiva],
may be fashioned in various designs from metal or wood.
O Lotus-born One, one should fashion those lotuses according to one's desired measurements, preceded by the propitiation of the mantra for all rites. (Pauṣa 29.163)
One should mark everything with the sectarian sign (lāñchana), including the pedestal, the water-pot (kalaśa), and so forth, as well as the seat and other personal requisites. Paus. 29.164.
One should likewise remove the pearl rings, ornaments such as bracelets and so forth,
and everything worn on the upper body, including the turban and other headgear. (Pausa 29.165)
Thus ends the twenty-ninth chapter, titled "The Characteristics of the Kuṇḍa," in the Pauṣkara-saṃhitā, a Great Upaniṣad within the Śrī Pāñcarātra.
Now begins the thirtieth chapter.
Pauṣkara said:
"O Blessed One, when the loss of [knowledge] has occurred for the devotees who practice mantras,"
O Acyuta, for one who is established in the yoga of knowledge and the like, and whose conduct is ever-virtuous, [there is no falling away].
I now wish to hear the means of protection by which, through its performance, devotees attain the fulfillment of their purpose. (Pauṣa 30.2)
The Blessed One said: "O Brahmin, how may one who is devoted to ritual action obtain the desired fruit within a year through his deeds, even without the performance of the *pavitrārohaṇa*?"
Just as the Aśvamedha sacrifice fulfills all desires for Brahmins and the Rājasūya for kings, so too is this the ornament of my devotees. (Pauṣa 30.4)
Just as the Kaustubha gem is known to be the most excellent ornament among all ornaments, so too should the Pavitraka be understood as the preeminent among the entire web of enjoyments.
Since it eternally fulfills for devotees their supreme divine activity for the attainment of both enjoyment and liberation, what enjoyment could possibly be superior to that? (Pausa 30.6)

Indeed, through constant devotion, she grants the state of being in the same world (sālokya) to her devotees, and to practitioners (sādhakas), she grants proximity (sāmīpya) endowed with various supernatural powers (siddhis). (Pauṣa 30.7)
It bestows union with its own mantra-self upon the foremost of practitioners once the summer solstice has passed and during the middle of the four-month period.
O Lotus-born One, one should perform [this rite] at the beginning or at the end, on all the twelfth lunar days, on all the solar transits (saṃkrānti), and on all the full moon days.
On all new moon days, as well as on the third lunar days,
under the asterisms sacred to Viṣṇu, and at all such auspicious moments.
On the twelfth day of the Cāturmāsya period, which is the divine Ṣaḍaśītimukha, whoever should perform the ritual installation on that day— ||| Paus_30.11 |||
The sacred thread of the Source of the World purifies his own lineage—past, present, and future. (Pauṣa 30.12)
There, the Blessed Lord Hari, the Supreme Self and the Infallible One, is personally present in various manifested forms, pleased with his devotees. (Pauṣa 30.13)
O you who are born from the lotus, although Nārāyaṇa, whose essence is the mantra, is himself eternally present and situated within the hearts of his devotees.
Nevertheless, because of the power of that desire for that ritual action,
the Lord, the King of Mantras, attains presence there for the sake of the practitioners.
Just as the sun, having reached the summer season, attains its sharpness without abandoning its own nature, so too does it come into closer proximity to the All-pervading Lord.

Indeed, for the sake of the stability of the seven [categories]—place, time, and so forth—from the beginning of creation, therefore the *pavitraka* [is performed]; for that [stability] is impossible in a state of mental distress. (Pauṣa 30.17)
One who is devoted to action with devotion performs his duty such that it becomes unfragmented;
such a person, dedicated to both knowledge and action, is one who acts without fragmentation.
Endowed with devotion, faith, and likewise enthusiasm, and possessed of the powers of yoga, O Pauṣkara, one attains identity with the single Brahman in no time at all. Pauskara 30.19.
With his entire being, he always protects the devotees' every virtuous activity born of mind, speech, and heart. (Pauṣa 30.20)
Therefore, [I shall explain] its nature as it truly is, arising from thorough knowledge, and by what means the fruit is attained for devotees through the completion of that practice. (Pauṣa 30.21)
That which is the unbroken, white radiance of the source of the universe, spreading infinitely,
undergoes fragmentation through its own manifold nature for those who lack discernment.
Know that the "world-thread" (jagatsūtra) is indeed like a golden thread and so forth; it is the sixfold conceit (abhimāna) which one assumes in the form of the *pratisara* amulet.
And it is colored by the passion for knowledge, joined with activities born of vigor,
enveloped by the *taijasa* mantras, and further encircled by power.

When the occasion for ritual service has arrived, one should perform the imperishable rite of sovereignty according to one's capacity; thus, O Lord, the Pavitraka ceremony has been fully explained, yet it does not belong to the Prabhū. Paus 30.25.
When Viṣṇu, the lord who pierces through the Brahman, is established in that form,
what is given with devotion and according to the rules bestows the state of the Blessed One.
And just as the gross, distinct [self] is to be conceptualized by means of those categories of objects established in common usage, so too is that which is determined by them.
The thread should be fine, firm, white, and smooth, spun by a girl born of the Brahmin caste,
or by a disciplined woman who is not aged.
Whether it has been prepared by a pure widow or obtained however one may find it, one should take it and purify it with the weapon-mantra.

O twice-born one, having looked upon [the deity] and meditated on the root-mantra, one should perform it fourfold; or, when there is consideration for the fourfold nature [of the deities], one should perform it eightfold.
But in the case of the different forms of the Blessed One, he is characterized by distinctions divided according to difference;
in Keśava and the others, he exists as the presiding principle with three or four qualities.
One should avoid using uneven threads for Viṣṇu, who is himself even;
since the act of purification (*pavitrika*) is inherently uneven, it does not belong to anyone [else]. (Pauṣa 30.32)
Purifying threads (pavitrakas) should be made from those well-spun fibers for the mantra-vessel, the weapon-vessel, and previously for the abode of the various mantras. (Pauṣa 30.33)
Of the principal deity called Maṇḍala, of everything situated therein, of the pervasive Lord residing in the pericarp, and of those dwelling among the filaments and petals; Paus_30.34.
The marks of the one whose form is the array of emanations, and those of the two women,
[are placed] on the head, the throat, the two arms, above the flower-offering, and upon the ground.
By means of the measurement, there are four [parts] for the image of the Lord of the World;
two indeed for the sacrificial pit and the fire, and two for the seat of the scripture.
Of the Lord who is the essence of speech and the reality of sound, and of the great-souled ones who possess the ritual implements beginning with the bell and the rosary; (30.37)
While his wife was bowed with devotion and intent on the worship of Hari,
as were his kinsmen, friends, and those who follow the dharma of the Blessed One— Pausa 30.38.
And of his subsequent companions, those servants who desired the fourfold self-nature, who were well-disposed toward him, and who performed sacrifices to Puruṣottama.
For the increase [of merit], for women, and indeed for purification,
a beautiful means of purification should be prepared in due order.

For the worship of the four locations belonging to him who is established in the six paths and the seats, who is the locus of various tantras, and who possesses the distinctions of qualities such as knowledge; Pausa 30.41.
O Lotus-born One, one should fashion the ornament of the Lord Mukhyamantra with one hundred and eight threads, or with half, or even with a quarter [of that number].

For this very reason, the number of recitations, oblations, and so forth—whether complete or deficient—is indeed equalized for devotees by means of that very Self (ātman) of the mantras. (Pauṣa 30.43)
With gold, excellent jewels, camphor, sandalwood paste, and saffron,
combined with all medicinal herbs and mixed with cinnamon, cardamom, and other ingredients.
One should fashion its braid using various purifying substances along with pure *picu* cotton,
marked by the number of threads prescribed for it.
O lotus-eyed one, [the breath moves] like a citron, a fresh myrobalan fruit, or a conch shell;
furthermore, the spaces between them are connected by an uninterrupted thread.
For the purpose of clearly understanding the divisions, one should compile [the sections] from nearby;
then, having arranged others according to one's desire, [one should proceed] for those who are to be initiated.
The two ornaments for the worshiper and the preceptor are profound, endowed with a multitude of ornaments consisting of the rotation of the Sūtras, and filled with meaning.
O Blessed One, because it has been prescribed through the ritual placement of mantras (*mantranyāsa*) and the meditation on identity (*tādātmyabhāvanā*),
the *pavitraka* should be fashioned without a core for others.
One should place an embryo situated within, colored with bāhlīka;
and it should be adorned above with golden figures. (Pauṣa 30.50)
Or with [images] made of gold, capable of being fashioned from cut leaves,
[bearing the marks of] the conch, the discus, the mace, the lotus, the garland, the śrīvatsa, and the kaustubha gem.
With their forms resembling the lord of birds, the *tāla* palm, the club, the *nandaka* sword, the bow, and the plow, they were like the *mandāra* flowers and comparable to the *pārijāta* trees.
It was adorned with the auspicious śrīvṛkṣa, mountains, lordly serpents, svastikas, chowries, jars,
the flames of the fire of piercing, fans, and parasols.
Whether for one person alone or for many, [the offering should be made] with rivers, oceans, bulls, serpents, and flocks of cranes, according to their respective places.
Having placed it in a copper vessel made of metal and covered with cloth,
one should cover it from above with unbleached cloth that has been fumigated.

Having performed his daily rites on the tenth day, the practitioner, restrained and pure, accompanied by the lord of guides, should be intent upon offering the *arghya* and flowers for the purpose of the preliminary consecration (*adhivāsa*).
Accompanied by the resonant sound of the Veda and by those reciting hymns of praise and auspicious verses,
he entered after performing the worship of the door-keepers at the hour of the moon’s rising.
Having sat down according to the prescribed rule in a pavilion adorned with ornaments and shaped like the world of Vairāja, one should begin the internal sacrifices.
Having performed the ritual placement (*nyāsa*) in its entirety first, one should prepare the water for the guest-offering (*arghya*);
then, having worshipped Gaṇeśa, this is done for the sake of attaining the fruit of success free from obstacles. (Pauṣa 30.59)
One should perform the Brahmakūrca rite and then purify the ground;
next follows the installation of the arches and other structures, their worship, and the consecration of the sacrificial pit.
One should perform everything— the arrangement of the mantra-weapon and the water-pot, the descent of the mantra into those two,
and their worship and so forth— in the same manner as the ritual procedure for initiation.
One should perform the divine activity while recollecting the All-pervading Lord through *kumbhaka* [breath retention];
since one cannot remain engaged [in this] incessantly, this is the prescribed remedy. (Pauṣa 30.62)
The mantra-practitioner should indeed visualize the *kaṃbhī* weapon for the sake of protection;
then, having brought down the Blessed One onto the sacrificial ground and worshipped his seat, [he should proceed]. (Pauṣa 30.63)
Having completed the entire ritual up to the end of the recitation, one should proceed to the presence of the image;
having prostrated with the eight limbs, one should offer the *arghya* water upon the head.
Then, with devotion, one should worship Puruṣottama together with his limbs and retinue by offering auspicious handfuls of flowers accompanied by fragrant unguents. Pausa 30.65.
Having set aside all that was prepared at midday, such as the flower worship and other offerings,
one should take it up with the head, pay homage, and perform the full adoration.
Having purified the image of the Blessed One along with its pedestal by means of the weapon-mantra of Viṣvaksena and with water, one should then purify the temple.
One should bathe the Lord of the gods with rites prescribed by rule,
using baths such as the *brahmakūrca* and others, prepared according to the application of mantras.

Then, one should worship according to the prescribed rite with fruits that correspond to the ritual substances, empowered by one's capacity and duly consecrated, and accompanied by gems and other offerings.
Having performed everything ending with prostrations, one should go to the lower abode by means of all unartificial enjoyments offered in due order with devotion. (Pauṣa 30.70)
There, having consecrated the fire, one should indeed perform the libation with mantras,
using the fire consecrated by the water from the jar and the arghya vessel.
One should cook a *caru* on the hearth with milk, ghee, and rice while reciting the *hṛdaya-mantra*;
having lifted it out, purified with ghee, and offered it in due order— Paus 30.72.
Then, one should offer a single portion of the substances used for the vase and the base;
afterwards, one should offer the full oblation (pūrṇāhuti) and fill the entire interior with sacrificial offerings (bali).
Having satisfied [the deities] with water-sprinkled offerings, one should then perform the oblation in sequence;
likewise, having fully prepared the clarified butter (*ājya*),
one should indeed perform the binding of the mudrās and so forth.
Having performed prostrations and so forth, one should then sprinkle the entire collection of ritual materials in front of that Lord with the Astra-mantra.
Having established everything in the direction of the wind (the northwest), preceded by the ritual lines,
with one clad in white garments and wearing the armor of the bark-garment.
Having worshipped it with the weapon-mantra (astra-mantra), one should then shield it with the armor-mantra (kavaca);
thereafter, all eight types of arrows are provided with their respective feathers on the outside.
Having offered clarified butter into the fire-altar while reciting the weapon-mantra in all directions and intermediate points,
[one should encircle it] with a firm thread of five colors or one that is very white.
Recalling the fourfold circumambulation, one should complete the armor [mantra];
likewise, one should encircle it from the interior of the mouthful to its exterior.
Facing east and seated upon his seat, he should drink the Brahma-kūrca poured from the hand of the Guru, and afterwards, he should eat the remainder of the caru oblation.
One should drink water from kusa grass infused with gold and gems, over which the heart-mantra has been recited;
thereafter, one should consume betel leaf together with a tooth-stick.
Seated upon a woolen rug provided with a blanket and a layer of kuśa grass,
one should recite the supreme mantra along with its ancillaries, while chanting auspicious and excellent hymns of praise.
Having completed the mandala while reciting the meritorious narrative of the Sovereign of All,
one should then perform the remaining rites for the ornaments as prescribed.
On the morning of the eleventh day, having performed worship preceded by ritual bathing,
one should duly offer oblations according to the prescribed rite until the completion of the final full oblation.
Having approached the vicinity of the water-pot, one should perform the offering; then, for the sake of inviting the Lord to enjoy special offerings, [one should proceed]. (Pauṣa 30.85)
A tooth-stick, betel with its accompaniments, mouth-perfumes, mirrors, sandalwood and other fragrant substances, and nutmeg and areca nuts; Pausa 30.86.
Then, having placed before the Lord of the World on his right side guggulu resin and refined incense, along with a lamp set within a copper vessel; Paus_30.87.
A decorative eye-ornament, a golden thread with bracelets, and yellow pigment and collyrium in a metallic vessel filled with honey and clarified butter. (Pauṣa 30.88)
One should offer the six flavors to the Great Form; then, one should present white and red cloths for the eyes to the Lord in the west, as well as the water of a sacred river.

One should place in a copper vessel for a crow the clay from a mountain, wood-apple fruits and the like, grassy ground, and blue *darbha* grass, along with water from sacred bathing sites (*tīrtha*) and food, for the purpose of enjoyment. (Pauṣa 30.90)
Then, O Puṣkara, one should offer to the Lord of Gods, the All-pervading One, garlands, the seven medicinal herbs, seeds, and fruits in the north.
Bowls of sesame and rice, milk, the essence of curd, and clarified butter; collections of perfumes, cinnamon, cardamom, and so forth; and minerals such as red ochre and the like. // Paus 30.92 //
A coconut with its fruit intact, and all products derived from sugarcane, shine when placed in a bell-metal vessel, provided that a lotus is present. (Pauṣa 30.93)
In the absence of these, the offering may be placed in a vessel made of sacrificial leaves;
for others, one should provide water with kuśa grass, betel leaf, and a tooth-stick.
White garments with upper cloths and sacred threads, and sandalwood perfumed with saffron, agallochum, camphor, and white sandalwood. (Pauṣa 30.95)
One should offer the blind-folded purifier (*vandhapavitraka*) to one who has entered the four stations;
thereafter, one should present the water for honor (*arghya*), flowers, and incense, and perform the binding of the mudrās.

At the beginning, middle, and end, one should recite the supreme mantra together with its ancillaries for the sake of perfect, uninterrupted peace; thereafter, with palms joined in reverence, one should recite [the following].
One should offer the hymn-mantra beginning with the two [syllables] preceded by the *praṇava* (oṃ):
"O you who consist of all mantras, infinite, eternally present, and imperishable. (Pauṣa 30.98)
O Lord of yoga, whose form is the enjoyment of meditative realization, the supreme Brahman Nārāyaṇa, Lord of the vital breaths, you who possess four forms! Pausa 30.99.
O you who pervade all, O unfallen one, O embodiment of existence, O omniscient Supreme Person!
From this moment until the day of your departure— Pausa 30.100.
O Lord, endowed with various groups of mantras,
abide in my presence within the divine image, its form, the ritual flask, and the ground of the maṇḍala.
In the rosary for counting, the rosary of beads, the fire, the form of the Guru, the bell, the seat of the scriptures, and the ritual implements for sacrifice; // Pausa 30.102 //

In all the sacrificial ladles and spoons, in the forms of the twice-born who are single-mindedly devoted, in the various classes of Viṣṇu’s attendants, and in those intent on their births and ritual duties; // Paus 30.103 //
For those who are purified by faith, skillful, and have you as their sole refuge,
regarding the rites such as the ritual baths performed during the past year— Pausa 30.104.
Today, for the sake of pacifying occasional, regular, and incomplete [impurities], and for your pleasure, I perform [this rite] according to the scriptures. (Pauṣa 30.105)
The ritual procedure for the purifying thread (pavitraka), which fulfills all rites, as well as the service consisting of mouth-perfumes and other offerings, has indeed been described. (Pauṣa 30.106)
Perform all the rites up to the end of the oblation for the consecration, making everything your own;
I worship you with devotion while you are in deep sleep, during the vigil. (Pauṣa 30.107)
O Blessed One, you have been made known here through the Brahma-sutras and their conclusions as the bestower of both enjoyment and liberation; you know everything that dwells within the heart.
"Out of affection for me, your devotee, you must grant me this favor.
Having thus invited Him, one should prostrate on the ground with the eight limbs [of the body]. (Pauṣa 30.109)
Having circumambulated [the deity] four times while recollecting the mantra in the heart,
[one should worship] with songs, dances, and other offerings, along with hymns accompanied by Vedic recitations.
One should pass the night in vigil accompanied by shouts of "Victory!";
then, having bathed during the Brahma-muhūrta and performed the auspicious rites for the marriage-thread ceremony, [one should proceed].
First, one should perform the worship at the gateway with great magnificence;
thereafter, O Pauṣkara, one should duly perform the worship of the Blessed One.
Through various tactile, gustatory, and other such metaphorical offerings,
fashioned with many variations and known as "heart-captivating," [he worships].
With various kinds of foods to be chewed, eaten, licked, and sucked,
as well as all the auspicious vegetables, roots, and fruits produced during the six seasons.

With purifying foods steamed over fire, accompanied by side dishes and the like, consisting of products from the cow, served on stable bronze vessels filled with honey and clarified butter; Pausa 30.115.
Filled with juices, rice, and milk like oceans situated in every direction,
they were provided with betel leaves, measured wealth, and appropriate internal furnishings.
Accompanied by excellent couches, purifying objects dear to oneself, and inexhaustible enjoyments for play arising from one's own country or foreign lands; Pausa 30.117.

With vessels made of gold, adorned with perfumes, garlands, and so forth, one should perform [the rite] in this manner in the presence of the mandala until the conclusion of the recitation and the mudrās. (Paus 30.118)
Having performed the sacrifice to the Blessed One, especially in the temple of the deity,
one should then take the vessel of ornaments, open it, and worship it.
Taking up the purifying thread (*pavitraka*), one should proceed to the vicinity of the ritual jar (*kalaśa*),
for that which constitutes the collection of limbs for worship is indeed the unmanifest reality (*tāttvika*).

Having indeed connected the third, which consists of both, as well as the triad beginning with the internal (adhyātma), one should remember it within that [state] by means of the intellect from the heart. (Pauṣa 30.121)
Therein, the collection of eight groups of eight, which is unmanifest and comprises the gathering of enjoyments—
the multitude of mantras and mudrās— is proclaimed as the essential reality.
Vedic recitation, singing, instrumental music, vows, observances, gifts preceded by festivals, and various occasional rites; Paus_30.123.
These [offerings], possessing both forms, bestow the goals of human life and grant delight to Janārdana, who dwells in the world as the very embodiment of mantra.
That which is their luminous, consciousness-constituted, pure, and imperishable form—subtle and lotus-like—that should be contemplated within the elements. (Pauṣkara 30.125)
O Mahāmati, that which resembles the sun, the moon, and fire, and is conceived as having a limited extent, should be meditated upon within the locations of the multitude of its knots.
The gross, the conventional, and the third, which is universal—these should indeed always be meditated upon when designating the collection of threads of that [reality]. (Paus 30.127)
O Pauṣkara, having thus characterized the internal pervasion, one should contemplate the mental pervasion known as the "deity within" (hṛddeva), which belongs to the mantra. (Pauṣkara 30.128)
That form which is inseparable from the four [elements], which is like nectar, filled with a multitude of diverse appearances, both manifest and unmanifest, and imperishable— Paus_30.129.
O Great-minded One, one should constantly contemplate the presence of the three—the crown, the Śrīvatsa mark, and the Kaustubha gem—as the supreme deity within oneself. (Pauṣa 30.130)
That beautiful and auspicious form, composed of the assembly of the five elements—earth, water, fire, air, and space—brings complete satisfaction to his devotees. (Pauṣa 30.131)
Therefore, its nature as the presiding deity over the elements should be understood according to the method of application;
having meditated thus, O Lotus-born One, one should utter [the mantra] at the end of the root mantra. (Pauskara 30.132)
With hands raised in reverence, one should recite that mantra adorned with the *praṇava*, which is the supreme, stainless knowledge, O God, that is the means for attaining you. (Pauṣkara 30.133)
"Accompanied by devotion and faith, the performance of sacred rites illuminates one's own nature;
indeed, you have declared that this is the means for the attainment of the indivisible [Brahman]. (Pausa 30.134)

By your grace, I have composed this work called the *Pavitra*, according to my ability, for the sake of those devotees whose souls are purified and who are devoted to both knowledge and action. (Pauṣa 30.135)
Now, meditate upon that Supreme Goddess as is fitting;
for from that arises action more auspicious than any other, and indeed, stainless knowledge.
You alone are indeed the other injunction arising from the collection of mantras, as well as the aggregate of substances;
you are the attainment and the fulfiller of all incomplete ritual actions. (Pausa 30.137)
O Blessed One, by this hawk, for one who is afflicted by the destruction of existence and is free from deceit, may all your ritual actions remain entirely unimpaired.
O Blessed One, I have made this request here out of my supreme longing for you, until your satisfaction is attained by you, the bestower of perfect knowledge. (Pauṣa 30.139)
But when a time of calamity has arrived, O Acyuta, ritual action and knowledge must not be abandoned by me intentionally; you know all this in its true essence.
O Lord, because you were not properly honored with appropriate enjoyments at the proper time and in the proper manner, my mind is filled with distress.
Worship with the enjoyment of sensory objects and satiation with the milk of sovereignty—
none of this is of any use to those who have accomplished their purpose in You.
For this entire [teaching] has been sown in a fertile field;
knowing this, I have previously declared that it will bear fruit entirely through immortality. (Paus 30.143)
O Lord, Sovereign of All, although I have accepted [this] from the mouth of my guru,
it does not flash forth clearly in my intellect as it truly is, nor has it been fully realized.

From the time of dawn until the end of night, due to the lack of independence and incapacity of the mind, and because of its instability, [the yogin remains unaffected] by the actions of mind, speech, and body.
O Lord, because of obstacles such as cold, heat, wind, and rain, as well as fevers and the like,
the constituent parts of the ritual cannot be fully accomplished by those who possess forms inferior to yours.
The daily ritual, which culminates in the attainment of supreme bliss until the cessation of worldly activity, is as previously described;
however, because it is not possible for the immortals in that manner, [it is different]. (Pauṣa 30.147)
To fulfill that [requirement], however, the most excellent worship known as *pavitraka*, which you have prescribed for every year, has been ordained. (Pausa 30.148)
Whatever pure [object] has been worshipped by me through direct perception, yet remains incomplete due to the performance of ritual action—lead that to purity for me. (Pausa 30.149)
Whether through knowledge or ignorance, whatever was spoken by me as prescribed, may all that be entirely fulfilled; may you always remain fully satisfied. (Pausa 30.150)
Oṃ, imperishable Lord of the World, eternal one whose form is mantra!
Protect me, O lotus-eyed one; forgive me, O Āja, be gracious, oṃ! (Pauṣa 30.151)
Having thus spoken the root mantra together with the marks of the heart and the other [limbs], one should then place it upon the head of the all-pervading Lord, whose nature is mantra.
[He is] the embodiment of all-knowing wisdom, activity, enjoyment, and virtuous intention;
thus [he is visualized] both within the mandala and situated inside the temple.
O Mahāmati, even for one situated in the midst of fire,
having placed [the object] within a vessel and having purified it with worship, it becomes a sanctifying purifier.
Then, having given the implements of the sacrifice to the teacher—who is the very self of the scripture—having placed him upon his heart, and having honored him like a god; Paus_30.155.
Then, being well-pleased, he [the sage] began to bestow a blessing for the sake of his complete success,
as he stood near the sacred fire together with his wife.
At the conclusion of the fire-oblation or at the end of the worship, for the others indeed in due order;
then, with coverings and gifts gathered according to one's means.

O Brahmin, [they were honored] with sacred threads and upper garments, accompanied by umbrellas and sandals, with various kinds of food, incense, and offerings such as the touching of the body (ālabhana).
O Pauṣkara, one should honor all the Brāhmaṇas as well as the ascetics who are well-prepared with soups; this should be done after concluding the rite within three nights or seven days.
Having first performed the great worship and concluded it with the final oblation (pūrṇā),
one should gradually withdraw [the ritual] oneself or through the Guru, the Self, or the Lord.
Having taken the vessel that has been honored and having worshipped it according to the rule,
he should place both knees upon the ground and prostrate before the preceptor.

Having first honored him with water for the feet, flowers, and other offerings, and having prostrated yourself, you should present that vessel, saying: "O Lord, may you show me your favor. (Pauṣa 30.162)
The preceptor should pronounce a blessing for him, expressing his delight in the Blessed One,
according to tradition and according to the scriptures, through the grace of the Four-Souled One.
"O Brahmin, may that year-long [observance] be perfectly fulfilled for you while you remain seated upon the throne, as he recites [the praises] over your head. (Pauṣa 30.164)
One should perform the dismissal of the Lord according to the sequence, preceded by worship, using the two-vessel mantra which bestows protection, good fortune, and liberation. (Pauṣa 30.165)
One should worship Viṣvaksena along with his limbs (attendants), and immediately thereafter offer libations;
afterwards, having withdrawn everything, one should indeed perform the ritual dismissal.
Having arranged the drinking of Soma as before for the sake of achieving flawlessness, [the vessel] should be fashioned from gold,
silver, or fine gems, or otherwise adorned.
Upon the wheel-base, within the wide vessel, in the center of the lotus,
with a neck marked by the lines of the Pāñcajanya conch and a beautiful face like a hundred-petaled lotus.

O Lotus-born One, upon the upper half [of the body] adorned with the circle of the Kaumudī garland, there is a stream of nectar-water flowing from the mouths of the sea-monsters of Śeṣa. (Pauṣa 30.169)
Adorned with rivers, the ocean, auspicious trees, fish, and garlands,
and thus endowed with these characteristics,
it is for the propitiation of the All-pervading Lord.

In the offering of water for the feet, the guest-water, the rinsing of the mouth, and the ceremonial bath; likewise during the annual festival, as well as in the rite of consecration with a thousand jars.
Thus has been described, O lotus-eyed one, the supreme Pavitrāropaṇa rite, which always protects the devotees on earth from all deficiencies, excesses, and other such faults. (Pauṣa 30.172)
Through the power of bringing that [state] to completion, one becomes a Brāhmaṇa learned in Vedic knowledge;
or indeed, a glorious Kṣatriya of exceedingly fierce power with an unbroken lineage.
The Vaiśya shall be endowed with wealth and grain, and the Śūdra shall be happy; indeed, he shall obtain the fruit of infinite gifts of cows, land, and gold. (Pauṣa 30.174)
For those who give for as long as they live, a man shall obtain that same fruit every day for a hundred years, even when the maximum lifespan is fully completed.
Having reached the appropriate time through his own intellect and having approached the abode of Hari,
he correctly remembers the Lord of Mantras and properly creates a body.
In vehicles resembling the moon and accompanied by celestial women,
he goes to heaven while being fanned and likewise honored by the immortals.
Having enjoyed vast pleasures arising from all the various worlds,
after a long time, he indeed returns once again to human birth.
He is born at an auspicious time, in an auspicious place, and into an auspicious family;
and when childhood has passed, his collection of faculties becomes manifest.

But when the principle of the intellect (buddhitattva) has been awakened through the power of practice over many births, one should become devoted to Nārāyaṇa in deed, mind, and speech. (Pauṣkara 30.180)
Constantly devoted to ritual action, wise, devoted to Brahman, and possessing the prowess of truth;
unchanging, pure in soul, and free from association with the wicked.
Freed from disease and sorrow, endowed with sons, wife, and other kin,
and liberated from untimely death, he attains stainless knowledge.
He arrives at Śvetadvīpa, which is very difficult even for the gods, the wise, and others to attain; there he beholds the Lord of the World.

That person who is devoted to those rites attains the state of the Supreme Brahman; for they behold the sacred thread of the Lord of the Universe being superimposed upon the Paśyantī level of speech. (Pauṣkara 30.184)
Likewise, others who rejoice in this go to Amarāvatī;
so too those who hear this sacred rite which destroys all sins. (Pauṣa 30.185)
And they indeed obtain the merit consisting of sacrifices and charitable works,
when a woman who has no other refuge is urged by her husband.
Devoted to him in deed, thought, and speech, that virtuous and faithful woman was ever free from malice toward her husband, remaining disciplined with all her faculties fully integrated.
And the lotus-born Brahmā places the pavitraka upon the Source of the World;
by this, one shall indeed obtain fortune and auspiciousness before long. (Pauṣa 30.188)
At the end of her body, she attains the status of being worshiped by celestial women and gods;
she gazes upon Arundhatī and the other foremost [sages] from above.
O Lotus-born One, at the end one attains that knowledge by which they go to the supreme state,
and by which one delivers one's kinsmen from their misdeeds.

O Brahmin, the mantra-practitioner, being of the nature of the mantra, gives an ornament to the all-pervading Lord preceded by affection and with the names of the ancestors, such as Janaka and others. (Pauṣa 30.191)
A man goes from an evil state to a happy state; as the water of the Ganges is to men, so is the nectar of the gods to the immortals—both being unstable [in their worldly states].

O Lotus-born One, just as the *svadhā* offering is for the ancestors who perform ritual acts, so too is the *pavitraka* thread a purifier that increases prosperity for those rich in sacred rites. (Pauṣa 30.193)
It destroys all faults and fears, annihilates all calamities, bestows all happiness, and reveals all secrets. (Pausa 30.194)
He who is a true devotee of the Blessed One, having undertaken the sacred mantras,
[engages] thus in this activity or through the constant practice of worship from birth.
Indeed, because of his non-difference from Viṣṇu, the supreme Self, this teacher must be sought with great effort by him. Paus 30.196.
O Lotus-born One, due to the absence of one's own guru and because he is not present, the initiation should be performed by another guru who has been requested to do so. (Pauṣa 30.197)
Neither by deed, nor by mind, nor by speech— nor by anything else, nor by one who is inferior—
should one who is established in another doctrine [be associated] with my devotees who are intent upon that alone.
For the spiritual teacher must be sought out for the sake of the *pavitrārohaṇa* and other rites, even though he knows me well and perceives my inner state. (Pauṣa 30.199)
Because his mind was fulfilled and he was so deeply devoted, I then considered him my guru;
I consider a disciple to regard his guru as a savior who has arrived, by the power of devotion. (Pauṣa 30.200)
Wherein there is equilibrium of the three— the mental fluctuations,
the disciple, the teacher, and the mantra— therein lie the liberation of the Tantra and the supernatural attainments.
He who, knowing this, behaves as one devoid of devotion toward his devotees, and likewise fails to bestow mantras upon his disciples, that lowest of men goes to hell. (Pauṣa 30.202)

The devotion previously accumulated by devotees gradually becomes manifest through contact with them and the practice of their conduct, as well as through the disparagement of the mantra and the deity. (Pauṣa 30.203)
Therefore, whatever [cognition] clearly arises from an object for another person or even for oneself, that is traditionally held to be the means of establishing that very object. (Pauṣa 30.204)
Wherever the spiritual teachers possess unwavering devotion, and wherever the disciples likewise have a desire for worship, right there [should it be performed]. (Pauṣa 30.205)
Then, O Lotus-born One, may the supreme mantra, being pleased, grant its presence;
for what indeed is the ritual action of one who is perfected, possessed of equanimous intellect, and free from activity?
Know that the ritual action of anyone other than him is preceded by devotion;
and that devotion directed toward him is considered equal to the conduct of a wife toward her husband.
Possessing the eight characteristics, complete, purified by faith, and bestowing liberation—
any other success (siddhi) bestows worldly accomplishments and yields results that are subject to deviation.

I stand as a neutral witness to everyone, yet I know their inner disposition according to reality; for when their devotion toward me is indeed unwavering, [I recognize it through those two]. (Pauṣa 30.209)
I favor the disciple through the essence of mantra by means of the guru’s mouth;
therefore, one who is not devoted should never be initiated, whereas a devotee is to be initiated.
One who is not devoted should not be joined with one who is excessively devoted in your worship;
for those who are devoted, devotion toward a guru who lacks devotion leads to torment.
Physical and mental suffering increases moment by moment;
through this, one's disposition becomes demonic, whereby one goes to the lowest state of existence.
O Lotus-born One, for devotees who have no other refuge than the Guru, the two kinds and three degrees of defects quickly come to destruction. (Pauṣa 30.213)
He truly cannot endure the great infamy or the hostility directed toward his guru—one who is worthy of favor yet lacks devotion, who is arrogant, and who has abandoned ritual practice. (Pauṣa 30.214)
And for one who has been initiated, the presence of unbearable defects [is a hindrance];
therefore, with every effort, one should act for the sake of attaining the unseen fruit. (Pauṣa 30.215)
Whatever task has been prescribed must be performed by both the disciple and the teacher;
one who lacks devotion does not attain consciousness, nor does one who lacks devotion attain meditative absorption.
One who possesses devotion understands the proper ritual procedure; one without devotion cannot be a knower of the scriptures.
Likewise, one should not worship an image, perform a sacrifice, or honor the sacrificial fire without devotion.
One should cause him to bind the *namudrā* and make him hear the *samayas*;
for he who, out of malice or greed, [binds it] for those lacking devotion toward the Teacher of the World— ||| 30.218 |||
If, out of delusion, one approaches those who understand the meaning of the contrary [teachings] and whose nature is intent on seizing [wealth], that preceptor goes to hell.
"O Lotus-born One, as for that which was asked by you, it has been stated: 'If one afflicted by suffering does not perform the previously mentioned expiation. (Pausa 30.220)
For the benefit of devotees residing within the three worlds, the auspicious Pavitrārohaṇa rite is performed once the rainy season has begun.
It should be told to humans, gods, and siddhas who follow [the teachings];
for they proceed with great speed through faith for every year.
In this great activity of the Supreme Lord,
while the All-pervading One remained lying down, during that time when the trees were thick with flowers and fruit.
While the sky was being overspread by clouds accompanied by cranes,
the surface of the earth was adorned with white, blue, and red lotuses.
In groves, orchards, and gardens, provided with green meadows and the like, endowed with rice crops and other grains, and beautified by the waters of ponds; Pausa 30.225.
The *pavitraka* rite performed for Viṣṇu, who dwells within, brings him great satisfaction;
O Brahmin, his practice of sleeping is always prescribed for that [period] beforehand. (Pauṣa 30.226)
Then, O Brahmin, on the aforementioned day, once that [rite] has been performed by those two, the sacrifice of action must certainly be protected by those devoted to ritual practice. (Pauṣa 30.227)
Thus ends the thirtieth chapter, titled "The Investiture of the Pavitra," in the Pauṣkara Saṃhitā, a great Upaniṣad within the glorious Pañcarātra.
Now begins the thirty-first chapter.
The Blessed One said: "O Mahāmati, having performed the Pavitrārohaṇa rite during the Cāturmāsya period..."
It should be brought to completion through various observances honored by the world.
One should worship this bed of the God and Goddess; hear now the procedure for that:
it should be adorned with gold and other jewels, and beautified in all its parts.
And upon a couch suited to the Blessed One, white as the moon,
adorned with a white parasol, yak-tail whisks, and excellent tinkling bells.
It was attended by the Vaijayantī host, adorned with golden-staffed pillars,
decorated with a divine canopy, and embellished with saffron and other fragrant substances.
It should be beautified above and covered with horizontal and vertical cloths,
filled with nutmeg and other spices, parched grain, and all kinds of seeds.
One should meditate upon this couch, which is furnished with variegated cloths at its corners, strewn with heaps of excellent flowers, and provided with jewel-lamps. (Pauṣa 31.6)

O high-minded one, [worship] the Lord of Nagas, who dwells in the midst of the glorious, vast ocean, whose crown consists of a thousand hoods, and who is as white as snow, the kunda flower, and the moon.

Having meditated upon [the deity] with the *praṇava*, one's own name ending in a consonant and accompanied by the *bindu*, and having worshipped, praised, prostrated, and propitiated [them]. (Pauṣa 31.8)
Having established there the ritual image, adorned with necklaces and armlets, anointed with sandalwood, saffron, and bāhlīka, and encircled with flowers; Pausa 31.9.
Covered with a cloth for the eyes, well-anointed and well-perfumed, one should [place] one's own seed-syllable mantra: "Oṃ, obeisance to the Lord of Lakṣmī. (Pauṣa 31.10)
Having mentally raised up that which is worthy of worship according to the sequence of the primary and secondary limbs,
one should do so with the twelve syllables joined with the words of one's own name.
But in the absence of an image made of ritual materials, having placed a beautiful cluster of *darbha* grass upon the seat according to the prescribed rule, [one should proceed].

Having placed that supreme mantra within it, [one should visualize it] situated in the midst of the cage of all the Śaktis, such as Gaṇḍā and the rest, emerging from the interior of the sky of one's own lotus.

Having led [the devotee] through the gift of the forms of the individual deities while absorbed in meditation, he should offer a garment that is honored by the limbs of the gods, unworn, and pure in nature. (Pauṣa 31.14)
Having worshipped above [the heart] with flowers, incense, and ointments,
one should deposit the power (śakti) of the mind, which is the synthesis of all tantras.
On the right, however, is the form named Abhimāna, raising a yak-tail whisk;
likewise on the left is Jñānaniśā, raising her hand with a palm-leaf fan.
One should meditate on her in the highest state, delighting in the massaging of hands,
standing at the region of his lotus-feet and caressing them with her own lotus-hands.
Having taken hold of her two divine feet, Śrī herself is present in his proximity;
she is the bliss that is the form of Brahman, the deity who is the supreme god above all gods. (Pauṣa 31.18)
With eyes filled with wonder born from the bliss of recollecting that [deity] within, they should be worshipped with their own names as mantra-syllables, preceded by the *praṇava* (OM). (Pauṣa 31.19)
O Lotus-born One, having thus properly installed this bed of the God of Gods according to the instructions, men who are intent on the Cāturmāsya vow should remain devoted to it.
Every day, worship should be performed here, along with cleansing and smearing the ground with clay or metallic preparations, or with fragrant substances such as sandalwood and the like.
The offering of incense and lamps, the fanning with a breeze raised by a fan,
and the hospitable treatment with cool water mixed with moon-like sandalwood paste.
Having brought about the cessation of perspiration with plantain leaves, white water-lilies, and lotuses mixed with blue water-lilies, one should perform worship repeatedly. (Pauṣa 31.23)
And when two months had thus passed, and the sound of clouds arose from the sky, there was a song accompanied by flute and lute, with a sweet melody. (Pauṣa 31.24)
O Brahmin, on the twelfth day of the month of Bhādrapada, at the onset of night,
the God of gods, Adhokṣaja, indeed resorts to a slight awakening.
For the sake of the immortals' stability, one should perform the ritual rotation,
leaving behind the supine posture with the assembly of limbs turned toward the south.
O Pauṣkara, resorting to yogic sleep and bringing about both manifestation and dissolution, [He remains] within the axle of the wheel of the vital breaths, as the seed of the universe.
Then, having cast off the covering garment from the lunar orb at Mūla,
this Supreme Lord remains [there] on the twelfth day of the month of Āśvayuja.
At night during the month of Kārttika, the Lord of the Immortals, having arisen and mounted his sovereign bird, should abandon his divine bed. (Pauṣa 31.29)
For the sake of pacifying the defects of all the streets of the entire multitude of worlds,
he whose self is immeasurable wanders about, bringing joy to the gods and others.
"Manifesting his own path of dharma in this world, his devotees should likewise perform that great feat of his. (Pauṣa 31.31)
With various auspicious festivals consisting of charity, recitation, and vigils,
accompanied by dancing and singing, and joined with graceful gestures and laughter.
O Brahmin, they always remained in one place, playing with flowers, self-restrained, bowed down before the Lord, and with minds fixed on no other.
Indeed, during the remaining month, those great men who are devoted to austerity and capable must once again protect [the site] in their own hermitage or in the sacred field of the immortals.
O Brahmin, O Lotus-born One, [one may perform the rite] with a twelve-night rite, a six-night auspicious rite, or, in case of incapacity, with a three-night or a one-day-and-night rite.
Then, by means of eating only at night, these four auspicious vows are observed by men who are devoted to fasting for a month and are supreme devotees of Viṣṇu.
For three nights, two nights, or one night beforehand, the vigil for Acyuta should be performed with recitations of meritorious narratives, preceded by hymns and songs.
With savory and sweet dances, with jests and songs of praise, with shouts of "Victory! and salutations accompanied by the clapping of hands.
One should worship Śrīnivāsa while offering oblations, meditating, and reciting prayers,
providing him with abundant enjoyments consisting of the six flavors and the sixty-four modes of service.
On the twelfth lunar day, during the Brāhma-muhūrta, one should worship Hari, who is the embodiment of mantra, with offerings of water for the feet, ointments, garlands, and refined incense.
O Great-minded One, [he was honored] with the sounds of conchs accompanied by the noise of dundubhī and paṭaha drums,
and with the various lofty words uttered by throngs of bards.
Then, having raised [the deity] from his bed with hymns characterized by awakening, accompanied by great shouts of "Victory! Victory! uttered again and again.
Then, with great magnificence, one should worship in due order within the mandala and other sacred sites,
preceded by a grand ritual ablution, using the complete enjoyments as prescribed.
With many great lamps, along with clusters of flower-pots containing sprouts, and fruits such as jackfruit and others, all anointed with honey, clarified butter, and sesame seeds.

With offerings of flowers, water for the feet, sandalwood paste, and other articles, adorned with the sacred thread (*brahmasūtra*), and with clusters of blossoms from *mālatī*, *mallikā*, and other such plants; (Pauṣa 31.45)
With rafts provided with straight branches of the kadamba, mango, and śrīvṛkṣa trees, bound together by cords, and well-honored with saffron and other offerings; Pausa 31.46.

Having thus performed the sacrifice up to the conclusion of the oblations with various gifts such as cattle, land, gold, and other auspicious coverings, [one should offer] a village, a city, or a house.
By means of a vehicle equipped with a purifier (pavitra), provided with wheels, auspicious,
joined with mantras, missiles, and a water-pot (kumbha), or else by means of that which has the interior of its body [shaped like] an image.
Accompanied by the sound of Vedic chanting and the music of song and instrumental performance,
the courtesans, who were devotees of the Blessed One, went along with the citizens.
Accompanied by wandering mendicants and celibate students devoted to silent recitation and praise,
[he was] indeed surrounded by a great retinue, adorned with banners and covered by white parasols.
Burning fragrant incense and various types of guggulu resin,
and having thus circumambulated the vehicle, one should bestow wealth upon those who seek it.
Then, having circumambulated him four times and prostrated with all his limbs like a staff upon the ground out of devotion toward the Supreme Person, he bowed down. (Pauṣa 31.52)
While standing before the chariot or within the temple, praising it with his mind and reciting prayers,
he should scatter parched grain, white mustard seeds, and fruits, along with offerings of water and flowers.
Whatever deity of the directions one visualizes, all directions become likewise;
by means of that, one indeed binds a stable state while wandering throughout the entire world.
For his devotees, the Blessed One is not obstructed by space, time, or other such factors within their devotion;
this is what is called "circumambulation," common to all embodied beings. (Pauṣkara 31.55)
When thoroughly practiced and fully mastered, it bestows the imperishable state;
one should perform it with both knees and hands, or alternatively with the two knees alone. (Pauṣa 31.56)
Once at the end of the year, or on the three junctions (trisaṃdhyā) and the twelfth days (dvādaśī),
or likewise at the conclusion of a sacrifice, one should [offer] with the head bowed down.
Then, having fully honored that state, it bestows the fruit for practitioners immediately after the end of the body; moreover, through gradual stages, the worlds of majesty are attained.
Having performed the sacrifice with supreme devotion, he thus bowed down to Adhokṣaja,
who is to be honored with circumambulations accompanied by prostrations.
Indeed, by visiting all sacred fields and wandering to all holy fords,
the Blessed One bestows the fruit upon the devotee who worships his feet.
By him who has performed circumambulation of the form of Hari, whose essence is mantra,
that man has been abandoned by the faults born of worldly existence after they themselves have circumambulated him.
For the devotees of the Blessed One who have purified their souls through the initiatory rites of action,
this excellent activity on the auspicious path is most meritorious.
Because it is equal to the sphere of gnosis and because it revolves like a wheel, it constantly bestows auspiciousness and exhausts the accumulation of afflictions. (Pauṣa 31.63)

For those devoted to the Blessed One who have reached the perfection of action, for those dwelling in divine abodes, or for others as well, [the body] consists of karma, speech, and the senses. (Pauṣa 31.64)
In the inner sanctum of Viṣṇu, or from within the womb-chamber, or in the hall of the face,
one should perform a multitude of prostrations, excluding the performance of circumambulations.
Since the sight of the back of the hand of the pervasive Lord residing within the fire causes defects for those whose forms are the mantras, so too does the body cause a lack of accomplishment.
Having performed a circumambulation by kneeling, O Brahmin, one should remain close within the presence of the Lord; for devotees, wandering away from His feet is another form of opposition.
Likewise, those wearing sandals or shoes, those holding an umbrella or a turban,
those seated in vehicles, on horses, or in palanquins, and those chewing betel and the like [should not be saluted].
Carrying a toy bird, a toy elephant, a stick, a mirror, and a fan, he would laugh or exult, sighing and babbling much. (Pauṣa 31.69)
One who, with a provoked mind, engages in playful dalliance and sport, being possessed by haste though seeking auspicious ends, shall not obtain any fruit from wandering here. (Pauṣa 31.70)

Therefore, one who desires auspiciousness should always perform their duties with a mind focused on nothing else, with that same inner self, whether at home, in a temple, or on a mountain. (Pauṣa 31.71)
For this reason, O Mahāmati, the Ekabera [form] yields abundant fruit with little effort;
it is infinite and the supreme means for attaining great liberation. (Pausa 31.72)
Having thus circumambulated [the deity] and offered a handful of flowers,
one should then descend from the chariot, preceded by the mantra-consecration of the wheel.
Furthermore, one should worship [the deity] again with hands joined in the mudrā;
then, having offered libations of clarified butter and other substances, one should present the auspicious final oblation (pūrṇāhuti).
One should ask forgiveness from Puruṣottama by offering water for the feet, incense, and other such items;
likewise, one should present a boat, an umbrella, and a sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā).
O Brahmin, having prostrated before his own guru, or in his absence before the twice-born, he should place both knees upon the ground and, with palms joined in reverence, recite this: (Pauṣa 31.76).
O Lord of All, by this act, may all people attain an entirely auspicious state; and may you, O God, experience supreme joy. (Pausa 31.77)
Thereafter, one should feed the Brahmins with various kinds of food and drink,
accompanied by offerings of sacrificial fees (dakṣiṇā) given with faith for the sake of satisfying the lineage of the ancestors.
Then, accompanied by his kinsmen and servants, he should perform the concluding sacrifice;
or, if he has the means, O Lotus-born One, it should be performed in this manner by those who are unperturbed.
The Lord should be beheld by the gods in the sacred field while seated in the Brahma-chariot,
or as the Sovereign stationed in a village, in an urban center, or within a celestial mansion.
Thus has been described the ritual for devotees known as the Kaumudī,
the fruit of which— beginning with residence in the same world as the deity— is established according to the power of one's inner disposition.
And the entire procedure beginning with the rite of the sacred thread (*pavitrārohaṇa*) for devotees of purified soul has been thus declared by me, O Lotus-born One. (Pauṣa 31.82)
O twice-born one, due to lack of independence, lack of capacity, or lack of wealth,
one may perform [the rites] in this manner during all the twelfth days within the course of another year.
Even when prohibited during the night, during the Cāturmāsya period, or while observing restraints,
one must sustain oneself with alms-food until the conclusion of the Tulā portion.
If [the moon] has waned on the twelfth day before the full moon,
one should perform the entire rite during the night, because that is the time when the lunar day reaches its culmination.
One should observe this excellent vow for five days on both occasions,
from the end of the eleventh day until the full moon, specifically during the periods when the sun is in Libra and Scorpio.
The renunciation of honey and meat, the avoidance of wine and women, the killing of various species of wild animals, and likewise the cutting down of trees; Paus_31.87.
And the burning of forests, the digging up of the earth with spades and such tools, the tethering of cattle, and the killing or binding of men. (Pauṣa 31.88)
One should diligently avoid wandering at night, socializing with those of low caste, and all things such as fine rice and oil massages. (Pauṣa 31.89)
O Lotus-born One, on the day following the day of conclusion, that which is ordained for the year for devotees and those possessed of faith [is performed]. (Pauṣa 31.90)
The consecration (abhiṣeka) must be performed for the attainment of well-being, peace, and auspiciousness;
therefore, it should be carried out by an excellent preceptor with a mind intent on bestowing grace. (Pauṣa 31.91)
In the absence of the guru, the practitioner may [seek permission] from his mother, his father, or from officiating priests who are older in age,
or from other practitioners.
Then, having placed [the deity] upon an auspicious seat marked with a svastika and a lotus,
one should prepare a nine-navelled lotus with eight petals according to the prescribed lines.
When it has been drawn with saffron and other pigments, or filled with flowers, covered with cloths for the eyes, and prepared with the prescribed powders; // Paus_31.94 //
It should be joined with bells arranged in their proper positions or with those already standing there,
as well as with vessels containing the seeds of the *jāta* plant, filled with auspicious barley, and marked with [the syllable] *ya*.
With curd, mirrors, white umbrellas, flowers, and auspicious ornaments;
with all kinds of seeds and the like, fragrant substances, and bilva fruits and the like.
With auspicious songs and musical instruments accompanied by the chanting of the Vedas,
[the rite was performed] by preceptors learned in the Pañcarātra and devoted to recitation and meditation.

Together with the sounds of gourds, lutes, water-drums, flutes, and bells, [the assembly] remained established in the true Brahman, which is the source and dissolution of all, according to the teachings of the authentic scriptures.
In the sacrificial hall, there were flames, flowers, full water-jars, auspicious trees, and clusters of blossoms, adorned by various maidens bearing ritual implements.
It was surrounded on all sides by cows and young calves, including bulls chewing upon *dūrvā* grass and other fodder, and it was crowded with throngs of bards.
