For the sake of increase, one should worship Parā Lakṣmī, who is endowed with all powers;
for the sake of attainment, one should worship Acyuta, the true, eternal, and imperishable state.
O Pauṣkara, this method of bathing has been prescribed for devotees;
having performed the preliminary consecration (adhivāsa) according to the previously mentioned procedure in due order, [the rite should be performed]. Paus_31.102.
A set of nine water-filled jars, made of gold or studded with gems and arranged according to the previously described method, should be placed there. Pausa 31.103.
First, one should meditate upon Varuṇa, who is mounted upon a chariot of serpents,
with hands granting boons and fearlessness, and emitting the essence of nectar.
That which is called *svādva* and known as *kṣīra* has attained a state of oneness;
it is mounted upon a variegated makara and holds a jewel-vessel raised in its hand.
One should meditate everywhere upon Varapāṇi and the ocean as being like water;
she who was born from the foot of Nārāyaṇa and who formerly bore the jar of people.
In the southeast, one should place Yamunā, who is mounted upon a tortoise and worshipped by the gods;
and in the south, Sarasvatī, seated upon a frog and a lotus.
[He saw] Śanaiḥpravāhasaṃjñā, who releases one from the bonds of the noose;
Nairṛtī, seated upon a bull; and in the west, Siṃhavaktrā.
One should place Airāvatī, seated upon an elephant, in the pitcher in the northwest;
here, in the center of the northeast lotus, one should place Vitastā, riding on a fish, in the pitcher.
[Namely] Narmadā, who is mounted upon a buffalo, Samāṅgā, and Devapūjitā; Vṛṣadvatī, Devikā, Paroṣṇī, and the one called Baḍabā.
Sindhu is in all eight Kakubh positions, arranged around her in due order;
or else, they are all situated upon lotuses in the secondary jars, holding water-pots raised aloft.
Adorned with flower clusters, their waters being stirred,
[the ponds] were filled with images of Vāsudeva and other deities, consecrated one hundred and eight times with mantras.

Having worshipped [the deities], one should bestow the consecration (abhiṣeka) for the attainment of all fruits, having meditated thus upon the lotus situated within the wheel, resting on a base of gold or other such materials. (Pauṣa 31.113)
As described for the river, the ocean, and Varuṇa, it was fashioned as before,
adorned with excellent pearls, gems, and the like, and decorated with svastikas and other auspicious signs.
In the [cakras] with twelve spokes, presided over by Keśava and others month by month,
and endowed with deities in all its limbs, another mantra is established.
Or one may perform the auspicious purificatory bath (*avabhṛtha*) with that water;
by daily placing that water upon the head and by offering salutations, [one attains purity]. (Pauṣa 31.116)
One is liberated from all defects and attains auspiciousness and prosperity,
[having come] from the group of holy fords including the oceans and rivers such as the Gaṅgā.
One whose self is purified and who has taken refuge in Acyuta obtains the fruit arising from the bath;
and when the concluding purificatory bath (*avabhṛthasnāna*) has been performed, the practitioner is then fully satisfied.
For the sake of attaining the state of the Blessed One, one should oneself [anoint] the feet of the Guru with water using the right hand alone, while mentally recollecting one's own mantra.
Having sprinkled [the water] upon the head with the mudrā called Śaṅkha, which faces upward,
and having discarded it once the garment has been moistened by the water, one should then put on another garment.
Then, having adorned the body with flowers, perfumes, and ornaments as before, starting with the uṣṇīṣa, one should sit upon a seat.
Then, one should perform the intimidation with the previously mentioned weapon;
having performed the ritual placement (*nyāsa*) and offered congratulations, one should proceed with the auspicious water-offering (*arghya*) and other rites.
Having received from the hand of the supreme guide all the royal regalia, ending with the parasol and the fly-whisks, he then rose from his seat.
Having paid homage to the Lord of the World, the Supreme Lord, the Infallible One,
he reached the abode of fire together with the preeminent teacher.
Having filled his joined palms with flowers, garlands, perfumes, incense, fruits, or seeds,
he should perform worship of the Lord within the fire-chamber.
Meditating upon the Lord of Mantras within his heart, he should sit facing the fire;
then, with a seat consecrated by the recitation of mantras and water, he should proceed.
One who is pure should touch everything from the feet up to the crown of the head with a mind fixed in meditation, as before;
then, having meditated upon the mantra within the palms of the hands, one should perform the ritual of the infused body (*vinyastadeha*).

One should offer that [flower], accompanied by perfumes, flowers, and water for honor (arghya), upon the head, the crown of the head, and the heart; or else, one should place the flower prescribed by the Sūtra on one's own garment, the girdle-thread, the sacrificial cord, or the elbow.
Having first performed the ritual restraint (*saṃyama*), one should place [the fire] into the lotus-hand of the disciple. (Pauṣkara 31.128) [...
Having thus brought about union with the fire that possesses qualities, for the sake of attaining the presence of all accomplishments until liberation, (Pauṣkara 31.130)
The preceptor should indeed perform the fire-oblation again, ending with the full oblation (pūrṇāhuti),
using seven types of fuel-wood materials mixed together and combined with sugar.

O Brahmin, one should offer one hundred and eight, or a thousand, or ten thousand oblations into the fire of the mantra-form situated in the center; thereafter, one should present the final oblation (pūrṇāhuti).
One should place the *sruva* spoon with its bowl facing downward upon the *sruc* ladle;
then, having worshipped the *sruc* with flowers and other offerings, one should place the *sruc* filled with clarified butter [upon it].
One should perform worship with fragrant flowers and waterless *arghya* offerings;
thereafter, one should offer clarified butter (*ājya*) in the prescribed number or half of that amount. (Pauṣa 31.134)

At the conclusion of the worship, O fair-eyed one, he should again offer the full oblation as previously described, whether it be a hundred, a thousand, ten thousand, or a hundred thousand times. (Pauṣkara 31.135)
The essence of knowledge (jñānātman) constitutes one-fourth of each of the preceding forms individually;
it is equal to that in the [mantras] beginning with the heart, and likewise in all those above.
O Pauṣkara, for the consorts of the Supreme Lord, one should offer all the marks, ornaments, and so forth with half that quantity, in due order. (Pauṣkara 31.137)

The libation with the sectarian mark (lāñchanatarpaṇa) is prescribed as half [the amount] for the six mantras of the shared seat (sādhārāsanamantra), which embody the nature of time, as well as for the gurus and others.
O Lotus-born One, having offered oblations to the essential protectors of the world who stand at the gates,
according to the sequence beginning with the Guru, one should offer half and half in due order.

O best of Brahmins, the number [of oblations] for the half-portion of the uneven [oblation], as well as for the ghee-oblation, should be increased by one; and it is exactly the same for the lotus and other [offerings]. (Pauṣa 31.140)
The sacrificial fuel sticks produced from the tree of the *brahmayajña* and those arising from the tree of worshipful knowledge—
these indeed come from milk-trees and are soaked in the three sweets.
The mantra-practitioner should offer oblations according to the ritual rules, reciting the collection of eye-mantras in sequence,
providing satisfaction through the offering of full oblations performed by means of fractional oblations.

O twice-born one, by means of a fire-oblation numbering according to one's own intellect, one who has conquered all obstacles should indeed satisfy one's own limbs with libations until the end of the full oblation; thus at the conclusion, the fire [is satisfied]. Paus 31.143.

When the array of mantras has been performed within the heart, one should lead it to satisfaction with the *pūrṇāhuti* at the end; once the fire-oblation (*homa*) has been thus accomplished, one should then offer a handful of flowers.
One should apply a *tilaka* or an upright sectarian mark (*ūrdhvapuṇḍra*) on the child with ashes at the appropriate places, using the Heart mantra, the Armor mantra, and the Head mantra in sequence.
The heart-mantra should always be employed in all rites;
one should always perform all actions by means of it. (Pauṣa 31.146)
One should perform the ritual in this manner for that which is called "the essence of all mantras. When the recitation is completed, drops of water fall from the mouth of the *sruc* ladle.

Then, with his hand, he should take [the water] from the *praṇītā* vessel and place it upon the head of the seeker of liberation who is free from desire; this is the *homa* previously described for such a person. (Pauṣa 31.148)
For one who possesses desire yet seeks liberation, and who is adorned with ornaments, the All-Knowing One dwelling within the heart does not grant the desired object. (Pauṣa 31.149)
Since he bestows even heaven upon his devotees without being asked, what indeed is there that he cannot give? Therefore, one should abandon making requests. (Pauṣa 31.150)
O one of great intelligence, this much alone is to be sought from the supreme Lord Acyuta by a living being who has performed worship at all times. Pausa 31.151.
Grant me supreme devotion, by which you may be pleased with me;
O Lord of Gods, when you are propitious, what on earth is not attained by me? (Pauṣa 31.152)
Thus addressed, O lotus-eyed one, having completed the ritual for consecration, one becomes qualified to hear the scripture of the Blessed One. (Pauṣa 31.153)
One indeed attains the divine station of Viṣṇu, by means of which, being intensely devoted, one is delivered from the perils of saṃsāra. (Pauṣa 31.154)
O Pauṣkara, once the offering of the water-pot has been performed, one should then offer groats, meat, and so forth,
starting from outside the mandala and proceeding in a clockwise direction.
O Blessed One, having offered a bali-oblation toward all directions together with water, along with sesame-water, honey, clarified butter, fragrance, and flowers; Pausa 31.156.

Once the offering of the bali has been made from the sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa) as if it were outside the mandala, the rite for the ancestors should be performed before the fire with cooked rice, as previously described.

Having sipped water and worshipped the goat from the pitcher, the sacrificial pit, and the mandala, he should then eat with forbearance for the sake of worship, being honored according to the prescribed rule. (Pauṣa 31.158)
Having fumigated it together with its limbs and its retinue in due order,
one should then offer a prayer for forbearance with waterless flowers and other offerings.
Having completed the worship of the fire and having prostrated according to the rule,
one should internalize its power within oneself by means of the heart-mantra and the *saṃhāra-mudrā*.

Having set aside the *sruk* and *sruva* ladles, he should perform the sprinkling with water around the sacrificial ground and upon his own head, taking up the water that has been brought forward. (Pauṣkara 31.161)
Then, having withdrawn that Acyuta who resides in the heart by means of the two [mantras],
and having performed the withdrawal of the sacrificial bed, one should then [bathe him] with honey, milk, and water.
O Lotus-born One, having reached the river Yamunā,
he cast everything into the water and, after performing the preliminary rites of offering (arghya), collected [the materials].
For the sake of favoring the disciple, one should perform the subsequent sacrifice (anuyāga);
the sacrifice for the Guru should indeed be performed in the same manner as the sacrifice to the Bhagavat.
Having given [the initiation] to the disciple, he should then depart once the self-sacrifice has been performed;
from this day forward, he should practice the propitiation of the mantra according to the rule.
O son of the Lord, one should not intentionally, with a mind characterized by faults such as delusion or laziness, neglect the worship [of the deity]. Paus_31.166.

Likewise, during the recitation of mantras, in the fire-chamber, at the time of bathing, in giving gifts as prescribed, in the chanting of hymns of praise, in reflecting upon the scriptures, and also in listening to them; Pausa 31.167.

Having performed a prostration at his feet and having received his command upon their heads, those of fortunate intellect, whose souls were devoted to Nārāyaṇa, [listened] to the exposition. (Pausa 31.168)
Then one should perform the sustenance of life by consuming the food offering (naivedya) and so forth;
for those who have observed the fast partake of the supreme meal of the Lord.

Those men whose bodies have been purified by what remains after the gift [of their flesh] are indeed worthy of salutation and honor among men, due to their continuous attainment of spiritual perfection.
The true nature of the self is always to be understood as that which has been ordained for him;
by means of that very self and through that sacrificial food, one accomplishes the realization of the self.
Know that to be the subsequent sacrifice performed by oneself within the self, which is offered with water and fruits remaining from the sacrificial feast. (Pauṣkara 31.172)
Those who daily perform the consumption [of the substance] before their meal do so for the purpose of seizing power over the vital breath (prāṇa), or indeed out of necessity. (Pauṣkara 31.173)
Endowed with heartfelt devotion, established on the true path, and firm in their vows,
they go without effort to the imperishable state at the end of the body.
Those men of meritorious deeds who observe this divine vow stand at the head of all those who observe vows and perform sacrifices.
One should understand that this auspicious act of sowing is again considered an offering made according to the proper rite to Viṣṇu, who is the essence of both mantra and Brahman. Paus 31.176.
This is that immortal Brahman; this is imperishable life;
this is knowledge, this is vigor, and this indeed is the splendor of Viṣṇu.
This very moon, remaining unbroken, exists by itself in the form of food;
the Lord Parjanya, for the sake of the perfection of the seasoning, resides within it.
The Supreme Lord, as the presiding witness, experiences [the world] through the nature of the fire within the heart;
because he is favored by that power, he is the person who has entered into primordial nature (prakṛti). 31.179.
In this way, the giver of food is to be known as the eater of food, and the food stands before him;
through the giving of his own [gift] to others, he attains full awakening.
Just as the powerful digestive fire residing within the body proceeds with water,
it acts as the cause for the sixfold taste of the six kinds of food.
Then, by means of that subtle cause, he should bring the selves into a state of presence as the Brahman-self; thereafter, he should slowly offer the food oblation.
Having divided [the mantra] into four parts by means of its final syllables, first with regard to the fourfold self,
one should offer three oblations solely by virtue of the requirement for the fourth.
Then, with a focused heart and the root mantra, one should eat morsel by morsel; finally, with mouth and hands purified, one should drink [water] consecrated by the mantra.
Or else, that water may be one that has flowed from the lotus-feet of his meditation,
or it may be that which previously resided in him who bore his form.
For all that has been attained brings about the destruction of all defects,
always pacifies all afflictions, and bestows all happiness.
O Lotus-born One, it is more purifying than all other sacred fords and mantras;
therefore, at the conclusion of a meal, the supreme gratification of the fire within the heart must indeed be performed. (Pauṣa 31.187)
Constantly devoted to heartfelt devotion, one should drink [the water] like clarified butter or milk;
while drinking at the Brahma-tīrtha, one should recite [the mantra] twice or four times in succession.
Furthermore, the incomparable majesty of that food which remains after giving—known as *prāpaṇa*—should be understood exactly as it has been described. (Pauṣa 31.189)
At the conclusion of the sacrifice, one should always offer libations to the worthy devotees, to the Supreme Lord,
and to the ancestors, out of compassion and for the pleasure of the All-pervading One.
He who knows thus the greatness of both the food offering and Acyuta,
and partakes of it according to the prescribed rite, attains equality with Acyuta.
By one who knows the vow, and especially by a devotee of the Source of the World, it must indeed always be protected even more than one's own life. (Pauṣa 31.192)
By means of this proper procedure, beginning with the gift of food and according to one's capacity,
the Supreme Lord indeed attains supreme delight for that person.
Whoever offers food, which is the supreme Brahman in embodied form, as worship, by him everything has been given to those who know the true nature of the Blessed One. (Pauṣa 31.194)
But at the conclusion of the vow, in sacred places such as shrines and the like, during auspicious moments characterized by favorable lunar days and astrological ascendants, ||| Pausa 31.195 |||
Having made an inexhaustible offering to the Blessed One, one attains the inexhaustible;
for when that is presented before the worthy recipients, Adhokṣaja is thereby satisfied.
One who is intent upon his own spiritual practice must strive to avoid those who are unworthy vessels, those who lack devotion, atheists, and the evil-minded. (Pauṣa 31.197)

For women, Śūdras, and animals—especially those who have eaten [forbidden food]—whether he is possessed of desire or free from desire, the knower of mantras remains steadfast in his virtuous vows. (Pauṣa 31.198)

For he who offers as an oblation what has been purified by mantra, even if he is already a perfected one (siddha), falls into a state of sin; how much more so, then, for one who merely desires to ascend? (Pauṣkara 31.199)
Pauṣkara said:
"O Lord of Gods, I wish to know that very compendium of the duties of the Blessed One which was briefly indicated by you as being worldly."

The Blessed One said: "Whether with abundant wealth or even a small amount acquired through righteous means, having dedicated it to the infallible Lord (Acyuta), whether it be auspicious or inauspicious," Pausha 31.201.
Whatever is offered for the pleasure of the Blessed One by those members of the assembly who are absorbed in him,
is remembered as being like a sacrifice that yields its own fruit and bestows heaven, even though it is traditionally known as such.
For those who possess desire, it indeed bestows that very fruit even there;
but for devotees who are free from desire, it surely grants the world of Acyuta.
Various austerities such as the *kṛcchra* and *cāndrāyaṇa* were performed for the sake of pleasing the Blessed One, granting whatever was desired.
Indeed, whatever is intended for these [deities] for as long as one lives,
that which is accepted for the sake of pleasing the Supreme Lord must be free from sweat.
That fruit indeed ripens in no time at all through the nature of divine knowledge;
having attained a meritorious field, one becomes imperishable there.
Or, on dry land, the practitioner who constantly worships with leaves, flowers, and so forth,
with devotion and with a mind focused on nothing else— at the end of his body, for that embodied soul— Pausa 31.207.
Through the grace of the God of gods, his status shall be universal;
he shall receive worship like that of Viṣṇu for as long as he lives.
At the time of the body's end, the wise man, devoted to devotion and faith and solely intent upon Nārāyaṇa, goes to Śvetadvīpa.
O Mahāmati, they shall travel by those celestial chariots along that path before long,
[passing] through well-known, fragrant, and auspicious trees with delightful fruits.

The first group consists of the verses ending with “*arcirādyān mahāmate*” [1.26–35]. Subsequently, the second group consists of nineteen and a half verses beginning with “*vibhavavyūha*” and ending with “*dehapādāmbupūrvaṃ tu tilasatphalacarvaṇam*” [2.1–19½]. And furthermore:

The twenty-two verses beginning with “suprasiddhaiḥ” and ending with “tadbhūtadarśitenaiva mārgeṇa mahatā mune” constitute the third group; after this follows the verse beginning with “kṛtvā cāghrāya.”
Having begun thus, it concludes with the chapter: "The fourth group, as in the second section—
whereas the first, second,
and third groups are written as before, the beginning of the fourth is different, as follows:"
Immediately after the third group, having again written the second group up to its end and set aside the third group,
the fourth group has been written in its entirety as a continuous sequence; thus, in both sections of the treasury,
the very reason for the inversion is the writing of the second and third groups in reverse order— here it is as follows.
Samādhi is the state in which the second and fourth heaps remain with their junctional bond unperceived; it sews together the sequence of the text and does not disjoin it.
Furthermore, as for that third group which has fallen in between, it cannot be reconciled in any way whatsoever with the fourth group.
On the contrary, it becomes well-joined with the first group and reaches its proper occasion;
beyond this, the second group is appropriately introduced.
It sustains the sequential order of the treatise;
therefore, following what has been shown, the arrangement of the text has been established.
Beyond this, the wise are the authority.
Whoever worships Acyuta with devotion in a forest or in the midst of mountains attains many desired objects, even those not sought after.
At the end of his body, he will be worshipped like the Blessed One by Indra and the other gods, either in a divine Vaiṣṇava temple or in one established by perfected beings or by men. (Pauṣa 31.212)
One should perform the great ritual action with a focused mind and devotion, including bathing with milk and other substances,
and anointing with sandalwood, agallochum, camphor, and bāhlīka.
O twice-born one, he should indeed wrap himself with divine, incomparable garments that are white, yellow, and reddish, along with an auspicious upper cloth and a sacred thread.
When wealth is available, one should then adorn [the image] with ornaments made of gold and inlaid with jewels,
and further decorate it with flowers down to the feet.
One should offer incense with auspicious guggulu resin sprinkled with clarified butter,
and with abundant great lamps filled with sesame oil and clarified butter.
Immediately after that, one should worship with interwoven offerings of unbleached, unwashed, very white, and dyed cloths,
which enclose within them cinnamon, cardamom, and other fragrant substances.
Then, having worshipped the Lord with curd mixed with honey and clarified butter, and with various pure offerings of food consisting of edible fruits and roots; Paus_31.218.
With purifying, clear, cool, and sweet drinks,
seasoned with cinnamon, cardamom, and other spices, fried, and scented with incense and camphor.
Immediately thereafter, [the deity] should be satiated with coconut water;
for the purpose of the food offering and the sipping of water, unsurpassed scented water should be offered.
Then [he should wear] white, unwashed, and large garments, or else those that have been squeezed dry;
furthermore, they should be infused with powdered camphor and rubbed with sandalwood paste.
And having offered excellent betel-leaf together with areca nuts, as well as rice, pulses, grains, sesame seeds, and white mustard; Paus 31.222.
Yellow pigment, the śrīphala fruit, flowers, dūrvā grass, the dhātrī fruit, curd,
new white silk cloth, and a white lotus that spirals to the right.

Having placed [the vessel] in a bowl made of metal, bamboo, or even wood, covered with leaves such as those of the *tamāla* tree, and having filled it with water for the guest-offering (*arghya*) along with flowers, one should then set [the object of worship] in its center.
Having placed his knees upon the ground and bowing his head, he should offer gold and silver of pure quality according to his own means. (Pauṣa 31.225)
O best of the twice-born, having taken [the offering] with both hands palms-upward and presented it to the Lord of the World for the sake of fulfilling all enjoyments— Pausa 31.226.
By which there is the attainment of all future desires for those seeking the fruit of reality;
indeed, by which [the self] is to be joined with the Supreme Self for those who are truly free from desire. (Pauṣa 31.227)
Leather items such as shoes and the like, other objects of enjoyment, those consisting of beds and seats, and stringed musical instruments; Paus_31.228 //
Beholding those vast [structures], which were bounded by cracked mṛdaṅga drums and noble company, and which, through his own discernment, bestowed joy upon his mind; (Pauṣa 31.229)

When all [the materials] are available, one should perform the sacrifice with the mind; when they are not available, one should sacrifice according to the power of faith and devotion, even with things that are not the most excellent.
Having enjoyed pleasures at will in the realms of heaven and other such true abodes, they shall,
after a period of time, [return] by the power of the Goddess's will.
O Sage, by means of that very great path consisting of the vision of reality,
he remains for many hundreds of eons amidst the manifestations and arrays of worlds.
Having attained gnosis there, he then descends to the surface of the earth and suddenly enters into dissolution within the Blessed One, whose nature is immeasurable.

This worship of the Immovable One, performed according to the sacred sites, shrines, and holy fords, has been briefly described for the sake of the devotees' peace from worldly existence. (Pauṣa 31.234)
Now, listen to the worship of Hari based on which time-period,
for the sake of destroying the worldly existence of devotees whose souls are solely intent upon Viṣṇu. (Pauṣa 31.235)
Furthermore, on auspicious days, one should perform sacrifices with abundant, purifying enjoyments acquired through righteous means, with faith and devotion.
At the times designated for specific rites, one should always remain undisturbed,
even during auspicious planetary conjunctions (lagna) and moments (kṣaṇa) known as celestial, atmospheric, and terrestrial.
Especially on the twelfth days of both fortnights,
and on those days well-known in the local tradition as recognized from other scriptures.

On days such as the *parividdha*, which are otherwise unsuitable for rites of honor because they involve the worship of other deities, one may instead perform [the rite] with milk, roots, fruits, and so forth. Pausa 31.239.
Then, for the purpose of cleansing the stomach, one should drink the five products of the cow (pañcagavya),
which has been infused with water from the feet of the image of the Blessed One and placed in a vessel made of leaves.
Together with water purified by gold, *darbha* grass, and excellent jewels,
and having likewise observed the fast, one should worship Keśava as before.
Having gratified the lotus-eyed Acyuta with gifts of gold, food, water, cows, land, black antelope skins, and so forth, as well as with offerings presented to him. (Pauṣa 31.242)
Having received that command upon his head, whoever bestows it upon one who is absorbed in Him, that seeker of fruit through devotion will surely attain the state of the Blessed One. (Pauṣa 31.243)
Furthermore, O Mahāmati, for one who seeks its fruit, the fruit of divine existence arises swiftly even after many hundreds of millions of eons.
For one endowed with long life, health, good servants, sons, wealth, and a wife,
the astrological calculation for the auspicious moment and whatever ritual has been forgotten must be performed.
Having first completed the remainder with a mind full of vigilance, one should complete the remaining ritual acts when the auspicious hour has arrived. (Pauṣa 31.246)

Having offered water for the feet, flowers, and so forth, along with golden cows and other gifts until the conclusion, [the rite lasts] for two days, one day, or a night, or indeed for three days or six days. (Pauṣa 31.247)
Having spent twelve days and two fortnights according to the prescribed rule,
prior to the day concluding the vow, one should perform the ritual vigil and other such observances.
It should be spent without sloth through recitation, fire-offerings, worship, meditation, prostrations, circumambulations, meritorious narratives, and hymns of praise. (Pauṣa 31.249)
Then, at the time of dawn, or during the night, or on an auspicious day,
one should perform the rites beginning with the bath and ending with the oblation into the fire of the vital breaths.
O twice-born one, it is improper to eat at night without the rising of the sun;
however, having prepared *siddhānna* (cooked food) accompanied by water for the twice-born, [one may do so]. (Pauṣa 31.251)

And one should offer before the Blessed Lady well-prepared oblations combined with clarified butter, preceded by water from the feet of the deity, as well as sesame seeds, excellent fruits, and chewed offerings. (Pauṣa 31.252)
Having offered the food oblation and smelled it, one should indeed touch it again;
before eating, one should partake of it for the sake of destroying inauspiciousness. (Pauṣa 31.253)
This very dawning of the day should always be saluted by those who know the vows and are absorbed in the Blessed One, for the sake of attaining bliss, happiness, and good fortune. (Pauṣa 31.254)
From the day the vow begins,
one who desires a good rebirth for their offspring must diligently avoid [these things] throughout the entire duration of the vow.
A day free from affliction by others should always be accepted as pure;
however, if it is joined with a portion of the preceding day, it is even more significant.
If the day of fasting is joined with even a small portion of the preceding day, it is always established as such in the world. (Pauṣa 31.257)
But for those devoted to fasting, that [eating] shall not bring about any fault; for such is the vow of devotees free from desire, O you who are intent on vows. (Pauṣa 31.258)

For those seeking fruits, who are subject to rebirth and whose minds are devoted to the power of karma, fasting is forbidden; for it has been established that even eating is permitted [in their case]. (Pauṣa 31.259)
Then, for the sake of bowing down to those devotees,
they approach them so that no turbidity arises in the mind during the worship of Acyuta.

For those who are unable even to observe fasts, yet whose souls delight in ritual action and the Brahman, know that they should always practice every form of giving, provided it does not cause suffering to others. (Pauṣa 31.261)
On this day, like one who has observed a fast,
being filled with the Blessed One and incapable of other duties, one should worship the Guru as soon as he has arrived.
Indeed, for the sake of the livelihood of the Teacher of the World, one should request patience with contentment,
whether it lasts for half a day, or less than that, or more.

Having thus joined the current day with the preceding one, and having made the following day stand before him, if he should perform his daily vow of eating only at night (nakta), making this his firm resolve; Paus_31.264.
On the day of the vow, by concluding all acts of giving at their final point, a fruit superior to that of ordinary fasting is produced for him. (Pauṣa 31.265)
On that very day, one who observes the fast should perform the sacrifice to the Self through the constant worship and other rites of Viśveśa until the end of that day.

If that which was performed on the following day remains incomplete, it will become as if it had not been done; otherwise, know that there is a contradiction for the embodied being who has already accomplished his purpose.

Through the renunciation of what is inexhaustible and through the power of non-grasping, one should first understand what is to be abandoned and what is to be adopted regarding guests who cause suffering to others. Pausha 31.268.
Having understood this, Vāsudeva, the infallible Lord who is the self of the lords of the lunar days,
should indeed be worshipped in due order by those observing fasts at the beginning of the festival and other occasions.
On both fortnights, or indeed during the bright fortnight according to one's wish,
the Lord whose self is the Grandfather (Brahmā), born from the lotus, [is worshipped] there on that first day.

And he should be worshipped according to the rules with a mind endowed with devotion, whether by one who possesses both the lotus and the elephant, or by one who worships with only one of them. (Pauṣa 31.271)
Having duly exhausted [the previous vows] with golden gifts according to his capacity,
the Creator himself becomes Hari on the second and third lunar days.
Then, on the fourth day, one should honor the self of Saṃyamana;
on the fifth day, the self of Amṛta; and on the sixth day, Śaktiśa.
On the seventh day he is indeed Jñānamūrti, and immediately after that, Viśvātmā;
then on the ninth day he is Siddhātmā, and thereafter the Blessed One is Dharmātmā.
Then on the thirteenth day, O great-minded one, he is the Īśāna-self, the Lord of Gods; then the Sūrya-self, the illuminator of the directions; then the Kāma-self; and then the Kalā-self.

The Blessed One, whose very self is the notion of the Father, is these various manifestations of the Lord of the World; they exist for the sake of those entitled to perform rites for specific desires, and for the constant attainment of what is desired.
One should worship [the deity] with offerings such as water for the feet and flowers accompanied by ritual acts;
for the sake of worship, one should sacrifice to Brahmā on the first day for the duration of a year.
Thus, one who desires the perfection of speech should worship the immutable Lord Dhātṛ, and Hari for the sake of destroying obstacles to liberation and for its attainment as well. (Pauṣa 31.278)
Then, for the pacification of unrighteousness, one should worship Yama, the restrainer;
and on the fifth lunar day, for the sake of increasing longevity and health, one should worship Amṛteśvara.
One should worship the infallible Śaktīśa on the sixth lunar day for the sake of attaining the power of Indra;
furthermore, one should properly worship the Lord of that Day in order to attain self-awareness.
Then, for the sake of abundance among the three kinds of accomplishments, the Soul of the Universe [is worshipped];
thereafter, for the sake of attainment, he who effects the acquisition of the true Dharma [worships] the Lord of the Ninth Night.
O great-minded one, on the tenth day, one should worship the Sun, the Lord of that day;
and on the eleventh day, a seeker of knowledge should worship Maheśvara, the Lord of Knowledge.
On the twelfth day, for the sake of great splendor and power, one should worship his lord;
and on the thirteenth day, for the sake of obtaining various women and jewels, one should worship his husband.
Then, for the sake of victory over Time and the deaths brought by Time, one should always worship Kālātman;
and for the pacification of the threefold debt, one should worship the Supreme Lord.
Thus, the lord of the fifteenth day (the Moon) is always to be honored;
even though, O twice-born one, it has been stated that the lords of the lunar days are to be worshipped on those respective days. (Pausa 31.285)
This is ordained for those twice-born who are single-mindedly devoted and who do not seek rewards,
on the eleventh day of both fortnights.

Even if two lunar days are mentioned by means of two lords of the lunar days, that which is prescribed as causing pain to others, or which is undesirable or reversed, [is to be avoided]. (Pauṣa 31.287)
"Even so, O best of the twice-born, the Ekādaśī and other such observances are secondary; they are not primary, for Acyuta is the primary reality. (Pauṣa 31.288)
For it is not only that, O Pauṣkara, but the entire web of other entities as well,
and even the sages who are the teachers of this conceptual proliferation.
Thus, everything has been set forth out of a desire to bestow grace upon devotees;
this [teaching], which is entirely composed of the Supreme Fullness, has been proclaimed from the state of the Lord of the Perfect State (Pūrṇabhāveśvara).
For the sake of his vows, he had made a sincere resolution for the fasts of the year,
preceded by the ritual casting of water.
In the twelfth month of that year, on the twelfth lunar day, all the concluding offerings of the Anuyāga were performed; otherwise, the fruit of the annual rite would not be attained.
Worship performed on the thirteenth day surely comes to naught;
one should instead perform it on the eleventh day, which is desired at will.

O Brahmin, for the sake of attaining the fruits of the three goals of life, one devoted to vows should perform a vow lasting one night or more with devotion, even without [seeking] those specific fruits. Paus 31.294.
Because he is unattached to all things, no fault arises for him;
he should perform the sacrifice and the self-offering on the thirteenth lunar day with a joyful mind.

Or, O twice-born one, when it is mixed with the Dharma, it lasts for a period ending at the first watch; however, when it is deficient or excessive by a watch, it is called the "twelvefold" [period]. (Pauṣa 31.296)
O Mahāmati, on the thirteenth day, having especially avoided it through lack of exertion and desire, [the moon] attains the state of being a constituent part [of the lunar day].
On the thirteenth day, he should perform his duties according to his own understanding; for that Vaiṣṇava who fails to do so, there will indeed be a great transgression.
For one who knows the mantras, the propitiation of the twice-born is superior even to that of the gods;
for one who knows the mantras, there is worship, fire-offerings, recitation, and giving according to one's own capacity. (Pauṣa 31.299)
Being joyful, observant of vows, and devoted to ritual action, one should exert effort so that the entire procedure of the primary rite is always successfully accomplished. (Pauṣa 31.300)
For those who have approached with devotion, free from deceit and guile, and who primarily observe their vows correctly, it is remembered that [the practice] is equal for all. (Pauṣa 31.301)
Lord Hari, the sovereign of all, truly dwells within the heart of everyone;
he knows their true intent and bestows a fruit corresponding to it.
Gold, gems, water, the six flavors, sesame seeds, clarified butter, a sacred thread, an umbrella, sandals, clothing, cattle, and land; Paus 31.303.
And by offering fragrant lamps, vessels, excellent fruits, and desirable objects collectively, these [deities] become granters of all desires. (Pauṣa 31.304)
Therefore, on the twelfth day (dvādaśī) falling on a Thursday, the two protectors of the ocean's depths should be propitiated with jars containing the wish-fulfilling cow (kāmadhenu).

For the sake of all desires, for the welfare of all sentient beings, for the purpose of destroying all dualities, and for the satisfaction of the ancestors, [he prepared] the water-pot for the Lord. (Pauṣa 31.306)
By this gift known as the "wish-fulfilling cow," the Supreme Lord, who is intent on the upliftment of the world, attains supreme delight. (Pauṣa 31.307)

Having considered the place, time, and other factors, the Imperishable One (Acyuta) should be worshipped with faith either at home or in a temple; thus, he becomes truly offered according to the prescribed rule.
If not, then it becomes an auxiliary [to merit] by virtue of the power of its inherent nature,
just as the water at the confluence of the Gaṅgā and Yamunā is a sacred ford (tīrtha) because of the presence of two waters.
Thus ends the thirty-first chapter, titled "The Dharma of the World," in the *Pauṣkara-saṃhitā*, a great Upaniṣad within the illustrious *Pāñcarātra*.
Śrī.
Now begins the thirty-second chapter.
Pauṣkara said:
"O Blessed One, Lord of the past and the future, for men who are devoted to mantras and sacrifices..."
What, however, would result from the thorough knowledge of that worship performed with conscious intent?

The Blessed One said: "O one of great intelligence, having first formed a formal resolve (*saṃkalpa*) accompanied by mantra during the worship with mantras, one should continue without despondency for as long as one lives. (Pauṣa 32.2)
And the rites for the deities who have been invoked must be performed with effort through action, mind, and speech, according to one's power and according to one's means. (Pauṣa 32.3)

When birth-impurity (sūtaka) or similar conditions have arisen due to lack of independence or incapacity, one should then worship the Guru according to the rules, preceded by formal supplication. (Pauṣa 32.4)
O Lotus-born One, [one should not look upon] a self-restrained son of the guru, a brother initiated together with oneself, or a younger or elder [brother], otherwise. (Pauṣa 32.5)
The expiation would be severe prior to the cessation of the initial resolve;
for others, however, their own respective mantras, mudrās, and so forth, are indeed half of that.
When the time for transmission has arrived, those men who have attained perfect accomplishment must not fail to speak;
yet he who, out of delusion, reveals his own mantras, mudrās, and so forth [to the uninitiated], [commits a fault]. (Pauṣa 32.7)
O twice-born one, for those others who are non-devotees, Mantreśvara,
together with his host of Siddhas, turns his face away from them. (Pauṣa 32.8)
And having caused great suffering, the officiating priests must therefore, with great effort,
keep their own mantra secret along with its ritual application.
Except for the guru, the son, the wife, and a sincere disciple, one should not perform the ritual of satiating the mantra-deities or worship in the presence of others. (Pauṣa 32.10)
In that regard, the one born from the lotus, being intent on what must be done, should recite the mantra mentally, but he should conceal the visualization of the mantra. (Pauṣkara 32.11)

Just as one indeed becomes a partaker of success through the mudrās and the rosary, so too is it [the case] for one who, without the formal undertaking of the mantra, [attains the same]. (Pausa 32.12)

Having consecrated an image of a deity with devotion and installed it in one's own home, one should employ it in worship, provided that one possesses the requisite capacity and other necessary qualifications. (Pauṣa 32.13)
A lord of the twice-born, knowing the five times of ritual observance and devoted to the six duties, should, when possible, maintain his livelihood in a constant and lawful manner.
That by which you possess an eternal fruit in this world and the next was not done through the oppression of others, nor out of fear, nor through deceit.

A wise person should worship the deity both regularly and on special occasions, for the sake of attaining fully complete results; this is the characteristic of the conduct of the virtuous. (Pauṣa 32.16)
For that purpose, he by whom worship was previously undertaken as a constant duty would indeed incur a transgression through its omission; therefore, he shall partake in the fruit of that [omission].

Therefore, one who desires merit should not speak thus regarding the cessation of ritual activity—whether it concerns occasional rites or the constant worship of those who are appointed [to the task]. (Pauṣa 32.18)

O Mahāmati, whatever means of subsistence one enjoys from anyone—whether they reside outside or are established within one's own house—and for whatever purpose it is intended; [that is what is meant here].
The fruit of that [action] arises from its cause, and the entirety of it proceeds from that very cause;
therefore, one who is devoted to spiritual practice should not neglect his livelihood.
O twice-born one, having understood through the mind the true inner disposition of householders who seek the mantra-form [of the deity], the deity indeed manifests to both. (Pauṣa 32.21)
"O Lotus-born One, knowing thus the true nature of the scriptures, one should apply oneself with effort; [the scripture] properly bestows the fruit or brings about an obstacle. (Pausa 32.22)

No form whatsoever belonging to the fourfold self of the All-pervading Lord— whether it be his essential nature or his majestic manifestation— should be disregarded, for it is preceded by wisdom and accompanied by a mind free from pride.

That image, whether fashioned from stone or wood, or painted on a cloth or a wall, should always be worshipped according to one's own capacity during periods of birth-impurity and other such times. (Pauṣkara 32.24)
Having recognized the time appropriate for one's lineage, one should protect the [lineage] by performing one's respective duties with a mind purified by faith. (Pausa 32.25)
One should perform worship until the time when [the image] becomes stainless;
for the sake of atonement, one should again perform worship preceded by a bath. (Pauṣa 32.26)
Having offered oblations into the fire according to the rules with devotion, one must also give sacrificial fees (dakṣiṇā) to the preceptor and others;
otherwise, there will indeed be atonement for the worshipper, O Brahmin.
Because men fail to worship the deities who have been installed within their homes, as well as those deities who are manifest [in images], [they suffer]. (Pauṣa 32.28)
O Lotus-born One, if this alone bestows such auspiciousness, how much more so when it is performed according to the rules, in its entirety, and endowed with all the necessary materials?
O twice-born one, together with the attainment of enjoyments, through devotion accompanied by faith, by following the path of right conduct, and with a perfectly purified intellect— Pausa 32.30.

The worship of the deities through mantras, mudrās, postures, and meditations, performed by the officiating priests as they are, constantly brings about the accomplishment of their goals. (Pauṣa 32.31)
Knowing this, O Lotus-born One, one who fears cyclic existence should not harbor pride regarding the failure to worship the gods during rites performed for specific desires or occasional observances.
And especially every day, let there be an obstacle for you [and others] through the separation from Brahmins and other devotees. (Pauṣa 32.33)

O Pauṣkara, having performed the bath appropriate for the gods and the ancestors, one should thereafter perform breath control (prāṇāyāma) and recitation (japa), primarily for those who follow [the path]. (Pauṣkara 32.34)
And from the practice of those great mantras and the scripture known as the Siddhānta, a fruit far superior to all else is obtained. (Pauṣkara 32.35)
And so, O Lotus-born One, the worldly conduct of gods, asuras, and humans is seen in this world to be born of their own inherent nature.
All those belonging to the various castes and stages of life were endowed with their own innate qualities as prescribed by birth;
they were masters of the Purāṇas and Smṛtis, and knowers of the Vedas and Vedānta.
O Mahāmati, even sages who are devoted to their own duties and the nature of reality do not attain supreme accomplishment without the grasping of mantras. (Pausa 32.38)
Why then do men of dull intellect practice the rituals prescribed by the Siddhānta and serve those who follow it for the sake of greed and delusion? (Pauṣa 32.39)

Having understood this, one should apply effort to the practice of mantra-adoration, to the propitiation of the gurus, and to the deep study of the established doctrines and other scriptures. (Pauṣa 32.40)
O one of stainless vision, because those who are devoted to that [knowledge] attain perfect liberation directly, it is not so for others whose nature is addicted to dry logic. (Pauṣa 32.41)
And for those devoted to knowledge and action, various perfections arise here;
yet they attain liberation in every way through the perpetual dissolution of the body. (Pauṣa 32.42)
Pauṣkara said: O Lord, I now desire to know the true nature of that ritual action (*karman*) which, when permeated by knowledge, bestows great supernatural power (*maharddhi*) upon practitioners.

The Blessed One said: Whatever consists of the mantras of the creators [of the world] and so forth, situated within the final phonemes of the vowels, indeed becomes a limb for the practitioners of mantra within the web of enjoyments. (Pauṣkara 32.44)
That very [reality] at the beginning must always be thoroughly known by the practitioner as the nature of pure consciousness, vibrating with its own radiance.
It is perfectly filled with the various powers of the instruments known as the objects, the senses, and the elements,
which are mutually either fully awakened or latent.
Furthermore, that which manifests in the form of pride and in enjoyment does so indeed of its own accord for the sake of achieving both worldly enjoyment and liberation. (Pauṣa 32.47)
Well-known by its very characteristic form to those who sacrifice with mantras, it enters into the state of being an auxiliary; such is the nature of its eternal abiding.
And now, O lotus-eyed one, those who have awakened must cast away that expectation of meditative cultivation,
for that object does not exist as a reality.

For those for whom the word of the authoritative teacher is paramount and whose souls delight solely in scripture, the reality of existence is established by the mantra; however, the means to that realization of true being [is the practice]. (Paus 32.50)
For those whose minds have been purified by devotion to the one who has truly descended, the state of being water [in fire] is indeed not logically possible, just as it is for fire. (Pauṣa 32.51)
In this way, the nature of fire can never arise from water; nor is such a reversal ever observed by a practitioner of mantra between these two.
O Lotus-born One, that mantra is indeed a magical illusion for devotees on the auspicious path; it is the impeller [of their progress], characterized by various forms of conviction.
The Blessed One, whose very form is knowledge, desiring to bestow grace upon his devotees, indeed enjoys [the world] himself by means of a portion consisting of the nature of enjoyment. (Pauṣa 32.54)
For the liberation of the officiating priests, however, there is a twofold collection of objects;
therefore, one should constantly practice it according to its two-fold division. (Pauṣa 32.55)
For indeed, when conjoined with knowledge, the agent and the action are thus clearly distinguished;
that which has been received from the mouth of a trustworthy teacher is rendered certain by means of scripture.
O Greatly Wise One, the mantra that has been properly received through the sequence of requests and so forth is indeed adorned by its existence when conjoined with the mudrās. (Pausa 32.57)

Due to negligence on the part of the unenlightened, whose minds are devoted to other activities, that [tradition] has become corrupted by the transposition of vowels and so forth, or has been lost through the omission of vowels and so forth. (Pauṣkara 32.58)
O Lotus-born One, it always produces even greater misfortune for practitioners of mantra there as well, and that very quickly. (Pauṣa 32.59)
Through the power of his extreme devotion, Vāca manifested in many forms;
he was employed in rituals such as bringing [the deity] face-to-face.

By virtue of his power to bestow grace, he grants whatever is desired to those beings who possess true devotion and have surrendered to him, even without following the prescribed sequence. (Pauṣa 32.61)
The Lord of Mantras becomes gracious toward those who have purified their selves in no time at all;
how much more so, O Pauṣkara, for those who are fully perfected in ritual action and knowledge?
And for those who are devoted to faith and have been awakened by their teachers, [the teaching occurs] without words of pride and with speech that gladdens the heart. (Pauṣa 32.63)
And [he taught] the great means of the mantras of the oceans,
which has come down through successive lineage and is indeed eternal, following the succession of gurus.
Then, O twice-born one, there is constant faith in that [truth], followed by its acceptance, and thereafter self-restraint accompanied by devotion and ritual action. (Pauṣa 32.65)
And thereafter, having understood the meaning of the scriptures as well as one's own direct experience,
one should again, with devotion, employ various means.
One who seeks both visible and invisible fruits should always serve a trustworthy person who knows the true scriptures, remaining constantly devoted to the sacred mantras. (Pauṣa 32.67)
O Pauṣkara, when such a possibility exists, one should daily and properly consider all matters concerning his security and well-being according to one's own capacity.
For in this saṃsāra,
it is the Supreme Lord Acyuta who has been set forth as the Guru by the power of the will of Īśvara.
O Great Sage, for one who wishes to advance by means of that [gate], his own mantra should first be recited with intense devotion; this is from the *Pauṣkara*. (Pauṣkara 32.70)
Therefore, out of devotion to the Son, or always during the ritual of the subsequent sacrifice,
one should offer the first portion of the cooked food with a completely satisfied mind.
O one of great intelligence, let it be for now whether he is his own guru or his son,
one who knows the sequence and the scriptures, or another who is single-mindedly devoted, or even one whose nature is the triple Veda.
Having performed his daily rites, well-contented, with thoughts stilled and undisturbed, he was indeed exceedingly devoted and had been entreated for a long time, O high-minded one. (Paus 32.73)

Or else, the one called the accomplishment of one’s own mantra consists of two, six, eight, or six syllables; it is known as *jita*, with the *praṇava* at the beginning and the seed-syllable at the end. (Paus 32.74)
In this way, they should be joined together in one place, like glowing embers rising upwards;
having placed them along with their limbs upon the palm of the hand, [one should project] those [elements], such as consciousness and the rest, into the body.
Taking that ego as his object, he who eats in whose house with favor—
that indeed becomes infinite for him, and it arises for him at that very moment.

But in the mandala and other rites, O Lotus-born One, the Lord of Mantras is not so gratified by all desired enjoyments nor by offerings of clarified butter and the like in the midst of the fire as he is when propitiated [in this way]. (Pausa 32.77)
He attains supreme joy, just as [he did] when it entered the body of his teacher;
therefore, having relied upon the causal sign, he should practice within the interval between [the arising of] opposing factors.
Likewise, O Lotus-born One, within a month, a year, or a period of six months,
one should especially worship one's own mantra in the presence of the Guru.
Thereafter, for the gratification of the ancestors and indeed for his own welfare,
he should worship the preeminent teacher until the end of the night.

Having propitiated [the preceptor] with enjoyments beginning with water for the feet and the arghya offering, up to the massaging of his feet, according to one's ability, and having offered the mother’s wealth as well; Paus 32.81.
O one of great intelligence, having followed him as he departs for his own home and so forth—those who have thus applied themselves to the practice of mantra-attainment; (32.82)
All the social classes, beginning with the foremost of the twice-born and preceded by the student (brahmacārin),
and ending with the mendicant (bhaikṣuka), indeed all of them attain perfection.
Pauṣkara said:
O Lord of the World, in former times, within whose house did the mantra-form exist—whether as one or many, arising from differentiation and characterized by its reflection? (Pauṣkara 32.84)
O twice-born one, [the image] may have been accepted out of devotion previously, or by oneself, or by ancestors;
it may have been installed with mantras, or even deposited by another. (Pauṣa 32.85)
Whether obtained through wealth from another, or from an unsuitable person such as a thief,
it has now been received from one's own guru for the sake of accomplishing both seen and unseen goals.
The mantra that generates clarity of mind and removes the suffering of saṃsāra is that which is applied to it, together with its limbs and its retinue. (Pausa 32.87)
"O Blessed One, has it been ordained for the seeker, or not? Or is there another way?
The Illustrious Lord replied:
"O Brahmin, O twice-born one, that which is self-manifested as well as that which is [established] by the hosts of Maruts."
The form of the accomplishment of mantra has been established by those who are identical with the Blessed One.

O Lotus-born One, the application of the mantras presided over by him, together with his own [application], has been prescribed for the sake of attaining proximity to him for human beings. (Pauṣa 32.89)
Thus, one's own mantra, along with its retinue, should not always be kept in the house;
rather, it should be employed in another form of mantra, beginning with the syllables *pa*, *da*, *i*, *sa*, and *pha*.
O twice-born one, it should be worshipped with its own mantra accompanied by the insignia and limbs; likewise, the mantra should be both enclosed within the image and released from it. (Pauṣa 32.91)
Moreover, O Mahāmati, the placement of all these self-manifested and complete mantras within one another brings about their mutual excellence.
He who is always disciplined in mind in the practice of mantra-adoration shall exhaust the remaining impermanent bondage of karma residing within his body. (Pauṣkara 32.93)
One should be impartial toward all beings and especially toward mantras;
apart from that [which is prohibited], there is no application of one's own mantra to others.
O twice-born one, because for someone, somewhere, and in some way, the mind does not become serene regarding its own self without the arising of pure knowledge, [one should practice]. (Pauṣa 32.95)
Worship with one's own mantra is nowhere prohibited;
rather, it is primarily through one's own path that worship is performed, whether at home or elsewhere in a mandala.
When there is worship according to the rites of mantra and tantra, there is no fault in using materials gathered for the sake of worship with one's own mantra; the same applies in sacred shrines.
When an image or a maṇḍala, having been separated from its path by means of mantra, is consecrated therein, then indeed the vision [of the deity] is ordained. (Paus 32.98)

O Lotus-born One, the offering of flowers is performed with one's own mantra, which is pervasive and free from impurity, because mantras indeed have the nature of pure consciousness alone. (Pauṣkara 32.99)
For the universal, consisting of the Word-Brahman (śabdabrahman), is indeed without distinction;
however, among those [beings], mutual distinctions arise through meditation, ritual placement (nyāsa), and so forth.
One's own mantra, which consists of the Śabdabrahman, arises as variegated and formidable, bestowing the fruits of malevolent rites, yet remaining intent upon grace. (Pauṣa 32.101)
O Lotus-born One, it manifests through the relationship of the sacrificer and the priest;
yet even that which is thus restrained does not manifest here without the cognition of its latent power.
But since it exists as the very self of the Word-Brahman, how can there be any [separate] power, given their identity?
It is like the oneness of space, which cannot exist without two distinct manifestations such as cloth.
Thus, through the two forms of sound, there is unity by way of grace;
and likewise, there is a noble birth from agitation even without a specific sacrifice. (Pauṣa 32.104)
"In one's own home, in a mandala, in a sacrifice, or even in a divine sanctuary," Pauṣkara said,
"O you who pervade the world, I do not see any higher path in this world."
For everything, both stationary and moving, has Vāsudeva as its self.
The Blessed One said:
"This is true, O one of great intelligence, exactly as you have stated it;
however, [it concerns] a living being who is engaged in ritual action and devoted to bhakti."
That in which there is repose in the ultimate sense, which wins over the heart— that indeed is the true path for the seeker; for that is the Vaiṣṇava way, characterized by purity.
He himself, desiring to favor the world,
manifests through the nature of his power and emanations as the pure essence whose self consists of the six qualities.
O Brahmin, know that to be the true path by which one approaches Him through scripture and ritual action—a path that eternally bestows the manifestation of Brahman. (Pauṣkara 32.109)
The pervasive Lord, abiding in the state of both manifestation and dissolution, expands whatever He wills by His own desire.
Having resorted to the natural field, which possesses those qualities and consists of the divine self.
Know that which consists of māyā to be permeated by qualities such as complete knowledge and the rest;
however, know that which consists of the [three] guṇas to be variegated and not entirely pure.
For that scripture which reveals it, as well as the prescribed procedure,
O Brahmin, know that to be a false path when viewed in light of what has preceded.
Therefore, that which is known as the manifestation of power (*vibhava-vyūha*) is remembered as the supreme cause for attaining the state beyond [suffering], the eternal and infallible form.
To those who have quickly sought refuge through action preceded by knowledge—
those performers of rites whose selves are purified— he grants the attainment of the true state.
O Lotus-born One, when the attainment of desired results through ritual acts is at hand, I consider there to be no other means for those who constantly long for enjoyments. (Pausa 32.115)
Having abandoned the extremely subtle and abundant splendor of those who sacrifice to the True Brahman,
the worldly fruit characterized by the attainment of heaven and the like is to be renounced.
For that which is constantly sought through sacrifices and other rites is never relinquished;
therefore, the host of deities belonging to the realm of illusion is not to be propitiated.
Since they have thus attained self-restraint when the true path has been pointed out, therefore, O Lotus-born One, one should always indeed exert effort [in this regard]. (Pauṣa 32.118)
One should indeed perform the propitiation of these mantras with devotion at every opportunity;
through their grace, the threefold suffering comes to an end. (Pauṣa 32.119)
"O Lotus-born One, [there are] the physical, the internal, and the divine.
Pauṣkara said:
"O Blessed One, regarding the constant worship of mantras by those who seek to propitiate them..."
What fruit is there from worshipping with offerings such as leaves and flowers at all times? (Pauṣa 32.120)
What is the fruit for those officiating priests who perform worship for them in detail with many flowers and other offerings? In this matter, I have a great doubt. (Pauṣa 32.121)

The Blessed One said: "O best of the twice-born, equality of fruit is established for devotees who are poor, even without fruits, flowers, and the like, by virtue of their internal devotion. (Pauṣa 32.122)
Whatever fruit is obtained from honoring those who are rich in Vedic learning but devoid of food,
that same fruit is obtained by honoring devoted followers who are always wealthy through fire-offerings and other rites.
Know that for poor devotees who worship with flowers and such,
the characteristic of a day and night is always to be understood as equal to a single moment.
O Lotus-born One, understand also the true meaning of that which pertains to the time of kings and the poor, and which is based on ritual action. Paus 32.125.
O Pauṣkara, one should perform the concentration (dhāraṇā) and meditation (dhyāna) of the mantras together with whatever pure collection of enjoyments has been obtained. Paus_32.126.
Indeed, through the constant and extensive practice of the union of the oceans, the sacrifice performed by those priests will swiftly bestow both worldly enjoyment and liberation. (Pauṣa 32.127)

That which is performed through the meditative concentrations (*dhāraṇā*) and so forth in a condensed manner yields immediate enjoyment; however, that which is achieved through the meditative concentrations and so forth with full ritual elaborations (*saṃbhoga*) results in enjoyment after a long time.
And he bestows upon his devotees the supreme state, devoid of worldly enjoyment;
therefore, for those seeking the highest good, it always leads to the attainment of the fruits of both enjoyment and liberation. (Pauṣa 32.129)
Having secured a portion of time with unwavering and undepressed devotion, one should apply oneself according to the rules, free from all other activities. (Pauṣa 32.130)
The sacrifice is indeed fully complete through the extensive practices such as *dhāraṇā*, even if it is accompanied by the fullness of enjoyments and prosperity for men. (Pauṣa 32.131)
Nevertheless, O Pauṣkara, there remains a superiority for those devoted to ritual action;
for [the attainment of] enjoyment and liberation is seized by deceit, which is clearly eliminated when that [devotion] is performed.
They arise among the officiating priests; therefore, one should not abandon enthusiasm for the constant ritual of mantra-adoration even in the absence of an abundance of material wealth.
For indeed, O Pauṣkara, whether one's state is that of the multitude of enjoyments,
or that of one who is intent on the fruit of attaining enjoyment, it is first for one whose self has not been disciplined.
Furthermore, for those with true discernment, there is no swift destruction of action that is rooted in liberation, eternal, and bestows the goals of human existence.
Pauṣkara said:
Indeed, for those worldly devotees whose minds are constantly distracted by the maintenance of sons, wives, and so forth, being devoted to various types of ritual actions; (Pauṣkara 32.136)
O Acyuta, how is their worship accomplished in detail?
For you have taught that from failing to worship them, the highest fruit is deficiency.
The Blessed One said:
"Indeed, that action which is performed according to the proper sequence brings about the highest good for men;
therefore, it should not be abandoned, whether it be concise or extensive. (Pauṣa 32.138)
O Lotus-born One, for what reason can the primary ritual (mukhyakalpa) in its full detail and the secondary ritual (anukalpa) that follows it be considered equal? Paus 32.139.
And even there, for those who are sincere, devoted, and of purified soul,
worship with leaves, flowers, and the like, along with enjoyments and words, has been prescribed.

O Great-minded One, without the continuity of actions, there is no [result] after a lapse of time—neither that which is called earth, water, fire, and air, nor that which belongs to space. (Pauṣa 32.141)
From the fivefold concentration (dhāraṇā), two abbreviated forms are prescribed— namely,
those called burning and nourishing— for the sake of total purification until the end of the body.
And from meditation on the nature of the supreme and the non-supreme, one [attains] the single, supreme, great heart-mantra for the performance of ritual services among all mantras. (Pauṣkara 32.143)

O Mahāmati, together with the ritual action and the mind, beginning with the syllable *praṇava*, there is indeed one mudrā to be propitiated; that is remembered as belonging to the yoga-mantra. (Paus 32.144)

Through recollection, one should perform the worship of the partless [deity] between the eyes by means of its own names, which contain the *namas* and the *praṇava*, while uttering it oneself. (Pauṣkara 32.145)
The supreme [form] of the mantra-embodiments, performed according to rule, is designated as "swift";
that second [form], characterized by subtlety, is distinguished by the seed-syllables (bījas). Paus. 32.146.

O Lotus-born One, that ritual of all mantras which is performed together with the *piṇḍas* consisting of the nectar of the [mantra’s] characteristics and its designations, up until the end of the recitation (*japa*), is remembered as the "Great" (*bṛhat*). Paus 32.147.
O Lotus-born One, one shall quickly attain absolute liberation after a short interval of time through the first [method],
but through the second, it occurs by means of a gradual process preceded by conscious deliberation.
O one of stainless vision, he bestows here and now the first group of six qualities beginning with knowledge, and the second group of eight beginning with atomization (aṇimā). Pausa 32.149.
But the third, O Pauṣkara, is indeed the sovereignty over all worlds; however, for all [beings], it is equality [only] upon the attainment of the supreme good (niḥśreyasa). Paus_32.150.
Indeed, even though the mantra designated by its own name possesses greatness, it [is mastered] quickly through the threefold time preceded by the [proper] signs. (Paus. 32.151)
Nevertheless, O Lotus-born One, in the worship of the directions beginning with the east,
one should recollect either the seed-syllable or the *piṇḍa-mantra* following the *praṇava*.
O Lotus-born One, this is the inner [mantra] of the Lord of Mantras, as well as of the Heart-mantra and others; it belongs to all other mantras known as "inner. (Paus 32.153)

And for those who abide on the lotus-seat and possess the characteristics of the Pradhāna, there is no contradiction; therefore, O Lotus-born One, they do not require other seeds or physical bodies. (Pausa 32.154)
To Vajralāñchana, Lokeśa, Tadastradhāra, Ārtinām, Tathāsanākhya, Vighneśa, and the eastern door-dwellers; Paus 32.155.
This applies to the celibate student, the independent householder, and even the ascetic;
how much more so for the householder who is devoted to worldly activity?

This indeed is for those who are lifelong celibates, whose souls are devoted to that [state], for practitioners possessing wisdom, and for those dwelling in solitude; it is beneficial for them. (Pauṣa 32.157)
He who, devoted to devotion and faith, correctly accepts and practices it, obtains therein the two-fold fruit previously described; such is the nature of the Self. (Pauṣa 32.158)
Together with the accomplishments of the practitioner, O Great-minded One, may there be no obstacles. (Pauṣa 32.159)
Thus ends the thirty-second chapter, titled "An Investigation into the Omission of Worship," in the Pauṣkara-saṃhitā belonging to the Śrīpāñcarātra together with the Upaniṣads.
Now begins the thirty-third chapter.
Pauṣkara said:
"The prior mode of worship for the Ninefold Form has been understood by me."
The fourfold nature [of the self] was not understood for the sake of liberation due to its manifold diversity.
The Blessed One said:
"From the worship of the Lord who is of fourfold nature, whose true essence is never abandoned, liberation arises; that [liberation] comes from that twofold worship. (Pauṣkara 33.2)
O Brahmin, listen further to the worship performed through various forms for the attainment of various fruits, exactly as it exists in its true state. Pausa 33.3.
One should first worship the all-pervading Supreme Self, the primordial god Adhokṣaja, who is to be honored everywhere, both at the conclusion of the ritual and in the center.
Then, by means of the yoga of emanation, one should worship the four [deities] beginning with Saṃkarṣaṇa and ending with Nārāyaṇa, in order, starting from the eastern petal.
Furthermore, by means of this yoga, from the state of a barren woman or one in distress up to the very end,
one should indeed worship [the deities] beginning with Nārāyaṇa and ending with Saṃkarṣaṇa.
Thus, in the fire-lotus, the group of four beginning with Pradyumna and ending with the deity Śabdabrahmā must indeed always be worshipped. (Pauṣkara 33.7)
On the right, however, beginning with Aniruddha and ending with Garuḍa as the seat,
the arrangement is prescribed, characterized by its origin and dissolution.
Then, one should worship [the deities] beginning with Nārāyaṇa and ending with Nṛsiṃha upon the lotus situated in the western direction;
likewise, one should worship [the deities] beginning with Brahmā and ending with Kṣmādhara upon the lotus situated in the western direction. (Pauṣa 33.9)
Ending with Saṃkarṣaṇa and beginning with Viṣṇu, [these are placed] in the wind and the lotus;
and Nṛkesarin and Varāha, starting from knowledge (jñāna) and so forth, are in the water and the east.
The triad beginning with Saṃkaṣaṇa and that which begins with Kṣmādhara in Īśāna must likewise be honored in sequence according to their respective origins.
O Brahmin, that which was first proclaimed as this group of nine arises from him; such is his power resulting from the worship of those [deities]. (Pauṣa 33.12)
The great [Lord] consists of nine forms;
he bestows the fruit of the fourfold self and the four aims of life upon those who have purified their souls.
For those who desire fruits, various results arise from worshipping these fourfold beings independently and constantly; indeed, such results manifest without delay. (Pauṣkara 33.14)
Whichever first [form] among the four forms of a particular deity has been proclaimed,
its power arises through the worship performed according to that sequence.

Indeed, this much has been said regarding the fruit resulting from the power of one's disposition; for through that, one's vigor and sovereignty are obstructed at the time of creation and dissolution.
That Brahmin was the mantra of those whose form is mantra, possessing incomparable radiance;
he was infinite, self-luminous, and peerless, the very lord of the world.
When there exists the thorough knowledge of the forms of the Supreme Lord, [He],
who is without beginning or end and infinite, becomes manifest for the realization of those engaged in action.

For the sake of accomplishing their deliverance from that [suffering], he himself has come as the Vyūha, manifesting in nine forms through his fourfold nature known as Prāṇa, Icchā, Śabda, and Kāla. (Pauṣkara 33.19)
Of that very Great-Souled God, whose nature is without distinction, who possesses all powers eternally present, and who is ever-arisen; (33.20)
And for those who have been led by the specific joys arising from the knowledge of sound,
I have taught this yoga for the sake of quelling the existence of living beings.
Even that which is not to be abandoned and is non-different from the Supreme Self— the conceptual proliferation of the truly existent— is indeed the perfect agitation that bestows the highest good.
By whose will the wheel of worldly illusion has again emerged, wherein even sages, along with gods and men, become deluded. (Pauṣkara 33.23)
As long as we have not been graced by this supreme one,
who possesses a fourfold nature and is the embodiment of the six qualities, appearing in the form of a human guide.
At the time of his worship, however, whether externally or within the sky of the heart,
one should vividly recollect him, manifest like a *kadamba* flower and radiant with the six qualities.
With a voice that is manifold, consisting of the four castes, and composed solely of vowels and consonants together with the *bindu*. (Pauṣkara 33.26)
But by means of some well-known external offering, which is indeed primary and intended as such, and which grants satisfaction to the mind; Paus 33.27.
O Lotus-born one, having first performed the placement (nyāsa) of his own limbs, which possess all complete qualities,
by means of worship with his own mantras, without distinction of location.
Now, within that mantra-globe resembling a kadamba flower,
[one should meditate] by means of the twelve-syllable mantra, which is indeed indivisible.

Having indeed brought it to manifestation within that [form], one should then establish the limbs and minor limbs according to the sequence of colors in their respective locations, such as the heart and so forth.
Then, [one should place them] on the heart, the head, the crest, the two shoulders, the middle of the hands, the two eyes, the belly, the back, and the two arms. (Pauṣkara-saṃhitā 33.31)
Then, on the two thighs, the pair of knees, and the two feet, the six syllables preceded by the *praṇava* are considered to be the ancillary limbs (*āṅgika*). (Pauṣkara 33.32)
There are others called the six Upāṅgas; hear their characteristics:
that which is well-established, pure, common, and unobstructed. (Pausa 33.33)
That awakened, radiant, and eternal knowledge is directly that which is infallible (acyuta),
by the power of whose own entire collection of energies everything exists.
Furthermore, as the cause of arising, persistence, and dissolution,
it attains a state of particularity through its constituent parts, yet without ever abandoning its own essential nature.
O twice-born one, the heart of the infinite lords of mantras and their mantra-powers, which possess various categories of capability, is like a jewel-lamp.
And likewise, that [nature] which reveals itself as well as strength and the other [qualities], and that sovereignty surpassing all, which is the quality of the Supreme Lord. (Pauṣkara 33.37)
That head of all mantras bestows glorious enjoyment and liberation;
it is indeed the supreme power of the Lord, filled with manifold potencies.
Know that the pure crest-lock (śikhā) is the mantra-essence which carries the fire upward;
it is that fortitude which, other than the vital breath characterized by steadfastness, never wavers.
Know that very thing to be the armor of mantras, for it is their essence of power—
that irresistible vigor, sovereignty, and the source of both manifestation and dissolution.
O Brahmin, that which is the infinite luminosity of the Lord of the World—beyond comparison and of matchless splendor—is the weapon of those whose forms are composed of mantra. (Pauṣa 33.41)
O Mahāmati, through the thorough knowledge of that, that supreme abode is perceived; and for some, it is dissolved together with the heart. (Pauṣa 33.42)
O twice-born one, having indeed abandoned one's own field, one should kindle the established knowledge; for the eye-mantra of mantras arises by the power of the Lord’s will.
In some places, the inner radiance of the four limbs, like that of the letter *ña*,
abides as a support within the jewels of the head, as if it were preceded by the crown.
Therefore, without a verbal description, those offerings consisting of the light of his command should be fully understood through those skilled in the rites of the Blessed One.
Thus, O one born from the Lotus, the bodily posture has been explained for all ritual applications; now hear the definitive rule regarding the ancillary gestures.
For by means of that very quality of knowledge, he always embraces even a slight external object, as well as its subordinate parts and his own belly. (Pauṣa 33.47)
O Mahāmati, others indeed consider it accomplished through metaphorical usage;
