furthermore, that which possesses the nature of a means [is so called] by virtue of its attainment of perfection and liberation.
And regarding all forms of giving, O pure-eyed one, that which is called the "conclusion" (pṛṣṭha)—the subsidiary limb consisting of the fruit of sovereignty—is the second [chapter]. Paus 33.49.

O twice-born one, that manifestation of the All-pervading Lord, whose nature is power, which is both extremely sharp and exceedingly gentle, consists of two aspects; that is the secondary limb known as the arms.

That which is the great field consisting of the manifest power of manifestation, containing manifold seeds, and composed of essence and potency— that is the very nature of that which is called the thighs.
That body of the Omniscient One, which consists of both knowledge and ignorance through His power, is indeed proclaimed as the fifth subsidiary limb (upāṅga) called Jānu. (Pauṣkara 33.52)

O Lotus-eyed One, that power of sustaining which remains unshaken and whose own quality is indeed distinct—that which is called "sustaining" (saṃdhārakatva) is declared to be the name of Your feet. (Pauṣa 33.53)
In the placement of the creation, maintenance, and withdrawal [of the universe], or within one's own self, O Lord,
there is the conceptualization of the primary limbs and secondary sub-limbs preceded by the twelve syllables.
Furthermore, O Supreme Lord, that [mantra], though its form may be deficient or excessive in its constituent parts, consists of very few syllables for those who possess many more. (Pauṣkara 33.55)
Thus they constantly worship me for the sake of ritual practice; moreover, one should honor me within one's own fields by name, with a prostration and the *praṇava*.

For mantras consisting of more syllables, one should perform this in the secondary limbs (upāṅgas); the utterance [of the mantra] occurs together with twelve measures (mānas) plus one syllable. (Paus 33.57)
By virtue of being a general term, she exists as the heart-born (hṛnmayī) indeed,
through the vowels beginning with 'a' or through the consonants beginning with 'ka', together with the bindu.
O best of the twice-born, wherever in ancient cities a gift was bestowed with the hand formed into a fist and mixed with well-prepared betel leaf; Paus_33.59.
The pervasion consisting of the limbs and secondary limbs should be recollected, or else it should be characterized otherwise:
as being free from the limbs and secondary limbs of cognition, and having the nature of the radiance of mantra-knowledge.
That supreme Prakṛti is Speech, whose form is consciousness, stainless and transcendent; she is filled by the Great Self, who is partless and the nature of pure perception.
Just as the body is distinct from the living soul,
so there is the gross element, and therein the subtle one known as the "city of eight" (puryaṣṭaka).
Just as the principle of the self residing in the body experiences enjoyment born of sense objects,
so too does the Lord, having attained full manifestation, take [upon Himself] that same experience.
In every way, however, one should [worship] the Lord of Mantras established in the form by means of his own mantra,
with enjoyments, recitations, various hymns of praise, and offerings to the fire.
Through gifts, distinguished sacrifices, and concluding rites of libation to the ancestors,
one should lead [them] to incomparable joy by means of these ritual applications and their corresponding recitations.
O Pauṣkara, thereafter one should perform the worship of the Mantreśas in due order;
for these are the honors for the Mantreśas, beginning with those who express their respective forms. (Pauṣkara 33.66)
O twice-born one, even for those possessing marks endowed with internal limbs, that [result] occurs in the land of enjoyment;
however, for you, it occurs in the land of enjoyment through your very form.
All those possessing the characteristics as previously described should be meditated upon in sequence,
within the mantra-body and the embodied form, blazing with radiating rays of light.
That supreme mantra-nature, moreover, due to its universal form,
manifests as various names and syllables, and likewise as various forms.
Therefore, O wise one, the gift of an image is not prescribed separately for each individual,
just as other mantras are not [prescribed] separately from the root mantra by means of their individual syllables.
Some lords of mantra have emerged from no cause, endowed with the qualities of speech and power; others, consisting of individual manifestations, [arose] by his will.
The one Lord of All, Ananta, out of compassion for living beings,
abides by his own will in the form of various mantras, just as he desires.

O Brahmin, though by nature she is one, she indeed becomes many for the sake of those great-souled ones who are to be supported; by the will of the Lord of the World, she is established in manifold ways.
That supreme mantra-nature, characterized as Vāsudeva,
has the six qualities as its body and is endowed with all powers, principles, and attributes.
Having become a treasury, she herself is characterized by bliss within her own subtle mantra-form,
which has the nature of pure luminosity.

Through recitation, through remembrance, and through worship of that which resides within one's own manifestation, the practitioner attains that supreme, non-dual, and profoundly peaceful state. (Pauṣkara 33.76)
Thus, for one who worships the imperishable, all-pervading Lord who has attained oneness,
both worldly enjoyment and liberation are held in the palm of his hand.
The Supreme Lord, however, manifests for the sake of revealing the arrays of the powers of their own mantras those whose nature is pure consciousness and who possess qualities such as knowledge.
O Lotus-born One, having by her own will manifested her inherent power of sound— which was previously unmanifested— within that [power], she assumed a body composed of mantra.
Then, endowed with the qualities of omniscience and characterized by the mantras as previously described,
they establish a firm abiding for the sake of favoring living beings.
In the arrangement of the letters, however, which consists of various seed-syllables (*bīja*) as a single mass,
whether solitary or combined, and numbering many, the nature of recitation (*japa*) is present. (Pauṣa 33.81)
The purity of the knower is consciousness presided over by the Lord, which is worshipped by the immortals;
and it is through this that even the ritual mantras attain their efficacy from the very root.
Furthermore, these mantras, whose bodies are sound and whose nature is contemplation,
do not deviate from their essential form, yet they assume manifoldness.
It is diverse due to the influence of various forms, and also due to the influence of various sentient beings;
it is diverse due to the influence of faith and devotion, and again, due to the influence of various fruits.
Furthermore, O Brahmin, due to various castes, various regions, various times, and the diverse application of various means, [the results differ].
And for the sake of the self-realization of those men solely intent on liberation,
as well as for the welfare of living beings whose minds are distracted by sense objects.
Pauṣkara said:
"O Acyuta, you have described the sacrifice for the Lord intended for a practitioner of pure being,
one who has conquered the senses, a devotee, and one who has attained perfection through mantra."
Furthermore, I wish to understand yoga for the sake of conquering reality—

that established knowledge which one who knows mantras obtains according to rule within the supreme state of meditative absorption (*samādhi*), which resembles a lamp unmoved in a windless place. (Pauṣa 33.88)
The Blessed One said:
"I have taught you the yoga of the primary principle (pradhānayoga) immediately following the yoga of action (karmayoga).
That is prescribed for the householder and the sage, but not for one who sacrifices to another. (Pauṣa 33.89)
Likewise, for the Paramahaṃsa who stands outside the world,
I shall therefore describe the yoga of reality, characterized by its distinct stages.

O Pauṣkara, for one who has received initiation for the purification of all principles, [this practice] is performed eternally and directly, without regard for various supernatural powers (*siddhi*). *Pauṣkara-samhitā* 33.91.
For the attainment of liberation and for the pacification of the veil of ignorance,
one abides in the Supreme Self by means of the nature of pure consciousness.

O high-minded one, he remains established within the self of the mantra, which is the very nature of the light of consciousness, having concealed himself through the activity of the yoga of manifold manifestations.
O Lotus-born One, that which remains perfectly concealed by the Supreme, the all-pervading Lord who is the essence of all powers—that is what must always be understood. (Pauṣa 33.94)
For one who has been favored by the Guru, who is devoted solely to the mantra, it is unmixed, incalculable, and perfumed by hundreds of latent impressions (vāsanās). (Pauṣkara 33.95)
That entire web of reality ceases in that way and not otherwise;
therefore, one who has attained the target and is devoted to the system of action [should proceed].
One must constantly practice the conquest of reality for the sake of attaining one's true nature;
having propitiated and meditated upon the all-pervading Self, which consists of all powers.

One should know that [the process] extends from the feet up to the head by means of the presiding deities of the principles (tattva), according to the distinction of locations as described in the initiation (dīkṣā). || 33.98 ||
Then, O twice-born one, like the core of a plantain tree and like a sweetmeat, one should thus practice that stainless yoga in three ways for the sake of attaining that [state]. (Pauṣa 33.99)
But now, from these [causes], there arises a delusion regarding what is similar.
O Lotus-born One, there is sleep, laziness, fatigue, labored breathing, and a vacant gaze.
Know that the characteristic of the six sheaths is obstructed by your own self;
through certainty, one should conquer this by means of the meditation on the weapon-mantra and even by its recitation. (Pauṣkara 33.101)
Having first achieved mastery over the vital winds, such as prāṇa and the others,
and being seated in a comfortable posture, one should indeed mentally worship the feet of the Guru.
Having propitiated [the deity] by means of its pervasiveness and having projected it into the body of one's own form,
one should then practice the mind as residing externally, while maintaining identity with that [deity].
O twice-born one, within the lotus of the heart, in the interior of the universe, is the supreme Brahman consisting of all powers, abiding in three abodes by means of the syllable *praṇava*.

Having practiced through the yoga of repeated cultivation, the twice-born should first meditate upon that; then, indeed, he should perform the practice for the conquest of reality according to this method. (Pauṣa 33.105)

With the heart-mantra (hṛdaya) enclosed by the Praṇava at the beginning and end, or with the mantra of one's own name preceded by it, one should indeed meditate upon the thousand-rayed sun and each individual web of principles (tattva) separately. (Pauṣa 33.106)
Through recitation, the knowledge of reality gradually comes to dissolution;
first into the sound of the *praṇava* as the support, then into the heart-mantra, and thereafter into that which consists of it.
In reality, one should dissolve the sound that bears that name [the syllable OM] into the interior of the Praṇava;
and the Praṇava-sound, which is one's own self, into Hari, who consists of the bliss of the Self. (Pauṣkara 33.108)
In this manner, O twice-born one, one should gradually achieve mastery over the elements beginning with earth, as well as their respective mantras,
and accomplish the complete conquest of one's own internal organs and sense faculties.
Thus, having conquered the thirty-three [gods] by means of the imperishable among the principles (tattvas),
he then [conquers] the mind, the ego, the intellect, and the collection of qualities in succession.
Having meditated upon and recited [the mantra] for *tamas*, *rajas*, and that which is designated as *sattva*, one should abandon them;
then, one should contemplate the subtle [self], designated as the "junction," which is distinct from its own qualities.
Having realized this and then renounced it, one should thereafter conquer the unmanifest,
which is the cause of this aforementioned phenomenal world and of that which follows it.
For one who is settled in various opinions and arisen from one's own conceptual constructions,
the reality of time— consisting of the past, the future, and the present— should therefore be contemplated.
O Great Buddha, that which purifies the infinite proliferation characterized by existence and non-existence—having meditated thus, one should abandon this triad. (Pauṣkara 33.114)
The characteristic of the means is indeed the fourfold characteristic of Dharma;
it is eternal, designated by the names of the powers known as knowledge, action, will, and protection.
One should directly realize [it] through recitation, meditation, and the practice of yoga, proceeding upwards from there;
therefore, O Brahmin, one should take up that which is all-pervading and eternal.
The divine state consisting of the seven consciousnesses should be meditated upon for the pacification of karma;
it is the culmination of the Brahman of Sound, which is to be known as eternally manifest.
The existence of the Supreme Self, who is the very nature of the Brahman of Sound,
who is formless yet possesses that form, consists of six attributes.
Having thoroughly practiced the Śabdabrahman, immediately after the six qualities,
one reaches that which is unutterable, devoid of phonemes, free from veils, and beyond sound.
That indeed expresses the true Brahman; it transcends the realm of speech and is imperishable.
And all [phonemes], consisting of vowels and consonants, are denoters of the forms of all [deities].

And due to their own specific distinctions, there are many [sounds] characterized by the definition of *daśūla*, consisting of the nature of vowels, consonants, phonemes, and articulated sounds (*ghoṣa*),
as well as the tones of passion (*rāga*).
O Great-minded One, there is sound (*dhvani*), the phoneme (*kūṭa*), and likewise the *sphoṭa* ending with the visarga;
from these, which possess mixed forms, [the sentence] arises through effort as the essence of the word (*vākya-tara*).

One who meditates upon this, becoming proficient therein, shall become a partaker of success and a bestower of all accomplishments until liberation; indeed, such a meditator attains the supreme Brahman.
Then, through practice and by pleasing the one who is easily propitiated, he correctly knows that meditation which is distinct from ordinary meditation, O Lotus-born One. (Pauṣa 33.124)

And that which appears externally as manifold within the nature of light and bliss—those two are the most subtle and stainless wave of the Lord who is the referent of the word "Being. (Pauskara 33.125)
Just as he who knows reality proceeds together with [the Self] to the imperishable state,
so too, having attained self-realization from the Supreme Lord, the Highest.

And it shall always belong to those who delight in knowledge and action, who practice faith and self-restraint, who are believers, who have conquered their senses, and who are devoted to the True Being.
This must never be spoken to one who lacks devotion, nor to an atheist,
nor to one who relies on fallacious reasoning, nor to one who has abandoned both ritual action and Brahman.
From the beginning of the night until dawn, that activity of the Supreme Lord is dear to the hearts of those Brahmins who have transcended the world.
Many others, engaged in worldly affairs, are not lords;
they are devoted solely to the void or Brahman, possessed of a mind occupied with the proliferation of speech.
Pauṣkara said:

"O Eternal One, I desire to know, according to the rules, the characteristics of what is to be abandoned and what is to be accepted through the various divisions of the collection of principles; explain that to me."
The Blessed One said:
"Just as the oiliness of milk does not exist apart from it, know that in this same way the Supreme Lord exists within all principles. (Pauṣa 33.132)
One should practice what has been taught regarding meditative absorption (samādhi) as both unity and diversity; for it is through that alone, as before, that one becomes detached and attains it.
That imperishable manifold, beginning from the collection of organs known as the senses and extending up to the highest manifest being, was withdrawn. Paus. 33.134.
Indeed, for those engaged in ritual action, there is a field of experience known as the manifold forms,
which is endowed with the qualities of pleasure and pain, and is firm, consisting of delusion and illusion.
Ignorance, however, increases moment by moment through attachment to that [world];
it dissolves through knowledge. Therefore, O twice-born one, it must indeed be constantly [overcome]. (Paus 33.136)
Although the means to be contemplated through the cultivation of what is to be abandoned is indeed clear for the attainment of the siddhis, even there it remains unstable.

Therefore, O best among the virtuous, having extracted the essence from that, one should employ the means for the perfection of yoga: namely, mind, intellect, ego, and the quality of purity (sattva). Pausa 33.138.
This fourfold group is unmanifest; it ceases upon the attainment of Brahman.
Then there is the divine equipment, characterized by the five powers.

O Mahāmati, that which is known as time, knowledge, action, will, and vital breath is the other eternal [reality] that cannot be abandoned; it brings about the accomplishment of those engaged in ritual action. Pausha 33.140.

Indeed, for the victory over the multitude of principles, for the attainment of the six qualities, for the thorough knowledge of the fourfold self, and for the realization of the Word-Brahman (śabdabrahman); Paus_33.141.
But for the attainment of the bliss of light and for reaching the state beyond conceptual construction,
one should first receive this ninefold method from the mouth of the Guru.
Through the natural state of Acyuta, by means of the reality consisting of the goal and the means,
there is nothing that the practitioner does not attain through direct realization.
Through the victory of accomplished meditation, it always bestows its respective fruit;
for this reason, that which is to be accomplished serves as the means for accomplishing another goal.
And that group of six beginning with knowledge is distinct from the reality of Brahman;
likewise is the group of eight beginning with *aṇiman*. Indeed, whatever else is pleasing [to one] is other than this.
O twice-born one, [he is] origin and dissolution, sovereignty facing every direction, pertaining to the self, pertaining to the divine, and pertaining to the elemental self.

However, regarding the meditative absorption (*samādhi*) on the practice of reality (*tattva*), those who contemplate reality must understand that the collection of principles begins from the state of the Word-Brahman (*śabdabrahma*) and extends down to the earth. (Paus 33.147)
Know that the supreme Brahman within is always common to all;
likewise, that which pertains to the divine should be known as the Praṇava together with its Lord. (Pauṣkara 33.148)
O lotus-eyed one, the respective nature of every [element], whether gross, subtle, or supreme, is to be known as its *adhibhūta* state. (Pauṣa 33.149)
This general method, preceded by internal [meditation], is to be meditated upon everywhere;
I shall now explain it with its specific details—listen with a one-pointed mind.
O twice-born one, the supreme Brahman, which is waveless, should be understood as the inner self within the uncreated Śabdabrahman through many millions of mantras. (Pauṣkara 33.151)

Always abiding in that very [state] by way of the presiding deity (adhidaivata), one should understand the elemental aspect (adhibhūta) to be that which consists of speech and the skin. (Pauṣkara 33.152)
The Śabdabrahman, as described above and known by its six internal qualities,
should be fully understood as the fourfold self, which is beyond form in its divine aspect.

Know that which they describe as the innumerable array of powers (*śaktivyūha*) arising from the qualities (*guṇa*), and which is the specific nature of those [powers], to be the *ādhibhautika* (pertaining to beings). 33.154.
Indeed, whatever sixfold quality belongs entirely to the vital energy (prāṇa-śakti) with respect to the internal self (adhyātma),
that is the eternal, lotus-eyed Vāsudeva with respect to the divine (adhidaivata).
The vital airs, beginning with apāna, which sustain the universe, constitute the *adhibhūta*;
the two powers of knowledge and strength stand as superior to the power of will (*icchā-śakti*).
That which is to be known is the divine (adhidaiva), and the Lord Saṃkarṣaṇa is the supreme;
and that which is power (sāmarthya) resting upon all the principles (tattva) is indeed the elemental (adhibhūta).
O Pauṣkara, know that the two [aspects] called sovereignty and vigor belong to the internal self;
as for the deity of the power of action, it is Pradyumna, the Supreme Lord.
O one of pure vision, the expansion of great light is the *adhibhūta*; that which is ever-arisen is *tejas*; the power (*śakti*) is the *adhyātma* of the twice-born; it is the unmanifest (*avyakta*).
O high-minded one, the triad of the sun, the moon, and fire is proclaimed as the presiding deity; the three unmingled qualities (guṇas) are the corresponding objective realm (adhibhūta).
And the internal function of the three qualities is their own aggregation:
Sattva has fire as its deity, while Rajas has you, the immortal, as its station.
Viṣṇu is the presiding deity over *tamas*; the state of being the sovereign of knowledge is the presiding deity over *sattva*.
O Mahāmati, non-attachment is to be known as the presiding deity over *rajas*. (Pausa 33.162)
For great delusion is proclaimed as the presiding deity over darkness;
internally, consciousness is the quality of the intellect, and its eternal presiding deity is [the element] water.
O Lotus-born one, passion (rāga) is the presiding deity (adhibhūta) of the faculty of sovereignty (aiśvarya);
that which consists of it is the intellect (buddhi) of the principle (tattva) called ego (ahaṅkāra), which is the internal self (adhyātma). Paus. 33.164.
The great Vaiśvānara of Time is to be fully known as the presiding deity (adhidaiva);
furthermore, the greatness of the mind is now explained as the elemental principle (adhibhūta).

Internally, however, the Lord of Creatures, the Boar of Men, is the ego; he is to be known as the deity (*adhidaiva*), while his volition (*saṃkalpa*) is the elemental state (*adhibhūta*). (Pauṣa 33.166)
The mind is traditionally held to be the internal [aspect] of the five sense-faculties;
know that time, the self, and the deity are the presiding powers, while pleasure and so forth are the objective elements.

The manifestation of speech and the other [organs] as the internal self (adhyātma) consists of the twice-born; however, that which pertains to the senses (indriyaka) should be understood as the divine (adhidaiva), known as Viśvarūpa and imperishable (acyuta). Paus 33.168.
O you of stainless vision, that which consists of the eight wombs— namely, activity and the objective world— is the internal state of the subtle elements together with the gross elements.
O Lotus-born one, understand the extremely subtle array of instruments; know the manifold majesty of the Lord’s manifestation as the presiding divinity. (Pauṣa 33.170)

For those seeking victory over the stages of reality, that which was previously described as the triad—beginning with the internal—consisting of the object to be understood and the objective world, has been taught for the sake of accomplishing yoga. (Pauṣa 33.171)
O Four-faced One, by means of its power and through a gradual process of replenishment,
that [state] is attained by all yogins through their repeated practice.

This practice of yoga is remembered as being for the purpose of dispelling the notion of a [static] reality and a Buddha; it extends from the earth up to the highest state, which is the imperishable essence of all powers. Pausa 33.173.
"For those who seek the fruit, the fruit would be distinct from the conquest of the principles; [therefore] the principle [is the goal].
Thus ends the section titled "The Exposition of the Principles" in the *Pauṣkarasaṃhitā*, a Great Upaniṣad within the illustrious *Pāñcarātra*.
The thirty-third chapter.
Now begins the thirty-fourth chapter.
The Blessed One said:
"In a sacred field, in a divine sanctuary, or at a place designated as a holy ford (tīrtha)..."
And in the auspicious grove and park, free from small insects, [he dwelt].
In an underground chamber, on a mountain peak, in a secluded temple, or considering a certain spot to be secure—whether in a cow-pen or in the residence of a twice-born; Pausha 34.2.
When the time has passed midnight, O Kamatrasambhava,
one should practice the cultivation of reality (tattvābhyāsa) right before the principal deity of one's mantra.

There, O high-minded one, when the threefold mastery of the breath has been attained, having offered the *arghya* at the head of the mantra and having presented incense accompanied by the sound of a bell; Pausa 34.4.
Having praised and circumambulated [the deity], one should [place it] upon a clean spot provided with a covering—
either a black antelope skin, a woolen rug, or a blanket.
O Brahmin, having indeed abandoned sleep and remaining on a pure bed, one should rise during the *brāhma-muhūrta* and perform the five-limbed bath (*pañcāṅga-snāna*). (Pauṣa 34.6)

O twice-born one, having performed the twilight rites according to the rules either while floating or in the midst of water, and having sat down before him with a stainless mirror, [one should proceed]. (Pauṣa 34.7)
Having displayed [the deity] and withdrawn it, one should establish the eternal mantra within the interior of the heart-lotus; without the mantra, there are no [entities] consisting of land or water.

Immediately thereafter, having withdrawn the mantras constricted by the limbs of the ritual action, one should indeed combine all the remaining offerings, such as the *arghya* and so forth, with that which was previously consumed. (Pauṣa 34.9)
Having offered water filled with his hand to Viṣvaksena,
and having cast it into the fire as before, he should then withdraw that entire [offering].
O best of Brahmins, one should also perform the withdrawal of the mantras from one's own body;
thereafter, one should effect the acquisition of enjoyments within the self by means of the mind.
For the sake of accomplishing the sacrifice to the Blessed One, one should solicit pure wealth from Vaiṣṇava recipients, and indeed not otherwise.
Pauṣkara said:
O Lord of the World, you praise the offering of incense, accompanied by the sound of a bell, more than anything else, again and again. (Pauṣkara 34.13)
I wish to know the greatness, the measure,
and likewise the characteristics of the two incense-bellows, as well as those of the one who maintains the incense-fire, exactly as they are.
"Let the essential nature and characteristics of incense smoke be proclaimed. The Blessed One said:
"O Lotus-born One, let the characteristics of that which has the Śabdabrahman as its single body be told."
And understand that the means of valid cognition is utterly pure, along with its objects of cognition.
Know that the *sama*, *ardhasama*, and *jyeṣṭha* [meters] are the longest;
the *madhyama* is equal to one-third of that, while the *kanyasa* is one-fourth. (Pauṣa 34.16)
The width is prescribed as being threefold: [the first] by one-third of its height, and [the other two] by a measure increased by twelve parts.
Having first laid out the cords running east-west and north-south,
one should thus first prepare a rectangular field that is square and elongated.
Then, having divided it by drawing threads horizontally and upwards,
one should lay down five vertical threads and eleven [horizontal] ones.
Now hear from me the division of those parts known as the arms:
the field of sound (śabdakṣetra) is prescribed to consist of five and a half parts.
There, having visualized the wheel and the lotus as visible everywhere,
one should likewise visualize the conch born from the lotus, the pearl necklace, and so forth, in their proper order.
One should fashion a perfectly circular pearl necklace situated within three concentric circles;
having omitted half of it from the front, one should leave half of that portion above.
With the remaining large portion, which is half of that part, above it,
a twelve-spoked wheel provided with a navel-region is prescribed.
O Brahmin, it may consist solely of knives, or be mixed with earth according to one's preference;
it may have sixteen spokes, or a hundred peaks, and be captivating to the mind.
O Lotus-born One, having fashioned a twenty-four-petaled lotus with its pericarp and filaments using one part and the upper portion [of the remaining material], Pausa 34.25.
Having mentally excluded the space between the hub of the wheel and the tips of the petals, [one should fashion it] according to the desired measurement, made very smooth and free from flaws.
One should fashion a beautiful mass of filaments fixed within the center, or one that is attached to the pericarp, elevated, and well-compacted. (Pauṣa 34.27)
Then, above, by means of the two paths and a portion, there is the auspicious characteristic;
resting upon the base of the pericarp, it is half-visible as the king of conchs.
Adorned by the threefold union of the worlds which has become a fold,
the *kumbha* is equal in measure to a portion of that [universe], having the form of the whirlpool of the syllable *Oṃ*.
Then, by means of half a portion upon the *kumbha*, one should gradually lead the *kalaśa* toward the state of being a *kuśa*,
step by step up to the limit of the location of the opening.
O Brahmin, up to the conch and the water-pot, one should shave [the hair] from two directions;
likewise, the fish-shaped mark should extend half and half from the two feet.
The first series of worlds has a width of four and a half parts;
the second is reduced by one part, and the third is measured by half a part.
O Lotus-born One, by means of one's own intellect, from the beginning up to the slightly elevated end,
the middle field is determined to be diminished according to the force of the proportions.
O Mahāmati, understand how it should be made upon the conch: its height shall be four and a half parts.
O twice-born one, the width of the portion known as the *muṣṭi* on the mace should be made with one and a half parts, and its height should be one part. Paus_34.35.
It should be either square or smooth and adorned with artistic work;
in the case of a circular [structure], it is prescribed to be square, while in a square [structure], it is remembered as being circular.
For that which is of equal form, O Brahmin, or has a hand-hold there, or is pointed like a spearhead, or is circular— it is remembered as being common in every respect. (Pauṣkara 34.37)
One should raise the fist upward; know that this is the *saptaparva* (seven-jointed) *gadā-stambha*, which, as before, is joined with knots and shells. (Pauṣa 34.38)
It is endowed with a multitude of pearl necklaces, possesses sharp edges and a square shape,
and is joined with the form of a bracelet as well as a cluster of stars.
Having completed it as circular with a collection of mother-of-pearl pieces, or simply as a smooth,
plain square devoid of ornamentation.
One should likewise construct a pillar for the mace (gadāstambha), marked with its own proportions and either octagonal or perfectly circular; then, upon its summit— Paus_34.41.
One should make it elevated by two parts, with either two arms or four arms;
its limbs should be proportioned as previously described and adorned with a circle of feathers.
O twice-born one, one should make the wings as wide as that [body] and equal to a fourth part;
then, both wings and the tail should indeed be extended by a third part.
The pair of primary hands should indeed be extended equally;
they should be placed together like a casket, arising from the *kamatra* [mudrā].
One who is like a winged bird, self-abiding, marked by the study of the Vedas,
devoted to the collection of mantras, or even one who is disciplined in detail, should be appointed.
Then, having spread it out according to this procedure upon the surface of the earth itself,
the artisan should examine it together with those who have not been [otherwise] fashioned by measurement.
If there is deficiency or excess due to this reason, one should personally complete it before him through the heart alone, by means of one's own intellect and action. (Pauṣkara 34.47)
O Lotus-born One, it measures the moving embryo by means of a sharp iron rod;
it is one and a half parts greater than the field and makes sound manifest.
O Lotus-born One, this much was ordained as the primordial, great fiery emanation, wherein the manifest totality of existence is supported, situated at the navel.
And therein, one's own group of twelve vowels is traditionally taught;
that same [group] becomes sixteen-spoked when joined with the neuter syllables.
O Lotus-born one, the threefold form of all phonemes is established in Vaikharī, preceded by Paśyantī, O Son of the Lotus. (Pausa 34.51)
Indeed, that supreme nature of speech which resides in the twelve-spoked [wheel] is present in that very sixteen-spoked [wheel], and likewise in the *akartarīs*.
For it exists eternally indeed in the form known as the Middle;
beyond this, that which consists of twenty-four syllables is the quality of the letters.
O Mahāmati, that lotus which is the lattice of petals should be fully understood;
know that the syllable *ma* is the color [of the lotus], and that is the pericarp of the lotus. (Paus 34.54)
The conch is the letter *ya*, while the mace is held at the fist;
the seven letters beginning with *ra* and ending with *ha* constitute the joints of the mace.
O Lotus-born One, know that patience is pierced by the mark of the bird;
likewise, the nature of the Śabdabrahman is characterized by the form of the bell. (Paus 34.56)
The power of the Blessed One is indeed to be known as being contained within the six qualities;
it is endowed with a multitude of splendors, and that splendor assumes the form of material substance.
Know this pair of qualities belonging to the presiding deity, called the Bell;
it is the Sound-Brahman (Śabdabrahman) to be abandoned, which resides in the center of the space of the heart.
It is eternally manifest, incomparable, and beyond the reach of the mind;
therefore, it is not possible to teach it to others who lack devotion.
O Lotus-born One, this is the characteristic of the mantras of the supreme nature:
that which exists within the tenfold sound beginning with the syllable *a* and ending with the *visarga*. (Pauṣkara 34.60)
And it abides in the form of various mantras, embodied in phonemes;
it is the mantra that bestows both enjoyment and liberation, which has been received from the mouth of a true guru.
Those devoted to divine rites should know that the object of knowledge resides in five locations:
externally in images and the like, on the tip of the tongue, and within the lotus of the heart. (Pauṣa 34.62)
And within the crest of incense smoke and the auspicious sound of the bell,
their own nature as light remains established, illuminating the heart.
O Mahāmati, know that in its intermediate form it is uninterrupted;
furthermore, understand that it rests upon the smoke of incense and possesses the manifest body (*vaikharī*).
When the bell is being rung, it is experienced without interruption;
indeed, those states which are based upon this [bell] must always be understood. (Paus 34.65)
At the time of constant worship,
however, practitioners longing for accomplishment [should meditate on] Ananta, who is joined with Kālavaikhānara, in the impeller of sound (śabdacodaka).
O Great Buddha, there is a conch resting upon a string of pearls, situated within the mouth of a bell; it stands firmly above that, supported by the sky.
In whichever region the twelve-fold Sun is situated within the wheel,
that very same [wheel] again abides in the blades of the scissors by way of the months.
The moon indeed consists of sixteen parts (*kalā*), and its body is composed of those parts;
for Varuṇa himself is present within all the circular fields. (Pauṣa 34.69)
The individual soul (jīva) indeed rests upon the unmanifest lotus-petal permeated by reality;
the Lord (īśvara), however, is situated on the pericarp within the filament of that lotus.
Know that the syllable *praṇava* is placed upon the conch, the *vidyā* rests upon the mace, and Garuḍa is the presiding deity of the vital breath (*prāṇa*); such is the host of deities.
Having meditated and worshipped with the primary offerings according to the ritual rules, and having performed the incense offering,
O Lotus-born One, one should establish [the image] upon the pedestal at the appropriate times.
Listen as I speak of those [mantras] to be employed among the Vedic rites;
thereafter, they are used in the worship of the deities situated within the seat of Gaṇeśa.
Especially during the offering of incense, at the time of the oblations and the mantras, at the conclusion of the recitation and praise, and when the satiation of the fire has commenced; Pausa 34.74.
At the offering of the final oblation (*pūrṇāhuti*), at the dismissal of the mantras, at the time of worshiping Viṣvaksena, and in the presentation of his offerings; Pausa 34.75.
Therefore, one who desires accomplishment must not act otherwise than what has been prescribed;
[the ritual] must possess the correct measure, be endowed with the defining characteristics, include the object of knowledge, and be accompanied by the deities.
It has been clearly declared that the form arising from the lotus is the primary one;
now learn of his other forms, which are mere semblances of the primary. (Pauṣa 34.77)
As it has been stated, the threefold measurement, designated by its breadth and length, is proclaimed as fivefold, beginning with the wheel and ending with Garuḍa. (Pauṣa 34.78)
O Brahmin, the arrangement of the feet of all [the verses] is prescribed by moving [the syllables] according to one's preference and by resorting to suitable positions. (Pausa 34.79)
Above that, one should fashion a lotus, fully blossomed with an upward-pointing pericarp, wide with long petals, and endowed with a mass of filaments. (Pauṣa 34.80)
O twice-born one, one should place the triad beginning with the conch upon its pericarp; or else, one may place only the discus near the line of the mouth.
Having first formed the three [symbols]—the lotus, the conch, and that [third] as previously described—and having completed everything as taught, with Garuḍa at the end; Paus 34.82.
O Lotus-born One, O Four-faced One, having fashioned a conch, a mace, and the king of birds upon the lotus-wheel of the liberated field, [place them] above.
Upon the door-panel is a lotus with a long petal-shade, facing downwards;
it is devoid of the conch emblem and is endowed with a mace, a stalk, and a bird.
Having fashioned a conch shell according to the prescribed method on the same level as the ground, a mace should be made above it, provided with the enemy of serpents (Garuḍa). Paus 34.85.
Alternatively, one should fashion a weapon with its face turned upward in the region of Garuḍa;
or else, a lotus with its face turned toward the sky is prescribed in that region.
And having likewise obtained a conch shell that spirals to the right and is adorned with three folds— one for each [of the three marks]— excepting the conch, the discus, and the lotus.
A bell that is very smooth and round, with a face like a cluster of pearls and stars, and free from any blemish, shall become a refuge for those beset by obstacles. (Pauṣa 34.88)
O Brahmin, for she indeed dispels obstacles when endowed with the mark;
therefore, she must certainly be made to bear the mark in order to obtain the fruit for her husband. (Pauṣa 34.89)
Thus ends the thirty-fourth chapter, titled "The Characteristics of the Incense Bell," in the Pauṣkara-saṃhitā, a Mahopaniṣad within the glorious Pāñcarātra.
Now begins the thirty-fifth chapter.
The Blessed One said:
"Thus has been described the characteristic of the incense bell, which increases prosperity."
O twice-born one, when she is moved during the offering of incense, [the following occurs].
The mantra constantly attends upon the worshiper;
then one should perform the measurement of the path using either one's own fingers or those made of gold.
O Brahmin, with twenty-four [fingers] one makes the supreme incense-burner;
its length, according to the craftsmen, should be as before, made of pure iron.
O Lotus-born One, having made that face four-cornered or circular with a measurement equal to one-fourth of itself, it should be adorned with three fires (nine triangles).
In the center of this eight-sided figure, one should indeed fashion a wheel together with a lotus,
or a lotus accompanied by the Lord [Iśa], or a svastika, or a house for the elephant.
It is properly adorned with a turban-band and a conch-shell mark at its summit;
now hear from me concerning that wheel, which is both square and circular.
For the characteristic, O Mahāmati, is according to its state and possesses specific distinctions;
having prepared a four-cornered field, or one that is circular and level. (Pausa 35.7)
In that interval, there is a lotus adorned with the stalks of a lotus-pond arising from a lotus;
it may be alone or accompanied by a wheel, and is to be enjoyed according to the prescribed rule.
Having first divided that [circle] into eight equal parts from the center,
one should then draw a circle with a radius of six parts, starting from the hollow of the pericarp.
O twice-born one, as it revolves within the hollow of the pericarp, one should bring it to a state of depression;
one should know its measure to be equal to half a sphere (golaka), just as it is when sealed.
With one-third of that measure, the height of the pericarp (karṇikā) is formed around the sixfold division;
it is well-surrounded by filaments (kiñjalkas) characterized by that same proportion.
That which remains from the seventh part, outside the series of filaments,
consists of two parts by which the network of petals is completed.
Having prepared the wheel as before, complete with pearl nets, one should likewise arrange it outside that [mandala] in sections according to the desired number.
O twice-born one, having taken a fourth part from the eighth part of the field according to the stated measurement, it should be assigned for the purpose of the altar.
One should fashion four conch shells in the four corners of the altar;
this is the square altar, adorned with conch shells, which has been described.
O Lotus-born One, this configuration of the zodiacal fields is not fixed;
it emerges from the back of the lotus in whatever circular shape is intended.
It may extend as far as the edge of the altar-ground or up to the rim of the wheel;
it may be shaped like a face or perfectly circular, according to the specific requirement of that site.
To support the altar, however, two lotuses are raised up;
in their center stands [the deity], endowed with the auspicious marks, seated in the lotus posture or other such postures. (Pauṣkara 35.18)
One should assume the form of Agni; his pair of feet indeed extended, his mouth directed toward the sky, and his ears reaching up to his tusks.
O twice-born one, having prepared the pericarp-lotus at the end of the stalk,
[one should worship] with Tathāgatas fashioned from lotus petals that are half-blown.
At its base, O Mahāmati, one should construct a foundation slightly higher than that, with a width equal to it; the ground-field should be provided with a svastika, well-perforated, and very firm.
Then, at the back of the lotus, one should fashion the wind-element together with its bindu as a foundation,
level with the elevation of the earth-element.
It is equal in extent to the diameter of the earth, or twice that, and it rests upon the rim of the wheel; it is dissolved therein and possesses a beautiful resonance.
Or else, the first [ornament] is a network of small bells, which is supreme for dispelling obstacles;
thus indeed has the specific characteristic been fully described. (Paus 35.24)
Now hear from me the general procedure for the mere incense of the mantra:
within a square enclosure, there is a lotus provided with a pericarp and filaments.
Having fashioned an eight-petaled lotus adorned with the sky and stars, or likewise provided with a pearl-thread and a pedestal; Pausa 35.26.
Then, in the middle, one should fashion a [mandala] with a twelve-spoked wheel together with a lotus, spread out with various petals, extending from the back limit.
In the place where the petals were fully blossomed, it was adorned with a turban and a silken cloth,
serving as a resting place for the face, and provided with a supporting rim.
Pure, with a very smooth stalk, and freed from the fibers of the lotus—
such is the form to be inferred by means of the desired measurement.
O Lotus-born One, that which is fashioned from all metals according to one's own capacity indeed bestows happiness upon ministers, householders, and devotees. (Pauṣa 35.30)
I shall describe the characteristics of that which is called the *samudgara*; let one understand it:
a hollow, circular cavity according to the dimensions specified for its breadth. (Paus 35.31)
Having first made them perfectly level, O Lotus-born One, like a casket,
he placed one of the two with its stalk upon the other in the middle above.
O Lotus-born One, the second [eye] is covered by a full-blown lotus with its face turned downward, while the other is covered by a lotus with its face turned upward. (Pauṣa 35.33)
For it was hollow, filled with a mass of seeds, and stood upright;
indeed, the elephant’s trunk, bent down from its root, could not grasp it.
Having fixed two [fibers] at the region of the stalk for the sake of stability,
thus has the characteristic of those [stalks] in full bloom been described.
Now listen, O high-minded one, to the characteristics of those who have arisen, according to their origin: it is a fourth part of the previous span in terms of width.
Having laid out a quadrangular field upon the surface of the earth,
one should then divide that length into eight equal parts.
O Lotus-born One, one should then construct a pedestal expanded fourfold [in width],
elevated by one-eighth part, and endowed with the arrangement previously described.
Extending from the feet up to the uṣṇīṣa, it should be spread out according to its full width;
it should be raised by half the height of the pedestal and measured as three parts of that width.
One should fashion a lotus in the center of the seat with two pericarp-circles,
possessing eight petals and filaments, adorned by a circular space.
It should be broad by half a part from its width, and again elevated by four and a half parts; it may be either octagonal or perfectly circular.
Or it may be a beautiful quadrangle, likewise arranged with its pillars established exactly as desired, O Lotus-born One. (Pauṣa 35.42)
That which is circular among these is indeed endowed with variegated ornamentation;
it rests upon pillars and arches, and for the most part measures one-eighth [of the total].
Equal in width to the pedestal, it is adorned with twelve spokes, provided with a hub and a broad rim, and decorated with pearl necklaces and other ornaments.
O Lotus-born One, having fashioned the wheel with its small bells as before,
it should be mounted upon the middle of its axle and raised by one and a half parts.
From the front, it should be equal to the pedestal; in width, it should be commensurate with the wheel;
in breadth, it should be half that portion; and it should be narrow according to the eightfold division.
And by means of gradual progression, its expansion is prescribed;
thus having prepared the mouth for the smoke-accompanied fire. (Pauṣkara 35.47)
Always, at all times, in the act of worshipping the All-pervading Lord,
[he offered] water-born, land-born, and even celestial beings, both those that move and those that are stationary.
With canopies of leafy creepers, conch shells, svastikas, and lotuses;
with clusters of pure flowers, and with siddhas, vidyādharas, and others.
And in all directions outside, there should be a residence for the celestial nymphs;
this applies to one who possesses a palace with a circular base and a square face. (Pauṣa 35.50)
O Lotus-born One, I shall explain to you exactly as it is the arrangement of the seat,
which is joined with three folds and resembles the face of a conch shell.
O Lotus-born One, one should fashion a lotus-shaped pedestal upon the seat;
it should be variegated, serving as a support for the pillar, and made of two *āmalasāraka* stones.
Then, one should erect a pillar fashioned with artistic design, previously smeared with blood,
or one resembling a series of rings, upon the top of the pillar-shaft.
O Brahmin, one should draw a lotus like a wheel, complete with filaments and twelve petals, with a wide pericarp;
above that, as before, one should draw a face.
Adorned with the aforementioned arrangement, it was circular all around,
provided with strings of pearls, and hung with a network of tinkling bells.

And regarding these, it was said: "Now, O Lotus-born one, there is indeed one [section] concerning the ritual procedure; the arrangement of the nature of water-born and land-born [beings], as well as those fashioned in the sky, has been composed by me. (Pausa 35.56)

And having thoroughly considered it, O Lotus-born One, that [calculation] should always be performed for everyone; for when it has been correctly applied to the limbs [of the body], its manifestation becomes clear.
...shines forth intensely. // Paus 35.57 //
Thus has been stated in brief the definition, as well as in detail,
of the act of burning incense and of its various forms.
Having thus accomplished [the rite], refined it, and brought it back to the state of ultimate reality,
one should empower it with one's own mantra and worship it as it rests upon its support.
Know that from the very beginning, in the place of the svastika, is the earth element with its five characteristics;
the water is the lotus, and the fire is the wheel of great luster.
Within the pericarp of the lotus is the sky, with a network of tinkling bells moved by the wind;
thus indeed is it accompanied by the adhibhūta and the adhidaivata.

That which was previously declared as that which must be meditated upon for the accomplishment of all rites is the complete form of the wheel, consisting of the hub, spokes, rim, and felly. (Pauṣa 35.62)
That which is partless and perfectly circular is indeed celebrated as the "orb of space" (vyomavṛtta);
one should worship the incense burner endowed with such characteristics.
Having performed the consecration according to the rule, O Mahāmati, one should recite the lineage of one's own family, having marked it with one's own name, and then offer it.
In the divine temple of Hari, frequented by gods and siddhas,
one should perform offerings at the three times of day, together with incense smoke.
One should ring a bell with a beautiful sound, accompanied by the sounds of kettledrums and other instruments;
one should circumambulate the divine abode many times while reciting hymns of praise. (Pauṣa 35.66)
O Great-minded One, having heard from outside the sound of a bell— the single seat of the Śabdabrahman— there arose great satisfaction for the assembly of Siddhas residing there.
To whom does this unstruck sound belong that has now recently become manifest, by which it has been revealed externally for the sake of instructing those who are capable? (Pauṣa 35.68)
Thus ends the thirty-fifth chapter, titled "The Characteristics of the Incense Burner," in the Pauṣkara-saṃhitā, a Great Upaniṣad within the Śrī Pāñcarātra. Oṃ.
Now begins the thirty-sixth chapter.
Pauṣkara said:
"O Blessed One, I desire to know that which has been uttered by you."
And it was observed to be possessed of the characteristics of a great soul.
Whatever divine abode or sacred site of the Siddhas there may be,
it serves as a means for both the ignorant and the wise among men.
O Lord, when the mantra of the practitioners first attains propitiation therein,
there arises constant clarity as well as great victory over reality.

For those who have completed their studies, for celibate students, for ascetics free from attachment, and for those who have desisted from the householder stage, [this] quickly becomes free from obstacles.
The Blessed One said:
"This world, distinct from the primordial matter (ākṣiti) and composed of illusion (māyāmaya),
consists indeed of the principles of the Lord known as the fields (kṣetra), together with the lords of the fields (kṣetranātha)."
Furthermore, he himself is present through those whose forms consist of various manifestations, preceded by an array of pervasive bodies,
and who possess the eternally pure sixfold divine attributes.
For the sake of favoring those who are destined for rebirth— whether they be ungrateful and of small intellect, or even devoted, or likewise non-devoted and atheistic— (he remains).
Indeed, when the island has become the axle of the earth-wheel, that field which is celebrated as beginningless bestows the fruit of one's own karma; yet its merit is indeed limited. (Pauṣa 36.8)
For the sake of favoring human beings, [the Lord], though formless, has presided over various locations through his own designations out of compassion, by means of those most excellent fields.
Likewise, O Lotus-born one, is she joined with the lords of the fields in their embodied forms, or does she remain on the earth in the state of a seed? (36.10)
Through knowledge and the rest, as well as the powers such as atomization (aṇimā) and others, which are unmanifest, consisting of the elements beginning with earth and fire,
taking the form of the seeds and digits of the principles (tattva), and endowed with the reality of Brahman.
Having descended into this world, they indeed manifest themselves prior to creation;
by their own nature, out of a desire to bestow grace upon all beings.
At the time of the withdrawal of the circle of the earth, together with the most excellent fields,
[he withdrew] those bodies which possessed mastery and granted boons, as well as the forms of the preeminent sages.
For in each respective field, which simultaneously bestows security and progress,
[the Lord manifests] a form consisting solely of His own will, as well as a form characterized by the conceit of individuality.
Having indeed manifested through the means of knowledge, beginning with the highest,
according to the appropriate times, by means of the cow of speech and the nature of stone.
Therefore, the lords of the fields on earth are indeed renowned by those very forms and names;
likewise, other gods with identical names are indeed known along with their respective abodes.
Thus is the land of action presided over by the lords of the fields and by the fields themselves—
both by the formless fields whose nature is consciousness, and likewise by the embodied lords of the fields.
Thus, those leaders of the fields who had entered [the path] through reasoning—
even they, after some time, themselves [realized] the defect consisting of stone.
O twice-born one, having perceived [this], they disappear due to the ruin of the country and other such calamities;
yet, through abundant deliberations, they once again become manifest as before. (Pauṣa 36.19)
Or he may, by his own power, impel the earth from within itself,
just as a cloud, without being impelled, produces a mass of rain from the ocean.

Thus, those who have taken refuge in me speak of their well-being and security, either in a dream or even in direct perception, or they do so themselves, being of a nature absorbed in me. (Pauṣa 36.21)
O Lotus-born One, that [mantra] shall always be true for those who are exceedingly devoted to its reality, but it shall be untrue for others; such is the case. 36.22.
Thus, their excellence is endowed with existence; [this is stated] for the purpose of refuting those who lack devotion, lest they [view it] as non-existent due to nihilism. (Paus 36.23)
Indeed, for the satisfaction of the believers and for the accomplishment of sacred sites and the like,
those Vāsudevas who are lords of the fields (kṣetreśas) reside within the hollows of the stones.
In some places he appears directly in the form of the wheel, conch, lotus, and mace;
especially so, indeed, on Mount Trikūṭa and on Raivataka.
O twice-born one, [he should bathe] at Sālagrāma, at Sahyādri, likewise at Viṣṇupada,
at Vyāvarta, at Kṛṣṇāśva, and at Kukṣi on the snowy mountain (Himavat).
On Mount Mahendra, Malaya, Vindhya, Pāriyātra, or Arbuda; on Hastivadra, where truth is observed, or on the excellent mountain Vikaṭa—Paus_36.27.
O Kamalasaṃbhūta, in my field of Siṃhācala, which is meritorious and most enchanting, and thus presided over by Vāsudeva.
Those who, by their own meditation, proceed to a field fashioned effortlessly through various and manifold distinct forms, whether by many or by some single one; Pausa 36.29.
Those who perish there while depending on the Lord of the Field (Kṣetranātha), or others at the end, or even in the middle portion of the earth; Paus 36.30.
Or else, when first seen by the divine vision, they gradually attain the state of being a sacred field (*kṣetra*) for that very person who has reached the ground of truth.
O one of pure vision, that [attainment] consists of sālokya, sāmīpya, and sāyujya; yet for a person devoid of discernment and lacking self-restraint, it is fruitless. (Pauṣa 36.32)
But even if one was previously an atheist who had come for refuge, O Pauṣkara, if he now approaches with faith and remains motionless, [he is to be accepted]. Paus_36.33.
O Lotus-born One, out of compassion, his kinsmen led him away while he was unconscious;
they threw him down before the Lord of the World, crying out, "Save us! along with women and children.
Having recognized him as one whose body was liberated, together with his subtle body (puryaṣṭaka),
they placed him upon an excellent chariot amidst the great sound of musical instruments.
Having forcibly conquered the fierce soldiers of Antaka with the servants of Kṣetrapati— [servants] who have the heads of lions, tawny monkeys, boars, dwarfs, horses, and serpents— // Pausa 36.36 //
With gentle countenances, they bore the lotus, conch, discus, and mace; some held the plow and the sword Nandaka, while others carried the thunderbolt, noose, goad, and bow.
Having brought [the spirits] with pestles and other implements, and with staffs in their hands and faces like those of Garuḍas,
they approach the Lord of the Field and cause them to descend.
O Lord of the Kurus, today let the five-elemental body of this protectorless man be duly released upon your own sacred field.
But Kṣaitranātha, having heard those words uttered by the Gaṇas,
gazed upon him with a gaze imbued with compassion.
But once he has reached his own place, that sanctuary where his sins were previously cleansed, there indeed remains a residue of fault for him once again.
Having brought about dissolution through association over time by these two means, whatever else has been assimilated into one's own self in this manner; Paus 36.42.
Having drawn that [deity] out from his own body by means of his own power and according to the [prescribed] signs,
and having ascertained its fitness for consecration, it is indeed for the attainment of perfect knowledge.
He grants birth in the land of action within a family of those who perform noble deeds, or in his own field or another’s field; for that is indeed what constitutes "vision" (sālokana) there.
And having, in due time, obtained his authority and performed, in brief, the pervasive practice as appropriate— the auspicious [practice] of thirteen kinds— Paus 36.45.
By that [first stage], one's purpose would be accomplished; by half of that, another;
and the third, O Lotus-born One, is joined with perfect knowledge.

For indeed, through time and by means of the manifestation of the senses characterized [by their objects], one who has previously observed the vow himself [attains] that [state] in the field with conscious intent, as before. (Pauṣkara 36.47)

Thereafter, with intense devotion, one should perform the renunciation of the body through vows and other means in the presence of the Lord of the Field; thus, that vow becomes free from all impurity.
Having made the individual body the fire-drill, when that pure and auspicious knowledge [of Dharma] arises, he instructs him therein on that very thing which is to be relinquished.
Or, O lotus-eyed one! (Pausa 36.49)
O Brahmin, having reached that supreme abode known as Vāsudeva, even the merits of the sacred pilgrimage sites of the yogins do not fall away.
Indeed, by virtue of being the eternal support, even those who possess knowledge attain the state of Hayagrīva and reach the most excellent and supreme yoga.
O Brahmin, they attain that which is eternally filled with knowledge without obstacle;
such, O Brahmin, is the supreme means for living beings arising from this very sphere.
Since this is so, for that reason, it should indeed always be cultivated,
just as the rays [are cultivated] by one of noble lineage for the sake of a stainless seed.
They destroy the powers that give rise to growth and their afflictions, yet this occurs without any loss of their own essential nature; for it is indeed just so.
By his own power indeed, through the auspicious rays of his own energy,
he completely eliminated the stains of the kalpa within the field for the sake of those dwelling in that field.
Thereafter, they bestow grace upon that person whose sins have been exhausted,
by means of earth, water, fire, wind, and the characteristics of space.
For that which is established here is constrained; hear from me that which is unestablished:
that which arises from the abandonment of food and water is known as *vāta* (wind). (Pauṣa 36.57)

O Pauṣkara, having correctly understood that which is the supreme non-appearance resulting from the closing of all doors, or else having brought about the fall of the body at the [proper] time, one attains liberation here. (Pauṣkara 36.58)
One who desires auspiciousness should strive with effort and devotion toward his service;
if he does not attain it in this life, it will be obtained through repeated practice in future births.
By means of which [virtue], the misfortunes that cause a man of cultivated intellect to go to ruin in birth after birth through exceedingly powerful sin— [save him from those]. (Pauṣa 36.60)
O Lotus-born One, even if that attainment has not yet arisen,
he is nonetheless not a fit vessel for the terrible teaching of Antaka.
He is to be revered even by the messengers of Yama, like a man who performs sacrifices;
for let alone human beings adorned with restraints and observances.
Other living beings as well, who were born there enriched by a particular devotion to the [deity],
due to the force of their prior impressions (*pūrvasaṃskāra*), are born again in another birth.
O Brahmin, those who are devoid of right discernment do not attain [this] when dead; nor do those who are my devotees, except for him who truly finds [this]. (Pausa 36.64)
Among men, he is indeed blessed, for he is not excessively oppressed by his misdeeds;
even though there is no destruction of actions that have not yet been experienced.
They attain a state of attenuation through the power of the greatness of the sacred field;
indeed, the destruction of karma occurs solely by virtue of the practice [of that place] throughout successive births.
O Mahāmati, by virtue of the power of the lords of the fields together with their fields,
those who give gifts to supplicants within such various fields [attain great merit].
Or, for the sake of propitiating the All-pervading One, they perform austerities with devotion;
they accomplish the mastery of the Lord of Mantras and offer libations of sesame seeds and other substances.
O Lotus-born One, those who worship the gods with sacrifices obtain the entire fruit [of their merit] through the well-known [mantras] beginning with the twelve syllables. (Pauṣa 36.69)

One should worship the Supreme Lord according to the prescribed rite with one's own principal mantra, using either mantras beginning with *jitaṃ te* or those ending with *matrānta*, as received from the mouth of the Guru.
O best of the twice-born, whatever is given to those authorized among the foremost of the twice-born who abide in the venerable sacred site, it belongs to the followers of the Pañcakāla.
That [result] is to be understood as inexhaustible for those who still desire existence and enjoyments;
however, for those whose passion has ceased through giving, it leads further to the attainment of liberation.
That which is given by many who are equal to oneself for the welfare of those dwelling within village boundaries, districts, other lands, or settlements,
one enjoys free from disease.
Know that, through one's own power, it is fulfilled in every birth, eternally;
and from that divine abode, it leads to infinite existence. (Pauṣa 36.74)
O Brahmin, that which is to be known as leading to a hundred thousand births comes from Siddhāyatana;
however, that which leads to a thousand births comes from the place prepared by the most eminent of Brahmins.
Know that what is performed by a Kṣatriya yields tenfold results in future existence, while that which is prepared by a Vaiśya yields half of that.
O best of the twice-born, that gift which is given in a temple constructed by a virtuous Śūdra to a Brāhmaṇa is indeed to be known as yielding twelvefold fruit. (Pauṣa 36.77)
When a gift is given to a sanctuary of the foremost of the twice-born that has been designated for castes who have no other refuge, does it indeed yield the same fruit? // Paus 36.78 //
But those who have constructed shrines by castes that perform mixed sacrifices bestow,
in due order, half of what was previously mentioned for each successive birth.
O Pauṣkara, for those who desire fruits, the Lord resides in all abodes; indeed, for those free from desire, He is established within all forms. (Pauṣkara 36.80)
Whether existing within another form or appearing as an incarnation,
he bestows the supreme state through his activity during those various manifestations.
Therefore, O twice-born one, one must strive with great effort, preceded by the propitiation of the mantra, to perform that rite which is distinct from consciousness. (Pauṣkara 36.82)
Therefore, for those men who are free from passion and who sacrifice to the Imperishable,
the unborn and all-pervading Vāsudeva, abiding within the activity of their own self, is revealed.
But when one whose mind is presided over by that [Brahman] performs sacrifice externally wherever it may be,
there and then the eternal Brahman is manifested for them.
Pauṣkara said:
For those men born in a temple who have committed inauspicious deeds,
when they die there, [they become] outcasts (vāhyas).
I wish to know the destination among them.
The Blessed One said:
"O Lotus-born one, by some previous action that was indeed pure, they perform [virtuous deeds], yet the mind of intelligence again commits evil."
Even though they know the greatness of the sacred field, they remain there helplessly and by force, dying due to the power of habitual tendencies from previous births. (Pauṣa 36.87)
And for the sake of pacifying their constant misdeeds, he [the Buddha] contracts the field of those [beings] and that of the Ender (Antaka) by means of skillful methods and unsurpassed teachings.
For you alone remove their taint— the residue of what they have consumed—
before long, even as they continue to perform unwholesome deeds.
Furthermore, O high-minded one, having received that command upon his head, he remained within our domain, [enjoying] the body [or its pleasures]. Pausa 36.90.
With a mind indeed imbued with compassion, they purify themselves;
thus, freed from faults, they proceed after the passage of time.
And through association, through completeness, and especially through contact with the virtuous,
those whose impurities have been utterly destroyed surely return to the Vedic path.
They practice that very thing by which they indeed attain union (*sāyujya*).
Pauṣkara said:
"If those born from that [practice] should indeed perish here as the most wicked of men..."
What is the destination of those most sinful men?
The Blessed One said:
"Yama purifies their misdeeds not by means of severe punishments;
for once their faults have been removed, they indeed return again to human birth. (Pauṣa 36.94)
O Lotus-born One, when the mind is intent on the destruction of the body with intense resolve,
it attains purification as before, just as men who have committed evil deeds do.
Those born there who are free from fault, having gone elsewhere to their dissolution,
now indeed proceed to the abode of Death by means of celestial chariots.
He should worship them, and then, with palms joined in reverence, he should say:
"May they indeed go to the Blessed One, who is the abode and the sanctuary of them all."
That state known as *sālokya*, which is stainless and brings about the destruction of the bonds of worldly existence,
is attained solely by this virtuous path shown by me.
As you set out there, may it be auspicious for you,
just as it is for the other inhabitants of that place who know the truth, O Blessed One.
Thus, for men devoid of discernment, even the fruit arising from a lotus would be [unattainable] through their sense-bases; how much more so, then, for others?

The earth is his feet, space is his navel, heaven is his head, and the moon and sun are his eyes; the worlds, preceded by the Great Principle (Mahat), are the hair upon the body of that All-pervading Lord.
The quarters are his ears, and the intermediate directions are indeed his arms;
his succession of netherworlds extends as far as the foundational power (Ādhāraśakti).
The station of that all-pervading, venerable, omnipresent, and great-souled one, who possesses an eternal form, is at the region of the soles of his feet.
Since everything consists of the Word (pada), for that very reason, O twice-born one, there is indeed no place on earth that is not a sacred abode for the devotees of the faithful. (Paus 36.104)
For the nihilists, all this world of the moving and the unmoving is composed of darkness;
however, O Mahāmati, let the well-established state [of reality] be set aside for now.
In whatever place it has been installed with devotion by the best of Brahmins and others—
whether immovable or movable, beautiful, and fashioned from variegated clay, wood, or stone— [there it remains].
Whatever image of Hari is made from metals such as gold, for those men who perish [while worshipping] it, by virtue of its majesty— Pausa 36.107.
Their residence in the triple heaven is characterized by nothing particularly exalted;
at the end, when they fall away, their rebirth occurs in various abodes.
O Great Buddha, those devoted to me should indeed understand the [karmic] sequence accordingly:
the direct manifestation belonging to the best of the twice-born arises in various fields and sub-fields.
O you born from the lotus, your birth occurred in a place fashioned by the gods, which increased from the abode of the Kṣatriyas and was frequented by true Vaiśyas.
O Lotus-born One, in the abode of Acyuta established by the sages,
a person shall not undergo rebirth from the lineage of Maudgalya through his worship.
A great abode fashioned by a man who has attained mastery over mantras indeed brings about the excellence of enjoyments for men, and likewise after the lapse of time. (Pauṣa 36.112)
O twice-born one, until the end ordained by those who know the mantras, there is another perpetual destruction of sin for the Kṣatriya immediately thereafter. (Pauṣa 36.113)
O Pauṣkara, by means of a canopy that is not too long,
there will gradually be a complete destruction of those defects over the course of time.
O Lotus-born One, having descended to the earth, he quickly exhausts his prior misdeeds right there through observances, by means of the remnants of what he has eaten.
As previously described, those who have been mentioned proceed in due order to the supreme state;
and those who have been ordained here for the auspicious act of relinquishing the body [attain it as well].
For those possessed of discernment, penances are not prescribed;
rather, [this practice] alone serves for the destruction of the misdeeds accumulated since birth. (Pauṣa 36.117)
By means of those [deeds] once they have been consumed by fire at the end of the body, they attain the imperishable state;
therefore, having reached this sacred field, one should perform expiation.
Having personally understood the fruit of evil and having resorted to the eternal being,
one whose mind and intellect were previously hostile attains thereby a state of auspiciousness.
Even for humans, a field that is powerful despite being faulty bestows a fortunate rebirth;
indeed, it does not abandon its own capacity for discernment, which is the second [factor]. (Paus 36.120)
The mind, along with the group of sense organs and the collection of instruments,
belongs to that [individual] who, at the end, has been thoroughly purified by great austerity.
The shrines and other sacred sites constantly bestow their grace upon that living being, whether he remains in this world or has gone to the next. (Pauṣa 36.122)
Even the virtues of the earth are not to be taken [forcibly] everywhere due to the weight of the prescribed rule,
just as supplicants do not take [wealth] from high-souled men.

They abandon one who is joyful for the sake of food and drink even if he knows their qualities, and they likewise abandon those who lack qualities even if they possess virtues, or conversely, they accept those with virtues even if they are otherwise.

Having thus understood the greatness of this sacred field, one should bring it to the highest state of splendor through asceticism, meditation, recitation, and the like, as well as through the satisfaction of action, speech, and mind.
The Blessed One said:
"By means of the four forms beginning with Vāsudeva previously mentioned,
by the twelve beginning with Keśava, and then by the ten beginning with Matsya."
The group of principles previously mentioned, numbering twenty-six and beginning with Earth, is pervaded by the Lord (Īśvara) and exists together with the twelve [Tattvas].
Enveloped by that [layer] which is suitably thick,
each principle (tattva) is reached in succession together with Vāsudeva and the others.
For such is the state of all the gods for the sake of the pacification of existence;
O Great-minded One, it is the universal form endowed with the six qualities.
For they always manifest [their effects] solely by virtue of their own specific functions,
and indeed only through the power of grace and the will of the All-pervading Lord.
The surface of the earth is always pervaded by all [beings] assuming various forms; yet each single manifestation possesses the same nature as Ananta in its full majesty.
Thus they proceed with various vehicles, weapons, and insignia belonging to their respective selves;
therefore, for the sake of the world, they act according to their will through their sovereign power.
Indeed, the status of all beings within their own respective domains is manifold;
it is fixed for those who bear weapons as well as for those who bear emblems.
Nevertheless, O Brahmin, all [these mantras] are traditionally held to be common to all beings; even so, understand from me regarding that matter as well.
Nor are these manifestations for the sake of pacifying other delusions through specific marks or banners;
rather, they should be understood as occurring solely by the power of their own inherent activity.
Likewise, there are other manifestations due to the influence of a portion [of that power];
some are the original creators, protectors, and supports, while others are distinguished by their banners and emblems.
"O twice-born one, in this way, the supreme group of manifestations of the three is indeed equal; others, such as Keśava and the rest, likewise bear it equally. (Pauṣkara 36.137)
"Along with their forms and characteristics, and indeed with their specific details.
Pauṣkara said:
"O Blessed One, I wish to hear about the characteristics and so forth of all [the deities]."
This is the specific distinction taught for the dissolution of existence for those subject to rebirth, in order to bring about the cessation of worldly becoming.
The Blessed One said:
"Listen, O one of pure vision, as I describe correctly and in due order, beginning from the Primordial God, the arrangement of the marks according to my instruction. (Pauṣa 36.139)
O one of stainless gaze, among the four hands, the first right hand should be held granting fearlessness or bestowing boons upon devotees. (Pauṣa 36.140)
Know that the left [hand] carries a conch in all four positions;
however, for the first [mudrā], it is held in the right and left hands with the palms facing backward.
Behold the time-wheel and the heavy mace of Acyuta;
[likewise] the plough accompanied by the pestle in his left hand and in his right.
In his pair of western arms, O Pauṣkara, Aniruddha holds a joined bow and arrow, as well as a shield together with the sword Nandaka.
"By means of the two rear hands, starting from the middle hand; indeed, this is the case for the fourfold form and for other forms as well. (Pauṣkara 36.144)
Listen now to the description of the abodes of those marked with the conch, the discus, the mace, and the lotus—the three deities belonging to the primordial goddess. Paus 36.145.
Know that there is a discus on the left rear hand and a conch on the right;
on the principal right hand is a lotus, and on the one next to it is indeed a mace.
For in this way, the Blessed One Keśava holds the lotus and other objects with his two primary hands— the right and left— while bearing the mace and the lotus.
In his left hands and so forth he holds the conch and the discus; he bears them in the two right hands.
Know him as the Blessed One named Nārāyaṇa, and [the one] named Mādhava. Paus 36.148.
In the primary frontal position, the Lord holds a conch and a mace;
in the two rear arms, he holds a lotus and a discus, while in all the preceding [frontal] pairs of arms, he holds the same.
These three divine forms, radiant as jasmine, the moon, and crystal,
together with the Blessed Vāsudeva, constitute his fourfold nature.

O Lotus-born One, the thorough knowledge of these three [deities] bestows liberation for some and the enjoyment of worldly existence for others; they belong to the three classes of gods known as the Kāmapālīs. Paushya 36.151.
"In the principal left hand there is a lotus, and indeed in the other, the right, a mace;
