A small collection of elements arising from forest lands—consisting of earth in its natural form—is prepared; that should be mixed with the [other] powder, O twice-born one. (Pausa 38.77)

And for the purpose of fashioning images, in a pure collection of great clay, one should [place] those made of mineral substances and those with a core of clay, together with the *hṛdaya* mantra. (Pauṣa 38.78)
O Lotus-born One, the application of powders derived from pearls, gold, and copper is always prescribed for the pacification of the burning sensation caused by the power of mantras. (Pauṣkara 38.79)
Everything from the charcoal and wood down to the edge of the forest is utilized;
all of that, when gathered according to the prescribed ritual, shall bring about success.
Having thus previously taken [the materials] from a forest or a grove of trees,
one should perform the fashioning of the image either there or in the vicinity of one's own home.
Having been instructed by the Guru, one should perform the sacrifice according to the rules in the ritual hall;
thereafter, one should worship the artisan, the master, and oneself, following the sequence arising from one's own [tradition].
A wise sacrificer should, from the very outset,
abandon any rajasic or tamasic disposition toward this most supreme undertaking.
"O Lotus-born One, that which is perfectly complete or even that which is beset by hundreds of obstacles certainly does not come to pass for those of defiled intellect. (Pauṣya 38.84)
O Lotus-born One, even for one of a sattvic nature, a deficiency of limbs arises through past karma alone, causing mental distress. (Pausa 38.85)
Now, learn from me the procedure that is prescribed there for the variegated image, using pigments, melted water, and so forth.
And the joining of the prescribed limbs is performed with perfumed powders and with purifying pigments such as white and red, which have been consecrated with mantras of the weapon (astra).
With clay mixed with honey, ghee, and milk, combined with silk-cotton powder, and sprinkled with golden water, one [should perform the rite] for images made of clay. (Pauṣa 38.88)
O Lotus-born One, when a split or a break occurs in something made of wood,
the application of cloth and weapons is prescribed preceded by rites for peace.
O Bṛhatkṣatā,
whenever a wound has been inflicted upon those born of stone, it is prescribed that a gem-stick be applied once the wound has become even slightly inflamed.
When the rubbing on a whetstone has been performed with a golden [tool],
and once the wound has been made even, the image will be beneficial in its qualities.
The installation of those [images] that have been damaged certainly brings death to the preceptor,
the patron, the foremost artisan, and the people of the region. (Paus 38.92)
A wound located on the circle of the sense organs brings misfortune to the agent;
one situated from the ear to the navel at the tip [of the nose] causes the death of a son. (Pauṣa 38.93)
In the latter two [sections], however, the hindquarters of the wife bring about the destruction of brothers;
from the waist down to the anus, there would be the loss of sisters.
And wherever there may be a wound from the root of the thigh down to the knee, it will cause the destruction of wealth, grain, and cattle before long. (Pauṣa 38.95)

From the knees down to the soles of the feet, he should proclaim [his own faults] for the sake of showing compassion to all and for his own reputation, as these are sources of reproach for his circle of servants.
O Lotus-born One, the artisan should restore to a state of flawlessness any injury sustained by the image being fashioned,
provided it has been cleared of beeswax.

Indeed, when a deficiency of parts has arisen, listen to this secondary alternative: at the commencement of the construction, there is the fault of injury; but once devotion to the Blessed One has arisen, and while that [devotion] persists, the abandonment of it and its destruction are each successively more contradictory [to that devotion]. (Paus 38.98)
Indeed, when considering large images and the like, the relinquishment of material substance is not appropriate, especially in the case of superior metals such as gold and others. (Pauṣa 38.99)
O Lotus-born One, when a deficiency of limbs has occurred, one should perform a sacrifice for the sake of pacification;
having again restored that limb, O Lotus-born One, according to the specific injunction.
One should apply pure gold to a wound on a golden [image] as it may be obtained; likewise, one should apply all powdered gems consecrated with the twelve-syllable mantra. (Pauṣkara 38.101)
O Mahāmati, in this same manner, one should fill other cavities arising from [other] elements with one's own element, using a small amount mixed with gold. (Paus 38.102)
O Pauṣkara, if by performing this rite in accordance with the rule mental purity does not arise, another ritual practice must be performed.
Having first performed worship as before, they should cause the preceptor, who is authorized by the elders,
to directly behold [the deity] and then lead it back to the formless state.
Furthermore, by means of that same material for the image, he should fashion another [image] that is unblemished,
complete in all its limbs, captivating, and extraordinary.
Since that [lotus] exists eternally without any interval of time,
O Kamalasambhūta, it arises perpetually from mere volition alone.
When she has reached her place, his ancestors— beginning with the great-grandfather— declare it so,
yet they dispute among themselves, beginning with the great-grandfather.
"Having mostly been freed from defects by our lineage, we shall attain the state of Vāsudeva, if he so desires. (Pauṣa 38.108)
Then, for the sake of pleasing these knowers of reality who possess the fourfold nature, he swiftly undertook the great sacrifice known as Pratiṣṭhā.
O Lotus-born One, [this is the account] of the sages, the gods, the ancestors,
and of human beings and all creatures dwelling within the belly of the three worlds.

O twice-born one, from a broken image made of metal that has arisen from a damaged scripture, one should fashion another image; in this way, [the merit] pertaining to the next world and so forth is secured. (Pauṣa 38.111)
Therefore, that very thing is prescribed, or its specific variety, because by following it, the agent obtains great merit arising from both worlds. (Pauṣkara 38.112)
And for those who reside in their own country and have been provided with wealth and other resources,
the measurement of the property should be carried out, divided according to the previously mentioned categories.
Indeed, for the sake of relatives and others, one should have an image of the Lord made;
freed from all defects, he goes to the world of Viṣṇu. (Pauṣa 38.114)
O Brahmin, a divine image may be self-manifested, or established by perfected adepts (siddhas), or installed by the wise; it may even be one set up by those beginning with Brahmins. Paushya 38.115.
The mantra that was placed there, together with the limb-mantras and their respective marks,
departs for its own abode, leaving behind the image without further ritual action.
Having cursed the preceptor and the architect, as well as the purpose for which it was established,
the Piśācas, Bhūtas, Vetālas, Yakṣas, and Rākṣasas likewise [departed].
They take refuge in the site, the seat, the image, and everything up to the banner;
having understood this, O Great Buddha, one who desires auspiciousness should act accordingly.
Just as auspiciousness is accomplished for an installed image through worship, fire-offerings, and gifts, accompanied by musical instruments and songs; (Pauṣa 38.119)

In one's own home, devotees should perform the offering of flowers, incense, and so forth for the mobile image at all times according to their ability, for the attainment of auspiciousness. (Pauṣa 38.120)
For as long as life lasts, the practitioner of mantra should worship his own mantra during the three periods of the day upon a mobile image that has been empowered by the mantras of reality.
Or previously, for the sake of the welfare of devoted followers who have attained realization, the Guru formerly established the common practice beginning with the twelve syllables.

Having thus withdrawn [the senses] according to the scriptures, one should, with devotion, offer [the offering] together with the *mātrās* to one's own guru for the attainment of the fruit of enjoyment and for the pacification of worldly existence.
Placing his hands at his feet and bowing his head, he made this request:
"At the time of your relinquishing the body, whether for yourself or for me who am worthy..."
The Vaiṣṇavas, desiring my grace, should indeed place [the vessel] full at the time of the renunciation of the body, out of compassion for their own disciple. (Pauṣa 38.125)
In this way, O high-minded one, the teacher should provide instruction to one who is fit, and he too, being self-restrained, should instruct another at the end of his body's life.
O Great-minded one, O Brahmin, because of the absence of that [devotion] in a householder, he must perform worship with reverence and remain in the temple. Paus 38.127.
But in the event that he does not obtain enjoyments, he should completely renounce food and drink for the sake of propitiating the All-pervading Lord,
being pure, having bathed, and with a serene mind.
Having offered water for the *arghya* oblation upon the head, either with flowers or alone—this is indeed the primary worship with water, for it is the very root of all enjoyments. (Pauṣkara 38.129)
Since all things consist of rasa, that rasa is the Supreme Lord, the Blessed One known as Nārāyaṇa; therefore, that is remembered as the most excellent arghya offering.
Furthermore, one should place the entire web of enjoyments at the feet,
for by being contained within the vessel of its own cause, it attains infinity.
Not long thereafter, although the devotees, ministers,
and mantra-performers possessed the power of the earth, fire, ether, and wind, [they were nonetheless overcome].
Flowers, incense, and other enjoyments ending with mantras have been proclaimed;
even there, their manifestation is indeed rooted in taste, for they are of that very nature.
O Lotus-born One, by means of that state of bliss which abides as the very essence of the elements beginning with space, everyone everywhere is seen to be a connoisseur of that flavor.
Thus, O Lotus-born One, the arrangement of the human shrines—
both those that are mobile and those that are immobile— has been fully described.
Except for the worship of the supreme Lord of the twice-born (Brahmā), one should not perform any other unstable Vaiṣṇava rites within the temple of the Blessed One,
nor those established in the forms of the Sun, Rudra, or Indra.
That which is prescribed for images produces negligence;
the forms of deities with multiple bodies do not possess the characteristics of a *vyūha*.
Those residing within the worlds should be fashioned according to the stable ritual procedure,
as indeed should the various manifestations of the primary manifestations.
Building residences on walls or in houses is forbidden; likewise, it is forbidden to construct a temple for the gods to the left of another building unless its height is equal to its length.
As it has been said: "He who, preceded by faith and devotion, desires to perform a reversal of the primary ritual (mukhyakalpa) on earth due to the influence of specific causes," Pauṣ 38.140.
And having first performed worship and oblations, one should obtain the command from the Guru,
as well as that which arises from the assembly of those residing within the various worlds.
He was never a source of opposition toward the gods who are worthy of worship, nor toward the inhabitants of the earth who follow the path of devotion. (Pauṣa 38.142)
And for those sacred seats (pīṭhas) whose forms have not been seen, there will be inauspiciousness;
likewise for those situated in the sense-bases (āyatana) that have occupied the interior.

When there is worship of the mantra-form, which possesses the manifestations of the array of emanations, the acquisition [of merit] for Vaiṣṇavas and for Brahmins and others is indeed ordained. (Pauṣa 38.144)

At the outset, for the sake of propitiation, one should indeed perform the entire sequence ending with the mantra as the primary method; however, in the alternative procedure, this may be done by means of other substances such as sacrificial altars (*sthaṇḍila*) and so forth.

O lotus-born one, when it is impossible [to perform all rites], even if there is a deficiency of eight times eight from the entire web of enjoyments, [one should still perform] all the enjoyments and ritual actions.

One who desires auspiciousness should constantly perform the supreme rite of pacification, characterized by the sacrificial ritual of the Blessed One, which encompasses meanings both deficient and abundant, as well as extensive. Paus 38.147.
Pauṣkara said: O Lord of the World, please instruct us on that supreme goddess of mantra-peace, which, when performed by teachers, pacifies all defects. Paus_38.148.
The Blessed One said: For those devotees of purified soul, the previously described lotus-wheel, which pacifies all defects, is beneficial; it is devoid of a dwelling place. (Pauṣa 38.149)
Or rather, because the worship beginning with the pedestal and ending with Viṣvaksena does not truly reach completion there without the worship of Sarveśvara.

One who knows the ritual procedure should establish the separate, desireless [deities] situated in the sky within the spaces of the sky; thereafter, one should cause them to be worshipped with Rigvedic hymns.
Having fashioned the seat (pīṭha) endowed with the vowels and the city (pura) endowed with the consonants,
one should perform there the previously mentioned ritual placement (nyāsa), beginning with the foundational support (ādhāra).
Having perceived him as one with his own body, and having remembered that which is revealed by the witness-consciousness,
he now [unifies] it with the general consciousness (citsāmānya) that constitutes the denoter of the form.
And just as here, having remembered [the states] such as "possessing sensation" (savedya) and so forth in one's own body,
there is indeed no fault of confusion when [the state] is presided over by direct perception.

In the same manner, the worship beginning with the Foundation Power (Ādhāraśakti) and ending with Viṣvaksena is faultless within the mandala; however, it must be preceded by the word "Bhagavat" [for each deity].
Having uttered the name of every [deity], one should say "namas to the Self" at the end;
in this manner is the worship of the deities of the seat, beginning with Dharma.

And thereafter, O Pauṣkara, having performed the worship of the mantra-forms that have been invoked within the mandala, according to their respective positions, *sthānabhedasthitānāṃ ca kṛtvā tadanu pauṣkara / maṇḍale mantramūrtīnām āhūtānāṃ samarcanam //* Paus_38.157 *//*
That which is complete leads to peace, while that which is incomplete leads to a lack of peace;
therefore, for the sake of peace, one should always perform the gift of a cow and the libation of fire according to one's own capacity.
But prior to the sacrifice to the Blessed One, [the ritual] is always prescribed everywhere;
and that is performed with rites permeated by knowledge, along with the water-offering (arghya) and other elements.
Having thus understood that the pure reality (samyaktva) exists as a sublime substance,
it is, like the seed and the sprout, non-different and beginningless. (Paus 38.160)
O Lotus-born One, in this world, for those who desire the fruit in order to attain that fruit, knowledge and action are indeed established as being mutually interdependent. (Pauṣa 38.161)
This should be understood through the intellect that is perfectly purified, owing to the lack of discernment regarding the Supreme Self known as the Blessed Vāsudeva.

For the sake of bestowing grace, out of compassion for those engaged in ritual action, he revealed the *ullāsa* (the radiant manifestation) endowed with knowledge and action, accompanied by mantra and mudrā.
Endowed with the power of reality (tattva-śakti) and possessed of qualities such as knowledge,
it is indeed accompanied by the eightfold supernatural powers (aṇimā and so forth), which are the seeds of accomplishment.

O best of the twice-born, for the pacification of all defects and for the perpetual attainment of the supreme state, the manifestation of the Supreme Lord and the manifestation of the Supreme Lord are non-different. (1)
It is to be fully understood, just as the auspicious flames of a smokeless fire.
Just as the waves of the ocean and the rays of the sun [arise from their source], so too,
through devotion preceded by resolve, [the deities arise] like the sun within the lotus of the heart.
Having performed sacrifices as before with enjoyments characterized by mental resolve during the great festival, he constantly brings about the arising of the Buddhas-to-be.
O Lotus-born One, he is subsequently gratified by more auspicious external offerings such as clarified butter and the like, within the support of fire, according to the prescribed rite.
And the guide, who is the very embodiment of the twice-born, having been brought to the highest satisfaction with food, drink, wealth, and other gifts, indeed bestows supreme peace.
Pauṣkara said: "O Lord, I wish to know the meditation upon this Sustainer of the World within the mandala and other supports for rites such as those for pacification. (Pauṣkara 38.170)
The Blessed One said:

O Lotus-born one, whatever manifestation is worshipped through knowledge and other qualities, that should be known as eternally endowed with the attributes of the All-pervading Lord in every respect. (Pauṣa 38.171)

For the sake of pacifying the suffering of saṃsāra, or for the complete pacification of that [suffering] which has arisen from it, one should indeed offer [the sacrifice], having made it the object of one's focus with devotion and true faith. (Pauṣa 38.172)
With mantras consisting of twelve syllables and so forth, one should constantly worship for the attainment of one's desired goals,
[visualizing the deity] in various forms with weapons, limbs, garments, garlands, ornaments, and the like.
Thus, completely filled with powers purified by grace as well as other personal means of accomplishment,
the infallible Lord manifests His form as consisting of pure consciousness.
One should remember [the Lord] in his human form for the sake of attaining the state of the virtuous,
with a body that is indeed beautiful, divine, and unchanging.

For those who practice meditation, the one who performs the ritual placement (nyāsa) is great, for he releases from the body a continuous light characterized by knowledge— a wisdom that arises without effort.
He was endowed with garlands, garments, and ornaments that were peerless and suited to him—
consisting of pure consciousness, self-luminous, and mutually delighting one another.
May he grant the delight arising from the mass of moonbeams, like a herd of cows, for the cooling of the sweat of those meditators who are afflicted by the fire of their past karma.
O Lotus-born one, know that the two powers called Vidyā and Kalā— consisting of knowledge and action, and conjoined with will— unite like a conch and a discus.

The Blessed One is possessed of infinite power; he is remembered as having infinite qualities, and is distinct from the principles of the sun, moon, and fire, which serve as examples for the perceptible world.
By the very condition of his own awakening, the limit of this [world] is established;
he is indeed everything, for what else could there be beyond all this? (Paus 38.181)
When that which is to be meditated upon shines forth within his own self, that is knowledge established in the Self;
through devotion and appropriate meditation, from this very state comes peace.
Thus, let those of contemplative and auspicious intellect understand his supreme form, which indeed bestows the highest bliss.
With divine [limbs] resembling dark collyrium slightly curved like a bow,
grey as camphor, and with interiors filled with flowers; Pausa 38.184.
It was adorned with beautiful hair crowned by a diadem and tiara,
possessing the radiant luster of ruby-red lotuses resembling land-born water-lilies.
With palms and soles of feet red, with faces beginning with the lips, with the ends of the nostrils and ear-cavities, and with teeth possessing the luster of pearls; (Pauṣa 38.186)
With eyes like slightly reddish cow’s milk and pure blue lotuses,
one should thus first meditate upon the lotus-eyed Acyuta within the heart-lotus.
The meditation on the radiance and splendor of various mantras shall grant all desires;
indeed, this external meditation within the mandala shall lead to the exhaustion of the suffering of existence.
It exists as non-different from the supreme reality of the Blessed One;
established herein, the array of mantras—the object of external knowledge—is perpetually manifest. (Pauṣa 38.189)
Since that which bestows liberation upon living beings exists in the form of various individual manifestations,
those [manifestations] previously mentioned should indeed be understood in their proper sequence.
O Brahmin, the powers beginning with Varāhī have their characteristics specified;
their visualization in sequence has been clearly explained previously as it truly is. (Pauṣkara 38.191)
O Lotus-born One, the eternal, pervasive, and stainless form of the Supreme Brahman known as Vāsudeva indeed exists in a state of non-difference [from him].
Just as flame, moonlight, and radiance belong respectively to fire, the moon, and the sun,
so he assumes at his own will the form called "ego-consciousness" (abhimāna), exactly as it has been described.
Indeed, O Blessed One, for the sake of bestowing grace, the powers of the mantras manifest their own supreme form characterized by self-conceit.
By taking you as the object of focus, through recitation, meditation, and worship,
the knower of mantras who remains established in devotion to you attains everything without delay.
O Lotus-born One, that which is innate, natural, and born of karma— the bondage of action— is indeed established like the blackness of copper remaining within its ore.
Having herself become the power of omniscience through the essence of the supreme mantra,
she effects the piercing of the principles of action and the self in due order.
Those who constantly attain that which is endowed with devotion and free from obstruction drink the supreme Brahman, the Lord, for the sake of attaining the nature of the mantra.
Having gradually attained their own lordly station through the authority they have gained, they depart by the power of mantra; because of that, they do not return again.

O Lotus-born One, having understood this, those mantras which are the most preeminent, as well as the forms of the Lord of the World, are indeed to be meditated upon and likewise worshipped. (Pausa 38.200)
Through propitiation, recitation, meditation, and thorough knowledge, they bestow their own auspicious state—that which is imperishable and infallible. (Pauṣa 38.201)
Just as fire burns away a great web of karma belonging to those whose nature is bound by karma, so too,
O Lotus-born One, having understood this, [one should act] with well-known expressive mantras.
With the twelve syllables at the beginning and the six or eight syllables at the end—
whether known by their own names or as their respective seed-syllables— these are received from the mouth of the teacher.
The Supreme Lords, known as Vāsudeva, are to be meditated upon in two divisions;
and there are four, ending with Aniruddha, according to the arrangement of the fourfold manifestation (caturvyūha).
In this same way, other [forms] such as Varāha and the rest, together with the fourfold manifestation (caturvyūha),
as well as those celebrated as the twelve beginning with Keśava, [are likewise established].
The worship of the fourfold Self, whose essential nature is never abandoned, who possesses manifold forms, and who exists in various states of transformation.

But that which is for the sake of accomplishing various goals, as well as for attaining qualities according to one's inclination—having correctly understood the sixfold policy (ṣāḍguṇya), there is greatness and supreme tranquility. (Pauṣa 38.207)
O Pauṣkara, whatever a wise person desires to attain quickly,
that should be worshipped according to its true state, for it is indeed nothing other than the limit of direct perception.
As before, with respect to the five manifestations (vyūha) and so forth of the forms of the Lord's manifestation,
he desires the sixfold qualities beginning with sovereignty, as well as the fourfold nature and the rest.
One should worship the foremost [deities], beginning with Vāsudeva, who has Pradyumna and Acyuta as his presiding overseers;
furthermore, he who desires the great multitude of virtues should worship them preceded by their formal manifestations (mūrti).
All various perfections of will, such as the powers beginning with *aṇimā*,
and the Lord of All must be understood to culminate in the Imperishable One who presides over the overseer.
However, for one who constantly practices worship in meditative absorption, that which culminates in Pradyumna is beneficial;
indeed, it is primarily characterized by the collection of qualities beginning with motion.
Furthermore, the venerable teacher’s steady face shines forth regarding its worship—
the sequence beginning with Vāsudeva, Acyuta, and Adhyakṣa, and ending with Pradyumna.
But he who desires the attainment of the sixfold group preceded by vigor, should then worship that Adhyakṣa, the infallible Apradyumna.
For one who desires the sixfold policy preceded by military power (*tejas*), the worship of that [power] is prescribed;
furthermore, the triad beginning with the superintendent (*adhyakṣa*) is enjoined for its worship. (Pauṣa 38.215)
Whether through worship prior to the formal installation of the images, or through worship alone,
the knower of mantras shall attain the state of liberation, which is the reality of the Blessed One.
Although that triad of forms exists at the end as all-pervading,
nevertheless, the Lord is truly the sovereign who, by his very nature, is the source of the universe's manifestation.
Having thus recognized that very one as worthy of worship immediately thereafter—
the Lord who is awake and the presiding overseer— you, together with your protector-self, [should honor him].
By worshipping first the triad beginning with Acyuta,
one should gradually propitiate the triad of the Ādideva within those respective positions.
Listen attentively to how a mantra-practitioner should perform this worship of the qualities according to the rule, by means of the fourfold self-union. Paus 38.220.
Knowledge, power, sovereignty, and valor—this tetrad, when differentiated through sacrifice, brings about accomplishment instantly. (Pauṣkara 38.221)
Strength, sovereignty, heroism, and splendor—this fourfold set culminates in *tejas*;
whatever one desires, by means of thorough knowledge, one shall obtain it.
O Lotus-born One, one should bestow this desired quartet upon the practitioners of mantra: splendor, power, knowledge, and strength ending with valor. (Pauṣa 38.223)
Having uttered the auspicious word beginning with the *praṇava* for the one whose nature is knowledge,
just as it has been stated for the quality of knowledge, so indeed is it for all.

Worship for the attainment of liberation and enjoyment is thus remembered as being manifold, performed either according to the unswerving sequence or by means of the aforementioned transposition. Paus 38.225.
Furthermore, one should worship the world-source, which is differentiated by divisions,
as non-differentiated within the great twelve-spoked wheel and within its interior of innumerable petals.
But the Lord who has transcended the qualities (guṇātīta) is, as before, within the pericarp;
indeed, [the lotus] upon the petals consists of the letters of that twelve-syllable mantra.

Salutations! For the attainment of those qualities that have come into being, [I offer] what is joined with the sixfold [set], beginning from the eastern quarter and proceeding clockwise, restrained by the Praṇava. (Pauṣkara 38.228)
One should worship, in due order, the three that have been traversed by the four divine forms, as well as the other three consisting of the qualities (guṇas), and the forms themselves. Paus 38.229.
Since those means lead to the attainment of the fruit, one should therefore perform sacrifice according to one's desire,
through action preceded by knowledge and endowed with devotion and faith.

O twice-born one, together with the dharma of your own caste and stage of life, and through perfect meditative absorption, [this should be maintained] until the time of your final liberation, for as long as you live.
And through the pacification of intense power and through propitiation, knowledge is attained—
either by this very body, or by that [other body], or by one or the other.
By virtue of being very gentle and by virtue of his disposition, he is worshipped by the immortals;
indeed, whoever performs worship through such authority [shall attain success].
Then, by means of the pure enjoyments as previously described and through various ritual acts,
once the completion of the limbs of the rite has been achieved, the sovereign of one's own mantras [should offer] the *arghya* with the heart-mantra and the weapon-mantra.
And having offered the prepared enjoyment of the Lord without fail, using the word preceded by *praṇava* and ending with the word *namas*, [one should perform the offering]. (Pauṣkara 38.235)
"I perform this" by name—that is the acquisition of enjoyments according to the rule;
it is the offering of those [enjoyments] with a mind [focused on them] and with the head bowed low. (Pauṣa 38.236)
In the act of offering, that which is to be known by the reciter [is to be understood] from the Lord of the Heart;
first for those [elements] residing within the heart through inhalation, and then sequentially for those situated outside.
That quintet beginning with the *arhaṇa* offering, known as the "heart-pleasing," was performed with the *añjali* mudrā and a mind purified by faith. (Pauṣa 38.238)
The offering should be presented in many ways, or as far as possible,
depending upon the supreme [deity], together with the senses well-restrained.
O Lotus-born One, by covering the nostrils with a cloth, one's own breath shall not strike [the face], just as it would not otherwise. Paus 38.240.
Just as there is no further germination of seeds that have been thoroughly roasted,
so too is there no rebirth from the fruits of actions for one who has first performed worship of Acyuta.

O one of great intelligence, let alone that which is designated as "karma" and devoid of benefit; for it is the supreme means for the destruction of existence, being fruitless and rootless. (Pausa 38.242)
Sacrifices such as the horse-sacrifice (aśvamedha) surely bestow the fruits of ritual action;
yet even they do not yield their own fruit to those who are devoted to the true mantras.

Sacrifices, indeed, have the nature of knowledge; having correctly understood the intention of the Supreme, they bestow supreme peace upon those who know the reality of the Blessed One. (Pauṣa 38.244)
O Lotus-born One, for others, the desired fruit is heaven and the like,
yet the fruit sought is the enjoyment of mortal existence, whether it be pertaining to the hereafter or to this world.
Having established this in one's intellect, O best of Brahmins, one should perform the recitation and other rites with faith,
accompanied by devotion and sincere intent.

Having thus worshipped the unborn and imperishable one, together with his limbs and his retinue, according to the sequence of the primary forms through the differentiation of powers and manifestations; Pausa 38.247.
Indeed, he alone is to be worshipped with the Ṛgveda and the Yajurveda;
by means of mantras and tantras in the state known as "Aciḥ," for the attainment of one's desired goal. (Pauṣkara 38.248)
The Supreme Brahman, the supreme abode, the pure, the sovereign lord—by virtue of his power, he is Acyuta, who is designated by the eyes as "Netra" (the Leader). Pausa 38.249.
Clearly, for him, the Supreme Brahman exists somewhere as the mark of the eyes;
indeed, it resides internally for those who possess secret mantras, while elsewhere it is manifest externally.
Therefore, O Mahāmati, the six limbs and the five limbs are indeed the designators and the designated, for they are joined through the act of propitiation.
When the reality of the Blessed One known as the Eye transcends the limbs, it resides in the head and in the space of the mantras, whether they be primary or subordinate. (Pauṣkara 38.252)
First, for the sake of stability, one should employ one's own seed-syllable, which is luminous in nature;
then, one should meditate upon the Lord of the Direction situated therein, in his form as both the supreme and the inferior.
But by means of the yoga of arising, having summoned the mantras from the supreme state according to their sequential positions for the occasion of worship, [one should proceed]. (Pauṣa 38.254)

And having established Hari, the Lord of All, according to the scriptures, with the weapons and armor as the final elements, when the sacrifice has been completed in accordance with the rules; Paus 38.255.
The practitioner who desires accomplishment should effect a gradual dissolution [of the elements].
Thus, indeed, the power of the Controller, known as Netra, belongs to the Supreme Lord.
By virtue of the radiance of the mantras, she exists as their non-departure;
she should be remembered externally in the lotus, or within the heart, inside the syllable *Ama*.
By means of her own seed-syllable called *niṣedha*, together with the *anusvāra*,
she shines with the brilliance of ten thousand fires, suns, moons, and boars.
Indeed, through the union of the signified and the signifier, everything that is desired in creation is always to be honored by means of the sound of the *sṛṣṭi* [vowel].
Furthermore, through worship, he bestows an unbroken seed of enjoyment that is contrary to the ministers, and which is eternally accomplished through ignorance.
At the time of concluding the daily recitation of the mantra,
as well as at its commencement, one should first understand the mantra exactly as it stands, according to the proper sequence.

The seed-syllable (bīja), the cluster (piṇḍa), that which is called the foot (pada), and likewise the mantra with its characteristics—these indeed are the divisions of mantras, each accompanied by its distinct fruit. (Paus 38.262)
Since the Lord of All exists in the form of various objects of expression,
He is figuratively designated by four kinds of pure designators.
For among the denoters and the denoted,
there exists this mutual manifoldness of forms, once the established rule of correspondence has been realized.

O Brahmin, even without the syllables of the *piṇḍa* known as names and characterized by words, one should effect the conceptualization of the denoted object by means of its own seed-syllables (*bījākṣara*). (Pauṣkara 38.265)
But for the twelve auxiliary limbs (upāṅgas) along with their primary limbs (aṅgas), [the worship is performed] by their own respective names;
however, for the six alone, or even for five, it may be done according to one's wish.
All these, joined with the anusvāra and placed within the *praṇava*,
should be performed by one who is self-possessed through the ritual placement (*nyāsa*) for the supreme worship of the mental form.
At the conclusion, however, one should place the salutation and so forth in accordance with the action;
likewise, when intending a specific result, the salutation is proclaimed [to be used]. (Paus 38.268)
O Lotus-born One, upon the attainment of the powers beginning with *aṇimā*, one should utter *svāhā*; but at the time of nourishment (*āpyāyana*), one should indeed utter *vauṣaṭ* in all cases.
For the purpose of subjugation, as well as for inciting enmity and the rite of expelling the wicked, the utterance *huṃ phaṭ* is prescribed; for mutual affection, *vaṣaṭ* is ordained. (Pauṣa 38.270)

O Brahmin, for the sake of satisfaction, for the offering of oblations, and indeed for the increase of splendor, [one should recite] without exception the word of salutation preceded by the *praṇava*. (Pauṣa 38.271)
There are other classes of mantras that effect the renunciation of karma;
these are prohibited for men who are proponents of established tenets (siddhāntins), even though they are endowed with their respective fruits. (Pauṣkara 38.272)
Especially for those who know the established tenets of mantra, for those who possess knowledge of mantra,
and likewise for practitioners of mantra who know other tantras, O Lotus-born One.

Accompanied by the community of one's own caste, the accomplishments of mantra are authorized by the ritual rules for those seeking fruits who are devoted to the enjoyment of their desires. (Pauṣa 38.274)
Those such as *mālā-mantras* and others which depend upon roots and suffixes, as well as those known as *stuti-mantras* which are accompanied by Vedic mantras; // Paus_38.275 //
O Lotus-born One, those who perform prostrations preceded by the *praṇava* and likewise offer the *tyāgapiṇḍa*, constantly captivate the minds of those who possess that knowledge. (Pauṣa 38.276)
The supreme power of those mantras of manifold meanings is indeed the eternally manifest, subtle Śakti, known as Sattā, whose characteristic is knowledge. (Pauṣkara 38.277)
O Lotus-born one, O Brahmin, their desire for the means of universal trust must be fulfilled; for that virtuous [desire] brings about expansion even in the granting of liberation. (Pauṣa 38.278)
And for the benefit of those devoted to acts of devotion who serve him constantly,
the wise one [bestows] medicinal herbs that grow upwards from the root, according to the prescribed rule.
On this earth, even those who have correctly understood the ritual procedures perform [the rites] by means of fire;
how much more so, then, those who know the scriptures, performing them with devotion according to the prescribed rules?
The instructors of the awakened perform what is beneficial for the mind;
they go into their private chambers, leaving behind all the clamor of bound sounds. (Pausa 38.281)
"Having relied upon the sequence of the beneficial words and mantras," Pauṣkara said:
"O Blessed One, I wish to know them together with their distinctions according to time."
The true nature of the perfected mantras and the scriptures, exactly as it exists.
The distinction of time— the Blessed Lord said: "O best of the twice-born, that which is one time [is divided] again by virtue of its various activities."
It appears as divided to [ordinary] agents, but indeed not so to those who are devoted to the Blessed One.
Indeed, that which is reckoned as a day and night consisting of sixty *nāḍikās* is divided into six seasons;
having divided it into five unequal parts from dawn onwards, one should proceed accordingly.
Having reached the *brāhma* hour, the knower of mantras, restrained and pure,
should purify his own body by means of the postures (*āyāma*) and other practices as prescribed.
Then, one should perform the worship of the mantra, arising from the body in which the mantras have been deposited,
beginning with recitation and hymns of praise, until the appearance of the sun.
Thereafter, one should perform the worship of enjoyments, such as flowers, roots, fruits, and so forth;
when the eighth part of the day has passed, one should carry out this practice preceded by a bath.
As before, one should perform the propitiation of the mantra until the end of the third watch;
thereafter, in the fourth watch, one should engage in the study of the scriptures.
Having performed reflection accompanied by hearing and exposition according to the desire of one's own intellect,
and once the sun has set, having reached the hall of worship, ||| Paus 38.289 |||
One should perform the worship of the mantra correctly, accompanied by recitation and meditation;
thereafter, having taken to the bed, one should remember the Lord of Mantras within the heart.
Having passed the portion of the night and then rising from his bed,
he should indeed practice the mantra-yoga within the lotus of the heart as before.
Having reached his bed once more, O Lotus-born One, he awakens;
rising and leaving his couch, he should then perform what was previously prescribed.
Know this to be the distinction of time; now the distinction of the scriptures is being stated:
that wherein the fourfold self is worshipped as something to be accomplished.
O Pauṣkara, know that the Āgama which was received by the Brāhmaṇas through their own traditional lineages is designated as the Siddhānta, and that [Siddhānta] came before it.
Indeed, that which consists of the twelve forms accompanied by various arrays, as well as the multitude of manifestations joined with other forms; Pausa 38.295.
Endowed with the intervals of manifestation,
it is supported by the heart-lotus and so forth,
along with Lakṣmī and others, those known as the conch and the discus, Garuḍa, and the lords of the directions.

O Lotus-born One, know that this scripture, which bestows all fruits and is known as the *Mantrasiddhānta*, consists of those who are devoted to the weapons (*astra*) along with their attendants. (Pauṣkara 38.297)
Where, in the absence of the fourfold form, the form of the Blessed One is represented by another through the mantra alone, conjoined with the sacrifice. (Pauṣkara 38.298)
O Pauṣkara, it is joined with the very array of Śrī and the others,
accompanied by beloveds, and surrounded by various ornaments and weapons in embodied forms.
That scripture, known as the *Tantrasiddhānta*, bestows both worldly enjoyment and liberation;
therein, indeed, lions and other animals appear according to the distinction between the primary and secondary modes of conduct.
When [the deity] has indeed been worshipped through the yoga of four, three, two, or more [limbs],
they are accompanied by their own respective retinues, or else remain enclosed within them.
Know that whatever is propitiated according to one's capacity is indeed another tantra;
thus, always understand this to be the commonality among the various scriptures.
And in the Pauṣkara, it is stated that there are two names for the Siddhānta, namely Pañcarātra;
each one exists with many divisions from its very root.
By the power of various dispositions, it has been revealed by the Siddhas and others as being concise, elaborate, and thirdly, both; (Paus 38.304).
Through the Itihāsas and Purāṇas, as well as the Vedas together with the Vedāntas,
those who have attained perfection over ten million births— of them, indeed, the end is recorded here.
Therefore, from this scripture, the supreme, imperishable Brahman known as Vāsudeva is attained through action preceded by knowledge.
Therefore, O Brahmins, the designations of his Siddhāntas are indeed meaningful;
for they consist of the Purāṇas, the Vedas and Vedāntas, as well as other works born of Sāṅkhya and Yoga.
O Lotus-born One, it should be known as fivefold, wherein the night is extended;
by virtue of the excellence of its fruit, it is remembered as the *Pañcarātra*.
The root known as the True Tradition (Sadāgama), which reveals the Supreme Brahman,
bestows divine accomplishments and brings peace to obstructive actions.
Thus ends the thirty-eighth chapter, titled "The Description of Qualifications," in the Pauṣkara Saṃhitā, a Great Upaniṣad within the glorious Pāñcarātra.
(Total number of verses:
313) Now begins the thirty-ninth chapter.
Pauṣkara said:
O Supreme Lord, I desire to know eternally the authority of the scriptures along with their designations, as well as the relationship between them and the gods and other beings. (Pauṣkara 39.1)
The Blessed One said: "It is concise and of three kinds—inferior, middling, and superior—and it consists of one hundred verses composed in the *anuṣṭubh* meter. (Pauṣa 39.2)
For that treatise known as the *Mūla* consists of two hundred verses and is designated by its feet;
that which numbers one hundred and fifty is remembered as the *Uddhāra*.
These three are indeed the divisions of deficiency, along with their respective increases and decreases;
yet, although they manifest in many ways for all [beings], their designation does not change again.
That which consists of two hundred and fifty [verses] is indeed to be thoroughly known as the *Uttara*;
and that which is known as the *Bṛhaduttara* would be double this amount.
That is declared to be a kalpa numbering one thousand;
however, the deficiency or excess for this triad should be understood as being in hundreds.
In this way, O Lotus-born One, there are many other scriptures with different names; all of them are but portions of the Kalpa, and they should be understood as such.
From three thousand five hundred up to six thousand and one, and reaching as far as twelve thousand, that scripture is known by the name *Saṃhitā*. (Pauṣkara 39.8)
And those others who indeed occupy the intermediate space by means of more than a hundred scriptural topics—
O Lotus-born One, it should be understood that for all of them, the designation "Saṃhitā" applies.
And those scriptures extending up to one hundred and twenty-five thousand verses,
as well as those exceeding that by a measure of one hundred thousand, have been proclaimed.
All of these, however, should be understood in sequence from the aggregate of eons (*kalpaskandha*),
consisting of many hundreds, thousands, and hundreds of thousands.
And that scripture known as the Tantra, up to three and a half million [verses], is said to be of nine types; thus the division of the triad has been explained.
Therein proceeds an incalculable enumeration of intermediate numbers,
through the awakening that follows the sequence of aeons and by means of the threefold power.
Through an extensive connection beginning with the divine and ending with the intermediate, there is an immeasurable designation; henceforth follows the reunion.

That which emerges together with Kāla from the Supreme Lord, being incalculable, is indeed established in the hearts of the perfected ones (siddhas) who have known all that is to be known. (Pauṣa 39.15)
By whom, through the measure of their own awakening, that which consists of ten million parts has been illuminated;
whose various divisions ending in the syllable *pāda* have indeed been proclaimed in succession.
Wherever it has arisen by its own will, along with various sectarian differences,
there are many other pure rites as well as those characterized by passion (rājasa) and darkness (tāmasa).
O Lotus-born One, the first among all scriptures is the scripture of the Supreme Lord;
it is purified by valid means of knowledge, beneficial, and belongs to the Sātvatas.
In the Siddhānta, those who know the reality of the Blessed One [attain it] from the perspective of ultimate truth;
and by them, that which has been obtained through the lineage is indeed for the liberation of living beings.
Pauṣkara said: O Lord, the supreme scripture of the Great Lord, which is immeasurable, vast, infinite, and like the sky, was first received by Sarveśvara. (Pauṣkara 39.20)
The Blessed One said:
[I shall proclaim] the scripture known as the *Aprameya*, concerning Vāsudeva, who is the Lord of all, the pervasive, the imperishable, the infallible, and the one who is to be expressed in words.
"Know, O twice-born one, that your own sound is not a separate characteristic;
for the self, which is designated as the nature of knowledge, has indeed been led away by its own will, O twice-born one. (Pausa 39.22)
For him who has attained his desires through his own nature and is independent,
this great [ego] called abhimāna, consisting of the power of the guṇas, arises from a portion of his knowledge.
Having himself assumed a form consisting of sound, that Blessed One, who is beyond the senses and imperishable, arrived there of his own accord by his own will.
But that all-pervading Saṃkarṣaṇa rested within the embodiment of knowledge;
and he himself [merged] his own infinite power with the one whose form is knowledge.
His form, consisting of the power of the qualities (guṇa) and called "Light" (prakāśa),
is the eternal Pradyumna, characterized by self-identification and imperturbable.
By that great being, the scripture, blazing with the luster of lightning, was breathed forth; and Vīryamūrti himself indeed entered into it.
Furthermore, O Brahmin, he who assumes an imperishable body called Aniruddha, which is generated from the great fiery essence that has expanded through the nature of *vīrya* (virility/energy).
This scripture, endowed with qualities, powers, and virtues, unconquered and imperishable,
was relinquished like a belch by the high-souled Pradyumna.
Having taken up that which was held within his heart by the self of Aniruddha,
the Lord created the deity Vāgīśa, who consists of the manifestation of the qualities (guṇas).
Unobstructed and of imperishable nature, that pair of meanings is the scripture;
it is not extracted [from elsewhere], is free from doubt, and has thus attained imperishability.
O embodiment of knowledge, that which was known from a portion [of you] has indeed been rendered imperishable within your own primordial form by the embodiment of knowledge.
And the state of being of equal flavor (samarasatva) has been set forth in the various treatises;
it was extracted by the Siddhas from Vāgīśvara and taught exactly as it was spoken.
Having correctly synthesized [these teachings] from the ocean as if from butter,
this has been revealed by the all-pervading Brahmā, the presiding deity of knowledge.
O twice-born one, by those deities headed by Rudra, Āditya, and Indra who were impelled [by him],
and by the Rudras and others born from his own portions, as well as by those born from their own portions who were seekers of his purpose— Pauṣya 39.35.
It was revealed by Brahmā to his own sons, Nārada and the others,
and from them it passed to the sages of purified soul dwelling within the three worlds.
It is solely by the power of his own intention, as well as by the power of various times,
various places, and various castes.
Thus, O one of great intelligence, this connection of the treatise has been told to you exactly as it stands; together with its secret, it must indeed be understood according to its true meaning.
Thus ends the thirty-ninth chapter, titled "The Determination of the Scriptures," in the Pauṣkara-saṃhitā, a Great Upaniṣad of the glorious Pañcarātra.
(Total number of verses: 38) Now begins the fortieth chapter. Pauṣkara said:
"O King, I have understood that great pacification of faults, which is supreme for bringing peace; indeed, through its reversal, it produces a state of mental well-being. (Pausa 40.1)

Through your grace, I have [explained] by way of incidental discussion everything up to the connection with the scripture, as well as that which is the foundation for various dharmas for living beings and bestows heaven. (Pausa 40.2)
Now, therefore, I wish to learn from you in brief the characteristics of the images and other details, along with their secret doctrines, concerning the Source of the World.

The entire procedure known as *pratiṣṭhā* (consecration), previously enjoined in its entirety, as well as the rites involving beeswax for those images that have incurred defects, have been declared. 40.4.
O God, you previously stated that these [measurements] are without honor or measurement; indeed, this characteristic extends from the hair at the top of the head down to the feet. (Paus 40.5)
"O Lord of the World, I did not understand this with full proficiency.
The Blessed One said: "In the past, O Pauṣkara, having established the foundation of various dharmas..."
For the sake of liberation, one should perform the supreme, pure, and imperishable consecration.
On a ground-site possessing auspicious characteristics, having first [prepared] with cow-products and food,
you [should know] the characteristics of the earth together with the accomplishment of the eastern direction.
That which is clearly stated for the purpose of consecration must indeed be understood as such:
the ground, beginning with the water-receptacle and so forth, adorned in various ways. (Pauṣkarasaṃhitā 40.8)

Together with forests, forested tracts, villages, cities, and so forth, he should accept them for the purpose of establishing [the shrine], according to the previous procedure and in accordance with the prescribed rites.
Having prepared an extensive area extending as far as a grove of flowers,
the guide should then perform the excellent concluding rite of the forest journey.
When the ascendant, beginning with the hour (horā), is honored by the moment (muhūrta), when there is an auspicious bird in the sky, and when Mars bestows happiness of mind. (Pauṣa 40.11)
When some portion of the time remaining [for his stay] has passed, he should dwell outside the forest on an auspicious planet, a favorable lunar mansion, and on a suitable day.
One should enter the forest, having first propitiated the forest deities there,
and taking with one a stone endowed with auspicious marks, such as a white one or similar.
One should [use] a tree that is very glossy, resonant with a beautiful sound, pure, free from defects such as cracks and the like, endowed with auspicious marks, uninjured, straight, and firm.

A tree that bears fruit and flowers, which is thick and milky, or one that has been abandoned [by others], belonging to various species, fit for ritual use, and bringing merit as an auxiliary to sacrifices—[such a tree should be chosen]. Paus 40.15.
Having first performed the offering of oblations to the presiding deity beginning with *Sattva*,
and having also performed the ritual dismissal (*visarjana*), the preceptor [should proceed] with [the sacrificial post] smeared with honey and clarified butter.
Then, with a tool, the artisan should strike it;
there, one should find sandalwood, *syandana*, and likewise fragrant sandalwood.
Aloe-wood, *karṇikāra*, *kāśmarya*, and red sandalwood;
*bilva*, *āmalaka*, and mango trees; as well as *tāla*, *varṇaka*, and *siṃhaka* trees. (Pauṣa 40.18)
Śrīparṇī, coconut, nāgamātṛka, pīnaka, products of the cow, kapittha, as well as camphor, tāla, and tamālaka. (Pauṣa 40.19)
The jujube tree, the khadira, the phalgu, the madhūka, the kiṃśuka tree, the phālaveta, the date palm, the nīpa, the nāraṅga, and the śiṃśupa.
The pippala tree, the aśvattha, the great pippalī branch, suradāru, harītakī, bakula, and also the udumbara. // Paus 40.21 //
Kālākhyam, Puṣpakūlam, another tree called Vaira, Phālāsyam, Bhūrjavṛkṣa, Palāśa, and Kṛtamardaka. (Pauṣa 40.22)
The *tinduka*, the heartwood of seeds, the great *mātuluṅga* tree,
the *rājavṛkṣa*, the *kohitaka*, the *sunābhi*, the *kuṭaja*, and the *arjuna*.
Sarala, kuṭaja, śāka, śamī, śrīveṣṭa, ketakī, asana, and spandana; and [the words] stabaka and stabaketa. (Pauṣa 40.24)
Those trees which are full of sap, well-prepared for sacrifice, and honored by the world—
all these excellent trees are to be taken for rites such as the installation ceremony.
By increasing the distance by one *tāla* at a time, up to the limit of the "end of the twelve" (*dvādaśānta*), there are thus sixteen images; this indeed is another [classification].
It is solely by virtue of necessity that these trees have been arranged in sequence for the purpose of making images, from the smallest among them to the largest. (Pauṣa 40.27)
Some rites are prescribed solely by virtue of their results for those seeking results;
others are prescribed for those free from desire, and all of them bestow every kind of fruit.
With these aforementioned seven components, auspicious archways (toraṇas) should be constructed;
indeed, the sacrificial ladles (sruva) and other implements suitable for the fire-ritual have been described.
O Puṣkara, the firewood, the sacrificial fuel, and the enclosing sticks in the fire are for the purpose of propitiating the mantras; they are auspicious seats. Paushya 40.30.
All the various forms of mantras, as well as their respective seats, and the diverse temples and other structures together with their surrounding walls.
Beds, seats, and other such articles for the deities, as well as chariots and the like for the purpose of processions during Vaiṣṇava festivals; Paus 40.32.
One should procure long flagstaffs for the tops of the spires according to the scriptures, having ensured they are dried in the shade.

One must certainly not take [substances] that have been defiled by breakage, division, worms, holes, or the claw-marks of lions and bears, nor those affected by defects such as lightning strikes and the like. Pausa 40.34.
Pauṣkara said:
"O Blessed One, [please describe] the characteristics of the auspicious seats (bhadrapīṭha), the images,
the pedestals for the goddesses, and likewise the temples."
I wish to know correctly the arrangement of the chariots and other vehicles, as well as the dimensions of the flagstaffs and the pavilions that adorn them. (Pauṣya 40.36)
The Blessed One said:
On an auspicious day favorable to oneself and approved by one's teachers, one should first determine the measurements everywhere in consultation with the artisan. (Pausa 40.37)
Then, O Brahmin, one should indeed accomplish everything together with a well-placed [deity]; for those places of manifestation of the All-pervading Lord which were previously mentioned, O Brahmin.
O Lotus-born One, among those two, the natural, auspicious throne is more excellent; it is divine in form and richly endowed with honor, weight, and measure.
In that regard, first, auspicious images of the Blessed One made from gold and other most excellent metals are prescribed; immediately thereafter, those fashioned from stone are likewise auspicious.
Wood, plaster, and likewise paintings are desired according to one's wealth;
among these, the practice of venerating the twice-born is traditionally held to lead to the attainment of liberation.
For the sake of the prosperity of those devoted to service, who are trustworthy and perform sacrifices to the immortals,
and for those intent on ritual offerings and oblations, it leads to the attainment of divine seats in heaven.
O Brahmin, for ascetics who are free from attachment, the most excellent and auspicious place of worship is Hari, the Lord of All, within their own hearts. (Pausa 40.43)
Through worshiping him, one attains incomparable clarity of mind;
having achieved this with effort and consecrated it with Vedic mantras.

One should perform [the purification] with fundamentally pure substances such as earth, ashes, water from sacred fords (tīrtha), and the like, using vessels made of gems, gold, silver, or copper. Pausa 40.45.
Like one's own body, it is composed of the systems of channels and their constituent parts, which are to be accepted,
as well as the bodily constituents (dhātus) and the qualities such as innate knowledge, together with the moon, sun, and fire.
That which, other than the collection of principles ending with earth, exists as a great reflection depending upon substance as its cause; Paus_40.47.
There, in the space of the heart-lotus, that which is placed through the meditation on Brahman—blazing with the light of the jewel of the mantra—bestows its corresponding fruit. (Pauṣa 40.48)
For those agents who are devoted to faith, the fruit comes forth steadily,
always according to the supreme Brahmanic realization and its specific form.
In the end, by virtue of that [practice], one attains the knowledge that illuminates the self;
therefore, now attend to the measurement of images.

One should gradually decrease each [measurement] by one finger-breadth (*aṅgula*) starting from the size of a palm tree (*tāla*), until it reaches a limit of four finger-breadths; thereafter, the measurement is as before.

O Brahmin, one should increase the measurement by one finger-breadth for each [deity] up to the limit of tranquility (śama), until the height reaches two palm-trees (tāla) for those images that are movable; beyond this point, it is not so.

For the immovable [images] and those for the worship of the twice-born, one should increase by two finger-breadths (dvyaṅgula) each in sequence up to a maximum of four cubits; beyond that, one should proceed as appropriate.
One should increase each [measurement] by one *tāla* up to the limit of the "end-maker" (*dvādaśāntakara*),
and from that point upward, one should increase it by one *tāla* plus a quarter.
From the excessive worship of the twice-born, another fourfold result arises;
for the sake of further increase from that prosperity, one should give [the gift] measuring twelve finger-breadths.
One should give a third part from the third part of the threefold measure, or more than that for its height, being half a *tāla* or even a full *tāla*.
For the second type of images, however, the height should be one *śama*;
beyond that, one should increase it for the purpose of determining the measurement.
"O best of the twice-born, there may be one image alone, or another that increases from this point upward,
gradually up to a limit of one hundred [units], measured by the *tāla* with its constituent parts."
For the sake of achieving one's desired height and for the attainment of one's goals,
one should repeatedly effect an increase in stature by virtue of the manifestation of one's form.
Furthermore, the greatness [of the image] in the rite of making the *bimba* is prescribed according to its purpose,
following the proper sequence along with its respective measurements and so forth.
Likewise, it should indeed be understood by one seeking results according to the nature of the result;
and for those free from desire, everything has been taught for the attainment of all fruits. (Pauṣa 40.61)
O twice-born one, it has been declared that there are many varieties according to the class of image, whether made of metal, clay, stone, or wood, according to their availability.
Having ascended his own tree, he assumes a posture with limbs separated by colors produced from it,
and is joined together by bound weapons, garments, and other such items.
O Lotus-born One, just as the bodies of living beings are formed from the various elements such as sinews, bones, and flesh,
so too is the manifestation of mantras through the dhātus and other components traditionally taught.

By both the unawakened and the awakened, she is worshipped with various enjoyments for the sake of attaining the fruits of the four aims of life; thus, through internal worship, she is honored externally as well.
O Brahmin, having set aside the great image made of variegated stone, how else could one fashion [an image] from clay, metal, or wood? (Pauṣa 40.66)
O Brahmin, without these distinct parts purified by valid means of knowledge, this much alone is declared to be the mere measure of the image.

For those devoted to devotion and faith, there is the movable and immovable [image] for the purpose of worship; therein, during the journey to shrines and holy places, there is movement. (Pauṣa 40.68)
And for those who are diligent in making images, one should give [the consecration] free from defects;
when worshipped, it bestows both success in this world and in the next.
Therefore, when installed on separate seats, whether in one's own hermitage or in another hermitage, a separate pedestal for movable images bestows auspiciousness. (Pauṣa 40.70)
For indeed, everything has been prescribed according to the distinction between the mobile and the immobile;
however, those made of clay, as well as the peripheral pedestals alone, have been described only briefly.
Now I shall describe in detail the characteristics of the *bhaṅgāsana*, as well as those of the auspicious seats (*bhadrapīṭha*) made of wood. Paus 40.72.
For that which pervades others— consisting of stone, gold, and so forth—
is, O Mahāmati, from a measure of twelve finger-breadths up to the limit of two cubits.
One should construct the auspicious *bhadrapīṭha* group by increasing the measurement by one finger-width at a time,
using the three types of finger-measures as previously described according to their desired characteristics.
All those with a maximum extent of twelve finger-breadths are known as having the "concise" characteristics;
those that terminate at exactly one cubit are proclaimed as being of "medium" size.
Beyond this, know that the first image is prescribed as being two cubits in extent; understand that its importance increases progressively with each subsequent one.
Through worship with abundant fruits along with *arghya*, flowers, and other offerings,
all [the pillars] shall possess conduits, four bases, and be endowed with excellent craftsmanship.
Those who stand on one leg with only a single garment should be understood by kings as being without water-channels,
yet adorned with limbs and feet.
O Great-minded One, the remaining [deities] should be fashioned like the surface of a mirror,
adorned with crescent moons resembling strings of pearls and accompanied by mirrors.
It was interspersed here and there with lotus petals from blossoming lotuses,
as well as with swans and vidyādharas.
Having now prepared it in such a way as to accord with its beauty,
the abundance of the auspicious pedestal was further adorned by a water-channel.
One should always perform that [rite] to the north of the one being propitiated, but on the southern side of oneself; now its characteristics are described.
In the center of the broad *bhadrapīṭha*, one-third of its width should be made smooth or adorned with artistic designs, according to the previously specified length.
One should then bury the water that appears as if it were the luster of bathing,
having divided it into three perfectly equal parts with portions of equal measure from the front.
Having cleared away two parts from the outside starting from the root at the neck-region,
one should make three points from the root, with the middle one emerging from the path of the arrow.
Know that even for one who delights in the enjoyment of water, above the two parts [of the body],
the Karmāṇinī— whose arrangement has been specified above— must be fashioned.
She who has the form of a crocodile's face and possesses the characteristics of Kapila should be abandoned;
she extends one-third of her width into the ground, with a continuous line of feet.
One should certainly not construct it with an abundance of ornamentation;
rather, like the Sarvatobhadra image, it should be provided with limbs in the center.
One should adorn the various parts of the body with flowers, leaves, and even sprouts,
or else, by means of one's own ingenuity, with marks in the shape of the crescent moon.
To the north of that, one should fashion a lotus, either together with a wheel or alone;
one should make it inclined outward, or else form a great, expansive opening.
Then, in the northeast direction, the face should be well-joined with the end of the portion,
and its extension should likewise be characterized by a clockwise curvature.
Focus one-pointedly on the arrangement of his own limbs, including those situated at the middle and the ends of the body, as well as the *prāsāda* and *bhadra* [postures]. (Pauṣa 40.92)
From half of the seat and from the arghya vessel, the area extending toward the back should be made square,
while that on the left side should be well-rounded.
One should place the head upon that very [pillar], which is abundant and wide;
the pillar should be well-rounded, fashioned smooth, or square.
The pillar-encasement should be eight-fold, or else fashioned with a beautiful design;
it is prescribed to be three times longer than its width.
Together with forests and groves rich in creepers, canopies, and leaves,
it was filled with lords of sages intent on meditation and devoted to the study of the Vedas.
O Mahāmati, [the forms] consist of the conch, discus, mace, and lotus, both manifest and unmanifest;
or else they have rosaries in their hands, being composed of the Blessed One for the sake of accomplishment.
O Lotus-born One, one should arrange these [mantras] in this manner, or otherwise, filling [the space] with full-blown lotuses provided with pericarp and filaments.
Or rather, by those utterly deluded, through their very same actions performed again and again, it must be arranged like a garland of stalks; it is not fit for a noble throne.
But that which is conceived as the portion on the back, beginning with the circle,
exists by nature as the support of the wheel, having the essence of an upward-facing lotus.
Having led it outside, one should fashion a wheel marked with all its constituent parts;
one should construct four pillars like tortoises as the supreme foundation.
O Mahāmati, the width of that which is to be seated with equanimity is indeed established as being one and a half times its [own] width.
In the forest of the earth, [the cloud] may have the shape of the Maheśvara-maṇḍala, or it may be circular,
or level with the region of the summit, or narrow due to its downward slope.
Having made it equal to one-third of its width at the base,
and having refined it as before, it should be provided with a dwelling.
Having brought the Lord of Mantras near for the sake of attaining liberation,
one should indeed worship with supreme devotion, or according to one's own capacity, for the attainment of fruits.
O Lotus-born One, these eight varieties of his have been established by practitioners residing in their own homes with great magnificence; they are eight-cornered.
They may be hexagonal, circular, or even square;
one should fashion that which is square so as to be provided with its own petals.
Therefore, O Mahāmati, for the sake of establishing the existence of this [soul], it has always been proven by means of a measure (pramāṇa) that is consistent with its non-existence. (Pauṣa 40.108)
Having thoroughly inferred [the proportions] by means of the arrangement of the construction and having completed it—
thus ends the fortieth chapter, titled "The Characteristics of the Auspicious Seat" (Bhadrapīṭhalakṣaṇa), in the Pauṣkara Saṃhitā, which is a Great Upaniṣad within the glorious Pañcarātra.
(Total number of verses: 109) Now begins the forty-first chapter.
Pauṣkara said:
"The ritual installation of mantras has indeed been indicated by the path you have described; I now wish to know that which was taught exactly as it is. (Pauṣya 41.1)

The Blessed Lord said: For men who are worshippers, whose souls are solely devoted to the mantra, and who have awakened to the nature of the mantra, worship performed in secret is beneficial. (Pauṣa 41.2)
Now, with a concentrated mind, learn of the arrangement and configuration of those made of wood and other materials arising from the elements, as well as those with pillars. (Pauṣkara 41.3)
Likewise, for pillars that are free from obstructions and whose bases rest upon the ground,
their thickness is traditionally held to be equal to one-third of their own width.
The water-channel should be equal in length to that [altar], or measured as half its width;
having divided it into well-proportioned parts, one should first construct a strong foundation.
The small [villages] are twelve in number, the middling ones are fourteen, and the extensive ones are sixteen; among these, the first category is situated in the middle.
The pedestal should be fashioned from six parts, smooth, level, and auspicious;
it may be perfectly circular or square, or simply in the form of its own lotus.
Alternatively, it is prescribed that the height [of the base] be equal to the combined [heights of the] wheel and the lotus;
its thickness is half [of that height], and for the lotus-stalk, it is one and a half times that.

O best of Brahmins, the previously described characteristics apply equally to those two [mandalas] together with their wheels and lotuses; however, for the square one, one should fashion it as prescribed.
O Lotus-born One, in the corners there should be no construction of conchs, nor should the four [conch-ornaments] beginning with the conch be made on the circular [mandala]. Paus. 41.10.

O Lotus-born One, regarding that which was stated concerning the wheel and the lotus—the four-cornered base being separated from the wheel and the lotus—it is said that their height is half [the diameter]. Pausa 41.11.
It is prescribed neither for one who is alone nor for one who is accompanied by a mantra; one should bury that lotus from the center, part by part, on all sides.
The excavated portion is made equal in width and half as long;
the water-retaining wall all around the excavation is equal in height to the slope on the outside.
The sacred thread (sopavīta) is prescribed when situated within the lines;
such is the determination of the portions for those [lines] made into twelve parts. Paus 41.14.

O twice-born one, the arrangements for the classes of wooden and even stone [images] were previously established according to their divisions, parts, and proportions, as they had been fashioned. (Pauṣa 41.15)
In the center of that, one should perform everything previously described according to the portions [assigned] by the sages;
and one should bury two portions each around it in due order.
The base of the birth [mandala] is traditionally held to be surrounded by one and a half parts;
whatever measurement was stated above that is indeed prescribed for it. (Pauṣkara 41.17)
Having divided that into sixteen parts, one should perform everything in the center with eight parts, together with a quarter of a part, just as before.
O Brahmin, one should bury the trough on all sides with two parts;
the reservoir of water, however, is prescribed with one and a quarter or two parts.
Having established the previously mentioned wheel, beginning with the lotus as described,
one should arrange the nine-lotus formation for the worship of the Lord.
In whatever manner one has calculated the expansion, in that same manner,
having taken [the earth] from the previously dug-out areas, one should join it together in the central region.
By which the field of the lotus is divided for you, as well as that of the nine lotuses, resting upon the supreme mantra. (Paus 41.22)
Just as a lotus is appropriately joined with its common stalk when worshipped, so too should the division of the extensive sections be performed exactly as described. (Pauṣkara 41.23)
Then, having prepared it, one should diligently construct an abundance of girdles and other ornaments,
starting from the water-reservoir and proceeding in sequence according to that specific instruction.
Having cleared away the majority [of the obstructions] from the four directions by means of the *anupāda* [mantra],
one should then perform the ritual service (*bhajet*) starting from the tail, using three, four, five, or six [verses].
Divided into three parts, it has a turban, a lotus, and three girdles;
divided into four parts, it has a turban situated among six girdles.
One should indeed fashion an auspicious lotus pond with two networks of small bells;
when there is an abundance of devotion to the sages, O Lotus-born One, it should be sixfold.
The uṣṇīṣa section, however, should be like the top of a relaxed limb;
below that, the thread is prescribed to be cut, shaped like a pearl-shell (śuktikā).
Below the portion of the oyster-shell design, one should fashion a circle with a pericarp;
and a circular seat is prescribed, or alternatively, a square one on all sides.
One should fashion three tiers below that as the well-characterized girdles;
each should be slightly less than one-quarter of the stated dimensions, in due order.

The stability [of the image] follows the intermediate sūtra; it is beneficial as that which generates the divisions, having abandoned the portion of the uṣṇīṣa-seat and [the figure of] Garuḍa with palms joined in reverence.
One should perform it with one's own mouth joined with the other [hand], or with both hands; I believe this applies to the Bhadrāsana as well.
Between the Gaṅgā and Yamunā, one should fashion Varuṇa, the lord of aquatic creatures,
in the middle of that [space], on the northern side of the auspicious throne (bhadrapīṭha).
On both sides of the measure, one should depict the ocean holding a jewel-vessel, with a gentle form and accompanied by divine aquatic creatures. (Pauṣa 41.34)
Therefore, the remaining four directions should be filled with clusters of small bells,
whether in a material image that is movable or one fashioned from finger-breadths.
Now, for the sake of the renown of kings and others who desire auspiciousness, I shall describe various types of residences that are beneficial for the wealthy and for others as well. (Pauṣa 41.36)
One should first practice the foundation of various dharmas therein—whether it be a king, a practitioner, or anyone else—that indeed bestows both worldly prosperity and heaven. (Pauṣa 41.37)
Having quickly brought about the cessation of that ritual action through the fruit of the rite of releasing a bull (vṛṣotsarga),
one should thereafter indeed perform the re-installation of Hari once again.
Wherein indeed the accumulation of specific karmas utterly subsides,
one does not incur even a livelihood based on unrighteousness through mere intention alone.
For by that very same [practice] which has been correctly completed,
in another birth he shall attain the supreme knowledge born of solitude, which grants the accomplishment of liberation.
For it is not by any other action, but by an action free from poison, that the highest peace is born; one who is subject to the Dharma bestows the imperishable.
Pauṣkara said: "O Blessed One, out of a desire for the welfare of the worlds, I wish to learn from you—the foundation of various dharmas—in order to still my doubts. (Pauṣkara 41.42)
The Blessed One said: First, having constructed an auspicious temple for the five deities, one should do so with a stainless mind entirely free from desire. (Pauṣa 41.43)
In that [city], one should establish a dwelling for the twice-born, dedicated to the purpose of the Dharma;
it is common to all worlds and brings about the destruction of all defects.
It is the supreme among all dharmas, always granting all desires,
the most excellent assembly of those who know the five times, and identical with the Blessed One.
Having recognized him as one devoted to the six duties, dedicated to the dharma of the three Vedas, pure among kinsmen, and free from mutual conflict, [he should be accepted].
Devoted to the study of the Vedas and engaged in the ten types of fire-sacrifices,
he dwelt in a place endowed with rivers, mountains, and forests, and free from harmful creatures.
In a region rich with crops, rice, and fruit, abounding in lush young grass, provided with sweet water, and adorned with strong ramparts; (41.48)
Having reached that auspicious place there and having worshipped the Lord of the World,
he then bathed, was anointed, and adorned himself with garments and ornaments.
Having first established a Brāhmaṇa with a copper-plate charter,
one should worship him as he sits upon the seats with water for the feet, the arghya offering, and flowers.
And with fragrant incenses and betel, O Mahāmati,
