one should offer water with *kuśa* grass into the hand at the places prescribed in due order.
One should cause [the disciple] to recite the twelve-syllable mantra, "pramādyam," and then perform the Sāman chant "pratiṣṭhāsi" as a prayer.
O lotus-eyed one, out of a desire to show me favor, you should be worshipped duly in your own home by means of the rites arising from your own lineage.

Together with his wife who shares the practice of the Dharma, he should, according to the scriptures, place fuel and other materials upon a prepared altar for the sacred fires, or for a single fire, as his capacity permits. (Pauṣa 41.54)
One must act with regard for the three periods of time, and one’s own duty must be fully observed;
entrance [into the order] must not be granted to those who have committed evil deeds.
One's own sons, daughters, servants, ministers,
and those born of one's own lineage should be consecrated according to the Vaiṣṇava rite so that they may become identical with the Blessed One.
From the Brāhma-muhūrta until the appearance of the sun,
one should perform the twilight rites (saṃdhyā) through bathing, worship, recitation of mantras, hymns of praise, and the reading of sacred texts.
Immediately following this is the acquisition of the means for sacrifice and objects of enjoyment;
thereafter, bathing according to the prescribed rule is beneficial, as described by the injunction.
In the evening, having performed the purification of the elements (ābhūtaśuddhi) and immediately thereafter the internal sacrifice (antaryāga),
one should then perform the external worship according to the prescribed rite.
Then follows the oblation to the fire, immediately after which comes the rite for the ancestors,
the offering of bali to the spirits, and the honoring of guests.
Immediately following this, he should perform the sacrifice of himself accompanied by his kinsmen and servants;
then, preceded by the Rig and Sama Vedas, he should engage in the study of his own sacred texts and reflection upon the Itihāsas and other scriptures.
Then, one should perform meditative concentration within the lotus of one's own heart;
thus is described the thirteen-limbed daily rite (āhnika) consisting of the Blessed One. (Pauṣkara 41.62)
Indeed, when the night has passed and the daily task has been performed with devotion, one should again practice renunciation and indeed undertake its formal reception once more. (Pauṣa 41.63)
Having thus received this command from the mouth of the preeminent guide for householders,
the performer should exit that place and perform a circumambulation.
Thus has the ritual procedure for the consecration of the Brahman been told to you;
it must be observed by Vaiṣṇavas and by lords of men for their own spiritual success.
Now, listen to the establishment of our own doctrine:
having constructed a monastery within the sacred precinct, free from artificiality and provided with a means of livelihood.
It was filled with merchant families and laborers, along with throngs of servants;
there stood water-tanks, water-mills, and nets, together with windows.

There, having first bathed together with the preceptor, one should prepare in abundance various kinds of food, including rice accompanied by condiments, as well as foods to be chewed and eaten. Pausa 41.68.
Having first performed the ritual placement (nyāsa) of his body with the twelve-syllable mantras,
the wise one should worship the Lord of the World, the Supreme Lord, the Infallible One.
Having summoned the Brahmins who have arrived and are masters of the Vedas, [he says]:
"This is that immortal food; this is the life-span bestowed by Prajāpati."
"This is Viṣṇu, this is Prāṇa, this is Jīva, this is the Supreme;
and for the sake of the welfare of all beings, the Anuyāga has been established. (Paus 41.71)
O Janārdana, whose form is food, source of the world consisting of the five elements,
remain present here until the dissolution of all beings.
One should recite the Ṛgveda hymns as before; the two subsequent Vedas, the Sāman and the Yajus, should be known;
and the Guru must indeed be requested for instruction beforehand by the disciple together with his family.
Furthermore, it must be engaged in and maintained together with the assembly of guests and others,
with a mind that is intent upon my grace.
Then one should satisfy the assembly with food that has been honored;
thereafter, one should clear away the remnants from those who are seated.
One should depart after circumambulating the gathered assembly of guests;
this is declared to be the establishment of the food for those destined for the imperishable state.
The foundation of knowledge (77–143) is the supreme means of deliverance and likewise the bestower of all happiness.
Now, therefore, attend to this foundation of knowledge.
By performing which indeed arises that knowledge accompanied by discernment.
Having collected the five pure collections of the Pañcarātra,
including all the *sadāgamas* and so forth, together with the Vedas and their auxiliary limbs (*vedāṅgas*).
Endowed with the Smṛtis and other traditional codes, accompanied by the Itihāsas, and encompassed by the sciences of logic (Ānvīkṣikī) along with grammar; Paus. 41.79.
Having filled various collections of colors with the pigments of Nandināgara,
he deposited them into inexhaustible caskets.
Having tied it with a very firm thread, such as black silk or the like,
[one should do so] on a site that is very stable, well-known, and frequented by kings and citizens.
In that mixed settlement inhabited by twice-born men and protected by a multitude of the virtuous,
there was nearby a stone house equipped with iron mechanisms.
It was provided with doors and bolts, white with plaster, and auspicious;
it was adorned by Vāgīśvarī, who sat upon a lotus and was decorated with variegated ornaments.
With her hands raised, holding the conch, discus, mace, and lotus,
she bears a rosary, while her other hand holds a collection of scriptures.

Then, having performed the ritual placement (*nyāsa*) as before, pure and wearing white garments, [he should worship] her who bestows boons and fearlessness, surrounded by the Siddhas and other supreme beings.
Having placed the books containing the compendia of the scriptures in due order upon that iron vehicle, which is presided over by the syllable Om and duly honored; Pausa 41.86.
Having worshipped them, anointed them, and covered them with cloths for the eyes, one should worship them with the twelve-syllable mantra and recite this: [Pauṣa 41.87]
O Viṣṇu, the Supreme Self, whose body is pure knowledge,
remain here indeed as the eternally established and imperishable soul of this scripture.
For the sake of assisting the ignorant and for the generation of awakening,
the immortals and others— who are themselves subject to decay— have thus abandoned you, the imperishable one.
Having spoken thus, one should worship again the embodiment of the Vedas and Vedāntas,
adorned with the true scriptures, the Bhagavata Purāṇa, and other such works.
Every day, with supreme devotion, one should worship the Seat consisting of the Śabdabrahman before the Vidyāpīṭha, upon the auspicious seat previously described.
O best of the twice-born, he should appoint a vigilant person to perform the worship;
then, having circumambulated [the deity] and offered incense, he should ask for forgiveness.
In the distribution of gifts to those who seek them, he should accumulate there a store [of wealth],
as well as a very abundant livelihood for the maintenance of the protection of the Teaching.
Having performed that instruction, he should give it for the preservation of the treasury of knowledge;
thereafter, in that temple, he should cause those who observe the vow of celibacy (brahmacārins) to recite it.
One should oneself recite the two mantras previously mentioned with palms joined in reverence for the sake of people who are blinded by the darkness of ignorance and lack discernment. (Paus 41.95)
Through the establishment of the seat of the scriptures, one attains stainless knowledge;
and by the great fruit arising from this very act, Hari [is attained].
May he attain supreme joy; no fruit of mine is required here, for this establishment of the Seat of Knowledge has been correctly revealed. (Pausa 41.97)
For those seeking fruits, it bestows the desired fruit of steadfastness in knowledge,
as well as the liberation of ponds, wells, tanks, and groves.
For those seeking fruits, the installation [of an image] of Viṣṇu indeed bestows heaven;
for those who have renounced ritual action, it grants that very state of Viṣṇu once again.
The Lord of the worlds, the Master of all, the Imperishable, has become the cause—
[he who is] the formless essence of sound, characterized by the nature of both knowledge and action.
Having attained its own true nature, it remains upon the earth,
having taken recourse to a body composed of that [nature], which is the supreme bliss of truth.
O Mahāmati, such is the power of the gods, the sages, and human beings— composed of various essences and embodied in the form of branches.
She was like a forest fire situated on a mountain peak,
manifesting through various distinct sounds mingled with young shoots, leaves, flowers, wind, and water.
The first portion of the earth is that which is immobile, known as the "footed" (the ground), which yields leaves, flowers, and fruits, and which is the very form of the gods' abode.
Then, from that [fragrance], there arose the moving form of another [deity] who had taken refuge in the abode of Saurabha,
consisting of the five Upanishads.
With the five consecrated mantras, beginning with the *Ṛg* and *Sāma* [Vedas], together with cow-dung and other substances in their proper order, and accompanied by water infused with *kuśa* grass.
Furthermore, for the sake of purification, one should first sprinkle water around that dug pit and subsequently lead it to a state of sanctity by filling it completely with water.
Or else, O twice-born one, by one who has descended to the earth, even with a slight or small offense.
With water that is non-saline, well-purified, and currently cool.
When possible, O friend, even by means of [a gift] purchased through the influence of place and time, or [obtained] from the Tāṭakas in the [forest] groves.
Nor by one who has not extracted [the essence].
Having gone to the presence of the cows and Brahmins, he cast a hundred paces or more into the middle of the pit; thus that pit was made vast and great. (Pauṣa 41.110)
Remaining in water for a long time, extending as far as desired, it should indeed be made so that it is accessible from all directions, lest instability arise. (Pauṣa 41.111)
One should always make it two bow-lengths in width, but deep in depth, so as to evoke intense affection from the elders among the women of noble families.
It may be equal to one and a half bow-lengths, or even ending at a single bow-length;
beginning from two bows, it extends indeed up to a hundred bows.
Once the width of the excavation has been determined, thereafter, according to your [requirements],
there are the earthen, the airy, the lunar, and the fiery [chambers].
Having made it square and elongated, endowed with auspicious characteristics,
and adorned with a multitude of pathways according to the proportions of its various sections.
It was filled with clusters of trees and creepers, adorned with grassy plots,
provided with guest-houses for travelers, and likewise equipped with resting pavilions and arched gateways.
Having acted thus according to the instructions, where there is ground shaped like a cow,
she should determine and maintain it, while effecting a reduction in the excavation.
Satisfying that water until the conclusion of the ritual procedure,
and having thus consecrated it, he should then look toward the eastern direction.

Then the officiant, standing on the western side together with the preceptor and the Brahmins, [should perform the rite] with water drawn from that [well], or otherwise with water available at hand. (Pauṣa 41.119)
At that time, one should smear the ground with clay mixed with cow dung,
using the twelve-syllable Gāyatrī, the Sāman, or the Vāsudeva mantra.
And having stationed, in due order, reciters of the Ṛg, Yajur, and Sāma Vedas in the eastern, southern, and northern directions for the purpose of the fire-oblation.
On dry land, or in ponds belonging to children, or in very beautiful basins,
one should perform the ritual placement (*nyāsa*) using either the twelve-syllable mantra or one's own [mantra].
Having taken a single lump of clay, he should fashion a bowl from its center and place it upon a seat adorned with silk and flowers.
Above that, one should place a golden-bellied jar filled with water,
properly wrapped in a cloth and smeared with saffron and other fragrant substances.
One should place a flower garland, flower clusters, dūrvā grass, darbha grass, seeds, fruit, water,
a white sacred thread, and a bright eye-ointment upon the wearer of the turban.

O Lord, one should meditate upon the immutable, all-pervading Master with the earth-element (pārthiva), which is empty yet endowed with life, together with the name accompanied by the bindu and the nectar. Paus_41.126.
One should contemplate Nārāyaṇa as the supreme form arising from the sweet sound;
at the end, the lotus should be joined to this triad of seed-syllables.
"O Blessed One, salutations then to Nārāyaṇa, the soul of all beings;
the installation preceded by the ritual bath should be performed according to the prescribed rule. (Pauṣa 41.128)
Having performed the fire-offering ritual up to its completion with either the twelve-syllable mantra, the eight-syllable mantra, or the six-syllable mantra, [one should proceed]. (Pauṣa 41.129)
Having honored, according to his ability, the best of the twice-born headed by his guru,
he should then take a full jar filled with water from a pond.
The performer should first place a lump of clay inside the bowl;
having poured out the water from the jar, he should utter this mantra: (Paus 41.131).
O formless Lord, O Protector, O Vāsudeva whose nature is nectar,
remain well-established for as long as the moon and stars endure.
O Lord, grant immediate protection to my followers, as well as to the gods, the ancestors, the Sādhyas, and all beings, who are always nourished by you. (Pauṣa 41.133)
May you attain supreme joy through this fruit arising here;
may there be satisfaction for all beings dwelling within the belly of the three worlds.

Having said this, he should cause those who know the Sāman, the best of Brāhmaṇas, to recite the Sāman beginning with "dhruva ā dyauḥ" and then the Ṛg-verses; and [he should recite] the Sāman beginning with "pratiṣṭhāsi. (Paus 41.135)
Afterwards, with various offerings and the water arising therefrom,
he should satisfy all the Brāhmaṇas as well as all those who performed the excavation.
Having propitiated the guides with gifts when one has the means, as well as the poor, the helpless, and one's servants, for the sake of attaining infinite fruit. (Pauṣa 41.137)
One should perform the gift of gold and land according to one's capacity,
as well as the gift of a maiden and the rite of releasing a bull, preceded by the ancestral śrāddha ceremony.

The fault arising from execution or imprisonment, as well as that arising from fines or confiscation of wealth, must be investigated by the lord of men after he has consulted with the people. (Pauṣa 41.139)
However, this other procedure is prescribed when possible:
[one should plant] a tree that bears the primary fruit, or else a branch of the *aśvattha* tree. (Pauṣa 41.140)
Having established the grove, performed the rites of consecration and bathing,
having anointed himself and adorned himself, he should enter it according to the prescribed rule.
Having wrapped it in a cloth and adorned it with a garland of flowers, one should perform all the rites up to the end of the fire-oblation (homa) as before, accompanied by the mantras. Pausa 41.142.
By that means, the practitioner goes to the further shore, the opposite bank of the ocean of saṃsāra.
Regarding the foundation of fruits,
roots, and food— listen, for I shall describe the foundation of fruits, roots, and food for those who seek such results.
In the three worlds, no gift is found superior to the gift of food.

The taste of food is said to provide immediate gratification, to be pleasing to the heart, and even to sustain the life-breaths of living beings, both at its production and during its preparation. (Pauṣa 41.144)
From food all beings come into existence; therefore everything is established in it.
And that upon which it is established—by that everything is established.
Together with his own self, he shall dwell in this world, in the heavenly realm known as Brahmaloka,
remaining free from disease and devoid of suffering for as long as he lives.
Through sons, wives, wealth, and food, he increases moment by moment;
he receives supreme honor, even greater than that from the most eminent. (Pauṣa 41.147)
The deities, the ṛṣis, and the siddhas constantly contemplate for him supreme increase in lifespan as well as exaltation.
Then, having become joyful and nourished, he is forever satisfied;
after enjoying vast pleasures, he finally reaches the abode of Nārāyaṇa.
Having remained in all the worlds, beginning with heaven, for many hundreds of kalpas, he departs in celestial palaces fashioned by the gods that resemble the moon.
Furthermore, in due course of time, he returns here to this most excellent and auspicious land,
obtaining birth in a family of the virtuous, a great and supreme birth among the highest caste.
He is born handsome, eloquent, and devoted to learning and wisdom;
he is always honored and most beloved even by all his enemies. (Pauṣa 41.152)
Virtuous, endowed with heroism, possessed of fortitude and energy,
always devoted to the twice-born and the gods, he is a donor intent on the welfare of all beings.
Devoted exclusively to him, truly knowing the Dharma, and having Nārāyaṇa as his supreme goal,
he enjoys the entirety of the three aims of life according to his desired characteristics.
Having performed again auspicious karma practiced throughout many births, which possesses infinite merit, one attains knowledge by means of which one proceeds to the supreme state. (Pauṣa 41.155)
Indeed, there is no worship of wells, ponds, or fragrant flowers;
one should bestow what is pure, for that constitutes identity with the deity, and one should perform the entire ritual procedure accordingly.
And having brought the herd of cows into this temple of the Blessed One,
he offered libations of clarified butter to the Lord after first providing them with baths and enjoyments.
For the sake of pleasing the cows, however, the teaching should be imparted;
that fire, accompanied by a cow-pen and provided with a lamp of ghee.
It must be protected like a deity as long as the moon and stars exist;
blazing incessantly, it shall dwell together with those who perform its service. (Pauṣa 41.159)
Having reached the auspicious time beginning with the Ṣaḍaśītimukha, which bestows merit,
one should construct a sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa) endowed with excellent characteristics within the home of a Vaiṣṇava, using divine and other materials.
Or else, one may perform the installation oneself upon the pillars of Dharma established in the past,
using auspicious Vaiṣṇava hymns and the twelve-syllable mantra and others.
With thousands of *ṛc*, *yajus*, and *sāman* verses that praise the God of gods,
the *hotṛ* priest should likewise recite them slowly once the rite for pacification has been performed.

Having consecrated the fire and the sacrificial pit with ghee and other substances, with unbroken grains, and with yellow, white, and black sesame seeds, according to the rite dedicated to Prajāpati; Paus_41.163.
One should offer oblations beginning from a thousand up to ten thousand,
or starting from a hundred up to a thousand, using a ladle made of copper.
Then one should offer clarified butter measured by an eighth part of the *pālīya* measure;
whether free from desire or possessed of desire, one should then offer the final oblation (*pūrṇāhuti*).
But Nārāyaṇa, whose self is the Veda, through the mouth of the Veda itself,
grants all desired objects as well as the ultimate means.
When this has been performed and accomplished, one should indeed bind [the vessel] upon the pedestal;
and for seven days, or alternatively for three auspicious nights, one should perform the Vasudhārā rite.
Alternatively, the procedure for performing it for a single day according to one's own capacity is now described:
[it should be done] in a smokeless, wide sacrificial pit using firm pieces of wood fit for sacrifice.

Having constructed a fire-altar on the ground of the girdle (mekhalā), either exceeding the height of a palanquin, or two bow-lengths high, or even higher than that, made of copper and well-spread; Paus. 41.169.
A cauldron should be joined to a firm wooden ring,
supported by four sturdy bamboo legs, and capable of withstanding the weight of the fire.
Then, it should be raised by four finger-breadths measured with a ruler;
the golden probe, produced from a measure of pure gold, must be uniform in every part.

One should perform the piercing with iron in a medium-sized crucible that is equipped with the proper measurements; then, one should take [the substance] after it has been filtered through cloth. Paus 41.172.
Having carefully poured into a cauldron clarified butter that is free from scum, fragrant, and possessing auspicious characteristics, and having previously performed the purification; Paus_41.173.
"Regarding the flow of time consisting of day and night, which is said to be threefold—starting from this point, you have spoken thus concerning the Lord, the Self, and the senses. (Pauṣa 41.174)
Or else, one should cause clarified butter to be offered from dawn until the end of the day, for one watch,
or for two watches, or even for three watches.
Or else, there are four *praharas*, depending on one's own capacity;
for it begins at a measure of six *prasthas* and indeed ends at four *prasthas*.
One should take up the flow according to one's capacity, or a *pālika* measure of clarified butter;
having spread it as clarified butter through the state of the inner self (*adhyātmatā*), enriched by the presiding elements (*adhibhūta*) and presiding deities (*adhideva*). (Pauṣa 41.177)

The sacrificial grass is the immortal Brahman; the clarified butter is indeed the supreme Self (adhyātma). The fire is the supreme deity (adhideva), and the herd of cows is the elemental substrate (adhibhūta).
For it has been declared by me that, considering wealth to be such, one who maintains his true nature acts according to the prescribed rule and the measure of its gates.
It was by his power that this entire world became truly impoverished;
for he had covered the cooking pot with a wide-open vessel.
And the Blessed One, Puruṣottama, is to be worshipped as a deity with offerings of water for the feet,
flowers, and so forth, within a vessel filled with wealth.
He himself remains a bestower of grace upon men who possess faith,
from the very commencement until the completion of their auspicious deeds.
Having worshipped and paid homage to Acyuta with the twelve-syllable mantra,
one should then offer unguents, as well as garlands of flowers and incense.
Then, with devotion, [he offered] a great oblation consisting of honey-mixture (madhuparka) and other foods, along with edibles and fruits,
to the Lord of All, the omnipresent one, stationed in his sanctuary.
Having performed the ritual preceded by bathing with great magnificence,
he should worship according to the rules with excellent and authentic hymns.
With the secret mantras consisting of eight or twelve syllables,
having placed both knees upon the ground, one should remain with the head bowed down in front.
Having first established this [mantra] which is the sole security, one should recite:
"The supreme wealth, the clarified butter, all this has been completely fulfilled by you. (Pauṣa 41.187)
O Lord, this supreme power, Tāreya, is worshipped as the sovereign;
its abode is like the southeast, and it indeed yields the fruit of sacrifice.
Having completed that village, which was situated within the district and endowed with a very large Gokula, by means of the edict of the Brahmins who were its guardians; Pausa 41.187.
In such a way that his great fame and supreme dharma are not cut off,
so must this be accomplished by the king for the increase of his glory and righteousness.
Whatever is auspicious beyond the group of six is proclaimed as a triad:
the cow-pen, the fire, and the lamp; these are the limbs within the sacred precincts.
And it must be protected by those who know the Dharma so that there may be no interruption;
for through the mouth of the fire alone, the thirty-three crores [of gods] [are sustained].
And every day they attain incomparable satisfaction for the gods by means of various products derived from cows, beginning with curd, milk, and clarified butter.
The Blessed One attains delight through offerings that are characterized by goodness (sāttvika);
like the supreme sun, he illumines everything with his splendor.
And by the power of the lamp that is always present, he who, having taken the Lord of the World as his object, [recites] during the sixty-four festivals (ṣaḍaśītimukha),... [Pauṣa 41.195]
On the lunar days, the Blessed One is to be worshipped in a water-pot, a mandala, or in fire;
[the worshipper], having fasted, being pure, bathed, and having performed the auspicious rites of kautuka, [should perform the rite].
With this mantra, beginning with *praṇava* and ending with *namaḥ*, let the Lord of Gods, the overseer of dharma, Vṛṣākapi, be pleased with me through my devotion. (Pauṣa 41.197)
The benefactor of cattle, the lord of cattle, and the protector stands encompassing everything;
therefore, on a smeared portion of ground, or indeed on a mere *kutapa* [woolen blanket], [the rite should be performed].
Having spread out a pure cloth that has not been worn or used, together with sesame seeds, unbroken rice grains, all kinds of seeds, kuśa grass, and white mustard seeds; Paus_41.199.
One should place that [substance] outside the fire-vessel, filling it completely starting from the east in due order;
there should be eight vessels containing milk, rice, curd, sugar-cane juice, and sesame seeds.
With ghee, all kinds of seeds, and cloths, there should be a curtain outside;
together with arrows, threads, peacock feathers, and well-prepared seats.
There were shallow bowls containing seeds, placed upon the mouths of full water-jars;
these were joined with branches laden with fruit and adorned with the boughs of trees.
Having placed [the vessel] along with lamps blazing in all directions, accompanied by the Rigveda and other [Vedas],
he should then bring down the cow Surabhi, adorned with ornaments, into its center.
It was adorned with ornaments and cloth, decorated with bells and chowries,
and embellished with gems, gold, and white lotuses upon its peaks.
With a tail like a pearl and coral, silver-colored feet, and a beloved mate;
with a mirror-like forehead, she was magnificent, possessing a splendid garland and a powerful crest. (Pauṣa 41.205)
In this very way, you should now honor Surabhi, who is adorned with ornaments,
established in her youth, and bold, on the left side of the bull.
It should be joined with a bronze milking vessel, consecrated on the preceding day,
and provided with the footprints known as Nandā, Sunandā, Surabhi, and Śītala.
Four milch-cows should be stationed there facing forward toward the east and other directions;
they should be endowed with great power and wealth, capable of yielding milk, and skillful in their movement.

Now, indeed, with reference to the directions and to one's chosen deity, [one should offer] cows that are pregnant, those with their calves, and those that have recently calved, each one by one. (Pauṣa 41.209)
One should cast it out with his own *hetu* mantra and sandalwood paste, along with the *vṛṣṇikṣetra*, provided that such materials are indeed available for him. (Pauṣa 41.210)
One should provide assistance according to one's ability, but its price must not be calculated;
having established the four Agnihotra fires outside [the village], one should offer them.
One should offer garments and ornaments, fragrant substances,
the earth or wealth for the sake of the earth, and whatever implements belong to a bull.
Having prostrated with devotion to the Guru, one should release the bull and Surabhi on the right side of the shoulder, using the weapon favored by him.
And it should be sealed in an instant with iron heated by fire;
having performed the renunciation of the bull in this manner, specifically for that purpose, once again— Pausa 41.214.
And one should indeed give abundant gifts of food along with ritual fees (dakṣiṇā), dedicating them to the Lord of Mantras for one's own sake or for the sake of another. (Pauṣa 41.215)
He who performs the rite of releasing a bull indeed goes to the world of Brahmā;
for the bull is the Blessed Dharma in this world, bound by desire and purpose.
By that which has been renounced, the eternal suffering of birth is indeed completely abandoned;
for Prakṛti, together with the eternal Surabhī, is truly perishable.
And due to that distinction, there are three powers whose nature is passion:
the first is the intellect [with the thought] "I am," and the next is the five sense organs.
All those who abide by relying on the spiritual lineage (gotra) turn back from [samsaric existence],
for the establishment in various dharmas occurs together with the release of the bull.
It has been spoken regarding that which was born from the lotus; now, pay close attention to that divine [teaching] which bestows liberation and has been indicated again and again. (Pauṣa 41.220)
The installation, O lotus-eyed one, is imperishable and bestows both worldly enjoyment and liberation.
Thus ends the forty-first chapter, titled "The Installation of Various Dharmas," in the glorious Pauṣkara-saṃhitā.
Now begins the forty-second chapter.
The Blessed One said: "In ancient times, the Lord of All [was worshipped] with mantras preceded by the twelve syllables."

The Blessed One is to be propitiated with devotion upon an altar, or in a water-pot, or on the ground; having gratified him with devotion through oblations of clarified butter and other offerings, one should then [worship] with mantras consisting of the Vedas.
The Blessed One, whose self is Viśvakarman, should cause Gaṇeśa to perform the sacrifice with various services,
such as flowers, incense, and ointments.
O Lotus-born One, when Viṣṇu has been dismissed along with the fire, those artisans who are skillful and worthy of honor [should be rewarded] immediately thereafter. (Pausa 42.4)
Moreover, with minds full of serene faith, they constantly perform [the rites];
by them, being purified and bathed, their own husband is to be gratified.
"Therefore, O twice-born one, you must accept a field that is pleasing to you—
whether it be uncultivated or cultivated, provided it is endowed with the qualities of the earth."
Having taken up [the site] which is free of thorns, favorable, approved by architects, and as extensive as desired for the purpose of establishing the foundation. (Pausa 42.7)

Mahendra, Varuṇa, Vāyu, and Viṣṇu, having reached their respective stations in the directions of the East, West, North, and South, should indeed perform [the rite] while resorting to divine abodes. (Pauṣa 42.8)
But preceded by the five sense-bases, the great and auspicious temple of the gods leads to success through one's own path; however, through a wrong path, it leads to failure.

This much has been stated regarding those who are liberated from their objects of desire; however, for others, it results in fault, since Hari is omnipresent within both their own path and the path of others.
When it flashes incessantly in the intellect, one should oneself [recognize] that Guru according to the scriptures;
then, under an auspicious and favorable lunar mansion, having paid homage to the omnipresent Lord Acyuta—

O twice-born one, having first warded off obstacles eternally, he should perform worship together with others who follow the Ekāyana path and those who recite the Ṛg, Yajur, and Sāma Vedas. (Pauṣa 42.12)
They were adorned with ornaments, wearing turbans and white garments,
decorated with ointments and garlands, and graced with finger-rings.
With the sounds of conch shells and musical instruments, with auspicious songs,
and with hands holding fruits, flowers, unbroken rice grains, nets, white mustard seeds, and so forth—
O twice-born one, having undertaken the rite with purity and accompanied by the preceptor, the performer should reach the site while remembering Vāsudeva in his heart. Pausa 42.15.

Having caused the declaration of an auspicious day (*puṇyāha*) to be recited, and having proclaimed the three *gāyatrīs* and so forth, as well as the *śākuna-sūkta* and the *śivasaṃkalpa*, [he should proceed]. (Pauṣa 42.16)
Accompanied by the Śrīsūkta and the excellent Bhadraśrīsāman, one should recite "Svasti bho" together with the commencement of the ritual action. (Pauṣa 42.17)

Then, having pierced the six *camasas*, immediately thereafter, the officiant, remaining there while reciting the eight-syllabled mantra beginning with "Śānta," becomes the teacher for those [disciples]. (Pauṣkara 42.18)

O Lotus-born One, having constructed outside the field, either in the northeast or in the east, a beautiful leaf-hut that is capable of withstanding wind and rain, (one should dwell there). Pausa 42.19.
There, having prepared flowers, water for honor, incense, and so forth, and having placed [the deity] upon an auspicious seat,
one should prepare the five products of the cow (pañcagavya) together with various mantras.

Having brought Nārāyaṇa, the embodiment of the waters, into proximity within an auspicious golden vessel, and having worshipped him upon a riverbank honored with water from sacred fords (tīrtha), [one should proceed].
Then, having prepared the arrangement here with gold, all medicinal herbs, and a garland of darbha grass, one should perform the ritual using the mantra-vessel and the weapon-vessel.
Having recognized that the seat is common to both of them, one should perform its worship;
having worshipped the Lord of Mantras together with his weapon in the heart according to the rule.
It should be placed upon the kumbha seat together with the vital breath and the mind, by way of the lunar channel; thereafter, indeed, the Weapon [mantra], the king of mantras.
O twice-born one, these three mantras are prescribed as common to all:
the mantra of six syllables, that of eight syllables, and likewise that of twelve syllables.

That thousand-spoked weapon, the Lord of Weapons (Hetīśa), which has been fully understood and obtained by one who has undergone initiation from a truly gracious guru—[that is the weapon]. Paus 42.27.

Having worshipped this auspicious weapon, together with its limbs and this specific [deity], along with all its constituent parts, by means of enjoyments ending with the sacrificial portions (mātrā), one should cause that limb to be attained.
Then, with excellent Ṛg-verses, Yajus-formulas, and Sāman-chants characterized by their appropriate occasions,
as well as with the manifesters of all the lords, one should perform the fire-oblation (homa).

The preceptor should thus perform [the rite] with sesame seeds mixed with unbroken rice, numbering one hundred thousand, using the mantras of the fire-pit (kuṇḍa) and the weapon (astra), purified by the gaze [of the deity]. Paus 42.30.
And having stationed four attendants of his own, who were experts in mantras and adorned with ornaments, upon the sandy banks and other such places in the east and the other directions; (Pausa 42.31)
Those four [Vedas] beginning with the Ṛgveda, from the Īśa up to the Vāyupatha,
are to be worshipped with devotion by those intent on ritual action for the purpose of oblations during the collection of the sacred field.
One should offer abundant clarified butter and other substances with those mantras characterized by the *bhrami* syllables,
using the four mantras pertaining to the fourfold self, preceded by the sixteen-syllable [mantra].
The other Brahmins, remembering Hari, the Lord of All,
should offer the oblations while he stands as the supervisor in the fourth corner, having assigned each one to his respective task.

For the purpose of the fire sacrifice in all the sacrificial pits, those who are pure, self-controlled, skillful, and trained in the science of architecture should perform the rite, having projected the deity’s form through the arrangement of mantras.
Having summoned those born of the lineage of Viśvakarman and seated them before him,
he should sprinkle them with the five products of the cow (pañcagavya) and other substances, while they are indeed clad in white garments.
Having observed those whose fingers and other limbs were adorned with garlands, sandalwood, and turbans,
and having purified them, he took them along with the water-pot.
One should place a very firm cotton thread, consecrated with the Sahasrāra mantra,
into the hands of the master builders along with a single rod.
Having sprinkled with the five products of the cow (pañcagavya) and consecrated with a thousand recitations,
he should scatter seeds mixed with parched grain and accompanied by white mustard seeds.
While reciting the Astra-mantra, one should perform three circumambulations clockwise around the discus,
from the starting point back to that same spot, accompanied by the auspicious sounds of the ringing bell.
Then, having taken the measurement of the site according to the desired cubits,
[one should proceed] by means of the portions of Viśvakarman residing in the disciple, the preceptor, or the agent.
Having extended that thread from the northeast corner and so forth toward the four directions,
one should seal the eight directions with stakes made of sacrificial wood.
Then, the wise man should offer the *bhūtabali* in a clockwise direction,
consisting of sesame flour, powder of turmeric, parched rice, curd, and barley meal.
This is declared to be "Bhūtakrūra"; with it, one should offer the *bali* to the spirits (*bhūta*).
Whatever spirits or even *rākṣasas* may dwell here [in this place], [they shall be satisfied]. (Pauṣa 42.44)
May all those [obstacles] depart today; I shall prepare this place for Hari by tying together trees with arrows, cane-sticks, creepers, bundles of hides, and other materials. (Pauṣa 42.45)
One should take spades known as *kuddāla*, which are shaped like the upper part of a drum, capable of holding white clay, not too heavy, and not sharp. (Pauṣa 42.46)
Standing upon the sacred site of the *brahmapada* and facing whichever direction one desires, one should worship the very firm elephant-footprints made from sacrificial wood. (Pauṣa 42.47)
Having recollected [the mantra] consisting of twelve syllables, the Blessed One, the creator of beings,
should meditate upon that which is characterized by the supreme self (adhyātma), known as the presiding deities (adhideva) and the presiding elements (adhibhūta).
There, [he beheld] the earth consisting of seven continents, complete with oceans and the like,
together with the seven netherworlds, and endowed with all beings, beginning with the mobile.
She is completely enveloped by all the powers (śaktis) residing in sound,
together with the seed-syllable *brahma* and the letter *la* accompanied by the nasal bindu.
Having first honored [the deity] by means of one's own mental conception,
and having meditated upon the state of the adhibhūta, one should thereafter recollect the ādhidaiva.
The supreme power of the Blessed Viṣṇu, the Lord of All,
is his great Vaiṣṇava form as the Boar, which is the ultimate nature of the inner self.
Thus much has been said regarding meditation in general for the acquisition of land;
one should also keep in mind the other specific [meditations] here, according to the nature of the temple site.
Having meditated upon the manifestation of the fourfold array of forms within the square,
one should contemplate this divine transmission of knowledge within the long square.
One should meditate on the wheel whose spokes have subsided and arisen, with its parts well-concealed;
one should contemplate the Lord reclining upon Ananta within the circular and rectangular chamber.
The pure "city of eight" (puryaṣṭaka), which bears the body of the lotus of time,
arose from the navel-cavity of Viṣṇu and abides as the essence of the eight directions.
In the temple, one should contemplate the earthly abode as having eight corners;
having meditated thus, one should do so repeatedly with the twelve-syllable mantra. (Pauṣa 42.57)
Having restrained [the breath] with the six-syllable mantra and bound the *mudrā* of the twice-born Acyuta,
[he remains] through the concentration of meditative visualization until the presence of the jar.
Then, as before, one should worship with extraordinary enjoyments using the eight-syllable mantra;
together with the brahmins, one should personally offer the final oblation (pūrṇāhuti) into the fire once again.
When the field has been consecrated for the purpose of all ritual actions,
one should indeed perform the installation of the feet on another most auspicious day.
Then, skillful laborers should be appointed in due order;
indeed, by satisfying them with food, drink, and other provisions, they will surely attain contentment.
The Blessed One said:
"When a portion of the earth has been thus taken up and cleared of thorns,
and when it is firm and free from pebbles, that young girl becomes the Earth herself, a bestower of wealth."
Did he perhaps seek some artificial purity and abandon that grove,
which was filled with great trees long established there? (Pauṣya 42.63)
It was crowded and filled with dense roots produced by that [tree];
its youthfulness was recognized, for it was traditionally held that its purity would surely manifest.
Cities, villages, and regions are not abandoned by the currents of rivers,
for they repeatedly shatter hopes while beholding great purity.
Having bathed and indeed having extracted the inner essence, one should give as a gift auspicious clay—white, free of grit, and smooth—or else one should bury it within the water. (Pauṣa 42.66)
Having seen the water and worshipped it, one should offer libations to the Lord of Aquatic Creatures,
together with the lords of the Nāgas and the assembly of gods stationed there.
For the sake of stability, it is filled with all kinds of stones and earth;
and having been filled with both earth and stones, it is then smoothed over with that same clay among the various layers.
Having repeatedly pounded [the ground] from the edge of the water-channel,
and having leveled and smeared it, one should then cause the herd of cows to dwell there.
It was filled with young calves together with herds of lordly bulls,
possessed rice fields full of water, and abundant stores of grass.
Having scattered sesame seeds there, once the cow dung and other materials have been removed,
he should then drive away the herd of cows and smear the ground once again.
Having worshipped [the deity], O Lotus-born One, the Sun-natured one should perform the attainment of the directions as before, [visualizing] the temple endowed with the form of the Blessed One.
Having first determined the direction facing one's preference,
one should then construct the sacrificial pavilion on that plot of ground.

If that [direction] cannot be obtained in the three directions, then [the site] should extend toward the north and south for the sake of suitability, purity, comfort, and freedom from obstacles. (Pauṣa 42.74)
There, the fivefold royal throne is arranged with reeds, kāśa grass, śara grass, and tufts of wool, either uncut or prepared by others, set apart with intervals.
Then, according to one's means, it may be seven, six, or five cubits;
or indeed four cubits, or even four and a half cubits.
O best of Brahmins, having excluded the intermediate spaces from all [the sections] by means of a sixth part of their respective extensive widths, one should then proceed with the height.
O Mahāmati, one should adorn all the corner pillars with their own respective twenty-fourth part of the width and height.
Having raised them to that same height above the tops of the pillars,
other beams were fashioned in various designs and extended crosswise.
All [the arches] arise from the large lotus and are provided with gateways (toraṇa) on the four directions;
the width of the gateways should indeed be one-third of the pedestal (pīṭha).
The height of all [the deities] is prescribed as three parts of their respective widths;
all of them, together with their wheels and Garuḍas, are [to be made] in the proportions of three, four, or five [parts]. (Pauṣa 42.81)
Having ensured that all of them possess auspicious characteristics, one should fix all the archways together with their pillars upon the ground at the prescribed intervals.
Furthermore, O twice-born one, the regions are square, while those in the middle are eight-cornered;
the upper portions are circular, all divided into equal parts.
The eastern and western portions of the street are equal to both seats;
each of the southern and northern sections constitutes a single seat-arrangement.
Having thus completed the sacrificial pavilion for the Blessed One with all ritual actions,
one should construct an altar marked with a lotus above the northern seat.
Circular or square, well-proportioned and auspiciously marked, it is known as the "Luminous" (prakāśa),
with its ground adorned by a girdle and inscribed with the symbols of the conch, discus, mace, and lotus.
For the purpose of consecrating the ritual substances,
one should perform the worship of the mantra, the weapon, and the vase upon the central seat within the mandala on the ground situated near them.
In the chamber for the medicinal herbs, one should arrange four jars for bathing;
elsewhere, however, one should place the bed upon that very bathing-platform.
Know that the fifth pedestal, provided with bathing materials, should be well-worshipped with sands and placed near the bathing pitcher. (Pauṣa 42.87)
Having thus prepared the great circular enclosure wall for the purpose of the consecration ceremony— equipped with six gates, windows, and doors provided with bolts— Paus_42.90.
Having abandoned the measurement of the temple site situated all around it,
one should draw an eightfold set of sacrificial pits (kuṇḍas) in the cardinal directions, together with their boundary lines (mekhalā) and pedestals (pīṭha).
In the case of a secondary alternative (anukalpa), however, one should construct [the pavilions] outside the eastern sector, or in the western part thereof;
they should share a single pedestal and be provided with archways (toraṇa).
Or there may be pillars with separate pedestals, distinct from one another;
on the eastern side is that called Cakrapadma, and on the southern side is Kevaleśvarī.
Or it may be fashioned as a square with a gada-belt, O Lotus-born One;
on the northern side of the lotus, one should place a conch shell, and [the other emblems] in the four corners.
O Brahmin, this is recorded as the arrangement of the sacrificial pits (kuṇḍas) for the rite of installation of deities such as the Cāturātmya in the foundation of the pedestal.
Listen to the arrangement of the sacrificial pits (kuṇḍas) in various directions and intermediate points, for the increase of great prosperity, good fortune, long life, and health. (Pauṣa 42.96)
Know that for the accomplishment of all activities and the removal of obstacles, there is a reversal of results; however, for liberation, it is equanimity.
O Brahmin, it is endowed with two pairs of maces in the eastern direction and four arrows in the north-east; the discus is in the southern direction, and then the conch is in the western direction.
In the northern direction, one should place a lotus with petals as desired; having prepared the southeast fire-pit in the shape of an *aśvattha* leaf. (Pauṣa 42.99)
One should fashion a *vimuktakamala* (lotus with released petals), a triangle, and a circle as before;
for the purpose of the fire-oblation (*homa*), there should be a sacrificial pit (*kuṇḍa*) in the direction of the Yātus (southwest), or an eight-sided one in the quarter of Vāyu (northwest).
Having first drawn the seat known as Śrīvatsa, characterized by a half-moon as described before,
one should mark it with its defining features in the northeast.
Beyond this, attend with one-pointed mind to another configuration:
the abode situated in the eastern quarter, in the south-eastern direction, having the form of the Kaustubha gem.
The discus is in the southern quarter; the bow-shaped [weapon] is in the direction of Yātu;
the water-born mace-shaped [weapon] is in the west; and that called the forest-garland is in the position of Vāyu.
The form of the northern direction is like a lotus, and the form of the north-east is like the Śrīvatsa;
indeed, for all [directions], it is ordained that they be equal in their extent.
As before, having rubbed away half of the lip by one-twelfth [of its width],
one should fashion a very level binding for the girdle, equal in width to that [lip].
O twice-born one, as before, all the uneven lines should be provided with girdles;
the yoni should be fashioned according to the prescribed characteristics, like the leaf of a *pippala* tree.
In the central region, one should draw a well-rounded fourth [line] marked with the Śrīvatsa;
or else, that same [line] should be outside the area of the temple ground at the northeast corner.
O Great-minded One, having performed the libation for all rites accompanied by honorific offerings, as well as for the deities who are limbs of the site and for the world-protectors; Pausa 42.108.
O Lotus-born One, having thus prepared the sacrificial hall together with the fire-pits for Vighneśa, the gatekeepers, Kṣetreśa, and the Earth, [one should proceed]. Paus 42.109.
Then, both from within and from without, one should adorn the army with various beautiful banners and those multitudes of Vaijayantī flags.
With lofty, purifying, and sturdy plantain-tree trunks, with clothed [vessels], with full water-jars, and indeed with clusters of blossoms and flower-stalks; Pausa 42.111.
Indeed, it is without a fire-house, yet possesses canopies of various forms,
along with arrows, peacock feathers, threads, and the presiding deities of the elements.
Previously, the Lords of the World and others had arrived, stationed as gatekeepers in the groves of the field,
with mirrors, variegated fly-whisks, and clusters of bells resonating with musical notes.
With bronze vessels completely filled with honey, clarified butter, curd, and milk, and with groups of green *pālikā* offerings placed upon the mouths of the jars; Paus_42.114.
With vessels of śāli rice accompanied by gold and filled with fruits, along with parched grain, white mustard seeds, and bowls of seeds endowed with the six flavors; Paus_42.115.
Then, with fragrant substances such as cinnamon and cardamom, with vessels and betel nuts, and with the three fruits— madhūka, badarī, and lākṣā— as well as other excellent fruits.
Just as with the many flowers produced from that [tree], arranged in various clusters, and with such diverse and purifying multitudes of enjoyments; Pausa 42.117.
The ground-levels outside the pedestal, surrounding all directions,
should be entered there along with the entire collection of abundant offerings that has been gathered.
Then, when the planet is auspicious and the lunar mansion is favorable and stable,
and when the ascendant is stable, situated in a stable division, completely pure, and endowed with excellent qualities— // Paus_42.119 //
For the purpose of establishing the base of the temple’s pillars, the patron, becoming one with the Blessed One,
having performed his daily rites, shall be accompanied by the foremost of the twice-born and by the preceptor.
Accompanied by the sounds of kettledrums, tabors, musical instruments, conchs, and the like,
they recite the praised Vedic hymns beginning with the Ṛg, Yajur, and Sāma Vedas.
Having performed the worship of the gatekeepers and entered the sacrificial hall,
one should recollect the pervasive presence [of the deity] upon one's own seat, perform the worship, and sit down.
Near the central pedestal, on the western foot, one should place [the deity] facing east;
and on the seats made of ṛks, those facing the eastern direction should be joined facing west.
One should employ the Yajurvedic mantras for the mechanism of the northern and southern directions, and having assigned the Sāmavedic mantras to the western part facing eastward.
And together with the Brahmins of the Ekāyana school, who were characterized by the designation "Mūrti," he then [saw] those in the northern direction who were devoted to their daily rites.
Then, having established the branches of the Atharvaveda in pairs,
he remained behind with good assistants, awaiting perfect knowledge.
And he should place the instructor of the mantras, together with the twice-born and others, in worship to his right, as a single portrait, composed in meditation. (Pauṣa 42.127)
Then, having mentally grasped the power of the deity who presides over the mantra, one should perform the ritual placement (*nyāsa*) with the form of the twelve-syllable mantra.
Then, with mantras consisting of the Vedas preceded by the eight-syllabled mantra,
one should first offer water for the feet and the vessel of honor (bhṛṅgāraka) according to the previously stated procedure.
Having prepared water for the feet and the *arghya* offering, as well as the five products of the cow (*pañcagavya*), one should worship the twice-born with ointments,
flowers, and the like, along with garments and finger-rings.
Having fumigated [the site] in due order with gold-adorned vessels containing purifiers,
the master builder, being self-restrained and accompanied by assistants, should cause [the officiant] to sit down.
Having granted permission to the sacrificer, [the vessels] situated on the sacrificial ground—whether made of gold, silver, or new copper—[should be offered]. Paus. 42.132.
O Lotus-born One, as for the secondary ritual, the jars may be made of stone or clay;
among them, the central jar should measure twenty-four finger-breadths.
That [pedestal] is broad in the middle and raised by two finger-breadths at each [end];
the opening is six finger-breadths [in width], and the mouth therein is known to be three finger-breadths.
O Lotus-born One, it should be known that the girdle is three finger-breadths above [the base];
and those lotuses of the directions are equal to half of this height.
Having filled it with various fruits and earth,
and having pounded it with strong khadira wood, they were gathered together with water.
Having dug a pit for the sake of filling it entirely,
and having leveled and smeared it, one should then perform the accomplishment of the directions as before.
One should adorn it with various banners and hoist victory-pennants;
one should beautify it with sturdy, purifying tree-branches, such as plantain trees and others.
With garments, full jars, flowers, silken cloths, and clusters of blossoms,
[one should act] when the planet is auspicious, the lunar mansion favorable, and the aspect of the stars is propitious.
When the ascendant is fixed, situated in a fixed sign, completely pure, and endowed with auspicious qualities,
the builder, indeed becoming one with the Lord, performs the consecration of the foundation of the temple.
Having performed his daily rites, accompanied by the foremost of the twice-born and the preceptor,
[he proceeds] amidst auspicious sounds such as the beating of kettledrums, tabors, and all kinds of musical instruments.
Accompanied by throngs of bards singing auspicious songs,
one should cause the venerable Vedas— the Sāma, Ṛg, and Yajus— to be recited.

Having sipped water and performed the ritual placement (*nyāsa*) with the twelve-syllable form, he should enter the earth-purifying ground prepared by the accumulation of provisions gathered with effort. *Pauṣkara* 42.143.

Then, having performed the foot-washing, the offering of water (arghya), and the five products of the cow (pañcagavya) together with the Vedic mantras beginning with the eight-syllabled one, he should worship the most excellent of the twice-born.
The master builder (sthapati), having offered the guest-water (arghya), flowers, and other honors, should proceed with the auspicious work;
he should cause each twice-born man to recite the Gāyatrī preceded by the syllable Om.
Having first recited the Gāyatrī Sāman and then the Kanikranda,
and likewise having first uttered the syllable Oṃ, one should thereafter perform the commencement of the ritual action.
Thereafter, one who knows the Ṛgveda and the Yajurveda should recite the Ekāyana, the Śivasaṃkalpa, and the Bhadra-ṛca, as well as the Samudīrya.
Bhadraśrīsāman, known as Sāmaja, who knew the rites and the Dharma from the beginning of the hundred [years], having divided the field as before, now purified it. (Pausa 42.148)
With all the purificatory Vedic mantras and those of the Pañcarātra,
one should place the girl in the northern direction or in the northeast within the enclosure.
Having drawn a four-sided mandala on a level earthen seat,
one should fashion the inauspicious Sarvatobhadra diagram, provided with two houses for subjugation.
Having placed two water-pitchers upon a noble seat,
adorned them with garlands and other ornaments, one should perform the ritual of accomplishment (*sādhana*) at one of them.
With the twelve-syllable mantra and the principal mantras declared in the Vedas, the Blessed One, Puruṣottama, [was worshipped] in that vessel which was supreme as a weapon.
Having reached the front of the pavilion with mantras consisting of the weapons and the liṅgas arising from the four Vedas, one should perform the worship that brings about the state of the heart.
Having brought [the deity] down, one should perform the external worship as previously described;
then, having offered libations according to the rule into the fire—excluding the final oblation (pūrṇāhuti)—one should proceed.
One should indeed worship Vāstu, the foremost of men, together with the host of gods as his limbs;
one should complete the rite by offering a hundred, fifty, or even twenty-five oblations.
Then [he should offer] sesame seeds sprinkled with clarified butter, followed by clarified butter itself,
with the Vāstuliṅga mantras belonging to the Sāmas, beginning with the Devavrata mantras.
Furthermore, one should prepare nine water-pots made of metal, perfectly level,
according to one's capacity, and certainly not less than twelve finger-breadths in size.
It may be made of stone or clay, well-baked, very firm, and auspicious;
it should be like a water-pitcher (bhṛṅgāra), octagonal, shaped like a conch, or tall.

Having offered the oblation, with a face free from attachment, one should perform the ritual bathing for the purification of all the materials according to the characteristics of the planets. Pausa 42.159.
O twice-born one, having accepted those [vessels] covered with cloths, either immediately or on another day,
he should gradually fill them with the appropriate materials while reciting Vedic texts that correspond to their characteristics.
With the eight-syllable Gāyatrī mantra, with the twelve-syllable vidyā, and with golden sands, gems, pearls, and the like— Pausa 42.161.
With all the [precious] elements, grains, and other substances such as pārata and the like, with seeds including white mustard, and with grains beginning with wild rice (nīvāra); Pausa 42.162.
One should further adorn the exterior with camphor, sandalwood powder, saffron, and agallochum, as well as silk ribbons, garlands, sandalwood paste, and other such items.
Having thus worshipped and consecrated her, one should place Lakṣmī in the center of the four [deities],
seated upon a lotus throne and surrounded by treasures.
Then, for the other four [jewels], there is the king of gems named Kaustubha;
it is accompanied by the lords of the treasures with their respective mantras and their own names.
The Blessed One, whose self is all-pervading power, should contemplate within himself the partless embodiment of sound by means of the six-syllable mantra.
One should lead the four-footed Brahma-field by means of the eight-petaled self,
having placed the pot of the Lord of All in the center, within the interior of the pericarp.

O twice-born one, one should place four jeweled jars in the eight directions of the circle of the quarters, starting from the eastern part in a clockwise direction, reciting either mantras or worldly formulas.
The target consists of four jars, beginning from the northeast (Īśa) and ending at the northwest (Vāyu).
Having thus performed the ritual placement (nyāsa), one should then perform the worship of the central [deity].
One should indeed worship the fourfold [deities] beginning with the Heart-mantra as residing within the jewel-pitchers;
however, one should worship the single mantra of all four for the *śrīkumbha* pitchers.
Having thus performed the placement of the partless (niṣkala) [mantra] for all of them in front with the eye-mantras and in the central jar, one should then proceed accordingly.
One should provide nine vessels made of either copper or stone, which are equal [in size],
well-rounded or square, well-fashioned, and twelve finger-breadths in length.
And there, within the central vessel, the four powers are restrained;
or rather, that supreme goddess who is power, capable of sustaining the entire universe.
Prabhā, Vaiśvarī, Jñānaśakti, and Amṛtā are indeed in the cardinal directions;
one should remember her, characterized by bliss, in the intermediate directions within the assembly of jars.
The power called Action is the unswerving energy, pure and bestowing birth upon the capable one;
having thus performed the placement, one should perform the worship of Śrī and the others by their own respective names.
Then one should worship the mantra of the treasures and their lords, together with its ancillaries;
thereafter, one should display the mantric mudrā, which is characterized by all-encompassing power.
One should perform the recitation with the twelve-syllable mantra and practice its complete restraint; [this applies] to the sixteen-syllable [mantra], not to the presence [of the deity].
Then, having urged one who knows the Yajus-mantras, "Apply the Yajus";
and one who knows the Sāman-mantras, [he should urge] the Puruṣa-sūkta, which is a Ṛk, and the Viṣṇu-saṃhitā.
Then, for Atharvan, one should perform the six-footed rite for the twice-born, followed by the Ekāyana;
thereafter, one should perform the four-fold mantra of names beginning with the manifestation of the Self (ātmavyūha).
Then, having chanted the Rathantara Sāman accompanied by salutations, he should indeed recite the Ṛgveda with great joy. (Pauṣkara 42.180)
One who knows the *sāman* should utter the *sāman* "Pratiṣṭhāsi"; then, immediately after that, [he should place] the water-jars... // Pauṣya 42.181 //
Then, indeed, the entire area should be smeared with lime,
and the eight directions of the field should be sealed with the eight Śaktis.
By means of confinement within a stone slab, or otherwise equal to the stones,
all [the lines] should be made level above, possessing the characteristics of the *sarvatobhadra* [mandala].
Having first been consecrated by bathing and other rites, adorned with garments, garlands, and colors,
and seated upon a throne of the eight jewels, one should properly install the eight [deities].

One should indeed place the eightfold mantra, distinguished by its syllables and having the *praṇava* (oṃ) at both the beginning and the end, starting from the east and ending in the northeast, distributed across the individual [deities].
O Great-minded One, [one should worship her] with the Praṇava and her own name ending in "namas":
she is the eternally powerful and heroic one, known as Anantā, steadfast and immutable.
The eighth among the twice-born is named Sandhyā, known as Dhṛti and Sthiti;
she proclaims the beginning and end of the Vedas along with the observances of the Yajurveda.
Then, O Lotus-born One, one should recite the Hayagrīva-vidyā and the Ṛgvedic hymns, followed by the Ekāyana; or else, having offered oblations with "yad ayāśca" and so forth. (Pauṣa 42.188)
Having offered the *pūrṇāhuti*,
the preeminent teacher, the performer, should then recite the mantra that is to be proclaimed, while recollecting the collection of mantras.
Accompanied by all the name-mantras beginning with Nyastaśrī and the rest, one who recites this single-vehicle mantra possesses a sevenfold intelligence. (Pauṣkara 42.190)
One should offer an oblation for the fulfillment of all rites;
thus much has been told by me to you, O lotus-eyed one, regarding the primary ritual procedure.
Therefore, I shall describe the secondary ritual procedure which brings benefit to all:
everything that is worshipped by the hosts of other fields is [to be placed] within this jar. (Pauṣa 42.192)
One should install the array of mantras as prescribed, including the *sthalaga* and *gopala*,
as the single, supreme power of the Lord which consists of all powers.
Having placed [the vessel] in the center of that [mandala], one should place the treasury of nectar and other substances therein;
then, with pigments such as saffron and the like, one should subsequently draw a lotus above it.
One should bring the remaining excavated portion of the ground to an even state on all sides;
then, by means of striking and other methods as previously described, [one should clear it] from all parts with the enemies.
Then, with a five-colored thread and firm stakes made of sacrificial wood,
the knower of mantras, reciting the weapon-mantra, should chant the *Jīmūta* [Sūkta].
Having sipped water and prostrated, one should indeed offer the previously mentioned oblation, accompanied by four garlands and sandalwood, for the fulfillment of desires, in the directions.
The King of Mantras, residing in the three places, having been patient [with the practitioner], then withdraws [the deity] by means of the twelve-syllable mantra, preceded by worship as before.
He shall act as the overseer for all those belonging to the cycle of worldly existence, from the outsiders on down;
and for the other flesh-eaters, he shall do so with Viśvakarman placed at their head.
One should provide food, sacrificial fees, and so forth for the foremost among the twice-born,
and give food and gifts of wealth according to one's ability to other supplicants.
Furthermore, according to the requirements of various regions, one should likewise construct a house and a seat,
as well as a diverse dwelling, endowed with their proper divisions.
And having then divided [the area] ending with the flagstaff-base (dhvajāsana) by means of one's own intelligence...
Thus ends the forty-second chapter, titled "The Installation of the Base of the Temple," in the Pauṣkara-saṃhitā, the Great Upaniṣad within the illustrious Pañcarātra.
(Total number of verses: 201) Now begins the forty-third chapter.
The Blessed One said:
Starting from a corner of the palace residence, one should construct a courtyard facing all directions as desired, and then design the surrounding wall.
In a temple with four doors, adorned with four forms, there should be a central hall containing a fire-pit and a street, or it may consist solely of the western wing. Pausa 43.2.
O Mahāmati, one should construct two pairs of watchtowers on the gates in every direction along the walls; likewise, one should build four or eight palaces.
For it may indeed be of a single form or possess various characteristics by the power of the Blessed One;
and according to one's inclination, it appears as a mere likeness of a palace.
O Brahmin, if one intends to construct an octagon there, a square made of baked bricks, stone, or wood should first be established in the four corners.
Then, one should arrange two palaces facing each other at the two locations of the door;
subsequently, one should place pairs of palaces with an interval between them in the three remaining directions.
O Great-minded One, the height of the door is declared to be equal to the measurement of the deity including its pedestal, according to the proportions of the deities who are elevated in stature.
One should bring about elevation by means of a pedestal for various short measurements;
it is free from the constraints of characteristics regarding its breadth and height.
It is a gateway easy to enter, which brings virtue even in times of distress;
it is well-prepared when performed under the asterism of Śuddha and followed by the constellation Ṛkṣa.
Having taken the continuous sequence of finger-breadths for both the width and the length,
one should multiply them by each other for the sake of auspiciousness and for the purpose of obtaining the lunar mansions (ṛkṣa).
Or one may purify it for the sake of gain by means of fist-casts while the fingers remain stationary;
one, three, five, or seven [throws] are auspicious, while all others are remembered as inauspicious.
Indeed, those [signs]—the banner, the tiger, the bull, and the lordly elephant—are in sequence;
thus, for the sake of obtaining the lunar mansions, one should again beautify that position.
From the Ādeka up to twenty-seven, one should joyfully perform the remaining rites;
or, with effort, one should increase the measurement by one finger-breadth for the two feet.
Having first deliberated thoroughly in this manner for the sake of auspicious constellations and success, one should indeed construct a temple for the gods of the earth. (Pauṣa 43.14)
Seated upon a bed or seat, or [seated] upon the Lord who is mounted on Garuḍa,
one should likewise place three [deities] in each of the three desired directions— or indeed, three in each of the three directions.
Seated in the southern direction, with its rear facing the western quarter,
the Garuḍa-throne is situated in the palace at the southern gate of the northern direction.
Regarding that which is proclaimed as the set of four for the four corners:
there, in the southeast direction, [the first] is placed, while at the northern gate, the last is in the east.

It is traditionally held that those called "limited" (iyattākhyāḥ) are attached to parts by virtue of the measure of their own awakening and the being they conceive themselves to be, due to the power of delimitation.
O Lotus-born One, that specific distinction known as *āsthāpana* occurs when the consecration of the *brahmapāṣāṇa* has been completed and the *paiṭhika* rite has also been performed. (Pauṣa 43.19)
When bathing alone has been performed for the purpose of pacifying defects in craftsmanship by means of rubbing with unguents, earth, ashes, cow dung, and so forth; Paus. 43.20.
When the gift of the eyes has been completed and the supreme bathing has been performed,
the Guru and others are raised up with great force by many guardians of the image.
O Pauṣkara, whatever various mantra has now been composed by means of insertion, when these three have attained oneness, it becomes as if sealed with adamantine glue.
When the rising of the ascendant has been declared, one should indeed perform the ritual placement of mantras (mantranyāsa) according to tradition;
likewise, through the contemplation of that power, there is the stabilization and establishment [of the deity].
On the inner walls of the palaces and in the sky and other such places,
the lords of practitioners have inscribed [the teachings] for the sake of accomplishment, up until the time of their success.
O twice-born one, the mantra and the ritual placement (nyāsa) of Kalabimba and indeed of Sāsana are for the purpose of constant propitiation, even during the ritual worship. (Pausa 43.25)
O Brahmin, that [earth] which is known as "moving" (calana) and also as "stabilizing" (sthitisthāpana),
and which is excessively defiled by defects such as the breaking of the ground preceded by floods of water— [is thus described].

Having lifted [the image] and placed it in this location of auspicious characteristics, its re-installation is proclaimed as "saṃsthāpana" (re-establishment) because of its being properly established once again. Paus 43.27.
One should remain seated on a seat that is eternally free from defects, having avoided those seats corrupted by faults such as lightning strikes or falls.
O Mahāmati, an image that is equal to that [original] and rich in the auspicious marks is worthy of veneration; it may be placed upon another pedestal or even elsewhere. (Pauṣya 43.29)
That which is to be understood is its specific distinction, namely, its establishment and its emergence;
this is because it is devoid of the assembly of cognitions and because it is perceived as being uniform in a single direction.
Furthermore, the circle of directions is [manifested] here primarily through one's own limbs due to mental impressions,
as well as by virtue of the states of lying down, sitting, standing, moving, and remaining still.
And there are many specific types known as *pratiṣṭhā* that grant all accomplishments (*siddhi*), due to their general configuration and indeed because of their particular qualities. (Pauṣkara 43.32)
And that which is established through imperishable purity is for those seeking the fruit of common worship;
its equality of fruit should be understood as occurring, however, in another birth. (Pauṣkara 43.33)
The establishment of the fourfold self bestows eternal knowledge,
having attained which a person shall never again undergo rebirth.
O Lotus-born One, he who, desiring rewards, should perform the installation of the four forms with supreme faith and devotion, [attains success] through that very resolve alone.
The paternal lineage, the maternal lineage, and the one called the wife—these seven lineages he uplifts upon attaining birth on earth once again. (Pausa 43.36)
O Lotus-born One, take refuge in devotion to Hari which is endowed with Dharma;
for one who has been born [in this world], the third [birth] indeed [occurs through it].
One should attain that which belongs to one possessing true discernment.
"By means of which one indeed crosses over from the terrible straits of saṃsāra—this is called 'Form' (rūpa) as the primordial foundation, O best of the twice-born. (Pausa 43.38)
Now, observe from these particular arrangements that,
having enjoyed the desired fruit in the divine worlds, [one returns].
Having attained an excellent birth, one should indeed practice once again that divine state established in Brahman which was [attained] in a previous life. (Pauṣa 43.40)
As before, consciousness bestows [the fruit] leading to the attainment of the state of the Supreme Lord;
this much is the difference stated, O Great-minded One, while there is equality in the rest. (Pauṣkara 43.41)
O Lotus-born One, [this is the fruit] of the supreme, divine, fruitful sacrifice of Acyuta,
who is imperishable and the bringer of the end of worldly existence.
Understand that distinction which exists merely by way of substance among the castes,
such as the Brāhmaṇas and others, whose souls are devoted to the householder’s life.

O Great-minded One, for those who have been initiated, for Brahmins previously [initiated], for those terrified by death and the like, and for those established in worldly affairs, there are the rites of consecration and so forth. (Pauṣa 43.44)
Those who have been initiated into nirvāṇa by their preceptor and who know the imperishable grant the fruit that has been described by me. (Pauṣa 43.45)

For those who have attained their authority through devotion, who are constantly engaged in worship, who are established in perfect meditative absorption, and for whom this birth is the last, [this is the state]. (Pauṣa 43.46)
O Lotus-born One, you have established a foundation for those whose minds are exhausted by conceptual construction,
for the sake of protecting their own families and so forth, and because of the arising of infinite beings.
O best among the wise, their observance is indeed prescribed for a period lasting as long as life, for the sake of satisfying the intellect. (Pausa 43.48)
Having understood this, one should, by means of wealth and power acquired through righteousness,
cause everything to be confiscated until the end of the banner and bring it to complete exhaustion.
Residing in the abode that is the dwelling of Viśvavāsa, facing south and seated upon a throne,
he is situated at the eastern gate in the house of Nirṛti.
Likewise, situated upon the back of the Lord of Birds (Garuḍa) in the temple of the quarter of Vāyu (the northwest),
it indeed grants the attainment of divine enjoyments along with [the fruits] from the celestial plane.
Having attained the status of Prajāpati by being situated in the directions as described,
they established the eternal stability of the three heavens and the rest above them.
By means of this vehicle, a person attains divine movement through the sky;
for those devotees who desire fruits, there are rewards such as elevated status and worldly prosperity. (Pauṣa 43.53)
All those established in the initiation of the fruit [seek] the fruits of cities for the sake of results; yet birth is the supreme festival, for it is the manifestation of the self. (Pausa 43.54)

Know that, O Lotus-born One, for the sake of the pacification of worldly existence, this shall be accomplished without delay by establishing [the deities] in the three directions according to the very sequence previously specified.
Or, O Great-minded One, the forms of Nṛsiṃha, Kapila,
and Kroḍa are prescribed in sequence for the four intermediate directions, as previously described.
One should place the horse-faced [deity] among the pearls, and the lion and others in their respective positions;
or alternatively, one may establish the tortoise and others in three directions.
For the sake of attaining the prior fruits for the gods who are lords of the Fish and Dwarf incarnations,
[the offerings] should be employed in the intermediate directions according to the sequence specified.
The Supreme Lord possesses a body of beautiful form, bearing a trident, a sword, and a weapon in his hands;
he is composed of all the gods and is the universal form itself.
Thus has the rule been stated; therefore, all others indeed, as well as the various other manifestations, O Lotus-born one, are likewise [to be understood].
This should be performed by those authorized by the gurus, and not by other sacrificers;
for then one may attain that delightful and desired hut together with the gods.
At the entrance, one should construct a structure resembling a pavilion, provided with a flight of steps and adorned with an altar; it stands as the locus for worship.

O Lotus-born One, thereafter, for the stability of other enjoyments and for the purpose of establishing the foundations of palaces, one should construct auspicious structures capable of withstanding wind and rain.
Whether in five or nine vessels, or even in a single pot of water endowed with all jewels, that which is the Supreme Lord has been placed.
One should worship him every day, together with his limbs, his marks, his mantras, and his retinue, as well as his own power.
