For the purpose of consecrating the mantra-image and for the pacification of obstacles caused by time,
O Mahāmati, otherwise an unavoidable obstacle arises.
Mantras always attain their presence through worship performed at the three times of day; through lack of worship, they bestow sorrow wherever one is obstructed. (Pauṣkara 43.67)
O Lotus-born One, the measurements for the forecourt and the placement of the deities have been described; now, please take them to heart. (Pauṣkara 43.68)
In the Middle Country (Madhyadeśa), however, on that ground, within an extensive and desired palace,
it is established under various names solely by virtue of its arrangement.
The characteristic of the investigation [of reality] belongs to the fourfold Self who stands upon the seat of the power of Brahmā, looking toward the four directions. (Pauṣkara 43.70)
That which is to be realized is that foundation which fulfills the array of the directions,
existing in the form of the power of steadfastness— formless and characterized by transcendence.

O Lotus-born One, for the sake of stability and for the purpose of ritual procedure, everything from the horizon down to the copper [layer] is established upon the Brahma-stone; all is rooted in the Brahma-stone. (Pauṣkara 43.72)
Furthermore, that formless [principle] indeed pervades from the very root both the material and the immaterial substance, characterized by its grasping of the pillar-like [support].
The uninterrupted persistence of a single, imperishable seed, established in each of the diverse objects,
is indeed firmly grounded.

O twice-born one, that which pertains to the manifestation of the entire multitude of forms— whether distinct, arranged in arrays, solitary, or complete— beginning with Brahmā and the others; ||| Paus_43.75 |||
When the abiding of a single [deity] occurs by its own will upon a single universal pedestal (viśvapīṭha), that specific distinction called *pratiṣṭhā* is designated as *sthāpana*. (Pauṣkara 43.76)

And having unified with a single-minded intellect the unmanifest aggregate of principles—which is permeated by the power of consciousness—and which is contained within the substance-form known as "motion. (Pauṣkara 43.77)
O twice-born one, at the time of consecrating the image, during that which is called the "infusion" (adhivāsa),
one should [fix] the excellent mantra with immobility, and again with the contemplation of movement.
Having indeed fashioned the desired [image] complete with its limbs and marks,
one should place it within the heart for the sake of propitiation, and then [place] that [mantra] again within his heart.
One should collect [the essence] because one's purpose has been fulfilled, either constantly or at another time; this is the other principle called "Being" (Sadākhya). // Paus_43.80 //
Indeed, it possesses various perceptions and likewise various dimensions;
it is likewise colored by various and manifold arrangements.
It was adorned with many variegated stages,
extending from the soles of the feet to the crown of the head, and the triad [of body, speech, and mind] was made to correspond accordingly.

One should perform [the rite] progressively higher and higher with various clusters of blossoms arising from the realms of Bhūr, Bhuvaḥ, Svaḥ, and so forth, including both stationary and moving beings and various perfected ones (siddhas).
With magnificent lords of serpents and royal nāgas, with beautiful lotus groves, and with divine vine-arbors bound together by chains of drums; (43.84)

Indeed, [he was honored] with water-born creatures such as lotuses, as well as with various nets of living beings born from the forest, those born from trees, and others beginning with the herds of deer and lions.
The Vāraṇas and Śabaras likewise [are distinguished] by their reliance on the haṃsa and padma [lotuses],
as well as other aquatic flowers such as the śaṅkha, svastika, and kahlāra.
With delightful, joyful manes rising like hundred-petaled lotuses, with yak-tail whisks adorned with tinkling bells, parasols, banners, and the like; Pausa 43.87.
Together with all those belonging to the earth and not belonging to the earth, along with the oceans and rivers,
with the nine types of requisites, and with the gods such as the moon, the sun, and fire.
With various divine manifestations accompanied by other manifestations,
with islands joined by other islands, and with the netherworlds (pātālas) together with their inhabitants; // Pausa 43.89 //

O Brahmin, [the world was filled] with great sages, lords of the realms of Tapa and Satya, possessing immense splendor, who were devoted to meditation and silence, accompanied by the twice-born and the gods of fire.
O Lotus-born One, one should thus adorn the auspicious [temples] with these and other [ornaments] resembling shanks and pillars, together with nose-ornaments for all directions.
From the center of the space within the inner sanctum, one should fashion [the area] marked with wheels and lotuses,
together with the gods beginning with Brahmā, as well as the Siddhas and Vidyādharas.

[He was attended] by those bearing flower-garlands and rosaries, by humble ones waving whisks and fans, and by those possessing the splendor of the forest-garland, mace, conch, discus, lotus, and other [emblems]. (Pauṣa 43.93)
[The deities] are marked by hands holding rosaries, numbering eight, four, and six respectively;
they stand outside the wheels and lotuses, acting as a protective enclosure.
One should adorn the interior wall with groups of all the gods, daityas, and other hosts, as well as others such as Nārada and his followers, who are intent on dance and song.
Having restrained that mantra there with the *praṇava* and his own name ending in *namaḥ*, he established the earthly realm (*bhūloka*) as his foot. (Pauṣkara 43.96)
In this way, one should visualize the Bhuvarloka situated upon the pedestal of the temple,
the Svargaloka within the shaft, and the Maharloka reaching the ground of the great spire.
*Stambha*, *talapa*, *caraṇa*, and *jaṅghā*;
likewise *sthāna*, *sthūṇa*, and *pāda*—these are synonyms. (Paus 43.98)
Janaloka is within that Vedyā, and the one named Tapoloka is in Daṇḍaka;
and the world named Satyaloka is at its crest in the abode of the gods.
And one should indeed meditate upon the supreme pervasion extending through the seven worlds,
O Brahmin, as consisting of the worlds above, within the chosen temple.
It is permeated by other factors such as the trees and so forth, which possess their own essential natures,
and by the characteristics of the "other" (the Supreme), which pervade everywhere in mutual relation.
O Brahman, it is devoid of a portion of the earthly realm (bhūrloka) and likewise abandoned by others;
indeed, due to the predominance of rajas and tamas, it possesses only a slight degree of the quality of sattva.
For this very reason, there are others whose forms consist solely of the quality of *sattva*,
as well as the *bhūrloka* situated separately, and the group of paths beginning with *pada*.
Once the deposition of the jewels has been performed, the three steps beginning with waking should be deposited upon the crest-lock known as the Kūrma-Brahmātman.

O Lotus-born One, he who is endowed with the state of the Fourth Brahman (turyabrahma) sits upon the seat that is the reflection of the path of mantra; by those two [feet], he stands upon the feet of another, which is this very principle (tattva). Paus. 43.105.
Then, one should contemplate the path of the digits (*kalādhvan*) from the navel up to the crown of the head;
that [path] is characterized by the *mantra-brahman* within the lotus of the aperture of Brahma (*brahmarandhra*).
In the pericarp is the Supreme Brahman, the universal, eternal, and all-pervading;
this state consisting of the paths, as it was described by me to you at the time of initiation, [is established there]. (Pauṣkara 43.107)
O Mahāmati, that is the perfection of temples up to their spires,
as well as of images together with their pedestals, characterized by the presence of spirits and other such features.
Therein, the Blessed One is indeed my internal self—embodied, peaceful, and infallible;
for he alone is the Virāj-self, the imperishable supreme deity.
The *adhibhūta* is the unmanifest (*avyakta*), O twice-born one, for it consists of all the principles (*tattva*) together with the others,
such as *vidyā*, *kalā*, and so forth, which exist for the sake of another.

O Great-minded One, just as [the elements] are established in their dissolution along with their seeds through the stages of the extremely subtle and so forth, so too do the principles (tattvas) and the objects such as sound terminate in the intellect (buddhi). Paus 43.111.
In the same way, O Brahmin, those [images] are considered to reside within the body of the temple presided over by the deity;
they consist of all powers and are pure, characterized by the quality of goodness (sattva).
Just as the mantra was imparted by the omnipresent Lord of All,
who is omniscient, all-pervading, and the sovereign creator of everything.
Know that the house of the mantra-deity is likewise [prepared] through ritual service;
therefore, with great effort and according to the rule, one should consecrate it together with its pedestal.
The installation of that image born of a living being is prescribed to be like that of a deity;
it should be provided with a flight of stairs and a well-proportioned base-platform (*jagatī*) endowed with auspicious characteristics.
And that pedestal of the palace should be understood as being of such a nature that it has attained a state of oneness with the coatings of lime mixed with iron filings.
It was constructed with baked bricks, as well as with stable clay and stones,
endowed with the correct proportions and characteristics, and possessed of a design created by the Omniscient One.
O twice-born one, that which is colored by the web of passion yields eternal fruit; yet, because it has become worn out, it must be performed again through the Svayambhuva and other rites.
O Mahāmati, when various images that are indestructible have been worshipped, the doer obtains a thousandfold fruit.
Trees dwelling by reservoirs of water took hold of the field of Puṣkara again and again through the true devotees, for the sake of pacifying their misdeeds.
O Lord of Men, those who protect through worship and other means that which has been lost due to contact with beginningless ignorance and also by the power of the decline of time; Paus_43.121.
At the end of their bodies, they go to heaven, unobstructed by the defects of sovereignty;
returning from heaven in due course, they attain stainless knowledge.
By this, the unbearable suffering of saṃsāra comes to an end;
indeed, such is said to be the fruit of entering a temple of the gods. (Pauṣa 43.123)
O Lotus-born One, let alone the abode of the gods, let there be for all devotees and even for kings who possess the contemplation of all paths. (Pausa 43.124)
By his mere will, the teacher brings about the pervasion consisting of the path of the worlds; out of a desire to bestow grace, he should reveal it to his devotees. (Pauṣkara 43.125)
O twice-born one, the builder who is endowed with auspicious marks, possessed of fortune, and free from deceit, obtains the previously mentioned full fruit, O brahmin. (Pauṣa 43.126)

Indeed, whatever fruit the builder obtains from the construction of palaces— whether through his own effort or through the work of artisans, such as gold, land, food, and so forth— that [fruit] belongs to the one who commissioned them without a mantra.
One obtains the fruit resulting from the gift of all one's possessions according to the prescribed rites,
whether it be small, middling, or great, by means of clay, wood, bricks, and so forth.

Whether it be a celestial abode crowded with gods, endowed with the characteristics of valid means of knowledge as previously described, or a village dwelling known as a mere hut, [one should enter it].
From the intermediate points of the compass, from the exterior, and from other directions, he is joined by others who have been dispatched—
those known as the *vibhava-vyūha* or by various other manifestations.

If, however, [the rite] is disturbed by defects such as earthquakes and the like, even for those who have bathed and performed their financial duties over a long period of time, [the merit is lost]. (Pauṣa 43.131)

The king, or his minister, or another person who is truly devoted and acts according to the king's command, should duly perform the extraction [of the image] with the consent of the preceptors. (Pauṣa 43.132)
Having obtained the supreme permission from the Lord for the performance of vows, worship, and other rites,
one should meditate upon the All-pervading Lord lying supine on a bed of darbha grass at Anantaśayana.
With the twelve-syllable mantra, the Blessed Lord Hari [worships] the Lord of Heaven ten thousand times,
or five thousand, or one hundred and fifty.
Then, under an auspicious constellation favorable to both the king and the city,
for the sake of pacification, [he performed the rite] which is the very life-force and which bears the qualities and form of the Lord of Mantras.
Having worshipped Traiguṇya according to the prescribed rite and having offered libations with many pieces of sacrificial wood in sequence, he extends his hand at the end of his life.
Just as Śakti consists of the path of the worlds (*bhuvanādhvan*) and the collection of manifestations (*vyaktisaṅgha*) as previously described,
so too does she consist of the fivefold group of existents (*sattābhūta*), namely the collection of words (*padasaṅgha*) belonging to the path of phonemes (*varṇādhvan*).
Having gratified and honored the host of elemental powers (bhūta-śakti-gaṇa), together with the presiding deities (sādhibhūtādhidaiva), as well as that which is exceedingly subtle and yet other.
O Brahmin, one should duly block the abode of the divine seat,
having recognized it as equal to the rising sun by means of its own specific names and mantra-words.
O Blessed One, protect once again this host of mantras— both those residing in manifest form and those that are unmanifest— beginning with the syllable *praṇava* and ending with *namaḥ*.

Indeed, that which stands at the measure of half an *udumbara* fruit, extending through the cardinal and intermediate directions, is pervaded by *darbha* grasses established upon the qualities of the intellect (*buddhi-dharma*) within the characteristic of the *vaimbala*. 43.141.
One should perform the continuous recitation because of the correct lack of full comprehension of that;
however, at the time of its conclusion, one should now perform the ritual placement (*nyāsa*).
And by means of the signs of extraction (*upoddhāra*) and the eight-limbed (*aṣṭāṅga*) Vedic [mantras],
having made each one manifest as the Self through inhalation (*pūraka*), like the orb of the sun.
Then, having placed [the deity] within a well-esteemed and honored water-pot, or within an image made of gold and other materials,
filled with water and sealed shut, one should worship it daily thereafter.
Having correctly introduced [the disciple] for the sake of the perfection of arising,
one must indeed again perform the re-establishment of the conditioned as it was extracted.
For the increase of kings, nations, and their territories, as well as for the prosperity of cattle and the twice-born,
and for the eternal attainment of that state by all beings together with the entire world.
O twice-born one, the restoration of palaces and images, as well as that of cows, land, gold, and so forth, and of the kingdom together with its king, should be performed in this same manner.
It arises for the sake of auspicious peace both in this world and in the next;
otherwise, O Lotus-born One, there would indeed be great fault. (Pauṣa 43.148)
And for those who seize palaces, whether outside or within,
by means of mantras such as the eight-syllable one and others, while the images are being moved.
One should perform the withdrawal of one's own mantras as previously placed,
just as fire is drawn from the sun by means of a sun-crystal gem.
O Pauṣkara, when the mantras have been gathered and are being recited,
if a fracture occurs in the images due to the force of karma or through negligence, [the following should be done].
Then, due to that very past sin, one should perform an expiation that produces clarity of mind and indeed brings about fame and well-being. (Pauṣa 43.152)
In that regard, one should perform the vow for one night, three nights, six days, or twelve nights, according to one's own capacity. (Pauṣa 43.153)
And by performing with diligence the rites beginning with the ritual bath and ending with the fire-oblation,
one should give gifts of sesame seeds along with gold and silver.

O high-minded one, one should provide food for many eminent brahmins according to one's ability, beginning with the rites of peace (śānti) and consisting of rice mixed with ghee and milk, and so forth. Pausa 43.155.
Having thus completed the vow arising from the preceptor and others, one should dwell,
taking refuge in a well-known sacred field frequented by the perfected ones.
Or, at a well-known sacred site (tīrtha), reciting the twelve-syllable great mantra repeatedly for one day or three days; (43.157)
One should perform the full rite at the time known as a *muhūrta*, specifically during the three junctions (*saṃdhyā*),
either in a divine abode or in a place designated as perfected (*siddha*).
When there is indeed equality in devotion, this expiation is prescribed as common for all castes, provided the offense was committed openly through the mind. (Pauṣa 43.159)

In the practice of recitation, a progressive increase in merit is indeed prescribed for the devotees of the Śūdra, Vaiśya, Kṣatriya, and Brāhmaṇa castes, provided they do not perform sacrifices for others.

For this has been stated in the *Prakāśa*: "Furthermore, for as long as clarity [of mind] persists, one should recite the mantra during that time; it is considered purifying to consume [the sacrificial substance]. (Pauṣa 43.161)
As long as one's own intellect, together with the mind, attains clarity, one should [recite] the twelve-syllable mantra which is indeed eight-syllabled in the unmanifest state. (Pauṣa 43.162)
O best of the twice-born, one should perform the three daily junctures (sandhyās) according to the six-syllable mantra in their proper sequence;
one should bathe as prescribed and, standing within the water, recite the mantra.
At the time of bathing, with undistracted mind and according to one's capacity, one should recite [the mantra] together with the three mantras—
the eight-syllable [mantra] repeated the prescribed number of times— in the morning, at midday, and at the close of day.
One should indeed perform the ritual at the proper place and time, and bathe once for each occasion;
the five-limbed consecration (pañcāṅgābhiṣeka) and the remainder are beneficial during the two junctions of the day (saṃdhyā).
Having thoroughly washed the lower part of the body down to the hips with nectar-like water,
he discarded his lower garment and took up a beautiful cloth.
Three days, six days, eight days, and twelve days—this is beneficial for those from Śūdras up to the twice-born, each succeeding one being better than the preceding. (Pauṣa 43.167)
O one of great intelligence, this sequence is the cause for the purification of the mind;
furthermore, another injunction accompanied by its fruit is now being declared.
The field, which is concise, common to all, situated on whatever level is desired, and measuring from four cubits up to twelve, is the [sacred] field... 43.169.
Successively less than the two preceding ones, down to the minimum,
it is divided by parts ranging from five hundred up to thirty.
The walls [should be] by two parts; the interval from the five-limbed [structure], however, is indeed [formed] by three and a half [parts];
from that, the inner sanctum (garbha) is by three and a half, and the two walls by two and a half.
Know that the layout of the ground measuring six cubits consists of parts reduced by one-eighth; thus, the inner sanctum (garbha) shall indeed be seven paces.
That which is to be fully known consists of four remaining parts as the walls;
the height of the eightfold hand-measure is formed by four and a half parts of the eighth division.
One should complete the arrangement of the walls with three and a half parts;
the womb-area (garbhakṣetra), including its limbs, consists of five cubits from the nine squares.
The remaining collection of cubits is declared to be the thickness of the walls;
for a sanctum measuring ten cubits, the width is six cubits.
By means of exactly two cubits, the assembly of walls is established;
from a field of eleven cubits, the inner sanctum (garbha) is six and a half cubits.
The measurement of the wall is declared to be four and a half cubits;
it should be seven parts of one-twelfth of the site, less a quarter.
The temple should be understood as being three-quarters of four cubits;
the walls should likewise be constructed by dividing that very measurement in the same manner.
Having made the fruit-bearing walls with thirteen parts,
when nine parts are completed by means of the eight [syllables], the temple of the Blessed One should be constructed.
Having achieved the accomplishment of the diminution of impurity by means of two finger-breadths or one finger-breadth,
one should cause the mind to descend from the walls of these [elements] which contain the essence of serenity.
Having set aside the excessive measure, one should apply it to the fields;
how much more so for the measure equal to an atom, let alone that of the finger-breadth and so forth?
It is considered to increase the prosperity of men; however, the fall of prosperity is inauspicious.
Therefore, O Pauṣkara, that [fall] must be brought back with great effort.
It was fashioned with beautiful structures and provided with four faces;
when considering the fourfold nature [of the deity], it had one or two doors... [as appropriate]. (Pausa 43.183)
One should face whichever direction is desired for the attainment of various supernatural powers;
one seeking long life should face the east, and one seeking fame should face the south.
One should have it face west for the sake of livelihood in an independent dwelling;
a temple facing north bestows wealth and grain.
O Pauṣkara, know that this much has been declared as the supreme worldly fruit for all [the rites], endowed with various enjoyments. (Pauṣkara 43.186)
In one's own field, which is vast and delightful, or on the ground of one's own lap, independently, or together with a previously established [image] in a temple of Hari; Paus 43.187.
This is remembered as the primary ritual procedure (*mukhyakalpa*) in the *Svāyambhuva* or the one called *Siddha*;
elsewhere, O ornament of the assembly of the wise, it should be understood as a secondary procedure (*anukalpa*).
On the ground spread out and shaded by the shadow of the palace's flagstaff, having been purified from all defects with bricks and lime-powder; (43.189)
Having established that [image] within that space, one should perform the installation along with the oblations and other rites as prescribed;
the image, together with its pedestal, should be of the same proportions as the temple door, being all-pervading and immutable.

Endowed with all the auspicious marks for the sake of his fame reaching to the ends of the ocean, he was born for the purpose of uplifting his own lineage that had long since passed away. (Pauṣya 43.191)
The very moment this resolve was formed, "I shall establish [the image]," at that very instant his fame attained an unshakable foundation.
What need is there to mention all other places, from the world of earth onwards,
for he who performs the consecration of the Source of the Universe by means of his own splendor?
He who performs the Vaiṣṇava consecration for his father, mother, or others who have passed away, according to his own capacity or wealth, [attains the highest state]. Paus 43.194.
Before long, they go forever to the abode of the Ender (Death),
and thereafter, after some time, to the supreme station of Viṣṇu.
Having obtained an auspicious portion of the earth together with noble lineage, character, and so forth,
they practice what is virtuous by which they attain rebirth.
Out of compassion, whoever should perform the consecration for Jātis or others, the fruit arising from that [act]... // Paus 43.197 //
And the lords of mantras, perfected through the sound of the *praṇava*, enter [the body] and,
after a short period of time, draw forth their own supernatural power (*vibhūti*).
Indeed, having had their defects destroyed, they were established again—unimpeded and stainless—by the perfected ones and others in sacred fords, sacred fields, and groves. (Pauṣa 43.199)

Those who, out of delusion, attempt to prevent the manifestation of the forms of the array of riches—their configuration, their measure, and their appearance—do not [prevent] the fault that arises after some time. (Pauṣa 43.200)
Vāsudeva and the others, who are of two types and belong to the Supreme Lord, are to be meditated upon;
they consist of four forms, ending with Aniruddha, according to the arrangement of the fourfold manifestation (caturvyūha).
In the same way, others such as Rāhu and the rest [are worshipped] together with the fourfold manifestation (caturvyūha);
likewise those beginning with Keśava, either with all [four] or with one or another of them.

O you who are worshipped by the immortals, he who performs worship according to his capacity, even if it be very slight or increasingly slighter due to the influence of his disposition, [attains success]. (Pausa 43.203)
Then, with the pure enjoyments as previously described and through various ritual acts,
once the constituent parts of the rite have been accomplished, the King of Mantras [is offered] the *arghya* with the heart-mantra and the weapon-mantra.
And having offered the prepared enjoyment of the Lord without first honoring it, [one should do so] with [the mantra] beginning and ending with the *praṇava*. // Paus_43.205 //
